Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

Page 172
(Surat al-Tawbah)
Madaniyyah, except the last two verses, which are Makkiyyah. Its verses number 129. It was revealed after al-Ma'idah.

The author of al-Kashshaf said: It has several names: Bara'ah, al-Tawbah, al-Muqashqishah, al-Muba'thirah, al-Musharridah, al-Mukhziyah, al-Fadihah, al-Muthirah, al-Hafirah, al-Munakkilah, al-Mudamdimah, and Surat al-'Adhab. He said: It is called al-Tawbah because it contains the repentance (tawbah) of the believers, and it is called al-Muqashqishah because it purges (tuqashqishu) one of hypocrisy, that is, it clears one of it. It is called al-Mubai'thirah because it searches out (tubai'thiru) the secrets of the hypocrites, seeks them out, stirs them up, digs for them, exposes them, punishes them, scatters them, disgraces them, and crushes them. 

It is reported from Hudhayfah: "You call it Surat al-Tawbah; by God, it did not leave anyone without touching him." And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas regarding this surah that he said: "It is al-Fadihah (the exposer). It kept on descending concerning them and touching them until we feared it would leave no one out." Surat al-Anfal was revealed concerning Badr, and Surat al-Hashr was revealed concerning Banu al-Nadir.

If it is asked: What is the reason for omitting the basmalah from its beginning?

We say: They have mentioned several reasons for this.

The first reason: It is related from Ibn 'Abbas who said: "I said to 'Uthman ibn 'Affan: What led you to place Surat Bara'ah, which is of the mi'in (surahs of about a hundred verses), and Surat al-Anfal, which is of the mathani (oft-repeated surahs), together, and did not separate them with 'In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful'? He said: The Prophet ﷺ used to say, whenever a surah was revealed to him, 'Place it in such-and-such a position.' Bara'ah was among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, and the Prophet ﷺ died without explaining its position. Its story resembled that of al-Anfal, so they were joined together." The judge (al-Qadi) said: It is far-fetched to say that he (peace be upon him) did not make clear that this surah follows Surat al-Anfal, because the Qur'an is arranged by God Most High and by His Messenger in the manner that has been transmitted. If we allowed, for some surahs, that their arrangement was not from God by way of revelation, we would allow the same in all surahs and in the verses of a single surah, and allowing that would undermine what the Imamiyyah say about allowing addition and omission in the Qur'an. That would remove it from being a proof. Rather, the correct view is that he (peace be upon him) commanded, by revelation, that this surah be placed after Surat al-Anfal, and that he (peace be upon him) removed "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" from the beginning of this surah by revelation.

The second reason: On this matter there is what is related from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, that he said: "They only supposed that because al-Anfal mentions covenants (al-'uhud), and Bara'ah mentions the repudiation of covenants (nabdh al-'uhud), so one was placed beside the other." The question mentioned above applies here too, because this reason is only complete if we say that they placed this surah after al-Anfal on their own account, for this reason.

Page 173

The third reason: The Companions disagreed as to whether Surat al-Anfal and Surat al-Tawbah are one surah or two. Some of them said: They are one surah, because both were revealed about fighting, and together they form the seventh of the long surahs, which are seven, and what follows them are the mi'un. This is an apparent view, because together they comprise two hundred and six verses, so they are like a single surah. Others said: They are two surahs. When the disagreement among the Companions on this matter became apparent, they left a gap between them to indicate the view of the one who says they are two surahs, and they did not write "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" between them to indicate the view of the one who says they are one surah. According to this view, we are not obliged to accept the doctrine of the Imamiyyah; for when this matter became uncertain among the Companions, they did not decide on either of the two opinions, and they acted in a way that shows this uncertainty existed. Since they did not tolerate even this degree of doubt, this shows that they were strict in preserving the Qur'an from distortion and alteration, and that refutes the view of the Imamiyyah.

The fourth reason: On this matter: God Most High concluded Surat al-Anfal by requiring that the believers be allies of one another and that they be completely cut off from the disbelievers. Then God Most High stated this meaning explicitly in His words: ﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger﴾. Since this is the very same statement, a confirmation and an affirmation of it, it necessarily follows that a separation falls between them. So placing a separation between them is an indication that they are two distinct surahs, and leaving out "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" between them is an indication that this meaning is the very same as that meaning.

The fifth reason: Ibn 'Abbas said: I asked 'Ali, may God be pleased with him: Why was "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" not written between them? He said: Because "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" is a guarantee of safety, and this surah was revealed with the sword and the repudiation of covenants, and there is no safety in it. It is related that Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah mentioned this meaning and reinforced it with the words of God Most High: ﴿And do not say to one who offers you peace, "You are not a believer"﴾ [al-Nisa': 94]. He was asked: Did not the Prophet ﷺ write to the people of war "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful"? He answered: That was an initiation on his part of calling them to God, and he did not repudiate their covenant to them. Do you not see that he said at the end of the letter: "And peace be upon those who follow the guidance"? As for this surah, it contains fighting and the repudiation of covenants, so the difference is clear.

The sixth reason: Our companions said: Perhaps God Most High, knowing that some people dispute whether "In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful" is part of the Qur'an, commanded that it not be written here, as an indication that it is a verse at the beginning of every surah; and since it is not a verse of this surah, it was therefore not written. This indicates that since it is written at the beginning of the other surahs, it must be a verse of every surah.

﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger, to those among the polytheists with whom you made covenants. So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape God, and that God will disgrace the disbelievers.﴾

God Most High says: ﴿A disavowal from God and His Messenger, to those among the polytheists with whom you made covenants.﴾ ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months, and know that you cannot escape God, and that God will disgrace the disbelievers.﴾

Page 174

In the verse there are issues:

First issue: The meaning of bara'ah (disavowal) is the cutting of protection. It is said: "I disavowed (bari'tu) someone, I disavow (abra'u) with disavowal (bara'ah)," meaning the protection between us has been cut and no bond remains between us. From here it is said: "I have disavowed the religion." Regarding the nominative case of ﴿bara'ah﴾ there are two views:

The first: It is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "this is a disavowal." Al-Farra' said: Its parallel is your saying, when you look at a handsome man: "Handsome, by God," meaning "this is handsome, by God." And His words ﴿min﴾ (from) denote the starting point, and the meaning is: "This is a disavowal reaching from God and His Messenger to those with whom you made covenants," just as you say "a letter from so-and-so to so-and-so."

The second: That ﴿bara'ah﴾ is the subject, ﴿from God and His Messenger﴾ is its qualifier, and ﴿to those with whom you made covenants﴾ is the predicate, just as you say "a man from the Banu Tamim is in the house."

If they say: What is the reason that the disavowal is attributed to God and His Messenger, while the covenant is attributed to the polytheists?

We say: God had permitted the making of covenants with the polytheists, so the Muslims, together with the Messenger of God ﷺ, made a covenant with them. Then the polytheists broke the covenant, so God required the repudiation of it to them; the Muslims were addressed with what warns them against that. It was also said: Know that God and His Messenger have disavowed what you covenanted with the polytheists.

Third issue: It is related that "when the Prophet ﷺ set out for the expedition of Tabuk, and the hypocrites stayed behind and spread rumours, the polytheists began to break the covenant, so the Messenger of God ﷺ repudiated the covenant with them."

If it is asked: How is it permissible for the Prophet ﷺ to break a covenant?

We say: It is not permissible to break a covenant except in three cases:

One: that some treachery on their part becomes manifest to him, hidden, and he fears their harm, so he repudiates the covenant with them, so that they stand equal in knowledge of the breaking of the covenant, based on His words: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people, cast back to them on equal terms﴾ [al-Anfal: 58], and He also said: ﴿Those with whom you made a covenant, then they break their covenant every time﴾ [al-Anfal: 56].

Two: that he had stipulated to some of them, at the time of the covenant, that he would keep them to the covenant for the stated period until God Most High commanded its termination; when God Most High commanded him to end the covenant with them, he ended it on account of the stipulation.

Three: that the covenant was fixed for a term, the term expires and the covenant lapses; and the purpose of declaring this disavowal is to make it clear to them that he will not return to the covenant, and that he is determined on war and fighting. As for beyond these three circumstances, it is not permissible at all to break a covenant, because that would be treachery and breach of word, and God and His Messenger are free of it. For this meaning God Most High said: ﴿Except those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, then they have not failed you in anything, nor have they supported anyone against you; so fulfil their covenant to their term﴾ [al-Tawbah: 4]. It was also said: Most of the polytheists broke the covenant, except some people among them, namely Banu Damrah and Banu Kinanah.

Third issue: It is related that the conquest of Makkah was in the eighth year, and its governor then was 'Attab ibn Usayd, and the descent of this surah was in the ninth year. "The Messenger of God ﷺ commanded Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, in the ninth year to be in charge of the pilgrimage season. When this surah was revealed, he commanded 'Ali to go to the people of the pilgrimage season to recite it to them. It was said to him: 'If only you sent it with Abu Bakr.' He said: 'None delivers on my behalf except a man from me.' When 'Ali drew near, Abu Bakr heard the roar of a camel and stopped and said: 'This is the roar of the she-camel of the Messenger of God ﷺ.' When he reached him, he said: 'Are you a commander or one commanded?' He said: 'One commanded.' Then they set out. When they were before Tarwiyah, Abu Bakr delivered a sermon and taught them about their rites. 'Ali stood on the day of sacrifice at the Jamrat al-'Aqabah and said: 'O people, I am the messenger of the Messenger of God to you.' They said: 'With what?' He recited to them thirty or forty verses, and according to Mujahid thirteen verses. Then he said: 'I have been commanded with four things: that no polytheist approach this House after this year, that no naked person circle the House, that no one enter Paradise except a believing soul, and that the covenant of everyone who has a covenant be fulfilled to its term.' They said at that: 'O 'Ali, inform your cousin that we have cast the covenant behind our backs, and there is between us and him no covenant except the thrust of spears and the strike of swords.'"

They differed about the reason why he commanded 'Ali to recite this surah to them and deliver this message to them. Some said: The reason is that it is the custom of the Arabs that none undertakes the confirmation or the breaking of a covenant except a man from the close kin; so if Abu Bakr had undertaken it, they might have said: "This contradicts what we know among ourselves about breaking covenants," and so they might not have accepted it. Their objection was therefore removed by entrusting it to 'Ali, may God be pleased with him. It was also said: When he specified Abu Bakr, may God be pleased with him, as commander of the pilgrimage, he specified 'Ali for this delivery to soothe hearts and to care for all sides. It was also said: He appointed Abu Bakr over the pilgrimage and sent 'Ali after him to deliver this message, so that 'Ali would pray behind Abu Bakr, and that would serve as a hint at the imamate of Abu Bakr. And God knows best.

Al-Jahiz affirmed this meaning, saying: The Prophet (ﷺ) sent Abu Bakr as commander over the pilgrimage and entrusted him with the season (al-mawsim), and he sent Ali to recite to the people verses from Surat Bara'a. So Abu Bakr was the imam (the one leading the prayer) and Ali was the one following him (al-mu'tamm), Abu Bakr was the preacher (al-khatib) and Ali was the listener (al-mustami'), and Abu Bakr was the one who raised the call at the season, the one who went ahead of them, and the one who gave them orders. This was not granted to Ali, may Allah be pleased with him. As for the Prophet's statement, peace and blessings be upon him: "None may convey on my behalf except a man from me," this does not indicate that Ali was superior to Abu Bakr. Rather, he dealt with the Arabs according to what they customarily recognized among themselves. The great chief among them, when he concluded an alliance (hilf) for a people or made a pact (ahd), would not dissolve that pact or agreement except by himself or by a man from his closest relatives, such as a brother or an uncle. It was for this meaning that the Prophet (ﷺ) said that statement.

Regarding His words, ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾, there are several discussions:

The first: The root meaning of *al-siyahah* (wandering, travelling) is roaming the earth, moving about freely, keeping far from cities and inhabited places, and eating and drinking little. A fasting person is called *sa'ih* (wanderer) because he resembles the wanderer in abstaining from food and drink. The exegetes said: ﴿fasihu fi al-ardi﴾ means "go wherever you wish in it." This is not a command in the strict sense. Rather, the intent is permission, release, and informing them that safety has been granted and fear removed, meaning: you are secure from being killed or fought during this period.

The second discussion: The exegetes said: This is a grace period (*ta'jil*) granted by God to the polytheists for four months. Whoever's treaty was for more than four months, it is reduced to four. Whoever's treaty was for less than four months, it is raised to four. The purpose of this announcement consists of several matters:

First: that they should reflect on their own situation and take precaution in this matter, and know that after this period they have only one of three options: Islam, or accepting the *jizyah* (poll tax), or the sword. This would compel them to accept Islam outwardly.

Second: so that the Muslims would not be blamed for breaking the covenant.

Third: God intended to encompass all the polytheists with jihad, so He generalized the disavowal (*bara'ah*) to all of them and gave them four months. This was due to the strength of Islam and to instilling fear in the disbelievers, and this could not be done without annulling the covenants.

Fourth: The Prophet ﷺ intended to perform the pilgrimage in the coming year, so he ordered this disavowal to be proclaimed so that the naked (*al-'urat*, those who circumambulated naked) would not witness it.

The third discussion: Ibn al-Anbari said: In His words ﴿fasihu﴾, the speech is implied, and the estimate is: "So say to them, 'Travel freely.'" Or this may be a shift from the third person (absence) to the second person (presence), as in His words: ﴿And their Lord will give them a pure drink﴾ ﴿Indeed, this is a reward for you, and your effort has been appreciated﴾ [al-Insan 76:21–22].

The fourth discussion: The scholars differed concerning these four months. It is reported from al-Zuhri that the disavowal was revealed in Shawwal, and the four months were: Shawwal, Dhu al-Qa'dah, Dhu al-Hijjah, and al-Muharram. It was also said: they were twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah, al-Muharram, Safar, Rabi' al-Awwal, and ten days of Rabi' al-Akhir. They were named *hurum* (sacred months) because killing and fighting were forbidden in them. So these sacred months, when killing and fighting were prohibited in them, were called *hurum*. It was also said: they were named *hurum* because one part of this period consists of sacred months, since the twenty days of Dhu al-Hijjah together with al-Muharram are among the sacred months.

It was also said: the beginning of that period was from the tenth of Dhu al-Qa'dah to the tenth of Rabi' al-Awwal, because the pilgrimage in that year took place at that time due to the *nasi'* (intercalation) that was practiced among them. Then it fell in the second year in Dhu al-Hijjah, which was the Farewell Pilgrimage (*hijjat al-wada'*). The evidence for this is his statement, peace be upon him: "Indeed, time has returned to its original form on the day God created the heavens and the earth."

As for His words ﴿And know that you cannot escape God﴾, it was said: Know that this respite is not due to incapacity, but for a wise purpose and kindness, so that whoever repents may repent. It was also said its estimate is: "So travel freely, knowing that you will never overcome God in any state." The meaning is: I have granted you respite and released you, so do whatever you are able to do, such as preparing instruments and equipment, for you cannot overcome God; rather, God overcomes you and subdues you. It was also said: Know that this respite is not because He fears escape, for wherever you are, you are in God's dominion and under His authority.

As for His words ﴿and that God will disgrace the disbelievers﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: by killing in this world and punishment in the Hereafter. Al-Zajjaj said: This is a guarantee from God, Mighty and Majestic, of the victory of the believers over the disbelievers, and of humiliation and abasement, together with the exposure of disgrace and shame, and ignominy and punishment that exposes them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 3:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj that Allah is free from obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger. So if you repent, it is better for you; but if you turn away, then know that you cannot escape Allah. And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment.﴾

Know that His saying: ﴿A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ is a complete sentence, specific to the polytheists. And His saying: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger to the people on the day of the greater Hajj﴾ is another complete sentence, conjoined to the first sentence, and it is general with regard to all people, because this is something that both the believer and the polytheist must know, since the ruling connected to it binds both of them together. So it is obligatory upon the believers to know the time at which fighting is permitted and the time at which it is forbidden. Therefore Allah, exalted is He, commanded this announcement on the day of the greater Hajj, which is the great gathering, so that this news would reach everyone and become widely known. And concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: al-adhan (the proclamation) is the notification. Al-Azhari said: it is said, "adhantuhu, udhinuhu, idhanan" (I notified him). So adhan is a noun standing in place of idhan (notification), and it is the true verbal noun. From this comes the adhan of the prayer. His saying: ﴿from Allah and His Messenger to the people﴾ means: a proclamation issuing from Allah and His Messenger, reaching the people, just as you would say: "a notification issuing from so-and-so to so-and-so."

The second issue: They differed concerning the day of the greater Hajj. Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Ikrimah, said that it is the Day of Arafah, and this is the view of Umar, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, Ibn al-Zubayr, Ata', Tawus, Mujahid, one of the two reports from Ali, and a report from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), that he said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delivered a sermon on the evening of Arafah, and said: 'Amma ba'd, indeed this is the day of the greater Hajj.'" Ibn Abbas, in the narration of Ata', said: the day of the greater Hajj is the Day of Sacrifice (Yawm al-Nahr), and this is the view of al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, al-Suddi, one of the two reports from Ali, and the view of al-Mughirah ibn Shu'bah and Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The third view is what Ibn Jurayj narrated from Mujahid, that he said: the day of the greater Hajj is all the days of Mina. This is the position of Sufyan al-Thawri, who used to say: "The day of the greater Hajj is all its days," and he would say: "the day of Siffin and the day of the Camel," meaning by it the period and the time, because each of these wars lasted many days.

The argument of those who said it is the Day of Arafah is his, upon him be prayers and peace, saying: "Hajj is Arafah." And because the greatest of the acts of Hajj is standing at Arafah, for whoever reaches it has reached the Hajj, and whoever misses it has missed the Hajj, and that only occurs on this day. The argument of those who said it is the Day of Sacrifice is that the acts of Hajj are completed on this day: the tawaf, the sacrifice, the shaving, and the stoning. And from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that a man took hold of the bridle of his mount and said: "What is the greater Hajj?" He said: "Your day, this one. Release my mount." And from Ibn Umar: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood on the Day of Sacrifice at the Jamarat during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and said: 'This is the day of the greater Hajj.'" As for the view of those who said the intended meaning is the totality of those days, it is far-fetched, because it requires explaining "day" as "many days," and that contradicts the apparent meaning.

If it is said: Why was that called the greater Hajj?

We say: there are several reasons for this:

The first: that this is the greater Hajj, because the umrah is called the lesser Hajj.

The second: that he made standing at Arafah the greater Hajj, because it is the most important of its obligations, since if it is missed the Hajj is missed. Likewise if the Day of Sacrifice is intended by it, because what is done on it is most of the acts of the greater Hajj.

The third: al-Hasan said: that day was called the day of the greater Hajj because the Muslims and the polytheists gathered on it, and because it coincided with the festivals of the People of the Book, and this had not happened before it or after it, so that day became great in the heart of every believer and disbeliever. Al-Asamm criticized this reason and said: "The festival of the disbelievers in it is an anger (of Allah)." This criticism is weak, because what is meant is that this day is a day which all the sects held great, and those who described it as "the greatest" were those.

The fourth: it was so called because the Muslims and the polytheists performed Hajj in that year.

The fifth: the greater is the standing at Arafah, and the lesser is the sacrifice, and this is the view of Ata' and Mujahid.

The sixth: the greater Hajj is the qiran (combined pilgrimage), and the lesser is the ifrad (single pilgrimage), and this is reported from Mujahid.

Then, exalted is He, explained what that proclamation was, saying: ﴿that Allah is free from obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾, and concerning it there are discussions:

The first discussion: One might say: there is no difference between His saying: ﴿A declaration of disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those among the polytheists with whom you made a covenant﴾ and His saying: ﴿that Allah is free from obligation to the polytheists, and so is His Messenger﴾. So what is the benefit of this repetition?

The answer to this is from several aspects:

The first aspect: the intent of the first statement is to inform of the establishment of disavowal, and the intent of this statement is to inform all people of what has taken place and been established.

The second aspect: the intent of the first statement is disavowal from the covenant, and the intent of the second statement is the disavowal which is the opposite of allegiance, operating in the manner of a rebuke and a threat. What indicates that this difference exists is that in the first disavowal it says "bari'a ilayhim" (disavowed toward them), and in the second: "bari'a minhum" (disavowed from them). The intent is that He, exalted is He, commanded at the end of Surah al-Anfal that the Muslims should be allies of one another, and by this He alerted that it is obligatory upon them not to ally with the disbelievers and to disassociate from them. Here He made clear that just as He takes the believers as allies, so He disassociates from the polytheists, censures them and curses them, and likewise the Messenger. For this reason He followed it with the mention of repentance, which removes the disavowal.

The third aspect: in the difference, He, exalted is He, in the first statement made manifest the disavowal from the polytheists who made covenants and broke the covenant, and in this verse He made manifest the disavowal from the polytheists without describing them with a specific attribute, to alert that what necessitates this disavowal is their disbelief and their polytheism.

The second discussion: His saying: ﴿that Allah is free from obligation to the polytheists﴾ contains an elision, and the estimated meaning is: ﴿And a proclamation from Allah and His Messenger﴾ that Allah is free from obligation to the polytheists, except that the preposition (bi) has been omitted because the context indicates it.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿So if you repent﴾, that is, from polytheism, ﴿it is better for you﴾, and this is an encouragement from Allah to repentance and to ceasing polytheism, which necessitates that Allah and His Messenger are described as disavowing it. ﴿But if you turn away﴾, that is, you turn away from repentance from polytheism, ﴿then know that you cannot escape Allah﴾, and this is a great threat, because this statement indicates that He, exalted is He, is capable of inflicting the most severe punishment upon them.

Then He said: ﴿And give tidings to those who disbelieve of a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter, so that one does not suppose that since the punishment of this world has passed and ceased, they have been freed from punishment; rather, a severe punishment is prepared for them on the Day of Resurrection. The word "tidings" (bishara) came here by way of mockery, as one says: "Their greeting is a beating, and their honouring is an insult."

**Verse 4 (Sura al-Tawba, 9:4):** "Except those of the polytheists with whom you made a covenant, who have not failed you in anything and have not supported anyone against you. So fulfil their covenant to them until their term. Indeed, Allah loves the righteous."

Al-Razi's commentary (Mafatih al-Ghayb), page 179 is marked.

Razi says: To what does this exception (*istithna'*, exception) refer? There are two views.

The first: al-Zajjaj said that it refers to the phrase "Disavowal" (﴿بَراءَةٌ﴾). The sense is: "A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger" to the polytheists who had covenants, except those who did not break the covenant.

The second: the author of *al-Kashshaf* said that its correct sense is that it is an exception from the phrase "So travel freely through the land" (﴿فَسِيحُوا في الأرْضِ﴾), because the address is to the Muslims. The sense is: "A disavowal from Allah and His Messenger to those with whom you made a covenant among them, who have not failed you, so fulfil their covenant to them."

Know that God described them with two things:

The first is His saying: "Who have not failed you" (﴿ثُمَّ لَمْ يَنْقُصُوكُمْ﴾).

The second is His saying: "Nor have they supported anyone against you" (﴿ولَمْ يُظاهِرُوا عَلَيْكم أحَدًا﴾).

The more likely meaning of the first is that they do not themselves initiate fighting, and of the second that they do not stir up other peoples, support them, or encourage them to war. Then He said: "So fulfil their covenant to them" (﴿فَأتِمُّوا إلَيْهِمْ عَهْدَهُمْ﴾). The meaning is that those who did not betray in these two respects should have their covenant fulfilled, and you should not make the faithful equal to the treacherous. His saying "So fulfil their covenant to them" means: discharge it to them complete and whole. Ibn Abbas said: "A clan of Kinana still had nine months remaining of their covenant, so it was fulfilled to them."

"Indeed, Allah" (﴿إنَّ اللَّهَ﴾) [Page 179] "loves the righteous" (﴿يُحِبُّ المُتَّقِينَ﴾). He means that the requirement of righteousness is that the two groups are not treated alike. Or the meaning may be that this group, because they disdained breaking and violating the covenant, deserved from Allah that their covenant also be protected from breaking and violation.

It is narrated that Bani Bakr attacked Bani Khuza'a while the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was absent, and Quraysh backed them with weapons. Then 'Amr ibn Salim al-Khuza'i came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and recited to him:

O Allah, I call upon Muhammad,
the covenant of our ancient father and yours.
Indeed Quraysh broke their promise to you,
and violated your firm binding pact.
They ambushed us at al-Hatim while we slept,
and they killed us while bowing and prostrating.

So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "May I not be granted victory if I do not support you."

It was also read as "lam yanqudukum" (﴿لَمْ يَنْقُضُوكم﴾) with the dotted ḍād (ض), meaning "they did not break your covenant" (*lam yanqudu 'ahdakum*).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then when the sacred months have passed, kill the polytheists wherever you find them, and seize them, besiege them, and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush. But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakah, then let them go their way. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: al-Layth said: it is said "salakhtu al-shahr" (I stripped the month) when you leave it. Abu al-Haytham clarified this meaning, saying: it is said, "ahlalna hilal shahr kadhā" (we sighted the crescent of such-and-such month), meaning we entered it and put it on. We then continue, each night until half of it has passed, to be clothed in it; then, after the half is complete, we strip it off ourselves piece by piece, until we have stripped it from ourselves. He recited:

"When I strip off the month, I begin again with its like; it is enough for the killer of months that I strip them and sight them anew."

I say: the complete explanation of this is that time encompasses a thing and is its container, just as place encompasses it and is its container. The place of a thing is the inner surface of the containing body that touches the outer surface, and of the contained body. When a thing is stripped from its skin, it has separated from the inner surface of that skin and that surface, which in reality is its place. Likewise, when the month is complete, it has separated from the encompassing of that month and entered another month. "Salkh" is the name for the separation of a thing from its specific place, so it was also used as a name for its separation from its specific time, because of the complete and strong correspondence between place and time. As for the sacred months, we explained them in His saying: ﴿So travel freely in the land for four months﴾, and they are from the Day of Sacrifice to the tenth of Rabi' al-Akhir. What is meant by their being sacred is that Allah forbade killing and fighting in them. Then, when these sacred months ended, He permitted four things:

The first: His saying: ﴿And kill them wherever you find them﴾ [al-Nisa': 89]. This is a command to kill them absolutely, at any time and in any place.

The second: His saying: ﴿and seize them﴾, meaning by capture; "akhidh" is a captive.

Page 180
The third: His saying: ﴿and besiege them﴾. The meaning of "hasr" is preventing someone from leaving an enclosure. Ibn Abbas said: it means, if they fortify themselves, then besiege them. Al-Farra' said: their siege is that they be prevented from the Sacred House.

The fourth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and lie in wait for them at every place of ambush﴾. "Marsad" is the place where the enemy is watched, from the expression "rasadtu fulanan arsuduhu," meaning I kept watch on him. The exegetes said: the meaning is, lie in wait for them on every road they take to the House, or to the desert, or to trade. Al-Akhfash said: there is an omission in the speech, and the sense is: lie in wait for them at every place of ambush.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if they repent, establish the prayer, and give the zakah, then let them go their way﴾. On this there are issues:

First issue: al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, used this verse to argue that one who abandons the prayer is to be killed. He said: because He, exalted is He, permitted the blood of unbelievers absolutely, by all means, then forbade it upon the combination of these three things: repentance from disbelief, establishing the prayer, and giving the zakah. So when this combination is not found, the permission to shed blood must remain on its original basis.

If they say: why can it not be that what is meant is affirming the two and believing in their obligation? The proof of this is that one who abandons zakah is not killed.

They answer: what you mention is a departure from the apparent meaning, and as for one who abandons zakah, specification has entered into it.

If they say: why is taking the specification preferable to taking the speech as referring to belief in the obligation of prayer and zakah?

We say: because it is established in the principles of jurisprudence that whenever there is a conflict between metaphor (majaz) and specification (takhsis), specification is preferable as the reading.

Second issue: It is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, that he used to say concerning those who withheld zakah: "I will not distinguish between what Allah has joined." Perhaps his intention in this was this verse, because He, exalted is He, did not command letting them go their way except for those who repent, establish the prayer, and give zakah. So he made fighting the apostates obligatory when they refused zakah. This was after they denied its obligation. But if they acknowledged its obligation and refused only to hand it over to him specifically, then it is permissible that he held that they should be fought because they refused to pay zakah to the Imam. His position was that this is known from the religion of the Messenger, peace be upon him, just as the other manifest laws are known.

Third issue: We have discussed the reality of repentance in Surat al-Baqarah in His saying: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37]. al-Hasan narrated that a captive called out, within earshot of the Messenger: "I repent to Allah, and I do not repent to Muhammad," three times. He, peace be upon him, said: "He has recognized the truth for its people, so release him."

Fourth issue: His saying: ﴿then let them go their way﴾. It was said: to the Sacred House. It was also said: to the management of their affairs. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾ toward whoever repents and believes. There is a subtle point in this: He, exalted is He, restricted all good things upon them and cast them into all calamities, then He explained that if they repented from disbelief, established the prayer, and gave zakah, they would be freed from all those calamities in this world. So we hope by Allah's bounty that the matter will be the same on the Day of Resurrection as well. Repentance is an expression for purifying the theoretical faculty from ignorance, and prayer and zakah are an expression for purifying the practical faculty from what is not fitting. This indicates that the perfection of happiness is bound to this meaning.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 6–7:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection until he hears the words of Allah; then convey him to his place of safety. That is because they are a people who do not know.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse:

The first issue: concerning the establishment of the connection of the composition (wajh al-nazm). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: A man among the polytheists said to ʿAli ibn Abi Talib: "If we wish to come to the Messenger after the expiry of this term, to hear the words of Allah or for some other need, will we be killed?" ʿAli said: "No. Allah the Exalted has said: ﴿And if any one of the polytheists seeks your protection, then grant him protection﴾, that is, give him security until he hears the words of Allah." The explanation of this statement is: We say that when Allah the Exalted made it obligatory, after the sacred months had passed, to kill the polytheists, this indicates that the proof of Allah the Exalted had been established against them, and that what the Messenger had mentioned before that, of the kinds of evidences and clear signs, sufficed to remove their excuse and their pretext. This requires that if any one of the polytheists seeks evidence and proof, he is not to be heeded; rather he is to be required either to accept Islam or be killed. When this idea was occurring to the heart, Allah therefore revealed this verse to remove this doubt. Its purpose is to show that if an unbeliever comes seeking proof and evidence, or comes seeking to hear the Qur'an, he must be given respite, it is forbidden to kill him, and it is obligatory to convey him to his place of safety. This indicates that the purpose of legislating killing is the acceptance of the religion and the affirmation of monotheism. It also indicates that reflection upon the religion of Allah is among the highest stations and the highest ranks, for the unbeliever whose blood had been forfeit, when he manifests in himself that he is seeking reflection and inquiry, that forfeiture is removed, and it becomes obligatory upon the Messenger to convey him to his place of safety.

The second issue: "aḥad" (anyone) is in the nominative by a verb that is elided and interpreted by the apparent verb, and its estimate is: "And if anyone (aḥadun) seeks your protection." It cannot be nominative by the inceptive (mubtada'), because "in" (if) is one of the governors of the verb and does not enter upon anything else.

If it is said: Since the estimate is what you have mentioned, what is the wisdom in leaving this true order? We say: The wisdom in it is what Sibawayh mentioned, namely that they put first what is more important and what they are most concerned with. We have shown here that the apparent evidence requires the permissibility of the blood of the polytheists, so its mention is put first, so that this indicates greater care in preserving his blood from being forfeited. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: if any one of them asks you to grant him protection from being killed until he hears the words of Allah, then grant him protection.

The third issue: The Mu'tazila said: This verse indicates that the words of Allah are heard by the unbeliever, the believer, the heretic, the sincere one, and what the majority of creation hears is nothing but these letters and sounds. This indicates that the words of Allah are nothing but these letters and sounds. Then it is known by necessity that letters and sounds cannot be eternal, because Allah's speaking with these letters is either all together or in sequence. If He spoke them all together, this connected speech would not have come about from Him, for speech does not come about ordered except when these letters come into existence in succession. If they came about all together and not successively, the ordering would not have come about, and so speech would not have come about. And if they came about successively, it would follow that the earlier one ceases and the later one comes into being, and that requires origination. Thus this shows that the words of Allah are originated. They said: If you say that the words of Allah are something different from these letters and sounds, this is false, because the Messenger did not indicate by his saying "the words of Allah" anything but these letters and sounds. As for the Hashwiyya and the foolish among people, they said: It has been established by this verse that the words of Allah are nothing but these letters and sounds, and it has been established that the words of Allah are eternal, so it is necessary to say that the letters and sounds are eternal.

Know that the Ustadh Abu Bakr ibn Fawrak claimed that when we hear these letters and sounds, we have also heard the words of Allah the Exalted. As for the rest of the companions, they rejected this view from him. That is because that eternal speech is either the very same letters and sounds, or it is something else distinct from them. The first is the view of the rabble and the Hashwiyya, and that does not befit intelligent people.

As for the second, it is false, because on this supposition, when we heard these letters and sounds, we have heard something else that differs from the reality of these letters and sounds. But we know by necessity that when we heard these letters and sounds, we did not hear anything other than them, and we did not perceive by the faculty of hearing any other matter distinct from them. So this claim falls.

The correct answer to the Mu'tazila's argument is that we say: this which we hear is not the very word of Allah according to your doctrine, for the word of Allah is nothing but the letters and sounds that He created initially. Rather, those letters and sounds have ceased, and these we hear are letters and sounds made by man. So whatever you impose upon us is binding upon you as well.

Know that Abu ʿAli al-Jubbai, because of the strength of this objection, adopted a strange doctrine, saying: The words of Allah are something distinct from the letters and sounds, and it remains with the recitation of every reciter. The Mu'tazila have unanimously agreed on the collapse of this doctrine. And Allah knows best.

The fourth issue: Know that this verse indicates that imitation (taqlid) is not sufficient in religion, and that reflection and inquiry are necessary. That is because if imitation were sufficient, this unbeliever would not have to be given respite; rather it would be said to him: either you believe, or we will kill you. Since that was not said to him, but we gave him respite and removed fear from him, and it became obligatory upon us to convey him to his place of safety, we know that this was only because imitation in religion is not sufficient, rather proof and evidence are necessary, so we gave him respite and delayed for him so that he would have the interval of reflection and inquiry.

Having established this, we say: There is nothing in the verse that indicates how long this respite is, and perhaps its length is known only by custom. So whenever signs appear in the polytheist that he is seeking the truth and investigating the way of inquiry, he is given respite and left alone; and whenever it appears of him that he is turning away from the truth, repelling the time with lies, he is not heeded. And Allah knows best.

The fifth issue: What is mentioned in this verse is his seeking to hear the Qur'an. We say: It is joined to it that he seeks to hear the proofs, and that he seeks answers to doubts. The evidence for this is that Allah the Exalted gave as the reason for the obligation of that protection his being one who does not know, for He said: "That is because they are a people who do not know." The meaning is: grant him protection because he is seeking knowledge, desiring guidance to the truth, and whoever has this reason is obligated to be granted protection.

The sixth issue: Concerning His saying: ﴿until he hears the words of Allah﴾, there are several views. It has been said: it means hearing the whole Qur'an, because the complete proof and clear signs are in it. It has been said: it means hearing the Surah of Bara'ah (al-Tawba), because it contains the manner of dealing with the polytheists. It has been said:

it means hearing all the proofs, and the Qur'an was specifically mentioned because it is the book that carries most of the proofs. His saying: ﴿then convey him to his place of safety﴾ means: bring him to the abodes of his people where they feel secure for their persons and their property. After that, it is permissible to fight them and kill them.

The seventh issue: The jurists said: When a hostile non-Muslim (harbi) enters the abode of Islam, he becomes spoils together with his property, unless he enters seeking protection for a legitimate purpose, such as hearing the words of Allah in hope of Islam, or he entered for trade. If he entered under the protection of a child or a insane person, their protection is considered a semblance of protection, so it is obligatory to convey him to his place of safety, which is that he should reach, guarded in his person and property, the place that is a refuge for him. Whoever of them enters the abode of Islam as a messenger, the message is a protection. Whoever enters to take property in the abode of Islam, and his property has protection, then there is protection for him. And Allah knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, verses 8–11**

His words, exalted is He: ﴿How can there be a covenant with the polytheists in the sight of God and in the sight of His Messenger, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque? So long as they remain upright toward you, remain upright toward them. Indeed God loves the God-fearing.﴾

His words, ﴿How﴾: it is an interrogative used in the sense of denial, as you say, "How can someone like you overtake me?" That is, it is not fitting that he should overtake me. In the verse there is an ellipsis, and its estimate is: "How can there be a covenant for the polytheists, given that they conceal treachery in what has occurred of the covenant, except for those with whom you made a covenant at the Sacred Mosque, because they did not break or violate [it]?" It was said: they were the Banu Kinanah and the Banu Damrah, so wait for their affair and do not kill them. "So long as they remain upright toward you in the covenant, remain upright toward them in its like." ﴿Indeed God loves the God-fearing﴾ means: whoever fears God fulfills his covenant with the one with whom he has made it. And God knows best.

﴿How, and if they gain the upper hand over you, they will not observe regarding you any kinship tie or covenant. They please you with their mouths, but their hearts refuse, and most of them are defiant transgressors. They have sold the signs of God for a small price and have averted [people] from His way. Indeed, evil is what they have been doing. They do not observe regarding a believer any kinship tie or covenant, and those are the aggressors.﴾

Know that His words, ﴿How﴾, are a repetition to express the improbability of the polytheists' steadfastness in the covenant. The verb is omitted because it is known, meaning: how can their covenant be, and their condition be that, if they gain the upper hand over you, after what preceded of confirmed oaths and pacts, they will not regard any alliance or covenant, "and they will not spare you." This is the meaning. It is necessary to explain the words mentioned in the verse. It is said:

"I gained the upper hand over so-and-so" when I overcame him, and "I rose over the roof" when I came to be above it. Al-Layth said: *al-zuhur* is the victory over a thing, and God made the Muslims gain the upper hand over the polytheists, that is, He made them superior to them. From this is His words, exalted is He: ﴿So they became victorious﴾ [al-Saff: 14], and His words: ﴿to make it prevail over all religion﴾ [al-Tawbah: 33], that is, to make it high. The verification of the matter is that whoever overcomes another acquires a quality of perfection, and whoever is like this makes himself manifest, while whoever becomes overcome becomes like one deficient, and the deficient does not display himself but hides his deficiency. So *al-zuhur* became a metonym for dominance, because it is one of its necessary consequences. Thus His words, ﴿if they gain the upper hand over you﴾, mean: if they gain power over you. And His words, ﴿they will not observe regarding you﴾: al-Layth said: "He watched the man (*raqaba al-insan*), watches him, a watching and a *ruqub*," which is to wait for him. The *raqib* of a people is their guard. And His words, ﴿and you did not observe my word﴾ [Ta-Ha: 94], that is, you did not keep it. As for the first [word, *il*], there are several views:

The first: it is the covenant. The poet said:

*We found them liars regarding their il, and the one who possesses the il and the covenant does not lie.*

meaning the covenant.

The second: al-Farra' said: *al-Il* is kinship. Hassan said:

*By your life, your il among Quraysh*
*is like the il of the young camel among the young ostrich.*

meaning kinship.

The third: *al-Il* is alliance. Aws ibn Hajar said:

*Were it not for the Banu Malik, and the il, a place of refuge,*
*and Malik among them, the bounties and the nobility...*

meaning alliance.

The fourth: *al-Il* is God, exalted and majestic. It is reported from Abu Bakr al-Siddiq (may God be pleased with him) that when he heard the babble of Musaylima he said: "This speech did not come forth from *il*." Al-Zajjaj criticized this view and said: the names of God are known from reports and the Qur'an, and no one has been heard saying: "O *Il*!"

The fifth: al-Zajjaj said: the true meaning of *al-il*, in my view, according to what the language requires, is the delimitation of a thing. From this is *al-illa*, the spear-head, and "a sharpened ear" (*udhun mu'allalah*). So *al-il* includes all that has been explained as covenant and kinship.

The sixth: al-Azhari said: *Il* is among the names of God, exalted and majestic, in Hebrew, and it is possible that it was Arabized and so was called *il*.

The seventh: some said: *al-Il* is derived from their saying: *alla yauullu allan*, when [something] becomes pure and gleams. From it is *al-ala*, the mirage, because of its shining. And "a sharpened ear" resembles the spear in its sharpness. He has *alil*, that is, a moan by which he raises his voice. A woman *raf'at aliliha* when she wailed. So the covenant was called *il* because of its clarity and its purity from the stains of treachery; or because when people made alliances they raised their voices with it and proclaimed it.

As for His words, ﴿nor any kinship tie﴾: *dhimmah* is covenant, and its plural is *dhimam* and *dhimam*. It is every matter that binds you, such that if you neglect it, a blame would attach to you. Abu 'Abd Allah said: *al-dhimmah* is that from which one feels shame (*yutadhammam minhu*), meaning that which one avoids in order to avoid blame. We detail the verses for a people who know.﴾ ﴿But if they break their oaths after their covenant and attack your religion, then fight the leaders of disbelief, for they have no oaths, so that they may desist.﴾

Know that when God Almighty described the state of those who observe neither kinship nor covenant with God, who break covenants, harbour hypocrisy, and transgress the limits set for them, He then explained what their ruling would be if they established prayer and gave zakat. He gathered all of that in His words ﴿then they are your brothers in religion﴾, which conveys the whole body of the rulings of faith. Explaining it in full would take a long time.

If it is said: what is conditional on a thing by the word "in" (if) is absent when that thing is absent. This implies that whenever these three things are not present, brotherhood in religion does not arise. This is problematic, because a person may be poor, or may be wealthy but not yet liable to zakat before the year has passed.

We say: we have already explained, in the commentary on God's words ﴿If you avoid the major sins that you are forbidden﴾ [al-Nisa': 31], that what is conditional on a thing by the word "in" does not necessarily imply the absence of that thing when the condition is absent. Thus this objection is dispelled.

Some people said: what is conditional on a thing by the word "in" is absent when that thing is absent. Here they said: the brotherhood of Islam among Muslims is contingent on performing prayer and zakat together, for God made them a condition for establishing brotherhood. Whoever is not eligible to be obligated to pay zakat must acknowledge its ruling. When he acknowledges this ruling, he enters the condition by which brotherhood becomes binding.

Ibn Mas'ud used to say: "May God have mercy on Abu Bakr; how deeply he understood religion!" He meant what Abu Bakr said regarding those who withheld zakat: "By God, I will not separate between two things that God has joined together."

Two points remain concerning God's words ﴿then they are your brothers in religion﴾:

The first: His words ﴿fa-ikhwanukum﴾. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is "then they are your brothers," with the subject (mubtada', the subject of a nominal sentence) omitted, like His words: ﴿But if you do not know their fathers, then they are your brothers﴾ [al-Ahzab: 5], meaning "then they are your brothers."

The second: Abu Hatim said: the people of Basra all said: "ikhwah" is used for kinship and "ikhwan" for friendship. This is an error. "Ikhwah" and "ikhwan" are both used for friends and non-friends alike. God said: ﴿The believers are but brothers﴾ [al-Hujurat: 10], and He did not mean kinship. He also said: ﴿or the houses of your brothers﴾ [al-Nur: 61], which refers to kinship. Ibn 'Abbas said: this verse made the blood of the People of the Qiblah (the Muslims) inviolable.

Then He said: ﴿We detail the verses for a people who know.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: this is a parenthetical interjection placed between the two statements. Its purpose is to urge and encourage reflection on what has been detailed regarding the rulings for the polytheists who are under treaty, and to urge preserving them.

Then He said: ﴿But if they break their oaths after their covenant and attack your religion.﴾ It is said: "Fulan broke his covenant" when he annulled it after confirming it, just as a woollen thread is unravelled after being twisted. From this is His words: ﴿after strength, into unravelled threads﴾ [al-Nahl: 92]. "Ayman" is the plural of "yamin," meaning an oath or swearing. "Yamin" is also said of an oath, and it is literally the word for the hand, because they used to extend their right hands when they swore or made alliances. It was also said that oaths are called "yamin" because of the "right" (yamin al-birr) in them. So His words ﴿if they break their oaths﴾ mean they annulled their pacts. On this there are two views:

The first, which is the view of most scholars, is that the intended meaning is their breaking of the covenant with the Messenger of God (ﷺ).

The second is that the intended meaning is taking the covenant to be Islam after faith, so the intended meaning would be their apostasy after belief. For this reason some read: "if they break their faith after their covenant." But the first view is preferred because of the well-known recitation, and because the verse was revealed concerning those who violated the covenant, since God divided them into two categories. When those who repent are separated from them, only those who persist in breaking the covenant remain.

As for His words ﴿and attack your religion﴾: it is said "tana'ahu bil-rumh yat'unuhu" (he stabbed him with a spear), and "tana'a bil-qawl al-sayyi'" (he attacked with evil speech). Al-Layth said: some people say "yat'unu" for spear-stabbing and "yat'anu" for attacking with speech, distinguishing between them. The meaning is that they disparaged your religion and found fault with it.

Then He said: ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾, that is, whenever they do this, then do this. On this there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi', Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read "a'immata al-kufr" with a single, unextended hamzah and softening of the second (the second hamzah is pronounced between hamzah and ya', "bayn bayn"). The rest read it with two hamzahs, fully pronounced. Al-Zajjaj said: the original form of "al-a'immah" is "a'immimah," since it is the plural of "imam," like "mithal" and "amthilah." But when the two mims come together, the first is assimilated into the second (idgham, assimilation), its vowel is transferred to the hamzah, and it becomes "a'immah." Then the ya' replaces the kasrah-bearing hamzah, because of the dislike of two hamzahs together in one word. This is the preferred view among all the grammarians.

Having understood this, we say: the author of al-Kashshaf said: the word "a'immah" has a hamzah followed by a hamzah "bayn bayn," where "bayn bayn" means between the place of articulation of the hamzah and that of the ya'. As for pronouncing both hamzahs fully, it is a well-known recitation, even if it was not accepted by the Basrans. As for pronouncing the ya' explicitly, it is not a recitation, and it is not permissible for it to be one; whoever pronounces it that way is a reciter who makes errors and distorts the text.

[p. 187]

The second issue: His words ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾ mean: fight the disbelievers as a whole, but God specifically mentioned the leaders and chiefs among them, because they are the ones who incite the followers to these false deeds.

The third issue: al-Zajjaj said: this verse requires the killing of a dhimmi (a non-Muslim under protection) if he openly attacks Islam, because his covenant is conditional on not attacking it. If he attacks it, then he has broken and annulled his covenant.

Then God Almighty said: ﴿for they have no oaths.﴾ Ibn 'Amir read "la iman lahum" with a kasrah on the alif, and this has two possible meanings:

One: "They have no security," meaning: do not grant them security. In this case it is a verbal noun from "iman," which is the opposite of causing fear.

The second: they are disbelievers who have no faith, meaning they have no true belief and no religion. The rest read it with a fathah on the hamzah, which is the plural of "yamin," and its meaning is: they have no oaths in the true sense, and their oaths are not oaths. Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, relied on this to argue that the oath of a disbeliever is not an oath. According to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, their oaths are oaths, and the meaning of this verse according to him is that, since they did not fulfil them, their oaths became as if they were not oaths. The evidence that their oaths are not oaths is that God described them as broken in His words ﴿if they break their oaths﴾, and if they had not been binding, it would not have been valid to describe them as broken.

Then God Almighty said: ﴿so that they may desist.﴾ This is connected to His words ﴿then fight the leaders of disbelief.﴾ That is: let your aim in fighting them, after the great offences they have committed, be that the fighting becomes a cause for them to desist from the disbelief they are upon. This is from the utmost of God's generosity and His grace in bestowing kindness.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 13:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths and resolved to expel the Messenger, and they initiated [hostility] against you the first time? Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Then fight the leaders of disbelief﴾, He followed it with mention of the cause that moves them to fight them, saying: ﴿Will you not fight a people who broke their oaths﴾.

Know also that He, may He be exalted, mentioned three causes, each of which would necessitate fighting them if it stood alone, so how much more so when they are combined:

The first: their breaking of the covenant. All the exegetes understood it as the breaking of the covenant. Ibn Abbas, al-Suddi and al-Kalbi said: it was revealed concerning the disbelievers of Makkah who broke their oaths after the covenant of al-Hudaybiyah, and they aided Banu Bakr against Khuza'ah. This verse indicates that fighting those who break oaths takes precedence over fighting other disbelievers, so that it may serve as a deterrent to others.

The second: His saying: ﴿and they resolved to expel the Messenger﴾. This is among the most emphatic reasons for which fighting is obligatory. They differed concerning it. Some said: the intended meaning is his expulsion from Makkah when he emigrated. Others said: rather, the intended meaning is from Madinah, because of what they undertook of consultation and agreement to kill him. Others said: rather, they resolved to expel him by undertaking what would call him to depart, namely the breaking of the covenant and the aiding of his enemies, so the expulsion was attributed to them figuratively, due to the matters that occurred from them which called to it.

His saying: ﴿and they resolved to expel the Messenger﴾ may be either in action or in intention to it, even if that action was not carried out in full.

The third: His saying: ﴿and they initiated [hostility] against you the first time﴾, meaning by fighting on the day of Badr, for when the caravan was saved they said: "We will not turn back until we uproot Muhammad and those with him."

The second opinion: He meant that they fought the allies of Khuza'ah, and so they initiated the breaking of the covenant. This is the view of the majority. He said ﴿they initiated [hostility] against you﴾ only to draw attention to the fact that the initiator is more unjust.

When He, may He be exalted, explained these three causes, He added to them, saying: ﴿Do you fear them? Allah has more right that you fear Him, if you are believers.﴾ This speech strengthens the motive for fighting in several respects:

The first: enumerating and detailing the strong causes strengthens this motive.

The second: when you say to a man, "Do you fear your adversary?", that is a stirring of him so that he disdains being described as afraid of his opponent.

The third: His saying ﴿Allah has more right that you fear Him﴾ conveys this, as if it were said: "If you fear anyone, then Allah has more right that you fear Him, since He is in utmost power, greatness and majesty, whereas the harm expected from them is at most killing, while what is expected from Allah is severe punishment in the Hereafter and the blame that necessarily follows in this world."

The fourth: His saying ﴿if you are believers﴾ means: if you are believers in faith, it is obligatory upon you to undertake this fighting, and its meaning is that if you do not undertake it, it is necessary that you are not believers. Thus it is established that this speech comprises seven kinds of matters that move them to fight those disbelieving covenant-breakers.

Some issues remain concerning the verse:

The first issue: al-Wahidi related from the scholars of meanings that they said: when you say "Do not do such-and-such," this is used for an act whose existence is anticipated, and when you say "Do you not do?", you say this regarding an act whose existence is established. The difference between them is that "la" negates the future, so when the alif (interrogative) enters upon it, it becomes an exhortation to do what is future, and it is not used to negate the present; when the alif enters upon it, it becomes for affirming the present.

The second issue: It is reported "from Ibn Abbas that he said: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿Will you not fight a people﴾ is an encouragement to conquer Makkah, and His saying ﴿a people who broke their oaths﴾ means their covenant, meaning the Quraysh when they aided Banu al-Dil ibn Bakr against Khuza'ah, the allies of the Messenger, peace be upon him. So Allah commanded His Messenger to march against them and support Khuza'ah. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ did that and commanded the people to prepare for Makkah, while Abu Sufyan was with Heraclius among the Romans. He returned and came to Madinah, and entered upon Fatimah, daughter of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, seeking her protection, but she refused. He said this to her two sons, al-Hasan and al-Husayn, and they refused. He addressed Abu Bakr, who refused; then he addressed Umar, who was harsh; then he addressed Ali, who did not answer him. So he sought protection through al-Abbas, who was close to him, and he granted him protection, and the Messenger granted him protection for the sake of his protection and let him go. Al-Abbas said: "O Messenger of Allah, Abu Sufyan has some pride, so give him something!" He said: "Whoever enters the house of Abu Sufyan is safe." He returned to Makkah and proclaimed: "Whoever enters my house is safe." They rose against him and struck him severely, and the conquest was achieved at that moment." This is what Ibn Abbas said. Al-Hasan said: it is not permissible that this be the meaning, because Surah Bara'ah was revealed a year after the conquest of Makkah, and the distinguishing of the right of this matter from its falsehood is not known except through reports.

The third issue: Abu Bakr al-Asamm said: this verse indicates that they disliked this fighting, due to His saying: ﴿Fighting has been prescribed for you, and it is hateful to you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 216], so Allah reassured them with these verses.

The judge said: He, may He be exalted, may urge the performance of an obligation upon one who is neither averse to it nor negligent in it. If he means that such exhortation to jihad benefits only where there is aversion to fighting, that is also not sound, because Allah, may He be exalted, may urge this kind [of people] to jihad so that the aversion which would have occurred without this exhortation does not arise.

The fourth issue: This verse indicates that the believer should fear his Lord and should not fear anyone other than Him.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 14–15:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fight them, and God will punish them at your hands, and will disgrace them, and give you victory over them, and heal the breasts of a believing people.﴾ ﴿And remove the rage of their hearts. God turns in forgiveness to whom He wills, and God is Knowing, Wise.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, said in the first verse, ﴿Will you not fight a people﴾ [al-Tawba: 13], He mentioned after it seven things, each of which requires them to advance to fighting. Then, in this verse, He repeated the command to fight, and mentioned in that fighting five kinds of benefits, each of which is great in its effect when taken alone. How much more so when they are combined?

The first of them is His saying: ﴿God will punish them at your hands.﴾ On this there are several points:

The first point: He called that a punishment, and it is true, for He punishes the disbelievers. If He wills, He hastens it in this world, and if He wills, He delays it until the Hereafter.

The second point: the meaning of this punishment is killing at times, capture at other times, and seizing wealth as spoils at still other times, so all that we have mentioned is included in it.

If they say: Did He not say, ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ [al-Anfal: 33]? Then how does He say here, ﴿God will punish them at your hands﴾?

We say: What is meant by His saying, ﴿God would not punish them while you are among them﴾ is punishment of annihilation (al-isti'sal), and what is meant by His saying, ﴿God will punish them at your hands﴾ is the punishment of killing and war. The difference between the two categories is that the punishment of annihilation may extend to someone who is not guilty, even if for him it is a cause of greater reward. As for the punishment of killing, it is apparent that it remains confined to the guilty.

The third point: our companions argued for their position that the act of the servant is created by God, exalted is He, from His saying, ﴿God will punish them at your hands.﴾ For the meaning of this punishment is killing and capture, and the apparent wording indicates that this killing and capture are the act of God, exalted is He, except that He brings it into existence through the hands of His servants. This is the explicit statement of our doctrine and our school.

Al-Jubba'i answered this, saying: If it were permissible to say that He punishes the disbelievers by the hands of the believers, it would be permissible to say that He punishes the believers by the hands of the disbelievers, and it would be permissible to say that He makes His prophets lie through the tongues of the disbelievers, and curses the believers through their tongues, because He is the creator of all that. Since this is not permissible according to the determinists (al-mujbira), it is known that He, exalted is He, did not create the actions of the servants. Rather, He attributed what we have mentioned to Himself by way of expansion (al-tawassu'), in that it came about by His command and His favors, just as all acts of obedience are attributed to Him on this interpretation.

Our companions answered him, saying: As for what you have imposed on us, the matter is as you say, except that we do not say it with the tongue, just as we know that He is the creator of all bodies, yet we do not say: O Creator of urine and excrement, O Fashioner of beetles and worms. So it is likewise here. Moreover, we agree that fornication, sodomy, and all other vices came about by the decrees of God, exalted is He, and His facilitation, yet it is not permissible to say: O Facilitator of fornication and sodomy, O Remover of the obstacles to them. So likewise here. As for his saying that what is meant is the decrees (al-aqdar), we say: This is turning the speech away from its apparent meaning, and that is not permissible except by a compelling proof, and the compelling proof on our side here is that the act does not proceed except when the motive (al-da'iya) that has arisen is present, and the arising of that motive is only from God, exalted is He.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and will disgrace them.﴾ Its meaning is the humiliation and abasement that befalls them when they witness themselves overpowered at the hands of the believers, abased and debased. Al-Wahidi said: His saying, ﴿and will disgrace them,﴾ that is, after your killing them. This indicates that this disgrace occurs to them in the Hereafter. This is weak, because we have explained that the disgrace occurs in this world.

The third: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and give you victory over them.﴾ The meaning is that since disgrace came to them through being overpowered, victory came to the Muslims through being the dominant ones.

If they say: Since the occurrence of that disgrace necessarily entails the occurrence of this victory, singling it out for mention is pointless. We say: The matter is not so, for it is possible that disgrace befalls them at the hands of the believers, yet the believers suffer some calamity from another cause. So when He said, ﴿and give you victory over them,﴾ it indicated that they benefit from this victory, conquest, and triumph.

The fourth: His saying: ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people.﴾ We have mentioned that the Khuza'a had embraced Islam, and Quraysh aided Banu Bakr against them until they inflicted punishment upon them. So God healed their breasts from Banu Bakr. It is well known that whoever has long suffered harm from his adversary, and then God empowers him over him in the best manner, his joy in it greatly increases, and that becomes a cause of strength of the soul and steadfastness of resolve.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts.﴾

One might say: His saying, ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people,﴾ means that He heals them from the pain of rage, and this is the very same as removing rage, so His saying, ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts,﴾ is a repetition.

The answer is that He promised them the occurrence of this conquest, so they were in the crush of waiting, as it is said: "Waiting is the red death." So He healed their breasts from the crush of waiting. On this interpretation, the difference between His saying, ﴿and heal the breasts of a believing people,﴾ and His saying, ﴿and remove the rage of their hearts,﴾ becomes clear.

These are the five benefits that God, exalted is He, mentioned in this fighting, and all of them return to calming the motives arising from the irascible faculty (al-quwwa al-ghadabiyya), namely the desire for vengeance, the seeking of retribution, and the removal of rage. He did not mention in them the finding of wealth or the attainment of food and drink, because the Arabs are a people created with zeal and pride, so He encouraged them in these meanings, which are suited to their natures. There remain here some points:

The first point: these attributes are suitable for the conquest of Mecca, because what took place in that event resembles these circumstances, and for this reason it is permissible to say that the verse was revealed concerning it.

The second point: the verse indicates a miracle (mu'jiza), because He, exalted is He, reported the occurrence of these circumstances, and they did occur in accordance with these reports, so this is a report of the unseen, and reports of the unseen are a miracle.

The third point: this verse indicates that the Companions were believers in the knowledge of God, exalted is He, with true faith, because it indicates that their hearts were filled with anger, with zeal for the sake of religion, and with an intense desire for the exaltation of the religion of Islam, and these states do not arise except in the hearts of believers.

Know that God's describing them with this does not negate that they are described as merciful and compassionate, for He, exalted is He, said of them: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 54], and He also said: ﴿severe against the disbelievers, merciful among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29].

Then He said: ﴿God turns in forgiveness to whom He wills.﴾ Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: This is mentioned by way of resumption (isti'naf), and it cannot be a response to His saying, ﴿Fight them,﴾ because His saying, ﴿God turns in forgiveness to whom He wills,﴾ cannot be made a consequence of fighting them against the disbelievers. They said: Its parallel is: ﴿If God wills, He would seal upon your heart﴾ [al-Shura: 24], and the speech ends here. Then He resumed and said: ﴿And God would erase falsehood﴾ [al-Shura: 24]. Some people said: This repentance may be made a consequence of that fighting, and its explanation is from several aspects:

The first: when He commanded them to fight, it may have been hard on some of them, according to what al-Asamm held. So when they advanced to fight, that action takes the place of repentance from that aversion.

The second: the achieving of victory and triumph is a great blessing, and when the servant witnesses the successive blessings of God, it is not unlikely that this becomes a motive for him to repent of all sins.

The third: when victory, triumph, and conquest are attained, and wealth and blessings increase, and his pleasures were being pursued by unlawful means, then, with the attainment of wealth and standing, it becomes possible to obtain them by lawful means, so the abundance of wealth and standing becomes a motive to repent from these matters.

The fourth: some of them said: The soul is strongly inclined to this world and its pleasures. When the doors of this world open to a person, and God intends good for him, he comes to know that its pleasures are base and trivial. Then the world becomes small in his eyes, and this becomes a cause for the soul's withdrawal from the world. This is one of the interpretations mentioned regarding His saying, exalted is He, quoting Solomon, peace be upon him: ﴿Grant me a kingdom that will not befit anyone after me﴾ [Sad: 35]. That is, after the attainment of this kingdom, the soul has no further occupation with seeking the world. Then he knows that upon attaining this kingdom, which is the greatest of kingdoms, there is no real benefit in the world, and no use in its pleasures and desires. At that point the heart turns away from the world and gives it no weight. Thus it is established that the occurrence of fighting leads to the five benefits mentioned, and the attainment of those benefits necessitates repentance, so repentance is connected to that fighting. He said, ﴿on whom He wills,﴾ because the finding of the world and the opening of its doors to a person may become a cause for the heart to withdraw from the world, and that is the case for one for whom God intends good, and it may become a cause for a person to be absorbed in it, to be consumed by it, and to be cut off by it from the path of God. So when the matter varies in the way we have described, He said: ﴿God turns in forgiveness to whom He wills.﴾

Then He said: ﴿And God is Knowing﴾, that is, of everything that is done and performed in His dominion and His kingdom, ﴿Wise﴾, that is, correct in His rulings and His acts.
