Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 38:

Page 48

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth? Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is little.﴾ There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: Know that when Exalted is He had explained the faults and disgraceful conduct of these disbelievers, He returned to encouraging fighting against them, and said: ﴿O you who have believed, what is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ The summary of the matter is that He, exalted is He, mentioned in the preceding verses many reasons that make fighting them obligatory, and He mentioned many benefits that result from fighting them, such as His saying: ﴿Allah will punish them by your hands and disgrace them and give you victory over them﴾ [at-Tawbah: 14]. He also mentioned their objectionable statements and their ugly deeds in religion and in worldly affairs. At this point, nothing remains to prevent a person from fighting them except the mere fear of being killed and the love of life. So Exalted is He explained that this obstacle is base, because the happiness of this world, in comparison with the happiness of the Hereafter, is like a drop in the sea, and abandoning a great good for the sake of a small evil is ignorance and foolishness.

The second issue: It is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas that this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of Tabuk. That was because when the Prophet ﷺ returned from al-Ta'if, he stayed in Madinah and commanded [the people] to fight the Romans. That time was a period of intense heat, the fruits of Madinah had ripened and were ready, and they regarded the campaign against the Romans as grave and feared it. So this verse was revealed. The verifying scholars said: People found this burdensome for several reasons:

The first: the severity of the season, in summer, and drought.

The second: the distance of the journey and the need for preparation far beyond what was customary in other campaigns.

The third: the ripening of the fruits in Madinah at that time.

The fourth: the intensity of the heat at that time.

The fifth: the awe of the Roman army. These many factors combined and necessitated the people's reluctance toward that campaign. And Allah knows best.

The third issue: It is said: The imam called the people (istanfara) to fight the enemy, and they went forth (nafarū, yanfirūna, nafran and nufūran) when he urged them and called them to it. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "When you are called forth, then go forth." The root of nafr (going forth) is going out to a place for a necessary matter, and the name of those people who go out is al-nafir. From this is the saying of people: "So-and-so is neither in the caravan nor in the nafir." His saying, ﴿you adhere heavily to the earth﴾, originally is tathaqaltum (you adhered heavily), and al-Aʿmash read it so. Its meaning is: you were slow. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿fa-iddaraʾtum﴾ [al-Baqarah: 72] and His saying: ﴿iṭṭayyarnā bika﴾ [an-Naml: 47]. The author of al-Kashshaf said: [The verb] was made to imply the sense of inclination and settling, so it takes ilā (to). The meaning is: you inclined toward the world and its desires, and you disliked the hardships and fatigues of travel. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿he settled toward the earth and followed his desire﴾ [al-Aʿraf: 176]. Although it is apparently a question, its purpose is emphasis in denunciation.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Are you satisfied with the life of this world rather than the Hereafter? But the enjoyment of worldly life, compared to the Hereafter, is little.﴾ The meaning is as if it were said: We have mentioned the many factors that call to fighting, we have explained the great benefits that result from fighting, and we have made clear the kinds of their disgrace and ugliness that should move any sensible person to fight them. Yet you have abandoned all of these matters. Does not your Lord command you to fight them, and do you not know that obedience to the Lord brings great reward in the Hereafter? Is it fitting for a sensible person to abandon a great reward in the Hereafter for the sake of a small benefit obtained in this world? The proof that the enjoyment of this world is little in comparison with the Hereafter is that the pleasures of this world are base in themselves, mixed with calamities and afflictions, and certainly cut off after a short time, whereas the benefits of the Hereafter are noble, lofty, pure and free from all calamities, and lasting, everlasting and perpetual. This necessarily entails the certainty that the enjoyment of this world is little, worthless and base.

Page 49

The fourth issue: Know that this verse indicates the obligation of jihad in every circumstance, because He, exalted is He, stated explicitly that their reluctance to engage in jihad is a reprehensible matter. Had jihad not been obligatory, this reluctance would not have been reprehensible. And it is not valid for anyone to say: Jihad is only obligatory at the time when the disbelievers are feared to attack, because he, peace be upon him, did not fear an attack by the Romans upon himself, and yet he made jihad obligatory along with them. The benefits of jihad are fully explained in Surat Al ʿImran. Furthermore, it is an obligation of sufficiency (fard kifayah): when some people undertake it, it is dropped from the rest.

The fifth issue: One may say: His saying, ﴿O you who have believed﴾, is addressed to all the believers.

Then He said: ﴿What is [wrong] with you that when you are told, "Go forth in the cause of Allah," you adhere heavily to the earth?﴾ This indicates that all the believers were reluctant regarding that obligation, and that reluctance is disobedience, and this indicates the consensus of the entire Community upon disobedience, and that undermines the claim that the consensus of the Community is a proof.

The answer: The address to the whole for the sake of some is a well-known metaphor in the Qur'an and in all kinds of speech, such as the saying:

"It is you I mean, yet listen, O neighbor" (Iyyaki aʿni wa-smaʿi ya jarah).

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 39:

The Exalted said: ﴿If you do not go forth, He will punish you with a painful punishment and will replace you with a people other than you, and you will not harm Him at all. And Allah is over all things competent.﴾

There are several issues concerning this verse.

The first issue: Know that when the Exalted encouraged them in the previous verse to fight in jihad by appealing to the reward of the Hereafter, He encouraged them in this verse to fight in jihad by appealing to other kinds of matters that strengthen motives. These are three kinds.

The first is the Exalted's saying: ﴿He will punish you with a painful punishment.﴾

Know that it is possible that what is meant is the punishment of this world, and it is possible that what is meant is the punishment of the Hereafter. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called the people to go forth, but they were sluggish, so Allah withheld the rain from them." Al-Hasan said: "Allah knows best about the punishment that would descend upon them." It has also been said that what is meant is the punishment of the Hereafter, since the word "painful" (alim) befits only that. It has also been said that it is a threat in every category: the punishment of this world, the punishment of the Hereafter, and the cutting off of the benefits of this world and the benefits of the Hereafter.

The second is His saying: ﴿and will replace you with a people other than you.﴾ The purpose is to alert them that He, the Exalted, has undertaken to grant victory to His religion over its enemies. If they hasten with Him to go forth, victory is achieved through them; and if they hold back, victory comes through others, and they incur censure, so that they do not imagine that the defeat of the enemies of the religion and the honour of Islam can be achieved only through them. There is no indication in the text that this meaning is from them. A parallel to this is the Exalted's saying:

[p. 50]
﴿O you who have believed, whoever among you reverts from his religion, Allah will bring forth a people He loves and who love Him﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 54].

Then the exegetes differed. Ibn 'Abbas said: they are the Successors (al-tabi'un). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the sons of Persia. Abu Rawq said: they are the people of Yemen. These views are not an explanation of the verse, because the verse contains no indication of them. Rather, that unrestricted statement has been applied to a specific instance that they had witnessed. Al-Asamm said: its meaning is that He would bring him out from among you, that is, from Medina. Al-Qadi said: this is weak, because the wording contains no indication that he (peace be upon him) would be moved from Medina to another place; so it is not impossible that Allah would raise up in Medina peoples who would support him in the expedition, and it is not impossible that He would support him with groups of angels while he is there.

The third is His saying: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all.﴾ The pronoun in al-Hasan's view refers to Allah, the Exalted, meaning: you will not harm Allah, because He is independent of the worlds. According to the others, it refers to the Messenger, meaning: you will not harm the Messenger, because Allah has protected him from the people, and because He, the Exalted, will not abandon him if you are sluggish toward him.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is over all things competent.﴾ This is an alert to the severity of the warning, from the standpoint that the Exalted is capable, and inability is not possible for Him; so when He threatens with punishment, He carries it out.

* * *

The second issue: Al-Hasan and 'Ikrimah said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by His saying: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. The verifying scholars (al-muhaqqiqun) said: this verse is addressed to those whom the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) called to go forth but who did not go forth; and on this reading there is no abrogation. Al-Jubba'i said: this verse indicates the threat (wa'id) against the people of the prayer (ahl al-salah), since it explains that if the believers do not go forth, He will punish them with a painful punishment, which is the punishment of the Fire; for abandoning jihad is only from believers. Thus the view of the Murji'ah, that the people of the prayer have no threat against them, is refuted. And if the threat against them for abandoning jihad is established, then likewise for other things, since there is no one who makes a distinction. Know that we have discussed the issue of the threat at length in the commentary on surah al-Baqarah.

* * *

The third issue: Al-Qadi said: this verse indicates the obligation of jihad, whether with the Messenger or without him; for He, the Exalted, said: ﴿O you who have believed, what is wrong with you that when it is said to you, "Go forth"...﴾ and He did not specify that the one who speaks is the Messenger.

If they say: the purpose must be the Messenger, because of His saying: ﴿and will replace you with a people other than you﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39], and because of His saying: ﴿and you will not harm Him at all﴾ [al-Tawbah: 39], since the purpose of these can only be the Messenger.

We say: the specificity of the end of the verse does not prevent the generality of its beginning, as we have established in the principles of jurisprudence (usul al-fiqh).

[Page 51]

**His saying, exalted is He:**

﴿If you do not help him, Allah has already helped him when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two; when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed Allah is with us." So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with hosts you did not see, and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest. And Allah is Mighty and Wise.﴾

Know that this is a mention of another way of encouraging them to engage in jihad. That is because He, exalted is He, mentioned in the previous verse that if they do not go forth when He calls them to it, and do not busy themselves with supporting him, then Allah will support him. The evidence is that Allah supported him and strengthened him when he had with him only one man. So here, it is more fitting (that Allah supports him). There are several issues in the verse:

**The first issue:** One may ask: how can His saying ﴿then Allah has indeed helped him﴾ be the answer to the conditional clause?

Its answer is that the implied meaning is: "If you do not help him, then someone who helped him when he had with him only one man, and that is no less than one, will help him." The meaning is that He will help him now as He helped him at that time.

**The second issue:** His saying ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾ means: Allah helped him at the time when those who disbelieved expelled him from Makkah. His saying ﴿the second of two﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl), meaning: in the state in which he was ﴿the second of two﴾. The explanation of His saying ﴿the second of two﴾ has already been given in His saying ﴿the third of three﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 73]. The clarification is that when two are present, each of them is the second to the other among those two. For this reason, they said: "So-and-so is the second of two," meaning he is one of them. The author of al-Kashshaf (Kashshāf, the Qur'anic commentary of al-Zamakhshari) said: it is also read ﴿thāni ithnayn﴾ with a sukun (on the nūn), and ﴿when they were﴾ is a substitute for His saying ﴿when He expelled him﴾. The cave (al-ghār) is a large hole in a mountain. That mountain was called Thawr, on the right of Makkah at a distance of one hour's walk. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ remained in it with Abu Bakr for three nights. His saying ﴿when he said﴾ is a second substitute.

**The third issue:** They mentioned that Quraysh and the polytheists in Makkah conspired to kill the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. So Allah revealed ﴿and when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ [al-Anfal: 30]. Allah commanded him to leave, he and Abu Bakr, at the beginning of the night, for the cave. The meaning of His saying ﴿who expelled him﴾ is that they made him like one compelled to leave. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ and Abu Bakr left at the beginning of the night for the cave. He ordered ʿAli to lie down on his bed, so that the darkness would prevent them from seeking him, until he and his companion reached what Allah had commanded. When they arrived at the cave, Abu Bakr entered the cave first, searching for whatever was in it. The Prophet ﷺ said to him: "What is the matter with you?" He said: "My father and mother be sacrificed for you! The caves are the abode of beasts of prey and vermin. If there is anything in it, let it be upon me and not upon you." There was a hole in the cave, so he placed his heel over it, lest something come out that would harm the Messenger. When the polytheists tracked the trail and drew near, Abu Bakr wept out of fear for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. He, peace be upon him, said: "Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us." Abu Bakr said: "Is Allah truly with us?" The Messenger said: "Yes." So he began wiping the tears from his cheek.

It is related from al-Hasan that whenever he mentioned Abu Bakr's weeping, he would weep, and whenever he mentioned his wiping away the tears, he would wipe the tears from his own cheek.

It was also said: when the polytheists appeared above the cave, Abu Bakr became anxious for the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "If you are struck today, the religion of Allah will be lost." The Messenger of Allah said: "What do you think of two whose third is Allah?" It was also said: when he entered the cave, Abu Bakr placed a thumāmah (a plant) at the entrance of the cave. Allah sent two doves which laid eggs at its base, and a spider wove its web over it. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "O Allah, blind their sight." So they kept going around the cave and did not see anyone.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** This verse indicates the virtue of Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, in several respects:

**The first:** When he, peace be upon him, went to the cave, it was because he feared that the disbelievers would attempt to kill him. Had he not been certain of the inner state of Abu Bakr, that he was among the sincere, verifying believers, the truthful, the ṣiddīqīn, he would not have taken him as a companion in that place. For if it were permissible that his inner state was contrary to his outward state, he would have feared that he would reveal him to his enemies, and also that he would attempt to kill him. When he chose him for himself in that situation, this shows that the Prophet, peace be upon him, was certain that his inner state conformed to his outward state.

**The second:** The emigration (hijrah) was by the permission of Allah, exalted is He. There were in the service of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ a group of sincere people, and they were closer in lineage to the tree of the Messenger of Allah than Abu Bakr was. Had Allah not commanded him to take Abu Bakr as a companion in that difficult and terrifying event, it would have been apparent that he should not single him out for this companionship. Allah's singling him out for this honor indicates a high rank for him in religion.

**The third:** All others besides Abu Bakr had left the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. As for him, he did not precede the Messenger as the others did, but rather he remained patient in his companionship, his constant attendance, and his service in this extreme fear, when no one else remained with him. This necessitates a great merit.

**The fourth:** Allah named him ﴿the second of two﴾, making him the second of Muhammad, peace be upon him, while they were both in the cave. The scholars have established that he, may Allah be pleased with him, was the second of Muhammad in most religious ranks. When the Prophet ﷺ was sent to mankind and presented Islam to Abu Bakr, Abu Bakr believed. Then he went and presented Islam to Talhah, al-Zubayr, ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan, and a group of other distinguished Companions, may Allah be pleased with them all, and all of them believed at his hands. Then he brought them to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ after a few days. So he, may Allah be pleased with him, was ﴿the second of two﴾ in calling to Allah. Also, whenever the Messenger of Allah ﷺ stood in a battle, Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, stood in his service and did not leave him, so he was the second of two in his assembly. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ fell ill, he took his place in leading the people in prayer, so he was the second of two there as well. When he passed away, he was buried beside him, so he was the second of two there too.

Some foolish Rafidis (Rawāfiḍ, a Shiʿi sect) criticized this point and said: his being the second of two with the Messenger cannot be greater than Allah, exalted is He, being the fourth of every three in His saying: ﴿There is no secret conversation of three but that He is the fourth of them, nor of five but that He is the sixth of them﴾ [al-Mujadilah: 7]. Furthermore, this ruling is general regarding both the disbeliever and the believer. So if this meaning from Allah, exalted is He, does not indicate the virtue of a person, then it is even more so that it would not indicate the virtue of a person when it comes from the Prophet.

The answer: this is a cold and forced argument, because what is meant there is that He is with all by knowledge and governance, and that He is aware of the inner thoughts of everyone. As for here, what is meant by His saying, exalted is He, ﴿the second of two﴾ is singling him out with this attribute in a context of honor. Also, we have shown, through the three aspects mentioned earlier, that his being with him in this situation is a decisive proof that the Prophet ﷺ was certain that his inner state was like his outward state. So where is the one side in relation to the other?

**The fifth:** Among the arguments from this verse is what has come in the reports, that when Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, grieved, the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "What do you think of two whose third is Allah?" There is no doubt that this is a lofty station and an exalted rank.

Know that the Rawafid in religion, when they swore, used to say: "By the truth of the five, the sixth of whom is Gabriel," and they meant that the Messenger ﷺ, ʿAli, Fatimah, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn had gathered under a cloak on the day of mubahalah (the mutual invocation of curse), and Gabriel came and made himself the sixth of them. They mentioned this to the Shaykh and Imam, my father, may Allah have mercy on him, that the people say this, and he, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "You have something better than this in His saying: 'What do you think of two whose third is Allah?'" It is known necessarily that this is more excellent and more complete.

**The sixth:** He, exalted is He, described Abu Bakr as being a companion of the Messenger, and this indicates complete virtue. al-Husayn ibn Fudayl al-Bajali said: whoever denies that Abu Bakr was the companion of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ is a disbeliever, because the Muslim community is unanimous that what is meant by ﴿when he said to his companion﴾ is Abu Bakr, and this indicates that Allah, exalted is He, described him as being his companion. They objected and said: Allah, exalted is He, described the disbeliever as being a companion of the believer in His saying: ﴿His companion said to him while he was arguing with him﴾
[p. 52]
﴿Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust?﴾ [al-Kahf: 37].

The answer: although He described him there as being a companion to him in mention, He followed it with something that indicates humiliation and degradation, which is His saying: ﴿Do you disbelieve?﴾ As for here, after He described him as being his companion, He mentioned what indicates honor and exaltation, which is His saying: ﴿Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us.﴾ So what relation is there between the two situations, were it not for extreme enmity?

**The seventh:** Regarding the indication of this verse on the virtue of Abu Bakr: His saying ﴿Do not grieve, indeed Allah is with us.﴾ There is no doubt that what is meant by this being-with is being-with through protection, support, guarding, and assistance. In sum, the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, shared with Abu Bakr this being-with. If they interpret this being-with in a corrupt way, it necessarily follows that they must include the Messenger in it. And if they interpret it in a noble and exalted sense, it necessarily follows that they must include Abu Bakr in it. To put it another way: the verse indicates that Allah was with Abu Bakr, and everyone with whom Allah is, is among the God-fearing and the good-doers, due to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is with those who are mindful of Him and those who are doers of good﴾ [al-Nahl: 128]. What is meant by it is restriction (ḥaṣr), and the meaning is: Allah is with those who are mindful of Him, and not with others. This indicates that Abu Bakr is among the God-fearing and the good-doers.

**The eighth:** In establishing this claim: His saying ﴿Indeed Allah is with us﴾ indicates that he was ﴿the second of two﴾ in the nobility resulting from this being-with, just as he was ﴿the second of two when they were in the cave.﴾ This is a station of utmost nobility.

**The ninth:** His saying ﴿Do not grieve﴾ is a prohibition against grief absolutely, and a prohibition necessitates permanence and repetition. This requires that Abu Bakr should absolutely not grieve after that event, before death, at death, and after death.

**The tenth:** His saying ﴿then Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾. As for the one who said that the pronoun in His saying ﴿upon him﴾ refers to the Messenger, this is false for several reasons:

**The first reason:** A pronoun must refer to the nearest of the preceding referents. The nearest of the preceding referents in this verse is Abu Bakr, because He, exalted is He, said: ﴿when he said to his companion﴾. The implied meaning is: when Muhammad said to his companion Abu Bakr: "Do not grieve." According to this implication, the nearest of the preceding referents is Abu Bakr, so the pronoun must refer to him.

**The second reason:** Grief and fear were present in Abu Bakr, not in the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, for he, peace be upon him, was secure and his heart was calm, due to what Allah had promised him, that He would help him against Quraysh. So when he said to Abu Bakr, "Do not grieve," he became secure. Thus, the tranquility was directed to Abu Bakr so that this would become a cause for removing his fear, which is more fitting than directing it to the Messenger ﷺ, given that before that he had been calm of heart and strong of soul.

**The third aspect:** If the intended meaning of "sending down tranquility" were that it was sent down upon the Messenger, then it would have to be said that the Messenger had been afraid before that. And if that were the case, he could not have said to Abu Bakr, ﴿Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us﴾. For how can one who is afraid remove fear from the heart of another? And if the matter were as they claim, it would have to be said: "So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him, and he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve.'" Since that is not the case, but rather Allah first mentions that he (upon him be blessings and peace) said to his companion, "Do not grieve," and then mentions with the particle of sequence (*fa*) the sending down of tranquility, which is His saying, ﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, we know that the sending down of this tranquility was preceded by the presence of tranquility in the heart of the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace). And if the matter is so, then this tranquility must have been sent down

[Page 54]

upon the heart of Abu Bakr.

**If it is said:** It must be that His saying, ﴿So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾, means that He sent down His tranquility upon the heart of the Messenger. The evidence for this is that He conjoined to it His saying, ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾, and this applies only to the Messenger. And the conjoined element must share in what it is conjoined to. So since this conjoined element refers to the Messenger, the element it is conjoined to must also refer to the Messenger.

**We say:** This is weak, because His saying, ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾, refers to the story of Badr, and it is conjoined to His saying, ﴿Allah had already given him victory﴾. The sense of the verse is: "If you do not support him, Allah had already given him victory in the event of the cave, when he said to his companion, 'Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us.' So Allah sent down His tranquility upon him and supported him with hosts you did not see at the event of Badr." If that is the case, then this objection falls away.

**The eleventh aspect:** Among the aspects indicating the virtue of Abu Bakr from this verse is the consensus of all that Abu Bakr is the one who bought the mount (*rahilah*) for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Abi Bakr and Asma' bint Abi Bakr are the two who used to bring them food. It has been related that he (upon him be blessings and peace) said: "I and my companion were in the cave for some ten days, and we had no food except dates." And they mention that Gabriel came to him while he was hungry and said: "This is Asma', who has come with *hays* (a mixture of dates, butter and cheese)." So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) rejoiced at this and informed Abu Bakr of it. When Allah commanded His Messenger to leave for Medina, he revealed this to Abu Bakr, and he ordered his son ʿAbd al-Rahman to buy two camels, two saddles and two sets of covering, and to set aside one of them for the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace). When they drew near to Medina, the news reached the Ansar, and they went out hastening. Abu Bakr feared that they would not recognize the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace), so he put his own garment on the Messenger of Allah so that they would know that the Messenger was the one. When they approached, they fell prostrate before him, and he said to them: "Prostrate to your Lord, and honor your brother." Then his she-camel knelt at the door of Abu Ayyub. We have related these narrations from the *Tafsir* (commentary) of Abu Bakr al-Asamm.

**The twelfth aspect:** When the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) entered Medina, no one was with him except Abu Bakr, and the Ansar saw no one with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) except Abu Bakr. This indicates that he (ﷺ) would choose him for himself from among his companions, in travel and at home. Our companions (the Ash'arites) went further than this and said: Since no one was present with him on that journey except Abu Bakr, if we suppose that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) had died on that journey, it would follow that no one would have taken charge of his affair except Abu Bakr, that no one would have been his executor over his community except Abu Bakr, and that no one would have conveyed to his community the revelation and the Qur'anic descent that occurred on that road except Abu Bakr. All of this indicates the lofty virtues and high ranks of Abu Bakr.

**Know that** the Rafidah (Shiʿa who reject the first caliphs) have argued from this verse and this event to impugn Abu Bakr, with weak and contemptible arguments, comparable to trying to hide the sun with a handful of mud:

The first: They said: "He (upon him be blessings and peace) said to Abu Bakr, 'Do not grieve.'" If that grief was right, how could the Messenger (upon him be blessings and peace) forbid it? And if it was wrong, it would follow that Abu Bakr was sinful and disobedient in that grief.

The second: They said, it may be said that he (ﷺ) singled him out for himself, because he feared that if he left him in Mecca, he might guide the disbelievers to him and inform them of his secrets and meanings. So he took him with himself to ward off this evil.

The third: That even if this situation indicates the virtue of Abu Bakr, he (ﷺ) ordered ʿAli to lie down on his bed. It is known that lying down on the bed of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) on such a dark night, while the disbelievers intended to kill the Messenger of Allah, exposes one's self to ransom (death). So this action by ʿAli is higher and greater than Abu Bakr being the companion of the Messenger. This is the sum of what they have mentioned on that subject.

**As for the answer to the first:** When Abu ʿAli al-Jubba'i related that doubt from them, he said: It must be said to them that in His saying, may He be exalted, to Moses (peace be upon him), ﴿Do not fear; indeed, you are the superior﴾ [Taha: 68], it would have to indicate that he was disobedient in his fear, and that would be a slander upon the prophets. And similarly in His saying about Abraham, when the angels said to him, ﴿Do not fear﴾, in the story of the roasted calf, and in their saying to Lot, ﴿Do not fear, nor grieve; indeed, we will save you and your family﴾ [al-ʿAnkabut: 33].

If they say that this fear arose only from human nature, and that Allah mentioned it in His saying, ﴿Do not fear﴾, to convey security and tranquility of heart, we say to them, in this matter, the same applies.

If they say: Did He not say, ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 67]? Then how did he fear despite hearing this verse? We say: This verse was revealed in Medina, and this event preceded its revelation. Furthermore, grant that he was safe from being killed, yet he was not safe from being beaten, wounded, and subjected to severe pain. And it is strange regarding them: if we supposed that Abu Bakr had not been afraid, they would have said that he rejoiced at the Messenger falling into trouble; and when he feared and wept, they raised this feeble question. This indicates that they do not seek the truth, but their aim is pure slander!

**As for the answer to the second:** What they have said is more base than the doubts of the Sophists. For if Abu Bakr had intended that, he would have shouted to the disbelievers when they reached the mouth of the cave and said to them, "We are here!" And his son ʿAbd al-Rahman and his daughter Asma' would have said to the disbelievers, "We know where Muhammad is, and we will show you him!" So we ask Allah for protection from a partisanship that drives a person to such a feeble statement.

**As for the answer to the third, there are several aspects:**

The first: We do not deny that the lying down of ʿAli ibn Abi Talib on the bed of the Messenger of Allah on that dark night was a great obedience and a high station. But we maintain that Abu Bakr, by his companionship, was present in the service of the Messenger (ﷺ), while ʿAli was absent, and the one present is higher in rank than the one absent.

The second: ʿAli bore the trial only on that night. After that, when they realized that Muhammad had departed, they left him and did not molest him. As for Abu Bakr, because he was with Muhammad (upon him be blessings and peace) for three days in the cave, he was in the most severe circumstances of trial, so his affliction was greater.

The third: Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) was well known among the people as one who encouraged people to the religion of Muhammad (upon him be blessings and peace) and called them to it. They witnessed that he invited a group of the senior Companions (may Allah be pleased with them) to that religion, and that they accepted that religion through his call. He used to oppose the disbelievers to the extent possible, and he used to defend the Messenger (ﷺ) with his self and his wealth. As for ʿAli ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him), he was young in age at that time, and no call or proof appeared from him, nor jihad with the sword and spear, because his fighting against the disbelievers appeared only a long time after they had migrated to Medina. So at the time of the Hijrah, no such state of his had appeared. Given this, the anger of the disbelievers toward Abu Bakr was undoubtedly greater than their anger toward ʿAli. And for this reason, when they realized that the one lying on that bed was ʿAli, they did not molest him at all, nor intended to strike him or harm him. So we know that Abu Bakr's fear for his own self in serving Muhammad (ﷺ) was greater than the fear of ʿAli (may Allah ennoble his face). Thus that rank was greater and more complete. This is what we say on this subject, in brief.

**As for His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾:** Know that the sense of the verse is that it is said, ﴿If you do not support him﴾, so he must be supported by two instances as evidence.

The first instance: He had already given him victory in the event of the Hijrah, ﴿when those who disbelieved expelled him, the second of two, when they were in the cave, when he said to his companion, "Do not grieve; indeed, Allah is with us," so Allah sent down His tranquility upon him﴾.

The second instance: The event of Badr, which is what is meant by His saying, ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾, because He sent down the angels on the day of Badr and supported His Messenger (ﷺ) with them. So His saying, ﴿and supported him with hosts you did not see﴾, is conjoined to His saying, ﴿Allah had already given him victory when those who disbelieved expelled him﴾.

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿and made the word of those who disbelieved the lowest, while the word of Allah is the highest﴾. The meaning is that on the day of Badr He made the word of polytheism low, base and contemptible, while the word of Allah is the highest, which is His saying, "There is no god but Allah." Al-Wahidi said: The preferred reading in His saying, ﴿and the word of Allah﴾, is the nominative (*raf*), and it is the reading of the majority, as a new sentence. Al-Farra' said: It is permissible to read *kalimata Allah* in the accusative, but I do not like this reading, because if it were in the accusative, the better form would be "and the word of Allah is the highest," as you say, "Your father freed his slave," and you do not say, "Your father freed his slave"... [a grammatical example of word order].

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is Mighty, Wise﴾, that is, Dominant and Victorious, who does nothing but what is right.

[Page 57]

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Go forth, whether light or heavy, and strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of Allah. That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, threatened those who do not go forth with the Messenger, and gave them the examples we have described, He followed this with a firm command, saying: ﴿Go forth, light or heavy.﴾ The meaning is: go forth whether you are in the state in which jihad is light for you or the state in which it is burdensome. This description includes many categories, which the exegetes (mufassirun) have mentioned:

The first: ﴿light﴾ in going forth, due to your eagerness for it, and ﴿heavy﴾ in going forth, due to its hardship upon you.

The second: ﴿light﴾ because your dependants are few, and ﴿heavy﴾ because they are many.

The third: ﴿light﴾ in terms of weapons, and ﴿heavy﴾ in terms of them.

The fourth: riding and on foot.

The fifth: young and old.

The sixth: lean and fat.

The seventh: healthy and sick. The correct view is what we have mentioned, since all of these are included in it, because the stated description is a universal description which includes all these particulars.

If it is said: Do you claim that this command encompasses all people, including the sick and the infirm?

We say: Its apparent meaning requires that. It is narrated from Ibn Umm Maktum that he said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Is it incumbent upon me to go forth?" He said: "You are none but light or heavy." So he returned to his family, put on his weapons, and stood before him. Then the words of Allah, the Exalted, were revealed: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ [An-Nur: 61].

Mujahid said: Abu Ayyub witnessed Badr with the Messenger (ﷺ), and he did not stay behind from the campaigns of the Muslims. He used to say: "Allah has said: ﴿Go forth, light or heavy.﴾ So I do not find myself except light or heavy."

It is narrated from Safwan ibn Amr that he said: "I was governor of Hims, and I met an old man, from the people of Damascus, whose eyebrows had fallen, on his mount, intending to go on a raid. I said: 'O uncle, you are excused before Allah.' He raised his eyebrows and said: 'O son of my brother, Allah has called us to go forth, light or heavy. Indeed, whoever He loves, He tests.'"

And it is narrated from al-Zuhri: Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab went out to a raid while one of his eyes had been lost. It was said to him: "You are sick, one who has a disability." He said: "Allah has called forth the light and the heavy. If I am unable to fight, I will increase the numbers and guard the baggage."

It was said to al-Miqdad ibn al-Aswad, while he was intending to go on a raid: "You are excused." He said: "Allah revealed to us in Surat Bara'a (at-Tawba): ﴿Go forth, light or heavy.﴾"

Know that those who hold this view which we have established say that this verse has been abrogated by the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾. 'Ata al-Khurasani said: It has been abrogated by His words: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [At-Tawba: 122].

One may say: They agreed that this verse was revealed concerning the campaign of Tabuk. They also agreed that he (peace be upon him) left behind the women and left behind some men. This indicates that this obligation is not an individual obligation (fard al-ayn) but a communal obligation (fard al-kifaya). Thus whoever the Messenger commanded to go forth is obligated to do so, light or heavy; and whoever he commanded to remain there is obligated to remain and to forgo going forth. Under this interpretation, there is no need to accept abrogation (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by a later revelation).

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿and strive with your wealth and your selves in the way of Allah﴾. In this there are two views:

The first view: This indicates that jihad is only obligatory upon the one who has wealth and self. Thus it shows that whoever does not have a sound self fit for jihad, nor wealth with which to strengthen himself to acquire the equipment of jihad, is not obligated to perform jihad.

The second view: Jihad is obligatory with the self when one is alone and capable of it, and with wealth when one is too weak to fight in person. It follows from this view that whoever is unable to send a group in his place with expenses from himself is a mujahid with his wealth, since it is impossible for him to do so with his person. Many scholars have adopted this view.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿That is better for you, if you only knew.﴾

If it is said: How is it correct to say that jihad is better than abstaining from it, when there is no good in abstaining from it?

We say: The answer to this is from two aspects:

The first aspect: The word ﴿better (khayr)﴾ is used in two senses:

One of them: in the sense of "this is better than that."

The second: in the sense that it is good in itself, as in His words: ﴿Indeed, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me﴾ [Al-Qasas: 24], and His words: ﴿And indeed, he is intensely attached to wealth (khayr)﴾ [Al-Adiyat: 8]. It is said: "Thareed is better (khayr) from Allah," meaning it is good in itself, and it has come from Allah, the Exalted. So His words ﴿That is better for you﴾ mean the second sense. In this aspect the question falls away.

The second aspect: Even if we grant that the intended meaning is that it is better than other things, the sense is that what is gained through jihad of the bliss of the Hereafter is better than what the one who sits out gains of ease, comfort, and enjoyment of them. This is why He said: ﴿if you only knew.﴾

[Page 58]

Because the good that is attained in the Hereafter through jihad cannot be perceived except through reflection, and it is only recognised by the believer who has come to know through proof that the claim of the Resurrection is true, and that the claim of reward and punishment is true and veracious.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 42:

God Most High said: ﴿Had it been a near gain and a short journey, they would have followed you. But the distance seemed long to them. They will swear by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you," destroying themselves, and God knows that they are indeed liars.﴾

Know that when God Most High had pressed them strongly to strive in the cause of God, and He had mentioned His words: ﴿O you who believe, what is wrong with you that when you are told to go forth in the cause of God, you cling heavily to the earth?﴾ [al-Tawbah: 38], He returned to establishing that they were reluctant. He showed that some people, despite all the preceding threats and exhortations to jihad, stayed behind during the expedition to Tabuk. He showed that ﴿had it been a near gain and a short journey, they would have followed you.﴾ There are several issues in this verse:

The first issue: al-'Arad (worldly gain) is whatever benefit of this world presents itself to you. It is said: "The world is a present 'arad, from which the righteous and the wicked both eat." al-Zajjaj said: there is an omitted element here. The meaning is: "Had the thing called to been a short journey," so the subject of kana (was) is omitted because what precedes it indicates it. As for His words ﴿and a short journey﴾, al-Zajjaj said: that is, an easy, near one. Such a thing is called qasid (moderate, direct) because whoever is midway between excess and deficiency is called muqtasid (moderate). God said: ﴿Among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate﴾ [Fatir: 32]. The underlying point is that what is midway between abundance and scarcity is aimed at by everyone, so it is called qasid. The explanation of qasid is dhu qasd (one with an aim), like their saying labin (having milk), tamir (having dates), and rabih (having profit).

As for His words: ﴿But the distance seemed long to them (bu'udat 'alayhimu al-shuqqah)﴾, al-Layth said: al-shuqqah is the distance of the journey to a far land. It is said: shuqqah shaqqah (a hard, distant journey). The meaning is: the hard, distant journey seemed long to them. The reason for this name is that it is hard for a person to travel it. The author of al-Kashshaf (a Qur'an commentary by al-Zamakhshari) reported from Isa ibn Umar that he read bu'udat 'alayhimu al-shuqqah with a kasra on the 'ayn and the shin.

The second issue: This verse was revealed about the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition to Tabuk. The meaning of the statement is: had the gains been near and the journey short, they would have followed you, out of greed for winning those gains. But the journey was long, so they were like those who despaired of winning the spoils, because they considered fighting the Romans a great matter. For this reason they stayed behind. Then God Most High informed that when he returns from the jihad, he will find them ﴿swearing by God, "Had we been able, we would have gone out with you,"﴾ either when he rebukes them for staying behind or initially, as a way of offering an excuse for staying behind. Then God Most High explained that they destroy themselves by this lying and hypocrisy. This indicates that false oaths bring about destruction. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "The yamin al-ghamus (a false oath that plunges its swearer into sin) leaves dwellings desolate."

Then He said: ﴿and God knows that they are indeed liars﴾ in their saying, "We were not able to go out," for they were able to go out.

The third issue: The verse indicates that His words ﴿Go forth, light and heavy﴾ apply only to one who is capable and able, since lack of capability is an excuse for staying behind.

* * *

[Page 59]

The fourth issue: Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i used this verse to refute the view that capability (al-istita'ah) exists together with the act. He said: If capability existed together with the act, then whoever goes out to fight would not have been capable of fighting. If that were so, they would have been truthful in their saying, "We were not able to do that." But since God contradicted them in this statement, we know that capability exists before the act. al-Ka'bi also used this line of argument, and he asked himself: Could it be that what is meant is: they had no provisions and no mount, and they did not mean capability itself?
He answered: If one who has no mount is excused from not going out, then one who has no capability is more deserving of excuse. Furthermore, the apparent meaning of capability is physical strength, not the existence of wealth. And if wealth is meant, it is meant because it helps a person with what he does through bodily strength. So there is no point in abandoning the literal meaning without necessity.

Our companions (the Ash'aris) replied: The Mu'tazilah (a rationalist school) conceded that the capacity to act does not precede the act except by a single moment of time. But that it should precede it by many moments is impossible. A person sitting in a place is not capable, at this time, of doing an act in a place far from him. Rather, he is only capable of doing an act in the place adjacent to his own place. Since it is established that, according to them, capacity does not precede the act except by one moment of time, then the people who stayed behind from the Messenger of God (ﷺ) were not capable according to the principles of the Mu'tazilah. Thus what they have imposed on us is binding on them from this verse. At this point, it is obligatory for us and for them to interpret capability as provisions and a mount, and then the argument falls away.

The fifth issue: They said: The Messenger (ﷺ) informed about them that they would swear. This is an announcement of the unseen that occurs in the future. When the matter happened as he had informed, this was an announcement of the unseen, and so it was a miracle. And God knows best.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 43:**

God says: ﴿May God pardon you. Why did you give them permission, until it became clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars?﴾

Know that by His saying ﴿Had it been an easy gain and a short journey, they would have followed you﴾, God made clear that a group stayed behind from that expedition. However, it does not make clear whether that staying behind was with the Messenger's permission or not. When He then said, ﴿May God pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾, this indicates that among them were those who stayed behind with his permission. On this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Some have used this verse to argue for the occurrence of a sin from the Messenger, on two grounds:

The first: He, exalted is He, said ﴿May God pardon you﴾, and pardon presupposes a prior sin.

The second: He, exalted is He, said ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾, and this is a question with the meaning of disapproval. This indicates that that permission was a disobedience and a sin.

Qatadah and Amr ibn Maymun said: "There are two things the Messenger did for which he was not commanded in either: his permission to the hypocrites, and his taking ransom from the captives. So God rebuked him, as you hear."

The answer to the first: We do not concede that His saying ﴿May God pardon you﴾ necessitates a sin. Why could it not be said that this indicates God's emphasis on honoring and reverencing him, just as a man says to someone else whom he holds in high esteem: "May God pardon you for what you did regarding my affair? May God be pleased with you. What is your answer to my speech? May God grant you well-being; you did not recognize my right!" His purpose in such speech is nothing but increased honor and veneration. ʿAli ibn al-Jahm said, addressing al-Mutawakkil when he had ordered his banishment:

May God pardon you. Is there no claim that would return me, by your pardon, from being exiled?

Have you not seen a servant who overstepped his bounds, and a master who pardoned, and a rightly guided one who guided?

Release me, release you, He who has never ceased, who protects you and turns away destruction from you.

The answer to the second: We say: it is not permissible to say that the intended meaning of ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ is disapproval. For we say: either a sin proceeded from the Messenger in this incident, or no sin proceeded from him. If we say that no sin proceeded from him, then on this assumption it is impossible for ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ to be a rebuke directed at him. And if we say that a sin had proceeded from him, then ﴿May God pardon you﴾ indicates that pardon was granted to him, and after pardon has been granted it is impossible for disapproval to be directed at him. Thus it is established that on all assumptions it is impossible to say that ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ indicates that the Messenger was sinful. This is a conclusive and sufficient answer. In light of this, ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ is understood as leaving what is preferable and more complete, especially since this incident was of the kind that concerns wars and worldly interests.

* * *

**The second issue:** Some people said: The Messenger, peace be upon him, used to judge by means of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning) in some incidents. They argued for this by saying that His saying ﴿So take warning, O people of insight﴾ [al-Hashr: 2] is a command to people of insight to take warning and to exercise ijtihad, and the Messenger was their master, so he was included in this command. Then they reinforced this with this verse, saying: Either it is said that God permitted him to give that permission, or He forbade him from it, or He neither permitted him nor forbade him. The first is invalid, since otherwise it would be impossible to say to him: "Why did you give them permission?" The second is also invalid, because on this assumption it would follow that he judged by other than what God had revealed, and so he would fall under His saying ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has revealed, those are the disbelievers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 44], ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 45], and ﴿those are the defiantly disobedient﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 47]. This is invalid by plain statement. Therefore only the third possibility remains: that he, peace be upon him, gave that permission in that incident of his own accord. Either this was based on ijtihad or it was not. The second is invalid, because it would be a judgment by mere whim, and that is invalid by His saying ﴿Then there succeeded them successors who neglected prayer and followed desires﴾ [Maryam: 59]. So there remains only that he, peace be upon him, gave permission in that incident on the basis of ijtihad, and this indicates that he, peace be upon him, used to judge by means of ijtihad.

If it is said: Then this would more fittingly indicate that it is not permissible for him to judge by ijtihad, since God forbade him from this judgment by His saying ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾.

We say: God did not forbid him from that permission absolutely, for He said ﴿until it became clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars﴾, and a judgment limited to a goal by the word ḥattā (until) must cease upon the attainment of that goal. This indicates the soundness of our position.

If they say: Why could it not be that the intended meaning of that clarification is clarification by way of revelation?

We say: What you have mentioned is possible, but on the assumption you have mentioned, his obligation becomes that he must not judge at all, and must be patient until revelation descends and the text becomes manifest. When he abandoned that, it would be a grave sin. But on the assumption we have mentioned, that error would be an error occurring in ijtihad, and so it falls under His, peace be upon him, saying: "Whoever exercises ijtihad and errs has one reward." Therefore interpreting the speech in this way is more fitting.

* * *

**The third issue:** This verse indicates the obligation of guarding against haste, the obligation of deliberation and patience, and avoiding being deceived by outward appearances, and of thorough investigation, so that one can treat each party according to what it deserves of closeness or distance.

**The fourth issue:** Qatadah said: God rebuked him, as you hear in this verse, then He granted him leniency in Surat al-Nur, saying: ﴿So when they ask your permission for some of their affairs, give permission to whom you will of them﴾ [al-Nur: 62].

**The fifth issue:** Abu Muslim al-Isfahani said: His saying ﴿Why did you give them permission?﴾ contains nothing that indicates what that permission was for. So it is possible that some of them asked permission to remain behind and he granted it, and it is possible that some of them asked permission to go out and he granted it, even though their going out with him was not proper, because they were spies for the hypocrites against the Muslims, stirring up strife and seeking calamities. For this reason there was no benefit in their going out with the Messenger.

The Qadi said: This is far-fetched, because this verse was revealed concerning the Battle of Tabuk, in the form of blame for those who stayed behind and praise for those who hastened forth. Also, what follows this verse indicates the blaming of those who sat back and the explanation of their condition.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 44–46 (part 1 of 2):

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive with their wealth and their selves. God knows well the God-fearing.﴾ ﴿It is only those who do not believe in God and the Last Day, whose hearts are in doubt, who ask your permission. They are hesitating in their doubt.﴾ ﴿Had they wished to go out, they would have made ready some preparation for it. But God disliked their setting out, so He held them back, and it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn 'Abbas said that His words ﴿do not ask your permission﴾ refer to the period after the expedition of Tabuk. The others said: this is not permissible, because what comes before this verse and what comes after it were revealed concerning the story of Tabuk, and the purpose of this discourse is to distinguish the believers from the hypocrites. For the believers, when they are commanded to go out to jihad, hasten to it and do not hesitate, whereas the hypocrites hesitate, become sluggish, and bring excuses and pretexts. This purpose is achieved whether it is expressed in the form of the present tense or the past tense. The point is that He, exalted is He, made asking for permission in that situation the sign of hypocrisy, and God knows best.

The second issue: His words ﴿those who believe in God and the Last Day do not ask your permission to strive﴾ contain an elided element, and the implied meaning is "in respect of striving." However, the elision is acceptable because it is evident. Here there are two opinions:

The first opinion: this statement is to be taken at face value without any further implied element. On this reading, the meaning is that it is not the habit of believers to ask your permission to strive. The senior figures among the Emigrants (muhajirun) and the Helpers (ansar) used to say: "We do not ask the Prophet ﷺ for permission to fight, for our Lord has urged us to it again and again, so what is the benefit of asking permission?" They were such that if the Messenger had ordered them to stay behind, it would have been hard for them. Do you not see that when 'Ali ibn Abi Talib was ordered by the Messenger of God ﷺ to remain in Medina, it was hard for him, and he was not content until the Messenger said to him: "You stand to me in the same position as Harun stood to Musa"?

The second opinion: there must necessarily be another implied element here. They said: because leaving off seeking the permission of the Imam for jihad is not permissible, and God censured these people for leaving off this seeking of permission, it is established that an implied element is necessary. The sense is: "These people do not ask your permission not to strive." The negative particle has been omitted, and a parallel is His words: ﴿God makes clear to you so that you do not go astray﴾ [An-Nisa: 176]. What indicates this omitted element is that what comes before the verse and what comes after it shows that the censure arose specifically from asking permission to remain behind, and God knows best.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿It is only those who do not believe in God and the Last Day, whose hearts are in doubt, who ask your permission. They are hesitating in their doubt.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: He clarified that this departure (from the duty of striving) does not happen except when there is no faith in God and the Last Day. Then, since the absence of faith may be caused by doubt about it, or may be caused by a firm and definite conviction of its absence, God, exalted is He, clarified that the absence of faith in these people was caused by doubt and uncertainty, and this indicates that the one who doubts and is uncertain is not a believer in God. Here there are two questions:

The first question: if knowledge is inferential (istidlali), then the occurrence of doubt about the evidence entails the occurrence of doubt about what the evidence establishes, and the occurrence of doubt about a single premise among the premises of an argument is sufficient for doubt about the soundness of the argument. This implies that a believer, whenever a question or difficulty occurs to him concerning one of the premises of his argument, would become doubtful about what is established by it, and this would imply that the believer leaves his faith at every moment, because a question or difficulty has come to his mind. It is known that this is false. Therefore it is established that the foundation of faith is not on argument but on taqlid (unquestioning acceptance of authority). Thus this verse indicates that the origin of faith is taqlid in this respect.

The answer: although the Muslim may be struck by doubt concerning the soundness of some premises of a single argument, all the other proofs remain free from criticism in his view. For this reason his faith always remains steady and continuous.

The second question: Do not your companions say, "We are believers, God willing"? That implies the occurrence of doubt.

The answer: We have thoroughly investigated this question in the commentary on His words in surah al-Anfal: ﴿Those are the true believers﴾ [Al-Anfal: 74].

The second issue: The Karramiyya said: faith is nothing but mere verbal affirmation, although He, exalted is He, testified against them in this verse that they are not believers.

The third issue: His words ﴿and their hearts are in doubt﴾ indicate that the locus of doubt is the heart alone. And when the locus of doubt is the heart, the locus of knowledge and faith is also the heart, because the locus of one of two opposites must be the locus of the other opposite. For this reason He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those, He has inscribed faith in their hearts﴾ [Al-Mujadila: 22]. And when the locus of knowledge and disbelief is the heart, then in reality it is the heart that is rewarded or punished, and the other parts follow it.

The fourth issue: His words ﴿so they remain hesitating in their doubt﴾ mean that the doubter who is uncertain remains wavering between negation and affirmation, not judging for either of the two parts and not firmly committed to either of two contradictories. Its explanation: belief is either firm or not firm. If it is firm and does not correspond to reality, it is ignorance (jahl). If it corresponds to reality and is based on certainty, it is knowledge ('ilm); otherwise it is the belief of the one who practises taqlid. If it is not firm, then if one of the two sides is preponderant, the preponderant side is conjecture (zann) and the outweighed side is illusion (wahm). If the two sides are equal, it is doubt (rayb) and uncertainty (shakk), and in that case the person remains hesitating between the two sides.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Had they wished to go out, they would have made ready some preparation for it.﴾ It is read ''uddatahu'' (with a definite object), and it is also read ''iddatan'' with the vowel of the 'ayn being i, without an annexation and with an annexation. Ibn 'Abbas said: he means provisions, water, and a mount, because their journey was long and in a difficult season, and their not making ready preparation is evidence that they intended to stay behind. Others said: this is an indication that they were well-off and able to obtain the equipment and provisions.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But God disliked their setting out, so He held them back.﴾ On this there are several issues:

The first issue: al-inba'ath means setting out to do something. It is said: "I made the camel rise, and it rose"; "I sent it for such a matter, and it set out"; and "He dispatched him on such a matter," meaning he carried it out. And al-tathbit means turning a person back from the action he had resolved upon. The meaning is that He, exalted is He, disliked their going out with the Messenger ﷺ, so He turned them away from it.

If it is said: their going out with the Messenger must either be considered a corruption (mafsadah) or a benefit (maslahah). If we say it was a corruption, why did He rebuke the Messenger for permitting them to remain behind? And if we say it was a benefit, why did He say that He disliked their setting out and going out?

The correct answer: their going out with the Messenger was not a benefit, as is shown by His explicitly stating after this verse and explaining those corruptions: ﴿Had they gone out with you, they would only have added to you nothing but confusion﴾ [At-Tawba: 47]. The remaining question is: since the more correct and beneficial course was that they should not go out, why did He rebuke the Messenger for granting permission? We say: we have reported from Abu Muslim that he said: there is no indication in His words "Why did you grant them permission?" that the Prophet, peace be upon him, had granted them permission to remain behind. Rather, it is possible to say that they asked him for permission to go out with him, and he granted them permission. On this reading the objection falls away. Abu Muslim said: the evidence for the correctness of what we have said is that this verse indicates that their going out with him would have been a corruption, so that rebuke must be understood as meaning that he, peace be upon him, granted them permission to go out with him. This is confirmed by other verses, among them His words: ﴿If God brings you back to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, ever."﴾ [At-Tawba: 83]. And among them His words: ﴿Those who stayed behind will say, when you set out for the spoils…﴾ [Al-Fath: 15] up to His words: ﴿Say: "You will never follow us."﴾ This is the answer to this objection according to the method of Abu Muslim.

The second answer: we grant that the rebuke in His words ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾ was indeed directed at him, because he, peace be upon him, granted them permission to remain behind. We say: that rebuke was not because remaining behind was a corruption, but because his granting them permission, peace be upon him, to remain behind was a corruption. Its explanation comes in several respects:

The first: he, peace be upon him, granted permission before completing the examination and before fully reflecting and pondering. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why did you grant them permission until it had become clear to you who were truthful and you knew the liars?﴾

The second: even if he, peace be upon him, had not granted them permission to remain behind, they would have remained behind on their own initiative, and that staying behind would have become a sign of their hypocrisy. When their hypocrisy became evident, the Muslims would have guarded against them and would not have been deceived by their words. But when the Messenger granted permission to remain behind, their hypocrisy remained hidden, and those benefits were lost.

The third: when they asked permission of the Messenger of God ﷺ, he became angry with them and said, as a rebuke: ﴿Sit with those who sit,﴾ as God related at the end of this verse, namely His words: ﴿And it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ Then they seized upon this expression and said: "He has granted us permission." So He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Why did you grant them permission?﴾ meaning: why did you mention to them this expression which enabled them to use it as a means of achieving their aim?

The fourth: those who say that ijtihad (independent juristic reasoning) is not permissible for the prophets, peace be upon them, said: he granted permission only on the basis of ijtihad, and that is not permissible, because when they had access to revelation, acting on ijtihad while having access to revelation is like acting on ijtihad when there is an explicit text. Just as that is impermissible, so is this.

The second issue: the Mu'tazila of Basra (al-Mu'tazila al-Basriyya) said: the verse indicates that He, exalted is He, is described by the attribute of will (muridiyya) and also by the attribute of aversion (karahiyya), as is shown by His words: ﴿But God disliked their setting out.﴾ Our companions said: the meaning of ''God disliked'' is that He willed the absence of that thing. The Basrans said: absence cannot be the object of a relation, because will is an attribute that requires the preponderance of one of the two possibilities over the other, and absence is pure negation. Moreover, a continuous absence cannot be the object of will, because making what already exists come into being again is impossible, and making absence into absence is impossible. Thus it is established that the relation of will to absence is impossible, so it is impermissible to say that what is meant by aversion is the willing of absence.

Our companions replied: we interpret aversion with respect to God as the willing of the opposite of that thing. Thus He, exalted is He, willed that they remain still, and the expression of this will was made by saying that He, exalted is He, disliked their going out with the Messenger.

The third issue: our companions argued on the question of divine decree and predestination (al-qada' wa'l-qadar) from His words: ﴿so He held them back﴾, meaning: He made them sluggish and weakened their desire to set out. The summary of the discussion on this point cannot be complete unless we state the truth clearly: the occurrence of an act depends on the arising of the motive for it. When the motive becomes weak and outweighed, the act cannot proceed from it. Then, whether the motive becomes firm or weak is either from the servant, which would lead to an infinite regress (tasalsul), or from God, in which case the intended conclusion follows, because strengthening the motive comes only from God. When that strengthening occurs, the act must follow, and in that case our statement on the question of divine decree and predestination is valid. Then He, exalted is He, concluded the verse with His words: ﴿And it was said: "Sit with those who sit."﴾ On this there are two issues:

Issue 1: The purpose of this statement is to alert to their blame and to associate them with women, children, and the infirm, whose custom is sitting in their homes. They are the ones who sit back and the ones who remain behind (al-khalifun wa'l-khawalif), as He mentioned in His saying: ﴿They were content to be with those who remain behind﴾ [al-Tawbah: 87].

Issue 2: Scholars differed over who said this statement. It is possible that the speaker was Satan, by way of whispering (waswasah). It is possible that some of them said it to others when they wanted to gather together in staying behind, because whoever undertakes corruption loves to multiply its kinds. It is possible that the speaker was the Messenger (ﷺ) when he gave them permission to stay behind, and so Allah rebuked him. It is possible that the speaker was Allah, glorified is He, because He disliked their going out for corruption, and the meaning was: if you are corrupters, then Allah dislikes your setting out in this manner, so He commanded you to sit back from this particular going out.
