Al-Kalbi said: "A man from among the hypocrites, called Abu al-Jawwaz, said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, 'Do you claim that Allah commanded you to place the charities with the poor and the needy, and you did not place them with the shepherds of sheep?' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, 'May you have no father! Was Moses not a shepherd? Was David not a shepherd?' When he had left, peace and blessings be upon him said, 'Beware of this man and his companions, for they are hypocrites.'" Abu Bakr al-Asamm, may Allah be pleased with him, related in his tafsir that "he ﷺ said to a man from among his companions, 'What is your knowledge of so-and-so?' He said, 'I have no knowledge of him except that you bring him near in the assembly and give him generously.' Peace and blessings be upon him said, 'He is a hypocrite; I maintain outward harmony with him because of his hypocrisy, and I fear that he will corrupt others.' The man said, 'If only you gave so-and-so some of what you give him.' Peace and blessings be upon him said, 'He is a believer; I leave him to his faith. As for this one, he is a hypocrite whom I placate out of fear of his corrupting [others].'"

**The second issue:** His saying: ﴿yalmizuka﴾ (﴿يَلْمِزُكَ﴾, "find fault with you"). Al-Layth said: *al-lamz* is like *al-hamz* in the face. It is said: "a man who is *lumaza*" (one who finds fault with you to your face), and "a man who is *humaza*" (one who finds fault with you behind your back). Al-Zajjaj said: It is said, "I *lamaztu* the man, *almizuhu*" with a kasra (i.e., the imperfect vowel *i*), and "*almuzuhu*" with a damma on the *mim*, when you find fault with him. Likewise, "*hamaztuhu, ahmizuhu hamzan*" when you find fault with him. And *al-humazatu al-lumazatu* is the one who backbites people and finds fault with them. This indicates that al-Zajjaj did not distinguish between *al-hamz* and *al-lamz*. Al-Azhari said: The origin of *al-hamz* and *al-lamz* is pushing. It is said: "I *hamaztuhu* and *lamaztuhu*" when you push him. Abu Bakr al-Asamm distinguished between them, saying: *al-lamz* is to point at someone with a fault of his companion, while *al-hamz* is to narrow one's eyes at someone's companion in front of that person.

Having understood this, we say: Ibn Abbas said, "yalmizuka" means "yaghtabuka" (backbites you). Qatada said, "yat'anu 'alayka" (reproaches you). Al-Kalbi said, "ya'ibuka fi amrin ma" (finds fault with you in some matter). There is no difference among these narrations except in wording. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: Here there is an omitted element, and the implied meaning is: "he finds fault with you regarding the distribution of the charities." Our master, the scholar and caller to Allah (al-Da'i ila Allah) said: The wording of the Qur'an, namely His saying ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾, does not indicate that this fault-finding was for this reason, except that the narrations we have mentioned indicate that the cause of the fault-finding was that. Were it not for these narrations, it would have allowed other possibilities besides them.

The first of these is that they might say: taking zakat in general is impermissible, because seizing a person's earnings from his hand is impermissible. At most one might say: he takes them in order to spend them on the poor. However, the ignorant among them used to say: Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, is the Enricher of the rich, so it is necessary that He be the one who takes charge of the interests of His poor servants; as for commanding us to do this, it is unreasonable. This is what Allah, Exalted is He, related about some of the Jews, that they said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is poor and we are rich﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 181].

The second: they might say: Grant that you take the zakat, but what you take is abundant, so you ought to be content with less than that.

The third: they might say: Grant that you take this abundance, but you spend it on other than its proper purpose. This is what the reports indicate the people intended. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: This verse indicates the baseness of the characters of those hypocrites and the lowliness of their natures. This is because, due to the intensity of their greed for taking charities, they found fault with the Messenger and attributed to him injustice in the distribution, even though he was the furthest of Allah's creation from inclination toward this world. Al-Dahhak said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to distribute among them whatever Allah gave him of little or much wealth, and the believers used to be content with what they were given and would praise Allah for it. As for the hypocrites, if they were given much, they rejoiced, and if they were given little, they became resentful. This indicates that their contentment and resentment were for the pursuit of a share, not for the sake of religion. It was also said: The Prophet ﷺ was winning over the hearts of the people of Makkah on that day by abundantly bestowing the spoils upon them, so the hypocrites became resentful. His saying ﴿at once they become resentful﴾: the word *idha* (إذا) here is for suddenness, meaning: "and if they are not given from them, they suddenly become resentful."

Then He said: ﴿And if only they had been content﴾, the verse. The meaning is: If only they had been content with what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave them from the spoils, and their souls were pleased, even if it was little, and had said: "That suffices us, and Allah will provide us with another spoil, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ will give us more than what he has given us today; indeed we are inclined toward the obedience of Allah, His bounty, and His kindness."

Know that the response to *law* (لَوْ, "if only") is omitted, and the implied meaning is: "it would have been better for them and more beneficial to them." This is because hypocrisy had overcome them, and faith had not taken root in their hearts so that they would rely upon Allah with the reliance due to Him. Omitting the response in this context is more indicative of magnification and awe, as when you say to a man: "If only you had come to us" and do not mention the response, meaning: "If you had done that, you would have seen a great matter."

**The second issue:** The verse indicates that whoever seeks this world ends up in hypocrisy in his religion. As for one who seeks this world to the degree Allah has permitted, and whose aim from this world is to use it as a means to the interests of religion, this is the right path. The principle in this matter is that one should be content with the decree of Allah. Do you not see that He said: ﴿And if only they had been content with what Allah and His Messenger gave them and had said, "Sufficient for us is Allah; Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger. Indeed, we are to Allah inclined [in hope]."﴾ In it He mentioned four levels:

**The first level:** Contentment with what Allah and His Messenger have given them, because of their knowledge that He, Exalted is He, is All-Wise, free from futility and error. "Wise" means that He is knowing of the outcomes of affairs, and whatever is His judgment and decree is truth and correctness, and there is no objection to it.

**The second level:** That the effects of that contentment appear on their tongues, which is His saying: ﴿and said, "Sufficient for us is Allah"﴾, meaning: "Others took the wealth, but since we are content with the judgment and decree of Allah, we have attained this great level in servitude, so Allah is sufficient for us."

[Page 80]

**The third level:** If a person does not reach that lofty rank at which he says "Sufficient for us is Allah," he descends from it to another level, which is that he says: ﴿Allah will give us of His bounty, and [so will] His Messenger﴾, either in this world if the decree requires it, or in the Hereafter, which is preferable and more excellent.

**The fourth level:** That he says: ﴿Indeed, we are to Allah inclined [in hope]﴾. Thus we do not seek from faith and obedience the taking of wealth or attaining positions in this world. Rather, what is intended is either acquiring the felicities of the Hereafter, or being absorbed in servitude, as the wording of the verse indicates, for He said: ﴿Indeed, we are to Allah inclined﴾ and did not say: "Indeed, we are inclined to the reward of Allah." It is related that Jesus, peace be upon him, passed by a people who were remembering Allah, Exalted is He, and said: "What moves you to this?" They said: "Fear of the punishment of Allah." He said: "You are right." Then he passed by another people remembering Allah, and said: "What moves you to this?" They said: "Desire for the reward." He said: "You are right." Then he passed by a third people occupied with remembrance, and asked them, and they said: "We do not remember Him out of fear of punishment, nor out of desire for reward, but to manifest the humility of servitude, the might of lordship, and to honor the heart through knowing Him, and to honor the tongue with words that indicate His holy and mighty attributes." He said: "You are the true ones, the verifiers."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 60 (part 1 of 4):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Charity is only for the poor and the needy, and those employed to collect it, and those whose hearts are to be reconciled, and for freeing captives and debtors, and for the cause of God, and for the wayfarer—an obligation from God. And God is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Know that when the hypocrites criticized the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding the sadaqat (obligatory charity dues), He explained to them that the disbursement of the sadaqat goes to these categories, that he had no personal stake in them, and that he did not take any share of them for himself. Thus, they had no further grounds to criticize the Messenger for taking the sadaqat. Here there are several discussions:

The first discussion: explaining the wisdom behind taking a small portion of the wealth of the rich and distributing it to the needy among people.

The second discussion: explaining the condition of these eight categories mentioned in this verse.

As for the first discussion, we say: the wisdom in the obligation of zakat (almsgiving) consists of several matters, some of which are benefits returning to the giver of zakat, and some of which return to the recipient of zakat.

As for the first category, it comprises several matters. The first: wealth is loved by nature, and the reason for this is that power is one of the attributes of perfection, loved for its own sake and for its very essence, not for something else. For it is not possible to say that everything is loved for the sake of something else, for otherwise either an infinite regress or a circular dependence would follow, and both are impossible. Therefore, the chain of loved things must end in something loved for its own sake. Perfection is loved for its own sake, and deficiency is hated for its own sake. Since power is an attribute of perfection, and an attribute of perfection is loved for its own sake, power is loved for its own sake. Wealth is a means of acquiring that power and its perfection with regard to human beings. Hence, the strongest means of power for human beings is wealth, and whatever something loved depends upon is itself loved. Therefore, wealth is loved. This is the cause of its being loved. However, being absorbed in its love causes the soul to forget the love of God and the preparation for the Hereafter. Thus, the wisdom of the Sharia required that the owner of wealth be obligated to remove a portion of it from his hand, so that this removal would break the intensity of his inclination toward wealth, prevent his soul from being entirely devoted to it, and alert him to the fact that human happiness is not attained by occupation with seeking wealth, but is attained by spending wealth in seeking the pleasure of God, may He be exalted. Thus, the obligation of zakat is a suitable and necessary remedy to remove the disease of love of this world from the heart. For this wisdom, God, may He be glorified, obligated zakat, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾ [At-Tawbah: 103]. That is: purify them and cause them to grow beyond being absorbed in the pursuit of this world.

The second aspect: abundance of wealth brings about intensity of strength and perfection of power, and the increase of wealth brings about the increase of power, and the increase of power brings about the increase of delight in that power, and the increase of these delights calls a person to strive to acquire the wealth that has become the cause of these increasing delights. In this way, the matter becomes a circular one, because when he strives greatly, his wealth increases, and that leads to an increase of power, which leads to an increase of pleasure, which drives the person to increase his pursuit of wealth. And since the matter has become circular, no end or termination appears for it. So the Sharia established for it another termination, which is that it obligated its owner to spend a portion of that wealth in seeking the pleasure of God, may He be exalted, so as to turn the soul away from that dark path that has no end, and to direct it toward the world of servitude to God and the pursuit of His good pleasure.

The third aspect: abundance of wealth is a cause for the arising of rebelliousness and hardness in the heart. Its cause is what we have mentioned, that abundance of wealth is a cause for the attainment of power, and power is loved for its own sake, and the lover, when he attains his beloved, becomes absorbed in him. Thus, a person becomes drowned in the pursuit of wealth. If something comes in his way that prevents him from pursuing it, he seeks help from his wealth and his power to repel that obstacle. This is what is meant by rebelliousness, and to it refers His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient﴾ [Al-Alaq: 6–7]. Thus, the obligation of zakat reduces rebelliousness and returns the heart to seeking the good pleasure of the Most Merciful.

The fourth aspect: the rational soul has two powers: the theoretical and the practical. The perfection of the theoretical power lies in glorifying the command of God, and the perfection of the practical power lies in compassion toward the creation of God. So God obligated zakat so that this perfection would be attained by the essence of the soul, which is its characterization as being beneficent to creation, striving to convey goods to them, and repelling calamities from them. For this very secret, peace be upon him said: "Take on the character of God."

The fifth aspect: when people know that a person strives to convey goods to them and to repel calamities from them, they naturally love him, and their souls incline toward him inevitably, as he, peace be upon him, said: "Hearts are created to love those who do good to them and to hate those who harm them." So when the poor know that a wealthy man allocates to them a portion of his wealth, and that the more his wealth increases, the more he allocates to them from that wealth, they support him with prayers and resolve. Hearts have effects, and spirits have warmth, so those prayers become a cause for that person's remaining in goodness and abundance. To this refers His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for that which benefits people, it remains on the earth﴾ [Ar-Ra'd: 17], and His saying, peace be upon him: "Protect your wealth through zakat."

The sixth aspect: independence from a thing is greater than independence through a thing. For independence through a thing necessitates need for it, although it is used as a means to independence from other things. As for independence from a thing, it is complete richness. For this reason, independence from a thing is an attribute of the Truth, and independence through a thing is an attribute of creation. So when God, may He be exalted, gave some of His servants abundant wealth, He had granted them an ample share of independence through a thing. When He commands them to pay zakat, the intent is to elevate them from the rank of independence through a thing to the station that is higher and more noble than it, which is independence from a thing.

The seventh aspect: wealth is called "mal" (wealth) because of the great inclination of everyone toward it. It comes and goes, it is quick to vanish, and it is on the verge of dispersal. As long as it remains in one's hand, it is as one on the verge of destruction and dispersal. When a person spends it on the paths of righteousness, goodness, and public benefit, it remains in a permanent state that cannot be removed, for it brings praise in this world and lasting reward in the Hereafter. I heard someone say: "A person cannot take his gold with him to the grave." I said: "Rather, it is possible for him to do so, for if he spends it in seeking the Greatest Good Pleasure, he has indeed taken it with him to the grave and to the Resurrection."

The eighth aspect: giving wealth is an imitation of the angels and the prophets, while withholding it is an imitation of the blameworthy miserly. Therefore, giving is more fitting.

The ninth aspect: the outpouring of goodness and mercy is among the attributes of the Truth, may He be glorified and exalted, and striving to attain this attribute to the extent of one's ability is taking on the character of God, and that is the culmination of the perfections of humanity.

The tenth aspect: a human being has only three things: the spirit, the body, and wealth. When he is commanded to believe, the essence of the spirit becomes absorbed in this obligation. When he is commanded to pray, the tongue becomes absorbed in remembrance and recitation, and the body becomes absorbed in those actions. What remains is wealth. If wealth is not spent on the paths of righteousness and goodness, it would follow that a person's stinginess with his wealth would exceed his stinginess with his spirit and body, and that is ignorance. For the degrees of happiness are three:

The first: spiritual happiness.

The second: bodily happiness, which is the middle rank.

The third: external happiness, which is wealth and status.

These ranks function as servants to the soul's happiness. So when the spirit has been devoted to the station of servitude, and then stinginess arises in giving up wealth, it becomes necessary to place the servant in a rank higher than the original master, and that is ignorance. Therefore, it is established that it is obligatory upon the intelligent person also to give wealth in seeking the good pleasure of God, may He be exalted.

The eleventh aspect: the scholars have said: "Thanking for a blessing means spending it in seeking the good pleasure of the Benefactor." And zakat is thanks for the blessing. Therefore, it is necessary to affirm its obligation, since it is established that thanking the Benefactor is obligatory.

The twelfth aspect: the obligation of zakat brings about the attainment of affection and harmony among Muslims, and the removal of hatred and envy from them, and all of this is among the most important matters. These are the considerations that are valid in explaining the wisdom arising from the obligation of zakat, which returns to the giver of zakat.

As for the benefits returning from the obligation of zakat to the one who receives zakat, they are numerous. The first: God, may He be exalted, created wealth, and what is sought from it is not its substance and essence, for gold and silver cannot be benefited from in their own forms except in a small matter. Rather, the purpose of their creation is that they be used as a means to achieve benefits and repel harms. So if a person acquires from wealth an amount sufficient for his need, he is more entitled to hold onto it, because he shares with all other needy people in the attribute of need, and he is distinguished from them by his striving to acquire that wealth. So his being entitled to that wealth is more appropriate than the entitlement of others. But if wealth exceeds the amount needed, and another needy person is present, then here two causes arise, each of which necessitates the ownership of that wealth. As for the owner, it is that he strove to earn and acquire it, and also the intensity of his heart's attachment to it, for that attachment is also a kind of need. As for the poor person, his need for that wealth necessitates his attachment to it. When these two opposing causes exist, divine wisdom requires that each of these two causes be respected to the extent possible. It is said: the owner has the right to earn and the right of his heart's attachment to it, and the poor person has the right of need. So we give preference to the side of the owner and leave him the greater part, and we give to the poor a small portion of it, in order to reconcile the evidences to the extent possible.

The second: when wealth exceeding basic needs is held by a person in his house, it remains idle, cut off from the purpose for which wealth was created. That is an effort to prevent the manifestation of God's wisdom, may He be exalted, and it is impermissible. So God commanded that a portion of it be spent on the poor, so that this wisdom would not be entirely rendered idle.

The third: the poor are the dependents of God, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no creature on earth but that its provision is upon God﴾ [Hud: 6]. And the wealthy are the treasurers of God, because the wealth in their hands is the wealth of God. Had God not placed it in their hands, they would not own a single grain of it. How many an intelligent and clever person strives with the utmost effort yet does not possess enough food to fill his belly, and how many a dull, boorish fool has the world come to him effortlessly and purely!

Once this is established, it is not far-fetched for a king to say to his treasurer: "Disburse a portion of what is in that treasury to the needy among my servants."

The fourth aspect: it may be said that wealth in its entirety is in the hand of the rich, although he does not need all of it, while neglecting the side of the poor person who is completely unable to earn is not befitting the wisdom of the All-Wise, the Most Merciful. Therefore, it is necessary that the rich be obligated to disburse a portion of that wealth to the poor.

**[Fifth aspect]** When the Law left most of that wealth in the owner's hand and gave only a small part to the poor, the owner could make up that loss by trading with what remained in his hand, earning profit, and so the loss would disappear. The poor man, however, has nothing at all. If no portion of the wealth of the rich were given to him, he would remain idle, with nothing to restore him. Therefore this is the better course.

**[Sixth aspect]** If the rich did not take charge of the needs of the poor, the severity of their need and the harm of destitution might drive them to join the enemies of the Muslims, or to commit reprehensible acts such as theft and others. So the obligation of zakat (obligatory almsgiving) achieves this benefit, and it is necessary to affirm that it is obligatory.

**[Seventh aspect]** The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Faith is two halves: half patience and half gratitude." Wealth is naturally loved, so possessing it requires gratitude and losing it requires patience. It is as if it were said: "O rich man, I gave you wealth and you gave thanks, so you became one of the grateful. So take out from your hand a share of it, so that you may be patient in losing that amount, and thereby become one of the patient. And O poor man, I did not give you abundant wealth and you were patient, so you became one of the patient. But I obligate the rich to give you a portion of that wealth, so that when that amount comes into your possession you will give thanks to Me and become one of the grateful." Thus the obligation of zakat is a cause for making all the responsible persons described by patience and gratitude together.

**[Eighth aspect]** It is as if He, glory be to Him, says to the poor man: "If I withheld abundant wealth from you, I have made Myself indebted to you. And if I gave the rich man abundant wealth, I obligated him to run after you and humble himself before you until you take that amount from him. Thus you are like one who bestows a favour upon him by delivering him from the Fire."

Then if the rich man says: "I have bestowed this dinar upon you," the poor man should reply: "Rather, I am the one who has bestowed a favour upon you, since I delivered you in this world from blame and shame, and in the Hereafter from the punishment of the Fire."

This is a collection of aspects of the wisdom behind the obligation of zakat; some of them are certain and some are persuasive. The one who knows the secrets of God's judgment and His wisdom is none but God. And God knows best.

* * *

**The second station: the interpretation of this verse.** It contains several issues.

**First issue:** His saying, ﴿Alms are only for the poor...﴾ The verse indicates that no one has a right to the sadaqat (alms) except these eight categories, and this is agreed upon. Moreover, the word ﴿innama﴾ ("only") denotes restriction, and this is shown by several aspects:

The first: the word *innama* is composed of *inna* and *ma*. *Inna* is for affirmation and *ma* is for negation. When the two are combined, each retains its meaning, so it must convey the affirmation stated and the absence of whatever is contrary to it.

The second: Ibn 'Abbas relied on the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ), "Usury is only in credit (*nasi'ah*)," to deny *riba al-fadl* (usury arising from unequal exchange of the same kind of commodity). Had this word not denoted restriction, the matter would not be so. Likewise some of the Companions relied on his saying (ﷺ), "Water is only from water," to hold that intercourse without ejaculation does not require *ghusl* (the major ritual bath). Had this word not denoted restriction, it would not be so. And He, exalted, said: ﴿Allah is only one God﴾ [an-Nisa': 171], and the purpose is to state the negation of divinity for any other.

The third: poetry. Al-A'sha said:
*"I am not the most numerous of them in pebbles, but glory belongs only to the multitude."*
And al-Farazdaq said:
*"I am the protector who defends the honour, and only I, or one like me, defends their noble lineage."*

By these aspects it is established that *innama* is for restriction. Among what indicates that the sadaqat are spent only on these eight categories is that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to a man: "If you are of the eight categories, you have a right to it; otherwise it is a headache in the head and a disease in the belly." And he said: "Sadaqah is not lawful for a rich person, nor for one who has sound strength."

**Second issue:** Know that when He, exalted, reported that the hypocrites find fault with the Messenger (ﷺ) regarding the taking of sadaqat, He explained that He takes them only for these eight categories, and does not take them for Himself, nor for his relatives and those connected to him. We have already shown that taking a small amount from the wealth of the rich in order to spend it on the poor in meeting their need is the specific wisdom and the necessary benefit. Since the matter is so, the faultfinding and reproach of the hypocrites is pure foolishness and ignorance. Therefore the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say: "I do not give you anything, nor do I withhold from you; I am only a treasurer who places it where he is commanded."

**Third issue:** The school (*madhhab*) of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, is that it is permissible to spend the sadaqah on only some of these categories. This is the view of 'Umar, Hudhayfah, Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu al-'Aliyah and al-Nakha'i. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "If I were to look at a household of Muslims who are poor and modest, and I gave them some of it, that would be more beloved to me." Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: it is necessary to spend it on all eight categories. This is the view of 'Ikrimah, al-Zuhri and 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz. He argued that God mentioned this division in the text of the Book, then emphasized it with His saying, ﴿an obligation from Allah﴾. He said: it is necessary to give each category at least three, since the least plural is three. If one gives the share of the poor to two poor persons, he is liable for the share of the third, which is one-third of the share of the poor. He said: there must also be equality among the shares of these eight categories. For example, if you find five categories, and you are obligated to give ten dirhams in sadaqah, the ten are divided into five shares, each share being two dirhams, and preference is not permitted. Then you must give each category two dirhams, and the least number of each is three, and you are not obligated to equalise among them. So you may give one dirham to one poor person, five-sixths of a dirham to another poor person, and one-sixth of a dirham to a third poor person. This is the description of the division of sadaqat according to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him.

The author, the one who calls to God, may God be pleased with him, said: The verse contains no proof for the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, because God made the sadaqat for these eight categories, and that does not require that the sadaqah of a particular person Zayd be for the whole of these eight. The proof for this is reason and transmission.

As for transmission: His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And know that whatever you obtain of spoils, one-fifth of it is for Allah and for the Messenger﴾ [al-Anfal: 41], and the rest of the verse. He established one-fifth of the spoils for these five groups. Yet no one has said that every item of booty individually must be distributed among these groups. Rather they agreed that the intent is to establish the whole of the spoils for these categories. As for whether every part of the spoils must be distributed among all of them, that is not so. Likewise here: the whole of the sadaqat is for the whole of these eight categories. But to say that the sadaqah of Zayd in particular must be distributed among these eight categories, the wording does not indicate this at all.

As for reason: a ruling established for a whole does not necessarily require its establishment for each part of that whole, and it does not follow that there is no difference between the whole and the part. By what we have mentioned, it is established that the wording of the verse contains no proof for what he (al-Shafi'i) stated. What indicates the soundness of our view are several aspects:

The first: a man who owns only twenty dinars, when it becomes obligatory upon him to pay half a dinar, if we were to burden him to divide it into twenty-four portions, each portion would become trivial and small, not beneficial for any significant purpose.

The second: if this exact specification were binding, the most deserving of observing it would be the senior Companions. Had the matter been so, this report would have reached 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, Ibn 'Abbas, Hudhayfah and the rest of the senior Companions. Had it been so, they would not have disagreed about it. Since they did disagree, we know that it is not binding.

The third: al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, himself has a difference of opinion regarding the permissibility of transferring sadaqat. No one has said that it is obligatory to transfer the sadaqat. If a person is in some village where there is no *mukatab* (a slave seeking emancipation by payment), no fighter engaged in jihad, no zakat collector, no one of those whose hearts are to be reconciled (*al-mu'allafah qulubuhum*), and no stranger passes by him, and it so happens that no one in debt is present in that village, then how is he to be obligated? If we say that it is obligatory for him to travel with what is due upon him of zakat to a town where he finds these categories, that is a view no one has held. And if we drop that obligation from him, then our view is sound. This is what we say on this subject. And God knows best.

* * *

**Fourth issue:** Defining the eight categories. The first and second are the *fuqara'* (the poor) and the *masakin* (the needy). There is no doubt that they are those in need whose expenses do not match their income. Then they differed: some said the one in greater need is the *faqir* (poor), and this is the view of al-Shafi'i and his followers. Others said the one in greater need is the *miskin* (needy), and this is the view of Abu Hanifa and his followers, may God have mercy on them. Some people said there is no difference between the *fuqara'* and the *masakin*: God described them with these two attributes, and the intended meaning is one thing. This is the view of Abu Yusuf and Muhammad, may God have mercy on them both, and the choice of Abu 'Ali al-Jubba'i. Its benefit appears in this matter: if a man bequeaths to a certain person and to the poor and the needy, those who said the poor are other than the needy say: to the certain person a third; and those who said the poor are the same as the needy say: to the certain person a half. Al-Jubba'i said: God mentioned them with two names to emphasise their importance in the sadaqat, because they are the origins among the eight categories. Also the benefit of it is that two shares of the sadaqat are given to them, unlike the others.

Know that the benefit of this disagreement does not appear in the distribution of the sadaqat, but appears in bequests. If a man says: "I bequeath two hundred to the poor and fifty to the needy," it is obligatory, according to al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, to give the two hundred to the one in greater need, and according to Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, to the one in lesser need.

The proofs of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, are several aspects:

The first aspect: God established the sadaqat for these categories only to remove their need and to secure their welfare. This indicates that the one mentioned first is in greater need, because the apparent principle is that the more important should be placed before the less important. Do you not see that it is said: "Abu Bakr and 'Umar," and whoever prefers 'Uthman over 'Ali, when mentioning them says: "'Uthman and 'Ali," and whoever prefers 'Ali over 'Uthman says: "'Ali and 'Uthman"? 'Umar recited the verse of the poet:
*"Grey hair and Islam suffice a man as a deterrent,"*
and said: "Why did he not put Islam before grey hair?" Since the mention begins with the poor, it follows that their need must be greater than the need of the needy.

The second aspect: Ahmad ibn 'Ubayd said: the *faqir* is in a worse condition than the *miskin*, because the root of *faqir* in the language is *maf'ur*, the one from whom a vertebra has been removed from the spine of his back, and then it was changed from *maf'ur* to *faqir*, just as it is said *matbukh* and *tabikh*, and *majruh* and *jarih*. Thus it is established that the *faqir* is so named for his crippling together with his severe need, since the crippling prevents him from moving about to earn. It is well known that there is no condition of poverty and wretchedness more binding than this condition. And they recited for Labid:
*"When Lubad saw the vultures scattering, he raised his primary feathers like a poor, unarmed man."*

Ibn al-A'rabi said: In this verse of poetry, "the poor man whose back is broken" is used as a proverb for every weak person who cannot turn himself about in affairs. Among the things that show that the word faqir (poor) implies great hardship is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And faces that Day will be gloomy﴾ ﴿Thinking that a calamity is about to be inflicted upon them﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 24-25]. Here the word fagirah (calamity) is used as a metaphor for the greatest kinds of evil and disasters.

The third aspect: It is reported that the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him used to seek refuge from poverty, and said: "Poverty nearly becomes disbelief" (كادَ الفَقْرُ أنْ يَكُونَ كُفْرًا). Then he said: "O Allah, let me live as a miskin (needy one), let me die as a miskin, and resurrect me among the company of the miskins." If the miskin were in a worse state than the faqir, the two reports would contradict each other, since he sought refuge from poverty and then asked for a state worse than it. But if we say that poverty is harsher than miskinah (neediness), then there is no contradiction at all.

The fourth aspect: That being a miskin does not contradict owning property, as is shown by the saying of God Most High: ﴿As for the boat, it belonged to poor men﴾ [al-Kahf: 79]. Here He described as miskin those who owned a boat among the boats of the sea, worth a considerable sum of dinars. We do not find in the Book of God anything indicating that a person is called faqir while he possesses something.

If they say: The proof for this is the saying of God Most High: ﴿And God is the Rich, and you are the poor﴾ [Muhammad: 38]. Here He described all of them as poor, although they possess things.

We say: This is more fitting to the opposite. For He described them as poor in relation to God Most High, since no one other than God possesses anything at all in relation to God. So our position is sound.

The fifth aspect: the saying of God Most High: ﴿or feeding on a day of hunger﴾ ﴿an orphan near of kin﴾ ﴿or a miskin lying in the dust﴾ [al-Balad: 14-16]. By the miskin "lying in the dust" is meant the poor man who has been pressed into the dust by the severity of his poverty. Restricting the miskin with this qualifier indicates that there may be a miskin who lacks the description of being "lying in the dust"; and he becomes that only on the assumption that he owns something. This shows that being a miskin does not contradict owning some things.

The sixth aspect: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: the faqir is the needy one who finds nothing. He said: They are the People of the Suffah (ahl al-Suffah), the Suffah of the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. They were about four hundred men who had no dwelling. Whoever among the Muslims had something to spare would bring it to them when evening came. And the masakin are the wanderers who ask people.

The basis of the argument: The extreme poverty of the People of the Suffah is known through mass transmission (tawatur). Since Ibn 'Abbas explained the fuqara' as them, and explained the masakin as the wanderers, and since it is established that the state of the needy one who does not ask anyone is harsher than the state of one who is needy and then asks people and goes around to them, it becomes clear that the faqir must be in a worse state than the miskin.

The seventh aspect: The word maskanah (neediness) is derived from sukun (stillness). So when the faqir asks people, humbles himself before them, and knows that whenever he humbles himself they will give him something, his heart becomes calm and fear and anxiety leave him. It may also be that he is called by this name because when he is answered with rejection and refused, he becomes still, is not agitated, and repeats the request. For this reason, tamaskun (making oneself humble and needy) is used as a metaphor for asking and humbling oneself before others. It is said: tamaskana al-rajul when he became gentle and humble. From this is the saying of the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him to one praying: "Be deliberate and make yourself humble" (تَأنَّ وتَمَسْكَنْ), meaning: be humble and submissive. This shows that the miskin is the one who asks.

Given this established, we say: God Most High said in another verse: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 19]. Since it has been established by what we have mentioned here that the miskin is the beggar, it follows that the mahrum (deprived) must be the faqir. And there is no doubt that mahrum is an intensive expression for establishing the matter of deprivation. So it is established that the faqir is in a worse state than the miskin.

The eighth aspect: He, the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him, said: "O Allah, let me live as a miskin" and the rest of the hadith. The apparent meaning is that God Most High answered his supplication and caused him to die as a miskin, and when he, the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him, died, he possessed many things. This shows that being a miskin does not contradict owning some things. As for the faqir, it indicates severe need, by His words, the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him: "Poverty nearly becomes disbelief." Thus it is established that poverty is a harsher state than neediness.

The ninth aspect: People agree that poverty and wealth are opposites, just as blackness and whiteness are opposites. No one has said that wealth and miskinah are opposites. Rather, they said: haughtiness (tarrafu') and tamaskun are opposites. Whoever is submissive to everyone, fearful of them, enduring their harm, silent in the face of their responses, and humbling himself before them, they say: "So-and-so shows humiliation and neediness," and they say: "He is a miskin, helpless." As for the faqir, they used it to denote the opposite of the rich. On this basis, they may describe a rich man as miskin when he shows submission, obedience, and abandonment of opposition; and they may describe a poor man as haughty, rising above humility and neediness. Thus it is established that poverty is the absence of property, while miskinah is the display of humility. The former contradicts the possession of property, while the latter does not contradict it.

The tenth aspect: the saying of the Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him to Mu'adh regarding zakat: "Take it from their rich and return it to their poor" (خُذْها مِن أغْنِيائِهِمْ، ورُدَّها عَلى فُقَرائِهِمْ). Had need been greater among the masakin, he would have said: "return it to their masakin," since mentioning the more important is preferable. These aspects we have mentioned indicate that the faqir is in a worse state than the miskin.

Those who argued that the miskin is in a worse state than the faqir presented several arguments:

The first: They argued by the saying of God Most High: ﴿or a miskin lying in the dust﴾ [al-Balad: 16]. He described the miskin as "lying in the dust," and this indicates the extreme of harm and hardship. Also, God made the expiations (kaffarat) of food to be given to him, and there is no greater need than the need to remove hunger.

The second: They argued by the verse of the shepherd poet:

"As for the faqir whose milch-camel was ∗∗∗ sufficient for his dependents, yet nothing of his fodder was left for him."

He called him faqir although he had a milch-camel.

The third: They said: the miskin is the one who stays wherever he is present because he has no house in which to dwell, and this indicates the extreme of harm and misery.

The fourth: They transmitted from al-Asma'i and Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that they both said: the faqir is the one who has something to eat, and the miskin is the one who has nothing at all. Yunus said: the faqir may have some of what suffices him, while the miskin is the one who has nothing. I said to a Bedouin: "Are you a faqir?" He said: "No, by God, rather I am a miskin."

As for the answer to their reliance on the verse: We have shown that this verse is evidence for us. For when He qualified the miskin mentioned here by being "lying in the dust," this indicates that there may exist a miskin without this description; otherwise this qualifier would have no benefit. As for their statement that it refers to the disbursement of the food required in expiations to him: we say, yes, He required its disbursement to the miskin qualified by being "lying in the dust," and this does not indicate that He required disbursement to the miskin in general.

As for their argument from the shepherd's verse: he mentioned that this one, who is now described as faqir, once had a milch-camel, and then his master left him nothing. Why, then, should it not be said: he had a milch-camel, and then, when nothing was left to him, he was described as faqir?

As for their statement: the miskin is the one who stays wherever he is present because he has no house: we say, rather the miskin is the wanderer among people who frequently goes about asking, and he is called miskin either because of his stillness when they rebuke and turn him away, or because of the stillness of his heart by knowing that people will not neglect him despite his frequent asking of them. As for the reports they mentioned from Abu 'Amr and Yunus, this is countered by the statements of al-Shafi'i and Ibn al-Anbari, may God have mercy on them both. Also, al-Qaffal transmitted in his Tafsir from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah that he said: "The fuqara' are the poor among the Emigrants (muhajirun), and the masakin are those who did not emigrate." And from al-Hasan: "The faqir is the one who sits in his house, and the miskin is the one who strives." And from Mujahid: "The faqir is the one who does not ask, and the miskin is the one who asks." And from al-Zuhri: "The fuqara' are the chaste ones who do not go out, and the masakin are those who ask." Our master, the Caller to God (mawlana al-Da'i ila Allah), said: All these statements agree that the faqir does not ask and the miskin asks, and whoever asks finds; thus the miskin was easier and had less need.

The third category: God Most High's saying: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾ (al-'amilina 'alayha), who are the collectors (al-su'at) of the zakat. These are given from the alms in proportion to the wages of their work. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and the view of 'Abd Allah ibn 'Umar and Ibn Zayd. Mujahid and al-Dahhak said: they are given one-eighth of the alms. The apparent wording agrees with Mujahid; however, al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, says: this is a wage for work, so it is determined by the amount of the work. The sound position is that the client (mawla) of a Hashimite or a Muttalibite may not be an agent over the alms so as to receive a share of them, because the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused to send Abu Rafi' as an agent over the alms and said: "Do you not know that the client of a people is one of them?" He said: ﴿and those employed to collect them﴾ because the particle 'ala indicates authority, as when one says: "So-and-so is over (ala) such-and-such a town" when he is its governor.

The fourth category: "God Most High's saying: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They are a group of notables from the tribes, whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave on the day of Hunayn. They were fifteen men: Abu Sufyan, al-Aqra' ibn Habis, 'Uyayna ibn Hisn, Huwaytib ibn 'Abd al-'Uzza, Suhayl ibn 'Amr from the Banu 'Amir, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Suhayl ibn 'Amr al-Juhani, Abu al-Sanabil, Hakim ibn Hizam, Malik ibn 'Awf, Safwan ibn Umayya, 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yarbu', al-Jadd ibn Qays, 'Amr ibn Mirdas, and al-'Ala' ibn al-Harith. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ gave each one of them a hundred camels and encouraged them toward Islam, except that he gave 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Yarbu' fifty camels and gave Hakim ibn Hizam seventy camels. Hakim said: "O Messenger of Allah, I did not think that anyone among people had a greater claim on your gift than I do." So he increased it by ten; then he asked again and he increased it by ten, and so on until it reached a hundred. Then Hakim said: "O Messenger of Allah, is your first gift, which I was averse to, better, or this one with which I am content?" The Prayer and Peace of Allah be upon him said: "Rather, the one you were averse to." He said: "By God, I will not take anything other than it." It was said: Hakim died while he was the wealthiest of Quraysh in property. Those gifts were a burden upon the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he reconciled them thereby. The author, may God have mercy on him, said: These gifts were given only on the day of Hunayn and have no connection to the alms. I do not know for what reason Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, mentioned this story in the explanation of this verse; perhaps the purpose was to show that in general it is not forbidden to spend wealth on those whose hearts are to be reconciled. But to make that an explanation of giving zakat to them is not fitting for Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Qaffal transmitted that Abu Bakr, may Allah be pleased with him, gave 'Adi ibn Hatim when he came to him with his alms and the alms of his people during the days of the apostasy (ridda), and he said: The intent is that the Imam may seek the help of such people in extracting the alms from the owners of property.

Al-Wahidi said: God, exalted is He, has made the Muslims independent of winning over the hearts of the polytheists. If the imam sees fit to win over the hearts of a people for some benefit that returns to the Muslims when they are Muslims, it is permissible, since it is not permissible to spend any of the obligatory zakat on the polytheists. As for those among the polytheists who are won over, they are given from the fay' property, not from the sadaqat.

I say: Al-Wahidi's statement that God has made the Muslims independent of winning over the hearts of the polytheists may give the impression that the Prophet (ﷺ) gave a portion of the zakat to them, but we have shown that this never occurred at all. Furthermore, there is nothing in the verse indicating that those who are won over are polytheists. Rather, He said: ﴿and those whose hearts are to be reconciled﴾, and this is general, covering Muslims and others. The correct view is that this ruling has not been abrogated, and that the imam may win over a people described in this way and give them the share of those whose hearts are to be reconciled, because there is no evidence at all for its abrogation.

The fifth category: His words ﴿and for the captives﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: there is an omitted element in it, and the implied meaning is: "and for the freeing of captives." The full discussion of this was already given in his commentary on Surat al-Baqarah, in His words ﴿and the needy and for the captives﴾ [al-Baqarah: 177]. Then, regarding the interpretation of "captives" (al-riqab), there are several views:

The first view: the share for captives is designated for mukatabun (slaves contracted to buy their freedom) so that they may gain their freedom with it. This is the position of al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, and of al-Layth ibn Sa'd. They argued with what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, that he said: "His words ﴿and for the captives﴾ mean the mukatab." This is reinforced by the words of the Exalted: ﴿and give them from the wealth of God which He has given you﴾ [al-Nur: 33].

Page 90

The second view: the position of Malik, Ahmad and Ishaq, that it is designated for freeing captives, by purchasing slaves with it so that they are set free.

The third view: the view of Abu Hanifa and his companions, and of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and al-Nakha'i, that a complete slave is not freed from zakat, but it is given toward a captive, and a mukatab is assisted with it, because His words ﴿and for the captives﴾ imply that the captive has a share in it, and that is incompatible with his being fully freed by it.

The fourth view: the view of al-Zuhri, who said: the share of captives is divided in two halves: half for the mukatabun among the Muslims, and half is used to buy captives from among those who have prayed and fasted and whose Islam is of long standing, so that they are freed from zakat. Our companions said: the safer approach regarding the share of captives is to give it to the master with the permission of the mukatab. The evidence for this is that the Exalted attributed the sadaqat to the four categories mentioned earlier using the preposition lam of ownership, which is His words ﴿Charity is only for the poor﴾. When He mentioned the captives, He replaced the letter lam with the letter fi, saying ﴿and for the captives﴾. This difference must have a purpose, and that purpose is that those four earlier categories are given their share of the sadaqat so that they may dispose of it as they wish, whereas for ﴿and for the captives﴾ their share is placed in freeing their necks from slavery; it is not handed to them, nor are they empowered to dispose of that share as they wish. Rather, it is placed toward captives by paying on their behalf. The same applies to the debtors: the wealth is spent on paying their debts; and for those fighting in the cause of God, the wealth is spent on preparing what they need for the campaign; and the wayfarer is likewise.

The conclusion: for the first four categories, the wealth is paid to them so that they may dispose of it as they wish, while for the last four it is not paid to them, but is spent on the needs that are recognised in the qualities for which they became entitled to a share of zakat.

The sixth category: His words, exalted is He, ﴿and the debtors﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the root meaning of ghurm in the language is the obligation of what is burdensome, and al-gharam is a painful obligatory punishment. Love is called gharam because it is a burdensome and binding matter, and from this comes: "so-and-so is mughram with women" when he is infatuated with them. Debt is called gharam because it is burdensome for a person and binding upon him. So the meaning of al-gharimun is those in debt. We say: if the debt arose from an act of disobedience, it does not enter the verse, because the purpose of spending the wealth mentioned in the verse is assistance, and disobedience does not merit assistance. If it arose not from disobedience, it is of two kinds: a debt incurred for necessary expenses or for some public benefit, and a debt incurred through guaranteeing others' obligations or reconciling disputes between people. Both are included in the verse. Al-Asamm related in his tafsir that when the Prophet (ﷺ) judged concerning the ghurrah (a payment for a fetus), the 'aqilah (paternal kin liable for payment) said: "We do not own the ghurrah, O Messenger of God." He said to Haml ibn Malik ibn al-Nabigha: "Help them with a ghurrah from their sadaqat." And Hamil was then in charge of the sadaqat.

The seventh category: His words, exalted is He, ﴿and in the cause of God﴾. The exegetes said: this means the fighters. Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: it is permissible for him to take from the zakat wealth even if he is wealthy, and this is the position of Malik, Ishaq and Abu 'Ubayd. Abu Hanifa and his two companions, may God have mercy on them, said: the fighter is not given anything unless he is in need.

Know that the apparent wording in His words ﴿and in the cause of God﴾ does not require restricting it to all fighters. For this reason al-Qaffal related in his tafsir from some jurists that they permitted spending the sadaqat on all forms of good, such as shrouding the dead, building fortresses, and maintaining mosques, because His words ﴿and in the cause of God﴾ are general in all of this.

The eighth category: the wayfarer (ibn al-sabil). Al-Shafi'i, may God have mercy on him, said: the wayfarer is one entitled to sadaqah, who wishes to travel in something other than disobedience but is unable to reach his destination without assistance. The companions said: whoever sets out on a journey from his town for a need may be given the share of the wayfarer. This is the discussion explaining these eight categories.

* * *

The fifth issue: concerning the rulings of these divisions.

The first ruling:

They agreed that His words ﴿Charity is only﴾ include obligatory zakat, because obligatory zakat is named sadaqah. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. And the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Nothing less than five camels (dhawd) is subject to charity, and nothing less than five wasqs is subject to charity." They differed on whether voluntary charity (sadaqah mandubah) is included. Some said it is included, because the word sadaqah is specific to the voluntary kind; so if we include obligatory zakat in it, then at least voluntary charity should be included as well, and the benefit would be that the expenditure of all charities is only for these people. The closer view is that the word sadaqat here refers to the obligatory zakat, and this is indicated by several points:

First: He, exalted is He, attributed these sadaqat to the eight categories using the lam of ownership, and sadaqah that is owned by them is only obligatory zakat.

Second: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the expenditure of sadaqat is only for these eight. This restriction is valid only if we take these sadaqat to be obligatory zakat. If we include voluntary acts, this restriction would not be valid, because voluntary charities may be spent on building mosques, hostels, schools, shrouding and preparing the dead, and all other purposes.

Third: His words, exalted is He, ﴿Charity is only for the poor﴾ are appropriate only if the charities and their divisions had already been explained, so that this statement refers to them. The charities previously explained and detailed are the obligatory ones, so this statement must be understood as referring to them.

The second ruling:

This verse indicates that this zakat is taken and distributed by the imam and whoever acts on his behalf. The evidence is that God, exalted is He, made a share in it for the collectors ('amilin), and this shows that the collection of these zakat payments requires a collector, and the collector is the one appointed by the imam to collect zakat. Thus this text shows that the imam is the one who collects zakat. This is reinforced by His words, exalted is He: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾. As for the view that the owner may himself pay the zakat on apparent wealth, this is known from another evidence, and one may rely on His words, exalted is He: ﴿And in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 19]. If that right belongs to the beggar and the deprived, it must be permissible for the owner to give it to them directly from the outset.

The third ruling:

The text of the Qur'an indicates that the collector has a right in the zakat wealth. They differed on whether the imam has a right in it. Some affirmed it, saying: the collector can only perform that work through the imam's authority and appointment, so the real collector is the imam. Others prevented it, saying: the verse restricts zakat wealth to these eight categories, and the imam is outside them, so this wealth is not spent on him.

The fourth ruling:

They differed on whether this collector, if wealthy, takes his share. Al-Hasan said: he takes it only if in need. The rest said: he takes it even if wealthy, because he takes it as a wage for his work. Then they differed: some said the collector in zakat wealth receives one eighth, because God divided zakat into eight categories, so he must receive one eighth, just as when someone bequeaths property to eight persons, each receives one eighth. The majority said: rather, his right is according to the amount of his expenses in collecting and gathering.

The fifth ruling:

They agreed that zakat wealth is not to be taken out of these eight categories. They differed on whether it is permissible to place it in only some of the categories. The proofs of these two issues have already been given. However, if we say that it may be placed in only some of the categories, this applies only to someone other than the collector. As for placing it entirely in the collector, that is not permissible by consensus.

The sixth ruling:

The collector and the mu'allafah are absent in this age, so the remaining six categories remain. It is preferable to spend zakat on these six categories according to what al-Shafi'i says, because that is the utmost in caution. If one does not do so, it is nonetheless valid, as we have explained.

The seventh ruling:

The general wording of His words ﴿for the poor and the needy﴾ includes both the disbeliever and the Muslim, but the reports indicate that it is not permissible to spend zakat on the poor, the needy and others unless they are Muslims.

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned these eight categories and explained their conditions, He said: ﴿an obligation from God﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "fari'dah" is in the accusative as an emphatic form, because His words ﴿Charity is only﴾ for these people is equivalent to saying: God has enjoined the sadaqat for these people as an obligation. This is like a warning against opposing this apparent meaning. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "God, exalted is He, was not pleased that the division of zakat be undertaken by an angel brought near, nor by a sent prophet, until He Himself undertook its division." The purpose of these emphases is to forbid taking zakat out of these categories.

Then He said: ﴿And God is Knowing﴾, that is, the most knowing of the measures of benefit, ﴿Wise﴾, who legislates only what is most correct and most beneficial. And God knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, verse 61:

God Almighty says: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet and say, "He is all ears." Say, "An ear of good for you: he believes in God, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe. And for those who harm the Messenger of God there is a painful punishment."﴾

Know that this is another kind of the ignorance of the hypocrites, namely that they used to say about the Messenger of God that he is "all ears," by way of disparagement and blame. In this verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** ʿĀṣim, in the transmission of al-Aʿmash and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān from Abū ʿIkrimah, from him, read ﴿أُذُنٌ خَيْرٌ﴾ ("ʾudhunun khayrun") with both words in the nominative and nunated, on the basis of the implied meaning: "If it is as you say, that he is all ears, then an ear of good for you is one that accepts from you and believes you, which is better for you than one that calls you liars." The rest read ﴿أُذُنُ خَيْرٍ لَكُمْ﴾ with the genitive construction (idafah), meaning: he is an ear of good, not an ear of evil. Nafiʿ read ﴿أُذْنُ﴾ with the dhal sukun in the whole Qur'an, while the rest read it with a damma. Both are dialectal variants, like ʿunuq and ẓufur.

**The second issue:** Ibn ʿAbbās (may Allah be pleased with him) said: A group of the hypocrites mentioned the Prophet (ﷺ) with words that are not fitting. Some of them said: "Do not do it, for we fear that what we say will reach him." Al-Jullās ibn Suwayd said: "Rather, we will say whatever we wish, then we will go to him and swear that we did not say it, and he will accept our word, for Muhammad is only an ear that listens." So this verse was revealed.

Al-Hasan said: The hypocrites used to say: "This man is nothing but an ear; whoever wishes can turn him wherever he wishes, he has no resolve." Al-Aṣamm narrated that a man from among them said to his people: "If what Muhammad says is true, then we are worse than donkeys." His stepson heard it and said: "By God, it is indeed true, and you are worse than your donkey." Then that reached the Prophet (ﷺ), and some of them said: "Muhammad is only an ear; if you meet him and swear to him, he will believe you." So this verse was revealed in accordance with his words. The speaker said: "O Messenger of God, I had never embraced Islam before today, and this youth is of great value to me. By God, I will thank him."

Then al-Aṣamm said: God Almighty exposed the aspects of their disbelief that they used to conceal, so that they would be a proof against them for the Messenger and so that they would be deterred. So He said: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you concerning the charities﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾, then He said: ﴿And among them are those who covenanted with God﴾ [al-Tawbah: 75], and so on, from the reports of unseen matters. In all of this there are proofs that he is truly a prophet from God.

**The third issue:** Know that God Almighty related that among the hypocrites there are those who harm the Prophet, then He explained that harm as their saying to the Prophet that he is "all ears." Their purpose by this is that he has no intelligence and no depth of insight, but rather he is simple-hearted and quick to be deceived by everything he hears. For this reason they named him "an ear," just as a spy is called "an eye." It is said: "So-and-so has placed an eye over us," meaning a spy who inquires closely into matters. So it is the same here.

Then God Almighty answered it with His saying: ﴿Say, "An ear of good for you"﴾. The implied meaning: Grant that he is an ear, but it is good for you. His saying ﴿ear of good﴾ is like saying: "So-and-so is a man of truth and a witness of justice." Then He clarified what kind of ear it is with His saying: ﴿he believes in God, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe﴾. God made these three qualities as things that necessitate that he, peace and blessings be upon him, is an "ear of good." So let us explain how these meanings entail that goodness:

As for the first, which is His saying ﴿he believes in God﴾: because everyone who believes in God fears God, and one who fears God does not proceed to harm falsely.

As for the second, which is His saying ﴿and believes the believers﴾: the meaning is that he accepts their word. That is, when they agree upon one word, he accepts that word from them. This contradicts his being simple-hearted and quick to be deceived.

If it is said: Why did the verb "believe" take the preposition bi- with God, and the preposition lam with the believers?

We say: Because the belief that is transitive to God is meant as affirmation (taṣdīq), which is the opposite of disbelief, so it takes bi-. And the belief that is transitive to the believers means listening to them and accepting their word, so it takes lam, as in His saying: ﴿And you are not one who believes us﴾ [Yusuf: 17]; ﴿But none believed in Moses except some offspring of his people﴾ [Yunus: 83]; and His saying: ﴿Shall we believe you, when the lowest have followed you?﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 111]; and His saying: ﴿Do you believe him before I have given you permission?﴾ [Taha: 71].

As for the third, which is His saying: ﴿and is a mercy for those of you who believe﴾: this also necessitates the goodness, because he treats your affairs according to the outward, does not search too deeply into your inner states, and does not strive to tear away your veils. So it is established that each of these three attributes necessitates that he is "an ear of good." When He clarified that he is a cause of good and mercy, He explained that whoever harms him deserves a painful punishment. Because if he strives to bring good and mercy to them, even though they are in the utmost depravity and disgrace, and then after that they repay his kindness with harm and his good with evil, there is no doubt that they deserve a severe punishment from God Almighty.

**The fourth issue:** As for the reading of the one who read ﴿أُذُنٌ خَيْرٌ﴾ with nunation in both words, there are several aspects:

The first aspect: The implied meaning is: "Say: an ear that is attentive and listens to the truth is better for you than this corrupt disparagement that you mention." Then He mentioned after it what indicates the corruption of this disparagement, which is His saying: ﴿he believes in God, and believes the believers, and is a mercy for those of you who believe﴾. The meaning: Whoever is described with these attributes, how is it permissible to disparage him, and how is it permissible to describe him as simple-hearted and quick to be deceived?

The second aspect: That one assumes an implied subject (mubtadaʾ), and the implied meaning is: "He is an ear of good for you," that is, he is an ear described as good in regard to you, because he accepts your excuses and overlooks your ignorance. So how do you make this quality a criticism of him?

The third aspect: This is a far-fetched aspect mentioned by the author of al-Naẓm (Ṣāḥib al-Naẓm), who said: "ʾUdhunun" (an ear), although it is apparently nominative as the subject (mubtadaʾ), its position is accusative as a state (ḥāl). Its interpretation is: "Say: he, being an ear, is good for you," that is: when he is an ear, he is good for you, because he accepts your excuses. A parallel is: "And he, as a guardian, is good for you," that is: he is in the state of being a guardian for you. But since it is deleted, the state is placed in the position of the subject. Its estimate is: "And he is a guardian, good for you." The implied pronoun "huwa" (he) is frequent in the Qur'an. God Almighty said: ﴿They will say, "They are three"﴾ [al-Kahf: 22], meaning: they are three. This aspect is extremely contrived, although al-Wāḥidī greatly admired it.

**The fifth issue:** Ḥamzah read ﴿وَرَحْمَةٍ﴾ ("wa-raḥmatin") with the genitive, as a conjunction after ﴿خَيْرٍ﴾ (khayrin), as if it were said: "an ear of good and mercy," meaning: a listener to speech that is a cause of good and mercy.

If it is said: Every mercy is good, so what is the benefit of mentioning mercy after mentioning good?

We say: Because the most noble category of good is mercy, so it is permissible to mention mercy after mentioning good, as in His saying: ﴿And His angels and His messengers and Gabriel and Michael﴾ [al-Baqarah: 98]. Abū ʿUbayd said: This reading is weak, because the conjoined word is far from the word it is conjoined to. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: Distance does not prevent the validity of conjunction. Do you not see that whoever read ﴿وَقِيلِهِ يَا رَبِّ﴾ ("wa-qīlihi yā Rabb") only takes it as conjoined to His saying: ﴿And with Him is knowledge of the Hour﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 85]? Its estimate is: "And with Him is knowledge of the Hour and knowledge of His saying."

If it is said: What is the reason for the reading of Ibn ʿĀmir: ﴿وَرَحْمَةً﴾ ("wa-raḥmatan") with the accusative?

We say: It is an object of purpose (ʿillah), whose cause is deleted. The estimate is: "And as a mercy for you, he grants permission," but it was deleted because His saying ﴿an ear of good for you﴾ indicates it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 62:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They swear by God to you in order to please you, but God and His Messenger have more right that they should please Him, if they are believers.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the ugly deeds of the hypocrites, namely their readiness to swear false oaths. It has been said: this is based on what preceded it, meaning: they harm the Prophet and speak ill of him, and then they swear to you. And it has been said: it was revealed concerning a group of hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. When the Messenger of God (ﷺ) returned to Medina, they came to him, offered excuses, and swore oaths, and the verse was revealed concerning them. The meaning is that they swore that they had not said what was reported of them, in order to please the believers with their oath. It was obligatory for them to please God through sincerity and repentance, not by displaying what they conceal contrary to it. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And when they meet those who believe, they say, "We believe"﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:14 and 2:76].

As for His saying ﴿that they should please Him﴾ after the mention of God and the mention of the Messenger, there are several reasons for it:

The first: He, exalted is He, is not mentioned together with another in a general manner; rather, He must be singled out for mention, out of exaltation of Him.

The second: the ultimate object of all acts of obedience and worship is God, so He alone was mentioned. It is related that one of the disbelievers raised his voice and said: "I repent to God and I do not repent to Muhammad." The Messenger, peace be upon him, heard that and said: "He has placed the truth in its proper place."

The third: it is possible that the intended meaning is "that they should please both of them," and so mention was confined to one of them, as in His saying:

We are content with what we have, and you are content with what you have, though our opinions differ.

The fourth: the Knower of secrets and hidden thoughts is God, exalted is He, and sincerity of heart is known only to God; for this reason God singled out Himself for mention.

The fifth: since the Messenger's pleasure must correspond to God's pleasure, and a difference between them is impossible, mention of one of them was sufficient, as one says: "The kindness of Zayd and his generosity have supported me and mended me."

The sixth: the implied reading is: "God has more right that they should please Him, and His Messenger likewise."

As for His saying ﴿if they are believers﴾, there are two views. The first: "if they are believers as they claim." The second: that they knew the truth of the Messenger's religion, but persisted in disbelief out of envy and obstinacy; for this reason God said: ﴿if they are believers﴾. In the verse there is evidence that God's pleasure is not obtained by displaying faith unless it is accompanied by inward assent of the heart, and this refutes the view of the Karramiyya, who claim that faith is nothing but verbal profession with the tongue.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, verse 63:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger, for him is the Fire of Hell, abiding therein? That is the great disgrace.﴾

Know that the purpose of this verse, too, is to explain the condition of the hypocrites who stayed behind from the expedition of Tabuk. In the verse there are several issues.

The first issue: The people of ma'ani (ahl al-ma'ani, scholars of the meanings and rhetoric of the Arabic language) said: His saying, "Do you not know" (alam ta'lam), is addressed to someone whom a person has tried to teach for a long time and has exerted great effort in teaching, yet he has not learned. So it is said to him: "Do you not know, after these long hours and this lengthy period?"

This was appropriate because the stay of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) among them was long, and his admonitions were many, warning against disobedience to Allah and encouraging obedience to Him. The pronoun in His saying, ﴿that he, whoever opposes Allah﴾ (annahu man yuhadidi Allah), is the pronoun of the matter and the affair (damir al-amr wa al-sha'n), and the meaning is: "The matter is such and such." The benefit of this pronoun is that if the subject and predicate were mentioned after the word "anna" (that), it would not have had a strong impact. But when you say, "The matter and the affair is such and such," it adds greater magnification and awe to that statement.

As for His saying, ﴿whoever opposes Allah﴾ (man yuhadidi Allah): al-Layth said: "Hadadtuhu" means "I opposed him." Muhadadah (opposition, hostility) is like mujanabah (avoidance), mu'adah (enmity) and mukhalafah (contrariness). It is derived from al-hadd (limit, boundary), and the meaning of "hadda fulan fulanan" is that he came to be in a boundary other than his boundary, just as "shaqqahu" means he came to be on a side other than his side. The meaning of ﴿yuhadid Allah﴾ is that he comes to be in a boundary other than the boundary of the friends of Allah, through opposition.

Abu Muslim said: Muhadadah is derived from al-hadid (iron), the iron of weapons. Then there are various expressions of the exegetes here: "He opposes Allah"; it has been said: "He wars against Allah"; it has been said: "He defies Allah"; and it has been said: "He is hostile to Allah."

Then He said: ﴿then for him is the Fire of Hell (fa-anna lahu nara jahannam)﴾, and regarding this there are several opinions:

The first: The estimate is: "Then it is certain that for him is the Fire of Hell."

The second: Its meaning is: "Then for him is the Fire of Hell," and "anna" is repeated for emphasis.

The third: We say: the response (jawab) of "man" (whoever) is omitted, and the estimate is: "Do they not know that whoever opposes Allah and His Messenger will perish; then for him is the Fire of Hell." Al-Zajjaj said: It is also permissible to read "inna" with a kasrah (kasra, the vowel i) by way of a new sentence after the fa', but the recitation is with the fathah (fatha, the vowel a) on "anna." Al-Ka'bi, in his Tafsir, reported that the recitation with the kasrah is also attested.

Abu Muslim said: Jahannam is one of the names of the Fire. The lexicographers relate from the Arabs that a deep well is called al-jihinnam among them, so it is possible that Jahannam is derived from this word. The meaning of the depth of its bottom is that its punishment has no end. Al-khalid (abiding) means the everlasting. Al-khizy may mean regret (nadam) and may mean shame (istihya'), and "regret" is preferable here because of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And they will conceal regret when they see the punishment﴾ [Yunus: 54].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrites are wary lest a surah be sent down against them, informing them of what is in their hearts. Say, "Mock on; indeed Allah will bring out what you are wary of."﴾

Know that they used to call Surat Bara'a (Surat al-Tawbah) "al-Hafira" (the Exposer), because it dug out what was in the hearts of the hypocrites (al-munafiqin). Al-Hasan said: "Twelve men from among the hypocrites gathered for a matter of hypocrisy, and Jibril informed the Messenger, peace be upon him, of their names. He, peace be upon him, said: 'Some people have gathered for such-and-such; let them stand up, confess, and seek forgiveness from their Lord, so that I may intercede for them.' But they did not stand up. Then he, peace be upon him, said after that: 'Stand up, O so-and-so, and O so-and-so,' until he reached them all. Then they said, 'We confess and we seek forgiveness.' He said: 'Now! I was at the beginning more inclined to intercede, but Allah was quicker in responding. Get out from me, get out from me!'" He kept saying this until they had all left entirely.

Al-Asamm said: "When the Messenger, peace be upon him, was returning from Tabuk, twelve men stood for him at the 'Aqabah to assassinate him. Jibril informed him, and they were masked on a dark night. He commanded him to send someone to strike the faces of their mounts. So he ordered Hudhayfah to do that, and he struck them until he drove them back. Then he said: 'Whom did you recognize from the people?' He said: 'I did not recognize any of them.' The Prophet (ﷺ) then mentioned their names and counted them for him, and said: 'Jibril informed me of that.' Hudhayfah said: 'Will you not send to them so that they may be killed?' He said: 'I dislike that the Arabs should say: Muhammad fought with his companions, and when he gained victory he began to kill them. Rather, Allah suffices us in that.'"

Page 97

If it is said: the hypocrite is a disbeliever, so how can he be wary of the descent of revelation upon the Messenger?

We say: there are several aspects to this:

The first: Abu Muslim said: this is a wariness that the hypocrites displayed in a mocking manner, when they saw the Messenger, peace be upon him, mentioning everything and claiming that it came from revelation, while the hypocrites used to deny that among themselves.
