So Allah informed His Messenger of that and commanded him to inform them that He would reveal their secret which they were wary of being revealed. And in His saying, ﴿Mock on﴾, there is an indication of what we have said.

The second: that the people, although they were disbelievers in the religion of the Messenger, nevertheless witnessed that the Messenger, peace be upon him, used to inform them of what they concealed and hid. Because of this experience, wariness and fear entered their hearts.

The third: al-Asamm said: they knew that he was a truthful Messenger from Allah, exalted is He, but they disbelieved in him out of envy and obstinacy. Al-Qadi said: it is far-fetched that one who knows Allah and His Messenger and the soundness of His religion would be opposed to them both. Al-Da'i ila Allah said: this is not far-fetched, because when envy grows strong in the heart it reaches a state where it disputes even matters that are perceived by the senses.

The fourth: the meaning of "wariness" (al-hadhar) is a command to be wary, i.e., let the hypocrites be wary of that.

The fifth: they were doubtful about the soundness of his prophethood, and they were not certain of its falsehood; and the doubter is fearful. So for this reason they feared that something would be revealed to him about their affair that would expose them.

Then the author of al-Kashshaf said: the pronoun in His saying ﴿against them﴾ and ﴿informing them﴾ refers to the believers, and in His saying ﴿in their hearts﴾ it refers to the hypocrites. It is also permissible that all the pronouns refer to the hypocrites, because when a surah is sent down concerning their meaning, it is sent down against them. And the meaning of ﴿informing them of what is in their hearts﴾ is that the surah is as if it says to them: "In your hearts is such-and-such," meaning: it broadcasts their secrets with a clear broadcasting, so it is as if it informs them.

Then He said: ﴿Say, "Mock on"﴾, and this is a command of threat, like His saying: ﴿And say, "Work"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 105]. ﴿Indeed Allah will bring out what you are wary of.﴾ That is: that which you are wary of, Allah will bring it out into existence; for when a thing comes into being after its non-existence, it is as if its doer brought it out from non-existence into existence.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 65–66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ ﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a faction among you, We will punish another faction because they were criminals.﴾

In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several things concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. The first: Ibn 'Umar narrated that a man from the hypocrites said during the Battle of Tabuk: "I have never seen people with more fearful hearts, more lying tongues, or more cowardly at the encounter than these people," meaning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers. One of the Companions said: "You lie, rather you are a hypocrite." Then he went to inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he found that the Qur'an had preceded him. That man came to the Messenger of Allah, while he had mounted his she-camel, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we were only playing and talking about the talk of travelers, cutting the road with it." He kept saying: "We were only conversing and playing," while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?" and he did not turn to him, nor did he add anything to that. The second: al-Hasan and Qatadah said: When the Messenger went to Tabuk, the hypocrites said among themselves: "Does he think he will prevail over al-Sham and take its fortresses and palaces? Far-fetched, far-fetched!" So upon his return he summoned them and said: "Are you the ones who said such and such?" They said: "That was not in earnest in our hearts; we were only conversing and playing." The third: It is related that those who stayed behind from the Messenger ﷺ were asked what they had been doing and what was the reason for their staying behind, and they said this statement.

The fourth: It is transmitted from Abu Muslim that he said, in explaining His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear lest a surah be sent down about them informing them of what is in their hearts﴾, that they displayed this fear by way of mockery; so He, exalted is He, made clear in this verse that when they were asked, "Why did you do that?" they said, "We did not say that in a spirit of defamation, but only because we were conversing and playing."

The fifth: Know that there is no need, in understanding this verse, for these narrations; for they indicate that they uttered corrupt speech by way of defamation and mockery, and when the Messenger informed them that they had said that, they became afraid and made excuses for it, saying: "We only said that in a manner of play, not in earnest." This is their saying: "We were only conversing and playing," that is: we only said that for the sake of play. This indicates that the word "innama" (only) confines the meaning, for if it did not, it would not follow from their being players that they were not mockers, and then this excuse would not be complete.

The answer: al-Wahidi said: The origin of khawd is entering into a liquid of water and mud, then it became common until it became a name for every entry into something in which there is defilement and harm. The meaning is: we were conversing and playing in vain speech, as a caravan converses to cut the road. The Messenger answered them with his saying: "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?!" And in this there are issues:

The first issue: There is a difference between your saying: "Do you mock Allah?" and your saying: "Is it at Allah that you mock?" The first implies denial of the act of mocking; the second implies denial of directing the mockery at Allah, as if he says: "Granted that you may proceed to mock, but how did you proceed to direct the mockery at Allah?" A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿No ghoul is in it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. The purpose is not the negation of ghoul, but the negation that the wine of Paradise be a place for ghoul.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, related about them that they mock Allah and His verses and His Messenger, and it is known that mocking Allah is impossible, so it must have an interpretation, and there are aspects to it:

The first: The intended meaning of mocking Allah is mocking the obligations of Allah, exalted is He.

The second: It is possible that the intended meaning is mocking the mention of Allah; for the names of Allah may be mocked by the disbeliever, just as the believer glorifies and exalts them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], so He commanded the believer to glorify the name of Allah. And He said: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who distort His names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. So there is nothing preventing it being said: "Is it Allah?" while meaning: "Is it by mentioning Allah?"

The third: Perhaps when the hypocrites said: "How can Muhammad conquer the fortresses and palaces of al-Sham?" some Muslims said: "Allah will help him in that and grant him victory over them." Then some of the ignorant hypocrites uttered a statement implying disparagement of the power of Allah, as is the habit of the ignorant and the atheists, so that was what was meant.

As for His saying: ﴿and His verses﴾, what is meant by them is the Qur'an and all that indicates the religion. His saying: ﴿and His Messenger﴾ is well known, and this indicates that the people only mentioned what they mentioned by way of mockery.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi transmitted from the lexicographers two views concerning the word i'tidhar (making excuse):

The first view: It is an expression for the erasing of a sin, from their saying: "i'tadharat al-manazil" when they were effaced (darasat). It is said: "I passed by a mu'tadhir dwelling," and i'tidhar is the effacing and the taking of the excuse from it, because the one making an excuse seeks to remove the trace of his sin.

The second view: Ibn al-A'rabi related that i'tidhar is cutting off, and from it one says of the foreskin: 'udhrah, because it is cut off; and the 'udhrat of a girl was named 'udhrah because she is "udhira," that is, cut. And it is said: "i'tadharat al-miyah" when the waters ceased. So the excuse, since it is a cause for cutting off blame, was called 'udhr. Al-Wahidi said: The two views are close, because the erasing of the trace of sin and the cutting off of blame are close to each other.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, made clear that this mocking was disbelief, and reason requires that proceeding into disbelief for the sake of play is not permissible. So it is established that their saying, "We were only conversing and playing," was not a genuine excuse for proceeding into that mockery. Since it was not an excuse in itself, Allah forbade them from making an excuse with it, because restraining from vain speech is obligatory. So He said: ﴿Make no excuse﴾, that is: do not mention this excuse in repelling this offence.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ indicates several rulings:

The first ruling: That mocking the religion, however it occurs, is disbelief in Allah; because mocking indicates belittling, and the great foundation of faith is the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, to the utmost possible, and combining the two is impossible.

The second ruling: It indicates the invalidity of the view of one who says that disbelief enters only into actions of the heart.

The third ruling: It indicates that their statement which proceeded from them was disbelief in reality, even though they had been hypocrites before, and that disbelief can renew itself in the disbeliever moment by moment.

The fourth ruling: It indicates that disbelief occurred only after they had been believers.

It may be asked: since they were hypocrites, how is it valid to describe them with this?

We say: al-Hasan said: The meaning is "you disbelieved after your belief which you displayed." Others said: Your disbelief became manifest to the believers after you had been Muslims in their eyes. The two views are close.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿If We pardon a faction among you, We will punish another faction﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: 'Asim recited: "in nA'fu wa nu'adhdhib" with the nun and with kasra on the dhal, and ta'ifatan in the accusative, and the meaning is that He, exalted is He, related of Himself that He says: "If We pardon a faction, We will punish a faction." The rest recited with the ya' and its damma, and with fatha on the fa', in the passive form: "in yu'fa 'an ta'ifatin" with the masculine, and "tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun" with the feminine. Sahib al-Kashshaf related from Mujahid: "in tu'fa 'an ta'ifatin" in the passive with the feminine. Then he said: The preferred form is the masculine, because the predicate attached to the adverbial phrase, as you say: "siira bi-l-dabbah" (it was journeyed with the animal), and you do not say "sirat bi-l-dabbah." As for the interpretation of his recitation, perhaps Mujahid went to the view that the meaning is as if it were said: "If a faction is shown mercy, you are likewise," and this is strange. The best recitation is the common one: "in yu'fa 'an ta'ifatin" with the masculine and "tu'adhdhab ta'ifatun" with the feminine.

The second issue: The exegetes mentioned that the two factions were three persons: two mocked and one laughed. So the first faction is the one who laughed, and the second is the two who mocked. The exegetes said: Since the sin of the one who laughed was lighter, Allah pardoned him; and the sin of the two mockers was graver, so Allah did not pardon them. Al-Qadi said: This is far-fetched, because He, exalted is He, ruled that both factions were disbelievers, and He does not pardon a disbeliever except after repentance and return to Islam; and also He does not punish a disbeliever except after his persistence in disbelief. But if he repents and returns to Islam, He does not punish him. So when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned that He pardons one faction and punishes the other, there is implied in it that the faction He informed He would pardon repented from disbelief and returned to Islam, and the faction He informed He would punish persisted in disbelief and did not return to Islam. Perhaps that one person, since he did not exaggerate in defamation and did not agree with the people in the mention, his disbelief was lightened; then Allah granted him success in faith and emergence from disbelief. This indicates that whoever plunges into a vain act should strive to minimize it, for it is hoped that by the blessing of that minimizing Allah will accept his repentance in all of it.

The third issue: They said: It is established by the narrations that the two factions were three, so one of the two factions must be a single person. Al-Zajjaj said: The word ta'ifah in the language originally means a group, because it is the quantity that can encircle a thing; then it is permissible to call one person a ta'ifah. Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿and let a group of the believers witness their punishment﴾ [al-Nur: 2]. Its minimum is one. Al-Farra' related with his chain from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "The ta'ifah is one or more." Regarding the permissibility of calling a single person a ta'ifah there are views:

The first: Whoever adopts a view and supports it will not cease to be defending it and supporting it, so it is as if with his heart he circles around it and defends it from all sides; so it is not far-fetched that one person be called a ta'ifah for this reason.

The second: Ibn al-Anbari said: The Arabs apply the plural word to a single person, so they say: "So-and-so went out to Makkah on camels," and Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿those to whom the people said﴾ [Al 'Imran: 173], meaning Nu'aym ibn Mas'ud.

The third: It is not far-fetched that when ta'ifah is intended to mean one person, its origin is ta'if, then the ha' was added to it for emphasis. Then He, exalted is He, gave as the reason for His punishing the second faction that they were criminals.

Know that since the two factions shared in disbelief, they shared in the crime, and punishment is specific to one of the two factions, and it is not permissible to explain a specific ruling by a general cause. Also, punishment is a ruling existing in the present, and His saying "kanu mujrimin" (they were criminals) indicates the occurrence of crime from them in the past time, and it is not permissible to explain a ruling existing in the present by a cause that is past; rather it would have been better to say "bi-annahum mujrimun" (because they are criminals).

Know that the answer to this is that this is an indication that the crime of the second faction was graver and stronger than the crime of the first faction, so the causation fell upon that severe crime. Also, there is in it an indication that that crime remained, continued and never ceased, so it necessitated the punishment.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 65–66:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you ask them, they will surely say, "We were only conversing and playing." Say, "Is it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?"﴾ ﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief. If We pardon a faction among you, We will punish another faction because they were criminals.﴾

In this verse there are several issues:

The first issue: They mentioned several things concerning the occasion of revelation of the verse. The first: Ibn 'Umar narrated that a man from the hypocrites said during the Battle of Tabuk: "I have never seen people with more fearful hearts, more lying tongues, or more cowardly at the encounter than these people," meaning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and the believers. One of the Companions said: "You lie, rather you are a hypocrite." Then he went to inform the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, but he found that the Qur'an had preceded him. That man came to the Messenger of Allah, while he had mounted his she-camel, and said: "O Messenger of Allah, we were only playing and talking about the talk of travelers, cutting the road with it." He kept saying: "We were only conversing and playing," while the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?" and he did not turn to him, nor did he add anything to that. The second: al-Hasan and Qatadah said: When the Messenger went to Tabuk, the hypocrites said among themselves: "Does he think he will prevail over al-Sham and take its fortresses and palaces? Far-fetched, far-fetched!" So upon his return he summoned them and said: "Are you the ones who said such and such?" They said: "That was not in earnest in our hearts; we were only conversing and playing." The third: It is related that those who stayed behind from the Messenger ﷺ were asked what they had been doing and what was the reason for their staying behind, and they said this statement.

The fourth: It is transmitted from Abu Muslim that he said, in explaining His saying: ﴿The hypocrites fear lest a surah be sent down about them informing them of what is in their hearts﴾, that they displayed this fear by way of mockery; so He, exalted is He, made clear in this verse that when they were asked, "Why did you do that?" they said, "We did not say that in a spirit of defamation, but only because we were conversing and playing."

The fifth: Know that there is no need, in understanding this verse, for these narrations; for they indicate that they uttered corrupt speech by way of defamation and mockery, and when the Messenger informed them that they had said that, they became afraid and made excuses for it, saying: "We only said that in a manner of play, not in earnest." This is their saying: "We were only conversing and playing," that is: we only said that for the sake of play. This indicates that the word "innama" (only) confines the meaning, for if it did not, it would not follow from their being players that they were not mockers, and then this excuse would not be complete.

The answer: al-Wahidi said: The origin of khawd is entering into a liquid of water and mud, then it became common until it became a name for every entry into something in which there is defilement and harm. The meaning is: we were conversing and playing in vain speech, as a caravan converses to cut the road. The Messenger answered them with his saying: "Was it Allah and His verses and His Messenger that you were mocking?!" And in this there are issues:

The first issue: There is a difference between your saying: "Do you mock Allah?" and your saying: "Is it at Allah that you mock?" The first implies denial of the act of mocking; the second implies denial of directing the mockery at Allah, as if he says: "Granted that you may proceed to mock, but how did you proceed to direct the mockery at Allah?" A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿No ghoul is in it﴾ [al-Saffat: 47]. The purpose is not the negation of ghoul, but the negation that the wine of Paradise be a place for ghoul.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, related about them that they mock Allah and His verses and His Messenger, and it is known that mocking Allah is impossible, so it must have an interpretation, and there are aspects to it:

The first: The intended meaning of mocking Allah is mocking the obligations of Allah, exalted is He.

The second: It is possible that the intended meaning is mocking the mention of Allah; for the names of Allah may be mocked by the disbeliever, just as the believer glorifies and exalts them. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High﴾ [al-A'la: 1], so He commanded the believer to glorify the name of Allah. And He said: ﴿To Allah belong the most beautiful names, so call upon Him by them, and leave those who distort His names﴾ [al-A'raf: 180]. So there is nothing preventing it being said: "Is it Allah?" while meaning: "Is it by mentioning Allah?"

The third: Perhaps when the hypocrites said: "How can Muhammad conquer the fortresses and palaces of al-Sham?" some Muslims said: "Allah will help him in that and grant him victory over them." Then some of the ignorant hypocrites uttered a statement implying disparagement of the power of Allah, as is the habit of the ignorant and the atheists, so that was what was meant.

As for His saying: ﴿and His verses﴾, what is meant by them is the Qur'an and all that indicates the religion. His saying: ﴿and His Messenger﴾ is well known, and this indicates that the people only mentioned what they mentioned by way of mockery.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Make no excuse; you have disbelieved after your belief﴾, and in this there are issues:

The first issue: al-Wahidi transmitted from the lexicographers two views concerning the word i'tidhar (making excuse):

The first view: It is an expression for the erasing of a sin, from their saying: "i'tadharat al-manazil" when they were effaced (darasat). It is said: "I passed by a mu'tadhir dwelling," and i'tidhar is the effacing and the taking of the excuse from it, because the one making an excuse seeks to remove the trace of his sin.

The second view: Ibn al-A'rabi related that i'tidhar is cutting off, and from it one says of the foreskin: 'udhrah, because it is cut off; and the 'udhrat of a girl was named 'udhrah because she is "udhira," that is, cut. And it is said: "i'tadharat al-miyah" when the waters ceased. So the excuse, since it is a cause for cutting off blame, was called 'udhr. Al-Wahidi said: The two views are close, because the erasing of the trace of sin and the cutting off of blame are close to each other.

The second issue: He, exalted is He, made clear that this mocking was disbelief, and reason requires that proceeding into disbelief for the sake of play is not permissible. So it is established that their saying, "We were only conversing and playing," was not a genuine excuse for proceeding into that mockery. Since it was not an excuse in itself, Allah forbade them from making an excuse with it, because restraining from vain speech is obligatory. So He said: ﴿Make no excuse﴾, that is: do not mention this excuse in repelling this offence.

The third issue: His saying: ﴿you have disbelieved after your belief﴾ indicates several rulings:

The first ruling: That mocking the religion, however it occurs, is disbelief in Allah; because mocking indicates belittling, and the great foundation of faith is the glorification of Allah, exalted is He, to the utmost possible, and combining the two is impossible.

The second ruling: It indicates the invalidity of the view of one who says that disbelief enters only into actions of the heart.

The third ruling: It indicates that their statement which proceeded from them was disbelief in reality, even though they had been hypocrites before, and that disbelief can renew itself in the disbeliever moment by moment.

The fourth ruling: It indicates that disbelief occurred only after they had been believers.

It may be asked: since they were hypocrites, how is it valid to describe them with this?

We say: al-Hasan said: The meaning is "you disbelieved after your belief which you displayed." Others said: Your disbelief became manifest to the believers after you had been Muslims in their eyes. The two views are close.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 67:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another. They enjoin what is evil, forbid what is good, and close their hands. They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them. Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient.﴾

Know that this is an explanation of another type of their disgraceful and vile conduct. The purpose is to show that their women are like their men in those reprehensible deeds and wicked actions. So He said: ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another﴾, meaning: in the attribute of hypocrisy, just as a person says, "You are from me and I am from you," meaning our affair is one, with no difference between us. Having stated this, He then detailed it, saying: ﴿They enjoin what is evil﴾. The word "munkar" (evil) includes every ugly thing, but the greatest of it here is denying the Messenger. ﴿And forbid what is good﴾. The word "ma'ruf" (good) includes every fine thing, but the greatest of it here is faith in the Messenger ﷺ. ﴿And close their hands﴾. It was said: from every good; and it was said: from every obligatory good, such as zakat, charity, and spending in the way of Allah. This second view is closer, because He censures them only for abandoning what is obligatory. It also includes not spending on jihad, and by this He alerts to their holding back from jihad. The basis of this is that the giver extends his hand and opens it in giving, so it was said of one who withholds and is stingy: "He has closed his hand."

Then He said: ﴿They have forgotten Allah, so He has forgotten them.﴾ Know that this statement cannot be taken on its apparent sense, because if we understood forgetting in its literal sense, they would not deserve blame for it, since forgetting is not within human capacity; and moreover, it is impossible with respect to Allah, exalted is He. So interpretation is necessary, and it is of two kinds:

The first: its meaning is that they abandoned His command until it became as though it were forgotten, so He recompensed them by making them, as it were, forgotten in regard to His reward and mercy. This is found in forms of speech such as His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil deed is an evil deed like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

The second: forgetting is the opposite of remembrance. When they abandoned remembering Allah through worship and praise of Allah, Allah abandoned remembering them with mercy and kindness. The use of forgetting as a metonymy for abandoning remembrance is apt, because whoever forgets something does not mention it, so the name of the necessary consequence is used as a metonymy for what it necessarily entails.

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, the hypocrites are the defiantly disobedient﴾, meaning: they are the complete ones in transgression. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 68–69:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein. It is sufficient for them. And Allah has cursed them, and they will have an enduring punishment.﴾ ﴿Like those before you, they were greater than you in strength and more abundant in wealth and children. They enjoyed their portion, so you enjoy your portion as those before you enjoyed their portion, and you indulged in vain talk as they indulged. Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter, and it is those who are the losers.﴾

Page 102

Know that when He, exalted is He, had previously explained concerning the hypocrite men and hypocrite women that He had forgotten them, that is, He recompensed them for their abandonment of adhering to obedience to Allah, He reaffirmed this threat and joined the hypocrites with the disbelievers in it, so He said: ﴿Allah has promised the hypocrite men and hypocrite women and the disbelievers the fire of Hell, abiding therein.﴾ There is no doubt that the everlasting Fire is among the greatest of punishments.

Then He said: ﴿It is sufficient for them.﴾ The meaning is that this punishment is sufficient for them, and nothing is more severe than it, and no addition to it is possible.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah has cursed them﴾, that is, He added to that severe punishment humiliation, blame and cursing.

Then He said: ﴿And they will have an enduring punishment.﴾ Someone may say: the meaning of the punishment being enduring (muqim) and its being everlasting (khalid) is one thing, so is this not a repetition?

The answer: it is not a repetition, and the difference can be shown in several respects.

The first: they have another kind of enduring, lasting punishment besides the punishment by the Fire and the everlasting abiding mentioned first, and it does not indicate that the punishment by the Fire is lasting. His saying: ﴿And they will have an enduring punishment﴾ indicates that they have, together with that, another kind of punishment.

Someone may say: this interpretation is problematic, because He said of the everlasting Fire: ﴿It is sufficient for them,﴾ and its being sufficient prevents adding anything else to it.

Its answer: it is sufficient for them in terms of pain and agony, and yet another kind is added to it as an increase in their torment. The second: the intended meaning of His saying ﴿And they will have an enduring punishment﴾ is the immediate punishment from which they never separate, which is what they suffer of the weariness of hypocrisy and the fear of the Messenger's gaining knowledge of their inner selves, and what they constantly fear of various kinds of disgrace.

Then He said: ﴿Like those before you﴾. Know that this is a turn from the third person to the second person (direct address), and this kaf is for comparison, and it admits of several aspects. The first: al-Farra' said: "You did like the deeds of those before you." The meaning is that He, exalted is He, likened the hypocrites to the disbelievers who were before them in commanding what is reprehensible, forbidding what is good, and withholding their hands from good deeds. Then He, exalted is He, described those disbelievers as being greater than these hypocrites in strength and more abundant in wealth and children, then they enjoyed the world for a period, then they perished, were destroyed, and turned to lasting punishment; so you, with your weakness and the scarcity of worldly goods with you, are more deserving to be like that.

The second aspect: He, exalted is He, likened the hypocrites in their deviation from obedience to Allah, exalted is He, for the sake of seeking worldly pleasures, to those disbelievers before them. Then He described them, exalted is He, with abundance of wealth and children, and that they enjoyed their khalaq (portion). Al-Khalaq is the portion, that which is created for a human being, that is, what good is decreed for him, as it is said of him "qasm" because it is a share and a portion; because it is "nusiba," that is, it is established. So He mentioned that they enjoyed their khalaq, and you, O hypocrites, have enjoyed your khalaq as those enjoyed theirs.

If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning enjoyment by khalaq regarding the earlier ones once, then mentioning it regarding the hypocrites a second time, then mentioning it regarding the earlier ones a third time?

We say: the benefit in it is that He, exalted is He, censured the earlier ones for enjoying what they were given of worldly portions, and for being deprived of the happiness of the Hereafter because of their being absorbed in those immediate portions. When He, exalted is He, established this censure, He returned and likened the condition of these hypocrites

Page 103

to their condition, and this is the utmost in emphasis. An example of this: whoever wishes to alert some oppressor to the ugliness of his oppression says to him: "You are like Pharaoh, who used to kill without a crime and torment without cause, and you do the same as he did." In sum, the repetition here is for emphasis.

When He, exalted is He, made clear the resemblance of these hypocrites to those earlier ones in seeking the world and in turning away from seeking the Hereafter, He made clear the existence of resemblance between the two groups in denying the prophets and in deceit, treachery and betrayal toward them, so He said: ﴿And you indulged in vain talk as they indulged.﴾ al-Farra' said: He means "like their indulgence which they indulged in," so "alladhi" is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun (masdar) indicated by the verb.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾; that is, their good deeds became void in this world due to death, poverty, and the transition from honor to humiliation and from strength to weakness, and in the Hereafter because they will not be rewarded, but rather punished with the most severe punishment: ﴿and it is those who are the losers.﴾ Since they exhausted themselves in rejecting the prophets and messengers, they found from it nothing but the loss of good in this world and the Hereafter, and nothing but the occurrence of punishment in this world and the Hereafter. The intended meaning is that when He, exalted is He, likened the condition of these hypocrites to those disbelievers, He made clear that those disbelievers obtained nothing but the nullification of their deeds and nothing but disgrace and loss, even though they were stronger than these hypocrites and more abundant in wealth and children than them. So these hypocrites, who share with them in these ugly deeds, are more deserving to be in the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, deprived of the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Al-Khalaq is the portion, that which is created for a human being, that is, what good is decreed for him, as it is said of him "qasm" because it is a share and a portion; because it is "nusiba," that is, it is established.
