If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning enjoyment by khalaq regarding the earlier ones once, then mentioning it regarding the hypocrites a second time, then mentioning it regarding the earlier ones a third time?

We say: the benefit in it is that He, exalted is He, censured the earlier ones for enjoying what they were given of worldly portions, and for being deprived of the happiness of the Hereafter because of their being absorbed in those immediate portions. When He, exalted is He, established this censure, He returned and likened the condition of these hypocrites

Page 103

to their condition, and this is the utmost in emphasis. An example of this: whoever wishes to alert some oppressor to the ugliness of his oppression says to him: "You are like Pharaoh, who used to kill without a crime and torment without cause, and you do the same as he did." In sum, the repetition here is for emphasis.

When He, exalted is He, made clear the resemblance of these hypocrites to those earlier ones in seeking the world and in turning away from seeking the Hereafter, He made clear the existence of resemblance between the two groups in denying the prophets and in deceit, treachery and betrayal toward them, so He said: ﴿And you indulged in vain talk as they indulged.﴾ al-Farra' said: He means "like their indulgence which they indulged in," so "alladhi" is an attribute of a omitted verbal noun (masdar) indicated by the verb.

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those are the ones whose deeds have become worthless in this world and the Hereafter﴾; that is, their good deeds became void in this world due to death, poverty, and the transition from honor to humiliation and from strength to weakness, and in the Hereafter because they will not be rewarded, but rather punished with the most severe punishment: ﴿and it is those who are the losers.﴾ Since they exhausted themselves in rejecting the prophets and messengers, they found from it nothing but the loss of good in this world and the Hereafter, and nothing but the occurrence of punishment in this world and the Hereafter. The intended meaning is that when He, exalted is He, likened the condition of these hypocrites to those disbelievers, He made clear that those disbelievers obtained nothing but the nullification of their deeds and nothing but disgrace and loss, even though they were stronger than these hypocrites and more abundant in wealth and children than them. So these hypocrites, who share with them in these ugly deeds, are more deserving to be in the punishment of this world and the Hereafter, deprived of the good of this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 70:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them: the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud, the people of Abraham, the companions of Madyan, and the overturned cities? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs. It was not God who wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, compared the hypocrites with the earlier unbelievers in their desire for this world, and in denying the prophets and going to extremes in harming them, He explained that those earlier unbelievers were among them, so He mentioned these six groups. The first of them: the people of Noah, whom God destroyed by drowning. The second: ʿAd, whom God destroyed by sending upon them the barren wind. The third: Thamud, whom God destroyed by sending the Shout and the thunderbolt. The fourth: the people of Abraham, whom God destroyed by depriving them of blessing; and it is related in the reports that He set a gnat upon the brain of Nimrod. The fifth: the people of Shuʿayb, who are the companions of Madyan, and it is said that they were descendants of Madyan ibn Abraham; God destroyed them with the punishment of the Day of the Canopy. The overturned cities (al-Mu'tafikat) are the people of Lot, whom God destroyed by making the high part of their land its low part, and rained down stones upon them. Al-Wahidi said: "al-Mu'tafikat" is the plural of "mu'tafikah," and the meaning of ʾi'tifak (overturning) in the language is inversion: those towns were overturned with their people, that is, they were turned over so that their upper part became their lower part. It is said: "afakahu fa-iftafak," meaning he turned it over and it was overturned. According to this interpretation, al-Mu'tafikat is an attribute of the towns. It was also said: their ʾi'tifak is the inversion of their conditions from good to evil.

Know that in the first verse He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Has there not come to them the news of those before them﴾, and mentioned these six groups. He said this because the news of these groups reached them at times by hearing these reports from people, and at times because the lands of these groups, which are the lands of al-Sham, are close to the lands of the Arabs, and their traces remain visible. His saying: ﴿Has there not come to them﴾, although it is in the form of a question, its intended meaning is affirmation, that is: the news of these peoples has come to them.

Then He said: ﴿Their messengers came to them﴾, and this refers back to all these groups.

Then He said: ﴿with clear proofs﴾, that is, with miracles, and there must be an implied element in the speech, the sense being: they denied, so God hastened their destruction.

Then He said: ﴿It was not God who wronged them, but they were wronging themselves.﴾ The meaning: the punishment which God brought upon them was not an injustice from God, because they deserved it by reason of their ugly deeds and their extremes in denying their prophets; rather, they had wronged themselves.

The Mu'tazilah said: this verse indicates that it is not possible for Him, exalted is He, to commit injustice, for otherwise praising Himself for it would not be fitting; and that indicates He never does injustice at all. That in turn indicates that He does not create disbelief in the disbeliever and then punish him for it, and it indicates that the doer of injustice is the servant, as in His saying: ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾. This discussion has been mentioned in this book many times, beyond counting.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 71:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another; they enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and they establish prayer and give zakat and obey Allah and His Messenger. Those — Allah will have mercy on them. Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, had emphasized the description of the hypocrites by their corrupt deeds and wicked actions, and then mentioned after it the various kinds of threat against them in this world and the Hereafter, He mentioned after that in this verse the believers being described with the qualities of goodness and the works of righteousness, in contrast to the qualities of the hypocrites. Then He mentioned after that in this verse the kinds of reward that Allah has prepared for them, the lasting reward and the enduring bliss. As for the qualities of the believers, they are His saying: ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another.﴾

If it is asked: What is the benefit in His saying, concerning the attributes of the hypocrites, ﴿The hypocrite men and the hypocrite women are of one another⁠﴾, while here, concerning the attributes of the believers, He says ﴿And the believing men and the believing women are allies of one another⁠﴾? Why did He use the word "min" (of) for the hypocrites and the word "awliya'" (allies) for the believers?

We say: His saying concerning the attributes of the hypocrites, ﴿some of them are of others⁠﴾, indicates that the hypocrisy of the followers is like a matter branching from the hypocrisy of the predecessors, and the matter in itself is so; because the hypocrisy and disbelief of the followers came about through imitation of those great ones, and through the demands of desire, natural disposition and habit. As for the agreement that exists among the believers, it came about not through inclination

Page 105
and habit, but through sharing in reasoning, success and guidance. Because of this cause, He, exalted is He, said of the hypocrites: ﴿some of them are of others⁠﴾, and said of the believers: ﴿some of them are allies of others⁠﴾.

Know that wilayah (allegiance, close bond) is the opposite of enmity, and we have mentioned earlier that the original meaning of the word wilayah is nearness, and this is reinforced by the fact that the opposite of wilayah is enmity, and the word for enmity (ʿadawah) is derived from ʿadā al-shay', meaning when one passes beyond something.

Know that when He, exalted is He, described the believers as being allies of one another, He then mentioned what serves as an explanation and elaboration of it, saying: ﴿They enjoin what is right and forbid what is wrong, and they establish prayer and give zakat and obey Allah and His Messenger.⁠﴾ He mentioned these five matters by which the believer is distinguished from the hypocrite. The hypocrite, as Allah described him in the preceding verse, enjoins what is wrong and forbids what is right, while the believer is the opposite of that. The hypocrite does not stand to prayer except with a kind of laziness, while the believer is the opposite of that. The hypocrite is stingy with zakat and the other obligations, as He said: ﴿and they withhold their hands⁠﴾ [al-Tawbah: 67]. The believers give zakat. And the hypocrite, when Allah and His Messenger command him to hasten to jihad, he holds himself back and discourages others, as Allah described him, while the believers are the opposite of them. This is what is meant in this verse by His saying: ﴿and they obey Allah and His Messenger⁠﴾.

Then, when He had mentioned the attributes of the believers, He made clear that just as He promised the hypocrites the Fire of Hell, He has promised the believers the future mercy, which is the reward of the Hereafter. Therefore He said: ﴿Those — Allah will have mercy on them.⁠﴾ He mentioned the letter sin (س) in His saying ﴿Allah will have mercy on them⁠﴾ for emphasis and intensification, just as one emphasizes a threat when saying: "I will take revenge on you someday," meaning that you will not escape me, even if that is delayed. Its parallels are: ﴿The Most Merciful will appoint for them affection⁠﴾ [Maryam: 96], ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied⁠﴾ [al-Duha: 5], ﴿He will give them their rewards⁠﴾ [al-Nisa': 152].

Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Exalted in Might and Wise⁠﴾, and this necessitates intensification in encouragement and warning, because the Mighty (al-ʿAziz) is the one who is not prevented from His will concerning His servants, whether mercy or punishment, and the Wise (al-Hakim) is the one who manages the affairs of His servants according to what justice and rightness require.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 72:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of perpetual residence (ʿAdn). And approval from Allah is greater. That is the great achievement.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the promise in the first verse in summary form, He mentioned it in this verse in detail. This is because He promised mercy, and then in this verse He clarified that this mercy consists of these things. The first of them is His saying: ﴿gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein﴾. The closer view is that He meant by them the orchards that are pleasing to the eye, because He said after it: ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of ʿAdn﴾. The conjoined element must be different from the element it is conjoined to, so their dwellings are in gardens of ʿAdn, and their scenic places are the gardens which are the orchards. Thus the benefit of describing them as ʿAdn (perpetual residence) is that they function as the house in which a person dwells. As for the gardens of the Hereafter, they function as the orchards to which a person may go for the sake of recreation and meeting loved ones.

The second: His saying: ﴿and pleasant dwellings in gardens of ʿAdn﴾. The scholars of narrations have said much about the description of the gardens of ʿAdn. Al-Hasan said: "I asked ʿImran ibn Husayn and Abu Hurayrah about His saying:
Page 106

﴿and pleasant dwellings﴾. They said: "You have come to the one who knows. We asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about that, and he (ﷺ) said: 'It is a palace in Paradise made of pearl, in which there are seventy houses of red ruby; in each house are seventy chambers of green emerald; in each chamber are seventy couches; on each couch are seventy mattresses; on each mattress is a wife from the Houris of wide eyes; in each chamber are seventy tables; on each table are seventy kinds of food; and in each chamber are seventy servant-girls. The believer is given strength in a single morning sufficient for all of that.'"

And from Ibn ʿAbbas: it is the House of Allah which no eye has seen and which has not occurred to the heart of any human. I say: Perhaps Ibn ʿAbbas said: it is the abode of those brought near to Allah, for he was too knowledgeable about Allah to affirm for Him a house. And from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him: I said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Paradise, what is its building?" He said: "A brick of gold and a brick of silver, its mortar is musk of strong fragrance, its dust is saffron, and its pebbles are pearls and rubies. In it is bliss without distress, and eternity without death; its garments do not wear out and its youth does not fade."

Ibn Masʿud said: the gardens of ʿAdn are the middle (buṭnān) of Paradise. Al-Azhari said: its buṭnān is its middle, and the buṭnān of valleys are the places where flood water collects; its singular is baṭn. ʿAtaʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbas: it is the capital of Paradise, its ceiling is the Throne of the Merciful, and it is the city in which are the messengers, the prophets, the martyrs and the leaders of guidance, and the rest of the gardens are around it. In it is the spring of Tasnim, and in it are palaces of pearl, ruby and gold. A pleasant wind blows from beneath the Throne and brings to them heaps of strong-scented musk.

ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr said: In Paradise there is a palace called ʿAdn, around it are the towers, and it has five thousand doors; at each door are five thousand guards. No one enters it except a prophet, a truthful one, or a martyr.

I say: The summary of the discussion is that regarding the gardens of ʿAdn there are two views. One of them: it is a proper name for a specific place in Paradise, and these reports and narrations which we have cited strengthen this view. The author of al-Kashshaf said: "ʿAdn is a proper name, as evidenced by His saying: ﴿gardens of ʿAdn which the Most Merciful promised﴾ [Maryam: 61]."

The second view: it is a description of Paradise. Al-Azhari said: ʿadn is derived from your saying: "So-and-so ʿadana in the place" when he remained in it, yaʿdinu ʿuduwwan. The Arabs say: "I left the camels of the sons of so-and-so ʿawadin in such-and-such a place," meaning that the camels remain at the place, become accustomed to it, and do not leave it. From this comes al-maʿdin (the mine), which is the place where gems are formed and whose source is from it. Those who hold this derivation say: all the gardens are gardens of ʿAdn.

The third type of the promises which Allah, exalted is He, mentioned in this verse is His saying: ﴿and approval from Allah is greater﴾. The meaning is that the approval of Allah is greater than everything previously mentioned. Know that this is the decisive proof that spiritual felicities are nobler and higher than physical felicities. This is because either the joy lies in his Lord being pleased with him, and he may use that approval as a means to some physical pleasure, or the matter is not so, but rather his knowledge that He is pleased with him necessitates joy and happiness for its own sake, without his using it as a means to another goal. The first is invalid, because what is a means to something cannot be of higher standing than that intended thing. If the intended thing of Allah's approval were that it be used as a means to the pleasures which Allah has prepared in Paradise, such as eating and drinking, then joy in the approval would be joy in the intended thing; but we have stated that joy in a means must necessarily be of lesser standing than joy in the intended thing. Therefore it is necessary that Allah's approval be of lesser standing and lower rank than the attainment of the gardens and the pleasant dwellings. But the matter is not so, because He, exalted is He, explicitly stated that attaining the approval is higher, greater, more majestic and greater. That is a decisive proof that spiritual felicities are more perfect and nobler than physical felicities.

Know that the correct and true doctrine is the obligation of affirming both together, as Allah combined them in this verse.

When He, exalted is He, mentioned these three matters, He said: ﴿That is the great achievement﴾, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: man is created from two substances: a subtle, higher, spiritual one, and a dense, lower, physical one. To these two is added the attainment of happiness or wretchedness. When physical goods are attained and spiritual felicities are added to them, the soul is successful with the felicities suited to it, and the body reaches the felicities suited to it. There is no doubt that this is the great achievement.

The second: He, exalted is He, explained in describing the hypocrites that they imitated the disbelievers who were before them in indulging in the world and its good things. Then He, exalted is He, explained in this verse the description of the reward of the believers, and then said: ﴿That is the great achievement﴾. The meaning: this is the great achievement, not what the hypocrites and disbelievers seek of indulgence in the good things of the world. It is related that He, exalted is He, says to the people of Paradise: "Are you content?" They say: "And what would stop us from being content, when You have given us what You have not given any of Your creation?" He says: "Shall I not give you something better than that?" They say: "And what is better than that?" He says: "I shall let My pleasure rest upon you, so I shall never be displeased with you ever after."

Know that the indication of this hadith that spiritual felicities are better than physical ones is like the indication of the verse, and its establishment has already been explained in full.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites, and be harsh with them. Their refuge is Hell, and what an evil destination.﴾

Know that we have mentioned that when He, may He be exalted, described the hypocrites with the evil attributes and threatened them with various kinds of punishment, and since God's custom in this Noble Book has been to mention the promise together with the threat, He therefore mentioned right after it the description of the believers with the noble, pure and good attributes, and promised them the lofty reward and the high ranks. Then He returned once more to explaining the condition of the disbelievers and the hypocrites in this verse, and said: ﴿O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites.﴾ There is a question regarding the verse, namely that the verse indicates the obligation of striving against the hypocrites, and that is not permissible, for the hypocrite is one who conceals his disbelief and denies it with his tongue, and when the matter is such, it is not permissible to wage war against him or to strive against him.

Know that people have mentioned opinions in response to this problem.

The first opinion: it means striving against the disbelievers and harshness of speech toward the hypocrites, and this is the view of al-Dahhak. This is far-fetched, because the apparent sense of His saying ﴿strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾ requires the command to strive against both together, and likewise the apparent sense of His saying ﴿and be harsh with them﴾ refers to both groups.

The second opinion: when He, may He be exalted, made clear to the Messenger ﷺ that he should judge by the outward appearance, he, peace be upon him, said: "We judge by the outward appearance," and the people used to show Islam and deny disbelief, so fighting against them was not permissible.

The third opinion, which is the correct one: striving (jihad) is an expression for exerting effort, and there is nothing in the wording that indicates that this striving is by the sword, or by the tongue, or by some other means. So we say: the verse indicates the obligation of striving against both groups, but as for the manner of that striving, the wording of the verse does not indicate it; rather, it is known only from another proof.

And when this is established, we say: the separate proofs indicate that striving against the disbelievers must be by the sword, and against the hypocrites by displaying the proof at times, by withholding gentleness a second time, and by rebuke a third time. ʿAbdullah (Ibn Masʿud) said regarding His saying ﴿strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites﴾: "Sometimes by the hand, sometimes by the tongue, and whoever is not able, let him frown in his face, and whoever is not able, then by the heart." Al-Hasan understood the striving against the hypocrites as the establishing of the prescribed punishments (hudud) upon them when they engage in their causes. Al-Qadi said: this is not something; for the establishing of the hadd is obligatory upon one who is not a hypocrite, so this has no connection with hypocrisy.

Then he said: al-Hasan only said that for one of two reasons: either because every sinner (fasiq) is a hypocrite, or because the majority of those upon whom the hadd was established in the time of the Messenger ﷺ were hypocrites.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 74:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it], but they did say the word of disbelief and disbelieved after their Islam, and they planned what they did not attain. And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty. So if they repent, it will be better for them; but if they turn away, Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter, and they will have no protector or helper on earth.﴾

Know that this verse indicates that groups of the hypocrites spoke corrupt words, then when it was said to them, "You have mentioned these words," they feared and swore that they had not said them. The exegetes have mentioned several views regarding the occasions of revelation:

The first: It is narrated that "the Prophet ﷺ remained during the expedition of Tabuk for two months, the Qur'an being revealed to him, and he reproached the hypocrites who had stayed behind. Al-Jullas ibn Suwayd said: 'By Allah, if what Muhammad says about our brothers whom we left behind in Madinah is true, though they are our nobles, then we are worse than donkeys.' Amir ibn Qays al-Ansari said to al-Jullas: 'Indeed, by Allah, Muhammad is truthful, and you are worse than a donkey.' This reached the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, who summoned al-Jullas, and he swore by Allah that he had not said it. Amir raised his hand and said: 'O Allah, send down upon Your servant and Your Prophet the confirmation of the truthful and the refutation of the liar.' Then this verse was revealed. Al-Jullas said: 'Indeed Allah has mentioned repentance in this verse, and I did say this statement, and Amir spoke the truth.' So al-Jullas repented, and his repentance was good."

The second: It is narrated that it was revealed concerning "Abdullah ibn Ubayy when he said: 'If we return to Madinah, the mightier will surely expel the meaner from it,' and he meant the Messenger ﷺ. Zayd ibn Arqam heard that and conveyed it to the Messenger, and Umar intended to kill Abdullah ibn Ubayy, but Abdullah came and swore that he had not said it," and then this verse was revealed.

The third: Qatadah narrated that "two men fought, one of them from Juhaynah and the other from Ghifar, and the Ghifari prevailed over the Juhayni. Abdullah ibn Ubayy called out: 'O sons of al-Aws, support your brother! By Allah, our likeness and the likeness of Muhammad is only as it is said: Fatten your dog and it will eat you.' They reported this to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and Abdullah denied it and began to swear."

Al-Qadi said: It is far-fetched that the meaning of the verse is these incidents, because His saying: ﴿They swear by Allah that they did not say [it], but they did say the word of disbelief﴾ up to the end of the verse are all plural forms, and taking a plural form to refer to one person is contrary to the original usage.

If it is said: Perhaps that one person said it in a gathering and the rest approved of it.

We reply: This too is contrary to the apparent meaning, because attributing a statement to those who heard it and approved of it is contrary to the original usage. Then he said: Rather, it is better to take this verse as referring to what is narrated: "that the hypocrites planned to kill him on his return from Tabuk, and they were fifteen. They agreed to push him from his mount into the valley when he ascended the steep path at night. Ammar ibn Yasir was holding the halter of his mount, and Hudhayfah was behind it driving it. Hudhayfah heard the sound of camels' hooves and the clatter of weapons, so he turned, and there were people wrapped in face-coverings. He said: 'Away from me, away from me, O enemies of Allah!' And they fled." The apparent meaning is that when they gathered for that purpose, they had thereby slandered his prophethood and attributed to him lying and fabrication in claiming the message, and that is the saying of the word of disbelief. This view is the one chosen by al-Zajjaj.

As for His saying: ﴿and disbelieved after their Islam﴾, one may say: they had embraced Islam, so how does this statement befit them?

The answer is in two respects:

The first: By Islam is meant peace, which is the opposite of war, for when they feigned hypocrisy they displayed Islam and inclined towards it; so when they openly declared war, fighting them became obligatory.

The second: They displayed disbelief after they had displayed Islam.

As for His saying: ﴿and they planned what they did not attain﴾, the meaning is their unanimous resolve to assassinate the Messenger, and Allah, may He be exalted, informed the Messenger, peace be upon him, of that, so that he guarded against them, and they did not reach their goal.

As for His saying: ﴿And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them from His bounty﴾, there are two discussions regarding it:

The first discussion: Concerning this bounty there are two views:

The first: These hypocrites, before the coming of the Prophet ﷺ to Madinah, were in hardship of life, not riding horses nor obtaining booty; and after his coming, they took the spoils, gained wealth, and found power, and this requires of them that they love him and strive with their lives and wealth for his sake.

The second: It is narrated that "a client of al-Jullas was killed, so the Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered his blood-money to be twelve thousand, and he became rich."

The second discussion: His saying: ﴿And they did not resent except that Allah and His Messenger had enriched them﴾ is an indication that there is nothing for which they could find fault with him; this is like the saying of the poet:

They found no fault with the Banu Umayyah except that they are forbearing when they are angry.

And like the saying of al-Nabighah:

There is no blemish in them, except that their swords have notches from the clashing of the battalions.

That is, there is no blemish in them. Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿So if they repent, it will be better for them﴾, and the meaning is to win their hearts after the great offence had come from them. Apparently it means only that if they repent they will gain good; as for whether they did repent, the verse does not say so, and we have already mentioned what was said about the repentance of al-Jullas.

Then He said: ﴿But if they turn away﴾, that is, from repentance, ﴿Allah will punish them with a painful punishment in this world and the Hereafter.﴾ As for the punishment of the Hereafter, it is known. As for the punishment in this world, it has been said: it means that when their disbelief became manifest among the people, they became like the people of war, so fighting them, killing them, taking captive their children and wives, and seizing their property became lawful. It has also been said: it refers to what befalls them at death and in witnessing the angels of punishment. And it has been said: it refers to the punishment of the grave. ﴿And they will have no protector or helper on earth﴾, meaning: when the punishment of Allah is decreed, no protector or helper will benefit them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private talk, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

Know that most of this surah is devoted to describing the hypocrites (munafiqun). There is no doubt that they are of various categories and kinds, and for this reason He mentions them in detail, saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61] ﴿And among them is he who criticizes you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49] – ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's property was delayed from him in Syria, so hardship befell him, and he swore by Allah while standing in some of the gatherings of the Ansar: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely fulfil from it the right of Allah," up to the end of the verse. The well-known account concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is: "That Tha'labah ibn Hatib said: O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth! The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Tha'labah, a little of which you render its thanks is better than a lot which you cannot bear.' He returned to him and said: By He who sent you with the truth, if Allah grants me wealth, I will surely give to everyone with a right his right. So he (ﷺ) supplicated for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for them. So he moved to a valley nearby, and he began to pray Zuhr and 'Asr and to leave off what was other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except for Friday, then he abandoned Friday too, and he began to meet the riders asking about news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked about him and was informed of his situation, and he said: 'Woe to Tha'labah!' Then the revelation came: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], so he sent two men to him and said: 'Pass by Tha'labah and take his charity.' At that, he said to them: 'This is nothing but a jizyah, or the sister of the jizyah,' and he did not pay the charity. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. It was said to him: 'Such-and-such has been revealed concerning you,' so he came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and asked him to accept his charity. He said: 'Indeed Allah has forbidden me from accepting it from you.' So he began throwing dust on his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I told you, but you did not obey me.' He returned to his home, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. Then he came to Abu Bakr with his charity, but he did not accept it, following the example of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then 'Umar did not accept it, following the example of Abu Bakr. Then 'Uthman did not accept it, and Tha'labah died during the caliphate of 'Uthman."

If it is said: Allah commanded him to bring out the charity, so how is it permissible for the Messenger (ﷺ) not to accept it from him?

We say: It is not far-fetched to say that Allah forbade the Messenger (ﷺ) from accepting the charity from him as a means of humiliating him, so that others might take a lesson from him and not refrain from paying charities. It is also not far-fetched that he brought that charity out only for show, not sincerely; Allah informed the Messenger (ﷺ) of that, so he did not accept that charity for this reason. It is also possible that when He said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity, by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾, this aim was not achieved in Tha'labah given his hypocrisy; for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from taking that charity. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that some of the hypocrites made a covenant with Allah that if He gave him wealth, he would spend part of it on the channels of good works. Then Allah gave him wealth, and that person did not fulfil that covenant. Here there are questions:

The first question: The hypocrite is a disbeliever; how can a disbeliever make a covenant with Allah the Exalted?

The answer: The hypocrite may be one who knows Allah, but who denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Because he knows Allah, he can make a covenant with Allah; and because he denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), he is a disbeliever. And how could I not say this, when most of this world is linked with the existence of the Creator, the Capable, and few among the kinds of disbelievers deny Him? All of them acknowledge that He, the Exalted, is the One who opens to man the doors of good, and they know that drawing near to Him is possible through acts of obedience and deeds of righteousness and kindness to creation. These are matters agreed upon by most people. Also, perhaps when he made this covenant with Allah the Exalted, he was a Muslim; then, when he became stingy with the wealth and did not fulfil the covenant, he became a hypocrite. The wording of the verse indicates what we have mentioned, where He said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾.

The second question: Is it a condition of this covenant that it be uttered with the tongue, or is there no need for utterance, such that if he intended it in his heart he enters under this covenant?

The answer: Some said: whatever he mentioned with the tongue, or did not mention but intended in his heart, is included in this covenant. It is narrated from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman that he said: A strong wind struck us at sea, and some of us vowed various kinds of vows, and I intended something but did not speak it. When I arrived at Basra I asked my father, and he said: "My son, fulfil it!" The proponents of this view said: the words ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾ refer to something they intended within themselves. Do you not see that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private talk﴾? The scholars who investigate (al-muhaqqiqun) said: this covenant is restricted to the case where it is uttered with the tongue. The evidence for this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, so long as they do not utter it," or words to this meaning. Also, the Exalted's saying: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity"﴾ is a report of their speaking this statement, and its apparent meaning indicates speech with the tongue.

The third question: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ means the bringing out of wealth. Now, bringing out wealth is of two kinds: it may be obligatory, and it may be non-obligatory. The obligatory is of two sorts: one sort is obligatory by the Law's binding from the outset, such as the obligatory zakat and the obligatory maintenance expenses; and another sort is not obligatory except when the servant binds himself by his own choice, such as vows.

Having known these three categories, does His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ encompass all three, or is the matter not so?

The answer: We say: As for the charities that are not obligatory, they are not included under this verse. The evidence for this is that He described them with His saying ﴿they became stingy with it﴾, and stinginess in the usage of the Law denotes withholding what is obligatory. Also, He blamed them for this abandonment, and one who abandons a recommended act does not deserve blame. As for the other two categories, what is obligatory by the Law's binding is necessarily included under the verse, such as the zakat and the wealth that is needed for expenses on the path of Hajj and jihad, and the wealth needed for obligatory maintenance expenses.

It remains to be said: Does this verse indicate that this speaker had bound himself to bring out wealth by way of vow? The more apparent view is that the wording does not indicate this, because what is mentioned in the wording is nothing but his saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾, and this does not imply a vow; for a man may covenant with his Lord that he will perform the obligatory expenditures that fall upon him if Allah grants him abundance. This indicates that what became binding upon them was bound upon them only by reason of this commitment, whereas zakat does not become binding by reason of this commitment, but becomes binding by reason of possessing the minimum amount (nisab) and the passing of a lunar year.

We say: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ does not necessitate that they do this immediately (on the instant), because this is a report of performing this act in the future, and this mere matter does not necessitate immediacy. So it is as if they said: "we will surely give charity at some time," just as they said: ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾, i.e., at the times when prayer is obligatory. Thus it emerges from the interpretation we have mentioned that what falls under this covenant is the bringing out of wealth that must be brought out by the requirement of the Law from the outset. This is strengthened by what we have narrated: that this verse was revealed concerning one who refused to pay zakat. It is as if He, the Exalted, was clarifying the condition of these hypocrites: just as they are hypocrites toward the Messenger and the believers, so too they are hypocrites toward their Lord in what they covenant with Him, and do not fulfil what they say. The purpose of this is to emphasise their description with hypocrisy. Most of these discussions are from the words of al-Qadi (al-Baydawi).

The fourth question: What is meant by "bounty" (fadl) in His saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty﴾?

The answer: It means the granting of wealth by whatever means, whether by way of trade, by way of profit, or by other means.

The fifth question: What is the derivation of "la-nassaddaqanna" (we will surely give charity)?

The answer: Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "la-natasaddaqanna," but the taa' was assimilated into the sad because of their proximity. Al-Layth said: al-Mussaddiq is the giver, and al-Mutasaddiq is the one who asks. Al-Asma'i and al-Farra' said: this is an error; al-Mutasaddiq is the giver, as the Exalted said: ﴿And give charity to us; indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The sixth question: What is meant by His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾?

The answer: The righteous (salih) is the opposite of the corrupt (mufsid), and the corrupt is one who is stingy with what is required of him in the obligations. Therefore the righteous must be one who fulfils what is required of him in the obligations. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Tha'labah had covenanted with Allah the Exalted: "If Allah opens to me the doors of good, I will surely give charity and I will surely..." And I say: there is no evidence for this restriction; rather, His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ points to the bringing out of the obligatory zakat, and His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾ points to bringing out every kind of wealth that must be brought out absolutely.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ This indicates that the Exalted described them with three attributes:

The first attribute: stinginess, which is withholding what is due.

The second attribute: turning away from the covenant.

The third attribute: refusing the commandments and orders of Allah.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

**The First Issue:** His saying, ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾, is a verb, and it must be attributed to something previously mentioned. What was previously mentioned is God, may His remembrance be exalted, along with the covenant-making, almsgiving, righteousness, stinginess, turning away, and aversion. It is not permissible to attribute the consequence of hypocrisy (*nifaq*) to the covenant, almsgiving, or righteousness, because these three are acts of goodness, and it is not permissible to make them the cause of the emergence of hypocrisy. Nor is it permissible to attribute this consequence to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, because the outcome of these three is that the person has abandoned an obligation. That cannot be made the cause of hypocrisy arising in the heart, because that hypocrisy is an expression of disbelief (*kufr*), which is ignorance and the abandonment of some obligation. It is not permissible that this should be the cause of ignorance arising in the heart. Firstly, because abandoning an obligation is a non-existence (*'adam*), while ignorance is an existence, and non-existence cannot cause existence. Secondly, because this stinginess, turning away, and aversion may be found in many sinners, yet hypocrisy does not accompany them. Thirdly, because if this abandonment caused disbelief to arise in the heart, it would cause it whether this abandonment was permissible in the Law or forbidden in the Law, since the difference in the legal rulings does not remove the cause from being a cause. Fourthly, because He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. So if the act of making a consequence were attributed to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, the meaning of the verse would become: "He made hypocrisy in their hearts a consequence of their breaking of promises, their aversion, and their turning away, because they broke the promise to God and because they used to lie," and that is not permissible, because there is a difference between turning away and the arising of hypocrisy in the heart because of the turning away, and it is well known that this is false speech. Thus it has been established by these considerations that this consequence cannot be attributed to any of the things previously mentioned except to God, glorified is He. So it is necessary to attribute it to Him, and the meaning becomes that He, exalted is He, is the One who causes hypocrisy to follow in their hearts. This indicates that the Creator of disbelief in the hearts is God, exalted is He. This is what al-Zajjaj (may God have mercy on him) said: its meaning is that, since they went astray in the past, He, exalted is He, led them astray from the religion in the future. What confirms that His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾ is attributed to God, may His remembrance be exalted, is that He said: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿they meet Him﴾ refers back to God, exalted is He, so it is more appropriate that His saying ﴿So He made it a consequence for them﴾ be attributed to God, exalted is He.

The Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: What is meant by His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts﴾ is that He made them suffer punishment for hypocrisy, and that punishment is the occurrence of grief in their hearts and the tightness of their chests, and the humiliation and reproach that befall them, and this continues for them until the Hereafter. We say: This is far-fetched, because it is a deviation from the apparent meaning without proof or doubt. If he mentions that rational proofs have shown that God, exalted is He, does not create disbelief, we will counter their proofs with rational proofs which, if placed upon the firm mountains, would have crumbled them.

**The Second Issue:** Al-Layth said: It is said, "I caused so-and-so to suffer regret (*a'qabtu fulānan nadāmatan*)," when you make that the outcome of his affair. Al-Hudhali said:

*"My sons perished and left me with grief after sleep, and with a tear that does not cease."*

It is also said: "So-and-so ate a meal which caused him illness (*a'qabathu saqaman*)," and "God caused him to have good (*a'qabahu Allāhu khayran*)." The essential point regarding this is that when one thing occurs after another, it is said: "God caused it to follow (*a'qabahu Allāh*)."

* * *

**The Third Issue:** The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that breaking a covenant and violating a promise produces hypocrisy, so a Muslim must strive greatly to avoid it. If he makes a covenant with God regarding some matter, he should strive to fulfill it. The position of al-Hasan al-Basri (may God have mercy on him) is that it necessarily produces hypocrisy, and he took as evidence this verse and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he prays, fasts, and claims that he is a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Guarantee for me six things and I will guarantee for you Paradise: when you speak, do not lie; when you promise, do not break it; when you are entrusted, do not betray; restrain your eyes, your hands, and your private parts: your eyes from betrayal, your hands from theft, and your private parts from fornication." ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) only mentioned his saying, "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite," regarding the hypocrites specifically, those who spoke to the Prophet (ﷺ) and lied to him, who were entrusted with his secret and betrayed him, and who promised to go out with him and then broke their promise.

It is reported that ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd explained the hadith, saying: When he speaks about God he lies about Him and about His religion and His Messenger; when he promises he breaks it, as mentioned regarding those who made a covenant with God; and when he is entrusted with the religion of God he betrays in secret, so that his heart is contrary to his tongue. It is also reported that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: A man came to al-Hasan and said to him: The sons of Jacob spoke to their father and lied to him in their saying, "The wolf ate him," and they promised him in their saying, ﴿And indeed we will surely guard him﴾ [Yusuf: 12], and then they broke their promise, and their father entrusted them with Joseph and they betrayed him. Shall we then judge them to be hypocrites? Al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) paused.

**The Fourth Issue:** His saying ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ indicates that this covenant-maker died a hypocrite. This report's content corresponded to it, for it is narrated that Tha'laba came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity and said: "Indeed God has forbidden me from accepting your charity." He remained in that state, and no one accepted his charity until he died. This indicates that the content of this report corresponded to it, so it was a report of the unseen, and therefore it was a miracle.

* * *

**The Fifth Issue:** Al-Jubbāʾī said: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists, those who liken God to creation) relied, in establishing the vision of God, exalted is He, on His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]. He said: Meeting (*liqāʾ*) is not an expression for seeing, as evidenced by the fact that He said, describing the hypocrites: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, and they all agree that the disbelievers do not see Him. This indicates that meeting is not an expression for seeing. He said: What strengthens this is His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath that is false in order to cut off the right of a Muslim man, will meet God while He is angry with him." And they all agree that the intended meaning of meeting here is meeting the punishment that is with God, so likewise here. The Qadi praised this statement. I say: I am greatly astonished at such eminent scholars: how their souls were satisfied with such weak considerations! This is because we have set aside the interpretation of the word "meeting" as "seeing" in this verse, and in this report there is a separate proof, so this does not bind us in all other instances. Do you not see that when we introduced specification into some general statements on the basis of a separate proof, we were not obligated to do the same in all general statements, to specify them without evidence? Just as this does not necessarily follow, that does not necessarily follow either. If he says: This statement is only strong if it is established that meeting in the language is an expression for seeing, and that is disputed, we say: There is no doubt that meeting is an expression for arriving, and whoever sees something has arrived at it, so seeing is a meeting, just as attainment (*idrāk*) is reaching. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed we are overtaken"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 61], meaning: "we are about to be caught up with." Then we interpreted it as seeing, so likewise here. Then we say: There is no doubt that meeting here is not seeing; rather, the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, that is, His judgment and decree. It is like a man's saying: "You will meet your deed tomorrow," meaning: "you will be recompensed for it." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. The meaning is: He punished them by bringing about that hypocrisy in their hearts because they had earlier proceeded to break promises and to lie.

[p. 115]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (*sirr*) is what their chests conceal, and the private conversation (*najwā*) is what some of them confer about with one another among themselves. It is derived from *najwa*, which is hidden speech, as if the two who confer together prevented others from joining them and moved away from others. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52]; and His saying: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾ [Yusuf: 80]; and His saying: ﴿So do not confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger, but confer together in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mujadila: 9]; and His saying: ﴿When you confer privately with the Messenger, offer a charity before your private conversation﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12].

Once you know the difference between the secret and the private conversation, the purpose of the verse is as though He, exalted is He, said: "Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation? So how do they dare to engage in hypocrisy, whose essence is concealment and private conferring among themselves, while knowing that God, exalted is He, knows that from their condition just as He knows the outward? And that He punishes for it just as He punishes for the outward?"

Then He said: ﴿And that God is the Knower of the unseen﴾. The one who knows much (*ʿAllām*) is an intensive form of the knower, and the unseen (*ghayb*) is what is absent from the creation. What is meant is that His essence necessitates knowledge of all things, so it must be that He has knowledge of all knowable things, and it is necessary that He is aware of what is in the inner thoughts and the hidden secrets. How, then, is concealment from Him possible? A parallel to the phrase "Knower of the unseen" here is the saying of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. As for describing God with the form ʿAllāmah (the one who knows exceedingly), it is not permissible, because it implies a kind of effort in regard to what is known, and effort with respect to God is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private talk, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

Know that most of this surah is devoted to describing the hypocrites (munafiqun). There is no doubt that they are of various categories and kinds, and for this reason He mentions them in detail, saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61] ﴿And among them is he who criticizes you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49] – ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's property was delayed from him in Syria, so hardship befell him, and he swore by Allah while standing in some of the gatherings of the Ansar: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely fulfil from it the right of Allah," up to the end of the verse. The well-known account concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is: "That Tha'labah ibn Hatib said: O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth!
