The more apparent view is that the wording does not indicate this, because what is mentioned in the wording is nothing but his saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾, and this does not imply a vow; for a man may covenant with his Lord that he will perform the obligatory expenditures that fall upon him if Allah grants him abundance. This indicates that what became binding upon them was bound upon them only by reason of this commitment, whereas zakat does not become binding by reason of this commitment, but becomes binding by reason of possessing the minimum amount (nisab) and the passing of a lunar year.

We say: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ does not necessitate that they do this immediately (on the instant), because this is a report of performing this act in the future, and this mere matter does not necessitate immediacy. So it is as if they said: "we will surely give charity at some time," just as they said: ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾, i.e., at the times when prayer is obligatory. Thus it emerges from the interpretation we have mentioned that what falls under this covenant is the bringing out of wealth that must be brought out by the requirement of the Law from the outset. This is strengthened by what we have narrated: that this verse was revealed concerning one who refused to pay zakat. It is as if He, the Exalted, was clarifying the condition of these hypocrites: just as they are hypocrites toward the Messenger and the believers, so too they are hypocrites toward their Lord in what they covenant with Him, and do not fulfil what they say. The purpose of this is to emphasise their description with hypocrisy. Most of these discussions are from the words of al-Qadi (al-Baydawi).

The fourth question: What is meant by "bounty" (fadl) in His saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty﴾?

The answer: It means the granting of wealth by whatever means, whether by way of trade, by way of profit, or by other means.

The fifth question: What is the derivation of "la-nassaddaqanna" (we will surely give charity)?

The answer: Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "la-natasaddaqanna," but the taa' was assimilated into the sad because of their proximity. Al-Layth said: al-Mussaddiq is the giver, and al-Mutasaddiq is the one who asks. Al-Asma'i and al-Farra' said: this is an error; al-Mutasaddiq is the giver, as the Exalted said: ﴿And give charity to us; indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The sixth question: What is meant by His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾?

The answer: The righteous (salih) is the opposite of the corrupt (mufsid), and the corrupt is one who is stingy with what is required of him in the obligations. Therefore the righteous must be one who fulfils what is required of him in the obligations. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Tha'labah had covenanted with Allah the Exalted: "If Allah opens to me the doors of good, I will surely give charity and I will surely..." And I say: there is no evidence for this restriction; rather, His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ points to the bringing out of the obligatory zakat, and His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾ points to bringing out every kind of wealth that must be brought out absolutely.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ This indicates that the Exalted described them with three attributes:

The first attribute: stinginess, which is withholding what is due.

The second attribute: turning away from the covenant.

The third attribute: refusing the commandments and orders of Allah.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

**The First Issue:** His saying, ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾, is a verb, and it must be attributed to something previously mentioned. What was previously mentioned is God, may His remembrance be exalted, along with the covenant-making, almsgiving, righteousness, stinginess, turning away, and aversion. It is not permissible to attribute the consequence of hypocrisy (*nifaq*) to the covenant, almsgiving, or righteousness, because these three are acts of goodness, and it is not permissible to make them the cause of the emergence of hypocrisy. Nor is it permissible to attribute this consequence to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, because the outcome of these three is that the person has abandoned an obligation. That cannot be made the cause of hypocrisy arising in the heart, because that hypocrisy is an expression of disbelief (*kufr*), which is ignorance and the abandonment of some obligation. It is not permissible that this should be the cause of ignorance arising in the heart. Firstly, because abandoning an obligation is a non-existence (*'adam*), while ignorance is an existence, and non-existence cannot cause existence. Secondly, because this stinginess, turning away, and aversion may be found in many sinners, yet hypocrisy does not accompany them. Thirdly, because if this abandonment caused disbelief to arise in the heart, it would cause it whether this abandonment was permissible in the Law or forbidden in the Law, since the difference in the legal rulings does not remove the cause from being a cause. Fourthly, because He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. So if the act of making a consequence were attributed to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, the meaning of the verse would become: "He made hypocrisy in their hearts a consequence of their breaking of promises, their aversion, and their turning away, because they broke the promise to God and because they used to lie," and that is not permissible, because there is a difference between turning away and the arising of hypocrisy in the heart because of the turning away, and it is well known that this is false speech. Thus it has been established by these considerations that this consequence cannot be attributed to any of the things previously mentioned except to God, glorified is He. So it is necessary to attribute it to Him, and the meaning becomes that He, exalted is He, is the One who causes hypocrisy to follow in their hearts. This indicates that the Creator of disbelief in the hearts is God, exalted is He. This is what al-Zajjaj (may God have mercy on him) said: its meaning is that, since they went astray in the past, He, exalted is He, led them astray from the religion in the future. What confirms that His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾ is attributed to God, may His remembrance be exalted, is that He said: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿they meet Him﴾ refers back to God, exalted is He, so it is more appropriate that His saying ﴿So He made it a consequence for them﴾ be attributed to God, exalted is He.

The Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: What is meant by His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts﴾ is that He made them suffer punishment for hypocrisy, and that punishment is the occurrence of grief in their hearts and the tightness of their chests, and the humiliation and reproach that befall them, and this continues for them until the Hereafter. We say: This is far-fetched, because it is a deviation from the apparent meaning without proof or doubt. If he mentions that rational proofs have shown that God, exalted is He, does not create disbelief, we will counter their proofs with rational proofs which, if placed upon the firm mountains, would have crumbled them.

**The Second Issue:** Al-Layth said: It is said, "I caused so-and-so to suffer regret (*a'qabtu fulānan nadāmatan*)," when you make that the outcome of his affair. Al-Hudhali said:

*"My sons perished and left me with grief after sleep, and with a tear that does not cease."*

It is also said: "So-and-so ate a meal which caused him illness (*a'qabathu saqaman*)," and "God caused him to have good (*a'qabahu Allāhu khayran*)." The essential point regarding this is that when one thing occurs after another, it is said: "God caused it to follow (*a'qabahu Allāh*)."

* * *

**The Third Issue:** The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that breaking a covenant and violating a promise produces hypocrisy, so a Muslim must strive greatly to avoid it. If he makes a covenant with God regarding some matter, he should strive to fulfill it. The position of al-Hasan al-Basri (may God have mercy on him) is that it necessarily produces hypocrisy, and he took as evidence this verse and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he prays, fasts, and claims that he is a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Guarantee for me six things and I will guarantee for you Paradise: when you speak, do not lie; when you promise, do not break it; when you are entrusted, do not betray; restrain your eyes, your hands, and your private parts: your eyes from betrayal, your hands from theft, and your private parts from fornication." ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) only mentioned his saying, "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite," regarding the hypocrites specifically, those who spoke to the Prophet (ﷺ) and lied to him, who were entrusted with his secret and betrayed him, and who promised to go out with him and then broke their promise.

It is reported that ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd explained the hadith, saying: When he speaks about God he lies about Him and about His religion and His Messenger; when he promises he breaks it, as mentioned regarding those who made a covenant with God; and when he is entrusted with the religion of God he betrays in secret, so that his heart is contrary to his tongue. It is also reported that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: A man came to al-Hasan and said to him: The sons of Jacob spoke to their father and lied to him in their saying, "The wolf ate him," and they promised him in their saying, ﴿And indeed we will surely guard him﴾ [Yusuf: 12], and then they broke their promise, and their father entrusted them with Joseph and they betrayed him. Shall we then judge them to be hypocrites? Al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) paused.

**The Fourth Issue:** His saying ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ indicates that this covenant-maker died a hypocrite. This report's content corresponded to it, for it is narrated that Tha'laba came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity and said: "Indeed God has forbidden me from accepting your charity." He remained in that state, and no one accepted his charity until he died. This indicates that the content of this report corresponded to it, so it was a report of the unseen, and therefore it was a miracle.

* * *

**The Fifth Issue:** Al-Jubbāʾī said: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists, those who liken God to creation) relied, in establishing the vision of God, exalted is He, on His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]. He said: Meeting (*liqāʾ*) is not an expression for seeing, as evidenced by the fact that He said, describing the hypocrites: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, and they all agree that the disbelievers do not see Him. This indicates that meeting is not an expression for seeing. He said: What strengthens this is His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath that is false in order to cut off the right of a Muslim man, will meet God while He is angry with him." And they all agree that the intended meaning of meeting here is meeting the punishment that is with God, so likewise here. The Qadi praised this statement. I say: I am greatly astonished at such eminent scholars: how their souls were satisfied with such weak considerations! This is because we have set aside the interpretation of the word "meeting" as "seeing" in this verse, and in this report there is a separate proof, so this does not bind us in all other instances. Do you not see that when we introduced specification into some general statements on the basis of a separate proof, we were not obligated to do the same in all general statements, to specify them without evidence? Just as this does not necessarily follow, that does not necessarily follow either. If he says: This statement is only strong if it is established that meeting in the language is an expression for seeing, and that is disputed, we say: There is no doubt that meeting is an expression for arriving, and whoever sees something has arrived at it, so seeing is a meeting, just as attainment (*idrāk*) is reaching. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed we are overtaken"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 61], meaning: "we are about to be caught up with." Then we interpreted it as seeing, so likewise here. Then we say: There is no doubt that meeting here is not seeing; rather, the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, that is, His judgment and decree. It is like a man's saying: "You will meet your deed tomorrow," meaning: "you will be recompensed for it." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. The meaning is: He punished them by bringing about that hypocrisy in their hearts because they had earlier proceeded to break promises and to lie.

[p. 115]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (*sirr*) is what their chests conceal, and the private conversation (*najwā*) is what some of them confer about with one another among themselves. It is derived from *najwa*, which is hidden speech, as if the two who confer together prevented others from joining them and moved away from others. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52]; and His saying: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾ [Yusuf: 80]; and His saying: ﴿So do not confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger, but confer together in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mujadila: 9]; and His saying: ﴿When you confer privately with the Messenger, offer a charity before your private conversation﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12].

Once you know the difference between the secret and the private conversation, the purpose of the verse is as though He, exalted is He, said: "Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation? So how do they dare to engage in hypocrisy, whose essence is concealment and private conferring among themselves, while knowing that God, exalted is He, knows that from their condition just as He knows the outward? And that He punishes for it just as He punishes for the outward?"

Then He said: ﴿And that God is the Knower of the unseen﴾. The one who knows much (*ʿAllām*) is an intensive form of the knower, and the unseen (*ghayb*) is what is absent from the creation. What is meant is that His essence necessitates knowledge of all things, so it must be that He has knowledge of all knowable things, and it is necessary that He is aware of what is in the inner thoughts and the hidden secrets. How, then, is concealment from Him possible? A parallel to the phrase "Knower of the unseen" here is the saying of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. As for describing God with the form ʿAllāmah (the one who knows exceedingly), it is not permissible, because it implies a kind of effort in regard to what is known, and effort with respect to God is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private talk, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

Know that most of this surah is devoted to describing the hypocrites (munafiqun). There is no doubt that they are of various categories and kinds, and for this reason He mentions them in detail, saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61] ﴿And among them is he who criticizes you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49] – ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's property was delayed from him in Syria, so hardship befell him, and he swore by Allah while standing in some of the gatherings of the Ansar: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely fulfil from it the right of Allah," up to the end of the verse. The well-known account concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is: "That Tha'labah ibn Hatib said: O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth! The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Tha'labah, a little of which you render its thanks is better than a lot which you cannot bear.' He returned to him and said: By He who sent you with the truth, if Allah grants me wealth, I will surely give to everyone with a right his right. So he (ﷺ) supplicated for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for them. So he moved to a valley nearby, and he began to pray Zuhr and 'Asr and to leave off what was other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except for Friday, then he abandoned Friday too, and he began to meet the riders asking about news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked about him and was informed of his situation, and he said: 'Woe to Tha'labah!' Then the revelation came: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], so he sent two men to him and said: 'Pass by Tha'labah and take his charity.' At that, he said to them: 'This is nothing but a jizyah, or the sister of the jizyah,' and he did not pay the charity. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. It was said to him: 'Such-and-such has been revealed concerning you,' so he came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and asked him to accept his charity. He said: 'Indeed Allah has forbidden me from accepting it from you.' So he began throwing dust on his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I told you, but you did not obey me.' He returned to his home, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. Then he came to Abu Bakr with his charity, but he did not accept it, following the example of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then 'Umar did not accept it, following the example of Abu Bakr. Then 'Uthman did not accept it, and Tha'labah died during the caliphate of 'Uthman."

If it is said: Allah commanded him to bring out the charity, so how is it permissible for the Messenger (ﷺ) not to accept it from him?

We say: It is not far-fetched to say that Allah forbade the Messenger (ﷺ) from accepting the charity from him as a means of humiliating him, so that others might take a lesson from him and not refrain from paying charities. It is also not far-fetched that he brought that charity out only for show, not sincerely; Allah informed the Messenger (ﷺ) of that, so he did not accept that charity for this reason. It is also possible that when He said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity, by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾, this aim was not achieved in Tha'labah given his hypocrisy; for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from taking that charity. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that some of the hypocrites made a covenant with Allah that if He gave him wealth, he would spend part of it on the channels of good works. Then Allah gave him wealth, and that person did not fulfil that covenant. Here there are questions:

The first question: The hypocrite is a disbeliever; how can a disbeliever make a covenant with Allah the Exalted?

The answer: The hypocrite may be one who knows Allah, but who denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Because he knows Allah, he can make a covenant with Allah; and because he denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), he is a disbeliever. And how could I not say this, when most of this world is linked with the existence of the Creator, the Capable, and few among the kinds of disbelievers deny Him? All of them acknowledge that He, the Exalted, is the One who opens to man the doors of good, and they know that drawing near to Him is possible through acts of obedience and deeds of righteousness and kindness to creation. These are matters agreed upon by most people. Also, perhaps when he made this covenant with Allah the Exalted, he was a Muslim; then, when he became stingy with the wealth and did not fulfil the covenant, he became a hypocrite. The wording of the verse indicates what we have mentioned, where He said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾.

The second question: Is it a condition of this covenant that it be uttered with the tongue, or is there no need for utterance, such that if he intended it in his heart he enters under this covenant?

The answer: Some said: whatever he mentioned with the tongue, or did not mention but intended in his heart, is included in this covenant. It is narrated from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman that he said: A strong wind struck us at sea, and some of us vowed various kinds of vows, and I intended something but did not speak it. When I arrived at Basra I asked my father, and he said: "My son, fulfil it!" The proponents of this view said: the words ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾ refer to something they intended within themselves. Do you not see that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private talk﴾? The scholars who investigate (al-muhaqqiqun) said: this covenant is restricted to the case where it is uttered with the tongue. The evidence for this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, so long as they do not utter it," or words to this meaning. Also, the Exalted's saying: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity"﴾ is a report of their speaking this statement, and its apparent meaning indicates speech with the tongue.

The third question: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ means the bringing out of wealth. Now, bringing out wealth is of two kinds: it may be obligatory, and it may be non-obligatory. The obligatory is of two sorts: one sort is obligatory by the Law's binding from the outset, such as the obligatory zakat and the obligatory maintenance expenses; and another sort is not obligatory except when the servant binds himself by his own choice, such as vows.

Having known these three categories, does His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ encompass all three, or is the matter not so?

The answer: We say: As for the charities that are not obligatory, they are not included under this verse. The evidence for this is that He described them with His saying ﴿they became stingy with it﴾, and stinginess in the usage of the Law denotes withholding what is obligatory. Also, He blamed them for this abandonment, and one who abandons a recommended act does not deserve blame. As for the other two categories, what is obligatory by the Law's binding is necessarily included under the verse, such as the zakat and the wealth that is needed for expenses on the path of Hajj and jihad, and the wealth needed for obligatory maintenance expenses.

It remains to be said: Does this verse indicate that this speaker had bound himself to bring out wealth by way of vow? The more apparent view is that the wording does not indicate this, because what is mentioned in the wording is nothing but his saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾, and this does not imply a vow; for a man may covenant with his Lord that he will perform the obligatory expenditures that fall upon him if Allah grants him abundance. This indicates that what became binding upon them was bound upon them only by reason of this commitment, whereas zakat does not become binding by reason of this commitment, but becomes binding by reason of possessing the minimum amount (nisab) and the passing of a lunar year.

We say: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ does not necessitate that they do this immediately (on the instant), because this is a report of performing this act in the future, and this mere matter does not necessitate immediacy. So it is as if they said: "we will surely give charity at some time," just as they said: ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾, i.e., at the times when prayer is obligatory. Thus it emerges from the interpretation we have mentioned that what falls under this covenant is the bringing out of wealth that must be brought out by the requirement of the Law from the outset. This is strengthened by what we have narrated: that this verse was revealed concerning one who refused to pay zakat. It is as if He, the Exalted, was clarifying the condition of these hypocrites: just as they are hypocrites toward the Messenger and the believers, so too they are hypocrites toward their Lord in what they covenant with Him, and do not fulfil what they say. The purpose of this is to emphasise their description with hypocrisy. Most of these discussions are from the words of al-Qadi (al-Baydawi).

The fourth question: What is meant by "bounty" (fadl) in His saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty﴾?

The answer: It means the granting of wealth by whatever means, whether by way of trade, by way of profit, or by other means.

The answer: Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "la-natasaddaqanna," but the taa' was assimilated into the sad because of their proximity. Al-Layth said: al-Mussaddiq is the giver, and al-Mutasaddiq is the one who asks. Al-Asma'i and al-Farra' said: this is an error; al-Mutasaddiq is the giver, as the Exalted said: ﴿And give charity to us; indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The sixth question: What is meant by His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾?

The answer: The righteous (salih) is the opposite of the corrupt (mufsid), and the corrupt is one who is stingy with what is required of him in the obligations. Therefore the righteous must be one who fulfils what is required of him in the obligations. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Tha'labah had covenanted with Allah the Exalted: "If Allah opens to me the doors of good, I will surely give charity and I will surely..." And I say: there is no evidence for this restriction; rather, His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ points to the bringing out of the obligatory zakat, and His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾ points to bringing out every kind of wealth that must be brought out absolutely.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ This indicates that the Exalted described them with three attributes:

The first attribute: stinginess, which is withholding what is due.

The second attribute: turning away from the covenant.

The third attribute: refusing the commandments and orders of Allah.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

The Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: What is meant by His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts﴾ is that He made them suffer punishment for hypocrisy, and that punishment is the occurrence of grief in their hearts and the tightness of their chests, and the humiliation and reproach that befall them, and this continues for them until the Hereafter. We say: This is far-fetched, because it is a deviation from the apparent meaning without proof or doubt. If he mentions that rational proofs have shown that God, exalted is He, does not create disbelief, we will counter their proofs with rational proofs which, if placed upon the firm mountains, would have crumbled them.

**The Second Issue:** Al-Layth said: It is said, "I caused so-and-so to suffer regret (*a'qabtu fulānan nadāmatan*)," when you make that the outcome of his affair. Al-Hudhali said:

*"My sons perished and left me with grief after sleep, and with a tear that does not cease."*

It is also said: "So-and-so ate a meal which caused him illness (*a'qabathu saqaman*)," and "God caused him to have good (*a'qabahu Allāhu khayran*)." The essential point regarding this is that when one thing occurs after another, it is said: "God caused it to follow (*a'qabahu Allāh*)."

* * *

**The Third Issue:** The apparent meaning of this verse indicates that breaking a covenant and violating a promise produces hypocrisy, so a Muslim must strive greatly to avoid it. If he makes a covenant with God regarding some matter, he should strive to fulfill it. The position of al-Hasan al-Basri (may God have mercy on him) is that it necessarily produces hypocrisy, and he took as evidence this verse and the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite, even if he prays, fasts, and claims that he is a believer: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays." And from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Guarantee for me six things and I will guarantee for you Paradise: when you speak, do not lie; when you promise, do not break it; when you are entrusted, do not betray; restrain your eyes, your hands, and your private parts: your eyes from betrayal, your hands from theft, and your private parts from fornication." ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabāḥ said: Jābir ibn ʿAbd Allāh narrated to me that the Prophet (ﷺ) only mentioned his saying, "Three characteristics, whoever has them is a hypocrite," regarding the hypocrites specifically, those who spoke to the Prophet (ﷺ) and lied to him, who were entrusted with his secret and betrayed him, and who promised to go out with him and then broke their promise.

It is reported that ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd explained the hadith, saying: When he speaks about God he lies about Him and about His religion and His Messenger; when he promises he breaks it, as mentioned regarding those who made a covenant with God; and when he is entrusted with the religion of God he betrays in secret, so that his heart is contrary to his tongue. It is also reported that Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ said: A man came to al-Hasan and said to him: The sons of Jacob spoke to their father and lied to him in their saying, "The wolf ate him," and they promised him in their saying, ﴿And indeed we will surely guard him﴾ [Yusuf: 12], and then they broke their promise, and their father entrusted them with Joseph and they betrayed him. Shall we then judge them to be hypocrites? Al-Hasan (may God have mercy on him) paused.

**The Fourth Issue:** His saying ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾ indicates that this covenant-maker died a hypocrite. This report's content corresponded to it, for it is narrated that Tha'laba came to the Prophet (ﷺ) with his charity and said: "Indeed God has forbidden me from accepting your charity." He remained in that state, and no one accepted his charity until he died. This indicates that the content of this report corresponded to it, so it was a report of the unseen, and therefore it was a miracle.

* * *

**The Fifth Issue:** Al-Jubbāʾī said: The Mushabbiha (anthropomorphists, those who liken God to creation) relied, in establishing the vision of God, exalted is He, on His saying: ﴿Their greeting on the Day they meet Him will be "Peace"﴾ [al-Ahzab: 44]. He said: Meeting (*liqāʾ*) is not an expression for seeing, as evidenced by the fact that He said, describing the hypocrites: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾, and they all agree that the disbelievers do not see Him. This indicates that meeting is not an expression for seeing. He said: What strengthens this is His saying (ﷺ): "Whoever swears an oath that is false in order to cut off the right of a Muslim man, will meet God while He is angry with him." And they all agree that the intended meaning of meeting here is meeting the punishment that is with God, so likewise here. The Qadi praised this statement. I say: I am greatly astonished at such eminent scholars: how their souls were satisfied with such weak considerations! This is because we have set aside the interpretation of the word "meeting" as "seeing" in this verse, and in this report there is a separate proof, so this does not bind us in all other instances. Do you not see that when we introduced specification into some general statements on the basis of a separate proof, we were not obligated to do the same in all general statements, to specify them without evidence? Just as this does not necessarily follow, that does not necessarily follow either. If he says: This statement is only strong if it is established that meeting in the language is an expression for seeing, and that is disputed, we say: There is no doubt that meeting is an expression for arriving, and whoever sees something has arrived at it, so seeing is a meeting, just as attainment (*idrāk*) is reaching. God, exalted is He, said: ﴿The companions of Moses said, "Indeed we are overtaken"﴾ [al-Shuʿara: 61], meaning: "we are about to be caught up with." Then we interpreted it as seeing, so likewise here. Then we say: There is no doubt that meeting here is not seeing; rather, the intended meaning is that He, exalted is He, made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, that is, His judgment and decree. It is like a man's saying: "You will meet your deed tomorrow," meaning: "you will be recompensed for it." God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. The meaning is: He punished them by bringing about that hypocrisy in their hearts because they had earlier proceeded to break promises and to lie.

[p. 115]

Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (*sirr*) is what their chests conceal, and the private conversation (*najwā*) is what some of them confer about with one another among themselves. It is derived from *najwa*, which is hidden speech, as if the two who confer together prevented others from joining them and moved away from others. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52]; and His saying: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾ [Yusuf: 80]; and His saying: ﴿So do not confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger, but confer together in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mujadila: 9]; and His saying: ﴿When you confer privately with the Messenger, offer a charity before your private conversation﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12].

Once you know the difference between the secret and the private conversation, the purpose of the verse is as though He, exalted is He, said: "Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation? So how do they dare to engage in hypocrisy, whose essence is concealment and private conferring among themselves, while knowing that God, exalted is He, knows that from their condition just as He knows the outward? And that He punishes for it just as He punishes for the outward?"

Then He said: ﴿And that God is the Knower of the unseen﴾. The one who knows much (*ʿAllām*) is an intensive form of the knower, and the unseen (*ghayb*) is what is absent from the creation. What is meant is that His essence necessitates knowledge of all things, so it must be that He has knowledge of all knowable things, and it is necessary that He is aware of what is in the inner thoughts and the hidden secrets. How, then, is concealment from Him possible? A parallel to the phrase "Knower of the unseen" here is the saying of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. As for describing God with the form ʿAllāmah (the one who knows exceedingly), it is not permissible, because it implies a kind of effort in regard to what is known, and effort with respect to God is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 75–78 (part 1 of 2):

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely be among the righteous."﴾ ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him, because they failed Allah in what they promised Him and because they used to lie.﴾ ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secrets and their private talk, and that Allah is the Knower of the unseen?﴾

Know that most of this surah is devoted to describing the hypocrites (munafiqun). There is no doubt that they are of various categories and kinds, and for this reason He mentions them in detail, saying: ﴿And among them are those who harm the Prophet﴾ [al-Tawbah: 61] ﴿And among them is he who criticizes you concerning the charities﴾ [al-Tawbah: 58] ﴿And among them is he who says, "Grant me permission and do not put me to trial"﴾ [al-Tawbah: 49] – ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty"﴾. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Hatib ibn Abi Balta'ah's property was delayed from him in Syria, so hardship befell him, and he swore by Allah while standing in some of the gatherings of the Ansar: "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity and we will surely fulfil from it the right of Allah," up to the end of the verse. The well-known account concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse is: "That Tha'labah ibn Hatib said: O Messenger of Allah, pray to Allah that He grant me wealth! The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'O Tha'labah, a little of which you render its thanks is better than a lot which you cannot bear.' He returned to him and said: By He who sent you with the truth, if Allah grants me wealth, I will surely give to everyone with a right his right. So he (ﷺ) supplicated for him. He acquired sheep, and they multiplied as worms multiply, until Medina became too small for them. So he moved to a valley nearby, and he began to pray Zuhr and 'Asr and to leave off what was other than them. Then they multiplied and increased until he abandoned the prayers except for Friday, then he abandoned Friday too, and he began to meet the riders asking about news. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asked about him and was informed of his situation, and he said: 'Woe to Tha'labah!' Then the revelation came: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103], so he sent two men to him and said: 'Pass by Tha'labah and take his charity.' At that, he said to them: 'This is nothing but a jizyah, or the sister of the jizyah,' and he did not pay the charity. Then Allah revealed: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾. It was said to him: 'Such-and-such has been revealed concerning you,' so he came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and asked him to accept his charity. He said: 'Indeed Allah has forbidden me from accepting it from you.' So he began throwing dust on his head. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I told you, but you did not obey me.' He returned to his home, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. Then he came to Abu Bakr with his charity, but he did not accept it, following the example of the Messenger (ﷺ). Then 'Umar did not accept it, following the example of Abu Bakr. Then 'Uthman did not accept it, and Tha'labah died during the caliphate of 'Uthman."

If it is said: Allah commanded him to bring out the charity, so how is it permissible for the Messenger (ﷺ) not to accept it from him?

We say: It is not far-fetched to say that Allah forbade the Messenger (ﷺ) from accepting the charity from him as a means of humiliating him, so that others might take a lesson from him and not refrain from paying charities. It is also not far-fetched that he brought that charity out only for show, not sincerely; Allah informed the Messenger (ﷺ) of that, so he did not accept that charity for this reason. It is also possible that when He said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity, by which you purify them and cleanse them﴾, this aim was not achieved in Tha'labah given his hypocrisy; for this reason the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) refrained from taking that charity. And Allah knows best.

The second issue: The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that some of the hypocrites made a covenant with Allah that if He gave him wealth, he would spend part of it on the channels of good works. Then Allah gave him wealth, and that person did not fulfil that covenant. Here there are questions:

The first question: The hypocrite is a disbeliever; how can a disbeliever make a covenant with Allah the Exalted?

The answer: The hypocrite may be one who knows Allah, but who denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ). Because he knows Allah, he can make a covenant with Allah; and because he denies the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ), he is a disbeliever. And how could I not say this, when most of this world is linked with the existence of the Creator, the Capable, and few among the kinds of disbelievers deny Him? All of them acknowledge that He, the Exalted, is the One who opens to man the doors of good, and they know that drawing near to Him is possible through acts of obedience and deeds of righteousness and kindness to creation. These are matters agreed upon by most people. Also, perhaps when he made this covenant with Allah the Exalted, he was a Muslim; then, when he became stingy with the wealth and did not fulfil the covenant, he became a hypocrite. The wording of the verse indicates what we have mentioned, where He said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow﴾.

The second question: Is it a condition of this covenant that it be uttered with the tongue, or is there no need for utterance, such that if he intended it in his heart he enters under this covenant?

The answer: Some said: whatever he mentioned with the tongue, or did not mention but intended in his heart, is included in this covenant. It is narrated from al-Mu'tamir ibn Sulayman that he said: A strong wind struck us at sea, and some of us vowed various kinds of vows, and I intended something but did not speak it. When I arrived at Basra I asked my father, and he said: "My son, fulfil it!" The proponents of this view said: the words ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah﴾ refer to something they intended within themselves. Do you not see that He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Do they not know that Allah knows their secret and their private talk﴾? The scholars who investigate (al-muhaqqiqun) said: this covenant is restricted to the case where it is uttered with the tongue. The evidence for this is his (ﷺ) saying: "Indeed Allah has overlooked for my community what their souls whisper, so long as they do not utter it," or words to this meaning. Also, the Exalted's saying: ﴿And among them are those who made a covenant with Allah, "If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity"﴾ is a report of their speaking this statement, and its apparent meaning indicates speech with the tongue.

The third question: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ means the bringing out of wealth. Now, bringing out wealth is of two kinds: it may be obligatory, and it may be non-obligatory. The obligatory is of two sorts: one sort is obligatory by the Law's binding from the outset, such as the obligatory zakat and the obligatory maintenance expenses; and another sort is not obligatory except when the servant binds himself by his own choice, such as vows.

Having known these three categories, does His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ encompass all three, or is the matter not so?

The answer: We say: As for the charities that are not obligatory, they are not included under this verse. The evidence for this is that He described them with His saying ﴿they became stingy with it﴾, and stinginess in the usage of the Law denotes withholding what is obligatory. Also, He blamed them for this abandonment, and one who abandons a recommended act does not deserve blame. As for the other two categories, what is obligatory by the Law's binding is necessarily included under the verse, such as the zakat and the wealth that is needed for expenses on the path of Hajj and jihad, and the wealth needed for obligatory maintenance expenses.

It remains to be said: Does this verse indicate that this speaker had bound himself to bring out wealth by way of vow? The more apparent view is that the wording does not indicate this, because what is mentioned in the wording is nothing but his saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty, we will surely give charity﴾, and this does not imply a vow; for a man may covenant with his Lord that he will perform the obligatory expenditures that fall upon him if Allah grants him abundance. This indicates that what became binding upon them was bound upon them only by reason of this commitment, whereas zakat does not become binding by reason of this commitment, but becomes binding by reason of possessing the minimum amount (nisab) and the passing of a lunar year.

We say: His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ does not necessitate that they do this immediately (on the instant), because this is a report of performing this act in the future, and this mere matter does not necessitate immediacy. So it is as if they said: "we will surely give charity at some time," just as they said: ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾, i.e., at the times when prayer is obligatory. Thus it emerges from the interpretation we have mentioned that what falls under this covenant is the bringing out of wealth that must be brought out by the requirement of the Law from the outset. This is strengthened by what we have narrated: that this verse was revealed concerning one who refused to pay zakat. It is as if He, the Exalted, was clarifying the condition of these hypocrites: just as they are hypocrites toward the Messenger and the believers, so too they are hypocrites toward their Lord in what they covenant with Him, and do not fulfil what they say. The purpose of this is to emphasise their description with hypocrisy. Most of these discussions are from the words of al-Qadi (al-Baydawi).

The fourth question: What is meant by "bounty" (fadl) in His saying ﴿If He gives us of His bounty﴾?

The answer: It means the granting of wealth by whatever means, whether by way of trade, by way of profit, or by other means.

The fifth question: What is the derivation of "la-nassaddaqanna" (we will surely give charity)?

The answer: Al-Zajjaj said: the original is "la-natasaddaqanna," but the taa' was assimilated into the sad because of their proximity. Al-Layth said: al-Mussaddiq is the giver, and al-Mutasaddiq is the one who asks. Al-Asma'i and al-Farra' said: this is an error; al-Mutasaddiq is the giver, as the Exalted said: ﴿And give charity to us; indeed Allah rewards the charitable﴾ [Yusuf: 88].

The sixth question: What is meant by His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾?

The answer: The righteous (salih) is the opposite of the corrupt (mufsid), and the corrupt is one who is stingy with what is required of him in the obligations. Therefore the righteous must be one who fulfils what is required of him in the obligations. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: Tha'labah had covenanted with Allah the Exalted: "If Allah opens to me the doors of good, I will surely give charity and I will surely..." And I say: there is no evidence for this restriction; rather, His saying ﴿we will surely give charity﴾ points to the bringing out of the obligatory zakat, and His saying ﴿and we will surely be among the righteous﴾ points to bringing out every kind of wealth that must be brought out absolutely.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿But when He gave them of His bounty, they became stingy with it and turned away while they were refusing.﴾ This indicates that the Exalted described them with three attributes:

The first attribute: stinginess, which is withholding what is due.

The second attribute: turning away from the covenant.

The third attribute: refusing the commandments and orders of Allah.

* * *

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So He caused hypocrisy to follow in their hearts until the Day they meet Him﴾, and concerning this there are issues:

**The First Issue:** His saying, ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾, is a verb, and it must be attributed to something previously mentioned. What was previously mentioned is God, may His remembrance be exalted, along with the covenant-making, almsgiving, righteousness, stinginess, turning away, and aversion. It is not permissible to attribute the consequence of hypocrisy (*nifaq*) to the covenant, almsgiving, or righteousness, because these three are acts of goodness, and it is not permissible to make them the cause of the emergence of hypocrisy. Nor is it permissible to attribute this consequence to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, because the outcome of these three is that the person has abandoned an obligation. That cannot be made the cause of hypocrisy arising in the heart, because that hypocrisy is an expression of disbelief (*kufr*), which is ignorance and the abandonment of some obligation. It is not permissible that this should be the cause of ignorance arising in the heart. Firstly, because abandoning an obligation is a non-existence (*'adam*), while ignorance is an existence, and non-existence cannot cause existence. Secondly, because this stinginess, turning away, and aversion may be found in many sinners, yet hypocrisy does not accompany them. Thirdly, because if this abandonment caused disbelief to arise in the heart, it would cause it whether this abandonment was permissible in the Law or forbidden in the Law, since the difference in the legal rulings does not remove the cause from being a cause. Fourthly, because He, exalted is He, said after this verse: ﴿Because they broke their promise to God that they had made to Him, and because they used to lie﴾. So if the act of making a consequence were attributed to stinginess, turning away, and aversion, the meaning of the verse would become: "He made hypocrisy in their hearts a consequence of their breaking of promises, their aversion, and their turning away, because they broke the promise to God and because they used to lie," and that is not permissible, because there is a difference between turning away and the arising of hypocrisy in the heart because of the turning away, and it is well known that this is false speech. Thus it has been established by these considerations that this consequence cannot be attributed to any of the things previously mentioned except to God, glorified is He. So it is necessary to attribute it to Him, and the meaning becomes that He, exalted is He, is the One who causes hypocrisy to follow in their hearts. This indicates that the Creator of disbelief in the hearts is God, exalted is He. This is what al-Zajjaj (may God have mercy on him) said: its meaning is that, since they went astray in the past, He, exalted is He, led them astray from the religion in the future. What confirms that His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them﴾ is attributed to God, may His remembrance be exalted, is that He said: ﴿until the Day they meet Him﴾. The pronoun in His saying ﴿they meet Him﴾ refers back to God, exalted is He, so it is more appropriate that His saying ﴿So He made it a consequence for them﴾ be attributed to God, exalted is He.

The Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: What is meant by His saying ﴿So He made hypocrisy a consequence for them in their hearts﴾ is that He made them suffer punishment for hypocrisy, and that punishment is the occurrence of grief in their hearts and the tightness of their chests, and the humiliation and reproach that befall them, and this continues for them until the Hereafter. Then God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation?﴾ The secret (*sirr*) is what their chests conceal, and the private conversation (*najwā*) is what some of them confer about with one another among themselves. A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿And We brought him near as a confidant﴾ [Maryam: 52]; and His saying: ﴿So when they despaired of him, they withdrew to confer privately﴾ [Yusuf: 80]; and His saying: ﴿So do not confer together in sin and transgression and disobedience to the Messenger, but confer together in righteousness and piety﴾ [al-Mujadila: 9]; and His saying: ﴿When you confer privately with the Messenger, offer a charity before your private conversation﴾ [al-Mujadila: 12].

Once you know the difference between the secret and the private conversation, the purpose of the verse is as though He, exalted is He, said: "Do they not know that God knows their secret and their private conversation? So how do they dare to engage in hypocrisy, whose essence is concealment and private conferring among themselves, while knowing that God, exalted is He, knows that from their condition just as He knows the outward? And that He punishes for it just as He punishes for the outward?"

Then He said: ﴿And that God is the Knower of the unseen﴾. The one who knows much (*ʿAllām*) is an intensive form of the knower, and the unseen (*ghayb*) is what is absent from the creation. What is meant is that His essence necessitates knowledge of all things, so it must be that He has knowledge of all knowable things, and it is necessary that He is aware of what is in the inner thoughts and the hidden secrets. How, then, is concealment from Him possible? A parallel to the phrase "Knower of the unseen" here is the saying of Jesus (peace be upon him): ﴿Indeed You, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ [al-Ma'ida: 116]. As for describing God with the form ʿAllāmah (the one who knows exceedingly), it is not permissible, because it implies a kind of effort in regard to what is known, and effort with respect to God is impossible.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who criticize the volunteers among the believers regarding charity, and those who find nothing to give except their effort, so they mock them—Allah will mock them, and for them is a painful punishment.﴾

Know that this is another type of their ugly deeds, namely their finding fault with those who bring charity willingly and voluntarily. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) addressed them one day and urged them to gather charity. 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf came to him with four thousand dirhams and said: 'I had eight thousand dirhams, so I kept four for myself and my dependents, and these four I have lent to my Lord.' He said: 'May Allah bless you in what you gave and in what you kept.' It was said: Allah accepted the Messenger's supplication concerning him, so that his wife Tumadir reconciled with him for a quarter of the eighth for eighty thousand. 'Umar came with something similar. 'Asim ibn 'Adi al-Ansari came with seventy wasq of dates from the charity. 'Uthman ibn 'Affan came with a great charity. Abu 'Aqil came with a sa' of dates and said: 'Last night I hired myself out to a man to draw water for his palm trees, and I received two sa' of dates. I kept one for my dependents and lent the other to my Lord.' The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) ordered that it be placed with the charities. The hypocrites said, in a spirit of disparagement: 'They only brought their charities out of showing off and seeking reputation. As for Abu 'Aqil, he only brought his sa' so that he would be mentioned along with the other notables, and Allah is not in need of his sa'.' Then Allah revealed this verse."

The discussion of the meaning of "lamz" (finding fault) has passed at His saying: ﴿And among them are those who find fault with you regarding the charities﴾. The "mutawwi'un" are the "mutatawwi'un" (those who volunteer), and "tatawwu'" is "tanafful" (voluntary performance), which is obedience to Allah Most High in what is not obligatory. The reason for assimilating the "ta'" into the "ta'" is the closeness of their points of articulation. Al-Layth said: "al-juhd" is a small amount by which the one of little means subsists. Al-Zajjaj said: "illa juhdahum" (except their effort), and "juhduhum" is read with a damma and with a fatha. Al-Farra' said: the damma is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz and the fatha is for others. Ibn al-Sikkit related from him a distinction between them, saying: "al-juhd" is capacity; you say: "hadha juhdi," meaning, this is my capacity.

Having known this, the intended meaning of "those who volunteer regarding the charities" is those wealthy ones who brought abundant charity, and by His saying: ﴿and those who find nothing except their effort﴾ is meant Abu 'Aqil, since he brought the sa' of dates. Then He related that the hypocrites mocked them, and then He clarified that Allah mocked them.

Know that bringing out wealth seeking the pleasure of Allah may be obligatory, as in zakat and all other obligatory expenditures, and it may be voluntary, which is what is intended by this verse. Then the one who brings a voluntary charity may be wealthy, so he brings a great amount, like 'Abd al-Rahman ibn 'Awf and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan; and he may be poor, so he brings a little, which is the effort of the one of little means. There is no difference between the two categories in deserving reward, because what is intended from outward deeds is the quality of intention and consideration of the state of motives and impediments. The little that the poor man brings may be more weighty with Allah Most High than the great amount that the wealthy man brings.

Then, those foolish hypocrites did not look beyond outward appearances, so they reproached that poor man who brought the small charity. That reproach may carry several aspects:

First: they may say: he is in need of it due to his poverty, so how does he give it away? However, this is among the things that necessitate excellence, as Allah says: ﴿and they prefer others over themselves, though they themselves are in privation﴾ [al-Hashr: 9].

Second: they may say: what effect does this little have? This is also ignorance, because when this man could only afford this, and he brings it, he has spent everything he is able to, so he is greater in standing with Allah than the deed of others, because he has cut the attachment of his heart from what was in his hand of the world, and has been content with reliance upon the Master.

Third: they may say: this poor man only brought this little so that he might join himself to the notables of people in this rank. This too is ignorance, because a person's striving to join himself to the people of goodness and religion is better for him than striving to join himself to the people of laziness and idleness.

As for His saying: ﴿Allah mocks them﴾, you have already known the principle in this matter. Al-Asamm said: What is meant is that He Most High accepted from these hypocrites the acts of righteousness they displayed, although He would not reward them for them, so this was like mockery.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 80:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Ask forgiveness for them, or do not ask forgiveness for them; even if you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them. That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger. And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "When the first verse was revealed concerning the hypocrites, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, ask forgiveness for us.' The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: 'I will ask forgiveness for you.' He busied himself with asking forgiveness for them, so this verse was revealed, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ abandoned asking forgiveness." Al-Hasan said: "They used to come to the Messenger of Allah and make excuses to him, saying: 'We only intended goodness and harmony and success,' so this verse was revealed." Al-Asamm narrated that "ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul used to stand up when the Messenger was delivering a sermon and say: 'This is the Messenger of Allah; may Allah honour him, strengthen him and grant him victory.' When he stood up in that position after Uhud, ʿUmar said to him: 'Sit down, enemy of Allah; your disbelief has become evident.' People rebuked him from every direction, so he left the mosque without praying. A man from his people met him and said: 'What turned you away?' He related the story. The man said: 'Return to the Messenger of Allah so that he may ask forgiveness for you.' He said: 'I do not care whether he asks forgiveness for me or does not ask forgiveness for me.' Then this was revealed: ﴿And when it is said to them, "Come, the Messenger of Allah will ask forgiveness for you," they turn their heads aside﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 5]. The hypocrites came after Uhud making excuses and pretending with falsehood that he should ask forgiveness for them."

The second issue: ﴿If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them.﴾ Al-Shaʿbi narrated: "ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul invited the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to the funeral of his father. He (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Who are you?' He said: 'I am al-Hubab ibn ʿAbdullah.' He said: 'Rather, you are ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAbdullah; al-Hubab is the Satan.'" Then he recited this verse. The judge said: The apparent meaning of His saying ﴿Ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ is like an indication that the people requested from him to ask forgiveness. I have related what has been transmitted in this regard of reports, and the closer view regarding the connection of this verse with what precedes it is what Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him, mentioned: that those who used to slander were the ones who requested forgiveness, so this verse was revealed.

The third issue: Some people said: specifying a definite number indicates that the situation beyond that number is contrary to it, and this is the position of those who hold the argument from the implication of speech (dalil al-khitab). They said: The evidence for this is that "when the saying of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times, Allah will never forgive them﴾ was revealed, he (peace be upon him) said: 'By Allah, I will increase beyond the seventy,'" and he did not turn away from that until the saying of Allah, exalted is He, was revealed: ﴿It is the same for them whether you ask forgiveness for them or do not ask forgiveness for them﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 6], so he refrained from them.

One may say: this argument in reverse is more appropriate, because when Allah, exalted is He, made clear to the Messenger (peace be upon him) that He would absolutely not forgive them, it became established that the situation beyond the stated number is equal to the situation at the stated number, and this indicates that restricting by a number does not necessitate that the ruling beyond it is contrary to it.

The fourth issue: Some people said: The Messenger (peace be upon him) busied himself with asking forgiveness for the people, so Allah prevented him from it. Others said: The hypocrites asked the Messenger (peace be upon him) to ask forgiveness for them, so Allah, exalted is He, forbade him from it, and the prohibition of a thing does not indicate that the one prohibited had already undertaken that act. We say that he (peace be upon him) did not busy himself with asking forgiveness for them, for several reasons:

First: The hypocrite is a disbeliever, and it has become evident in his law (peace be upon him) that asking forgiveness for a disbeliever is not permissible. For this reason Allah commanded His Messenger to follow Abraham (peace be upon him) except in his saying to his father: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. If this is well known in the law, how is it permissible to undertake it?

Second: Asking forgiveness of one person for another does not benefit that person if he persists in ugliness and disobedience.

Third: His undertaking to ask forgiveness for the hypocrites would be like encouraging them to commit sin.

Fourth: If Allah were not to respond to him in it, the supplication of the Messenger (peace be upon him) would remain rejected before Allah, and that would necessitate a diminution of his station.

Fifth: If this supplication were accepted from the Messenger, then its few would be like its many in obtaining a response. Thus it is established that the intended meaning of this statement is that when the people asked him to ask forgiveness for them, Allah prevented him from it, and the purpose of mentioning this number is not to limit the prohibition. Rather, it is like when one says to someone who asks him for a need: "Even if you asked me seventy times, I would not grant it to you," and he does not mean by that that if you exceed it, he will grant it. The same applies here. What confirms this is His saying in the verse: ﴿That is because they disbelieved in Allah﴾. He made clear that the cause for which the Messenger's asking forgiveness would not benefit them, even if it reached seventy times, is their disbelief and their defiance, and this meaning exists in the increase beyond seventy. So this reasoning serves as evidence that the purpose is to remove the hope that the Messenger's asking forgiveness would benefit them while they persist in disbelief. It is also confirmed by His saying: ﴿And Allah does not guide the defiantly disobedient people﴾, meaning that their defiance prevents guidance. Thus it is established that the truth is what we have mentioned.

The fifth issue: The later exegetes said: Seventy, in the usage of the Arabs, is an extreme limit, since it is an expression for multiplying seven by ten. The number seven is a noble number, since the number of the heavens, the earths, the seas, the climes, the stars and the limbs is this number. Some of them said: This number was specifically mentioned here because it has been narrated that "the Prophet (peace be upon him) pronounced takbir over Hamzah seventy times," so it is as if it was said: "If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times" in correspondence to your prayer over Hamzah. It was also said: The origin of this is His saying: ﴿The likeness of those who spend their wealth in the way of Allah is like a grain that grows seven spikes, in each spike a hundred grains﴾ [al-Baqarah: 261]. And he (peace be upon him) said: "A good deed is multiplied tenfold up to seven hundredfold." So when Allah, exalted is He, mentioned this number in the context of multiplying for His Messenger, it became the basis for it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 81–82:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who were left behind rejoiced in their seat, contrary to the Messenger of Allah, and they disliked to strive with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah, and they said, "Do not go forth in the heat." Say, "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they understood."﴾ ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much, as a recompense for what they used to earn.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the ugly deeds of the hypocrites, namely their rejoicing at sitting (at home) and their aversion to jihad. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: It refers to the hypocrites who stayed behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in the expedition of Tabuk. And al-mukhallaf (the one left behind) is the one who was abandoned from among those who had gone.

If it is said: They contrived until they stayed behind, so the better phrasing would have been: "those who stayed behind (al-mutakhallifun) rejoiced."

The answer comes in several aspects:

The first: The Messenger, peace be upon him, prevented groups of people from going out with him, because he knew that they would cause corruption and disruption. These were thus "left behind" (mukhallafin), not "those who stayed behind" (mutakhallifin).

The second: Those who stayed behind became "left behind" in the verse that comes after this verse, which is His saying: ﴿So if Allah returns you to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, then say, "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me."﴾ [al-Tawbah: 83]. When Allah, exalted is He, prevented them from going out with him, they became "left behind" because of this cause.

The third: Whoever stays behind from the Messenger, peace be upon him, after his going out to jihad with the believers is described as "left behind," in that he did not rise up, so he remained and stayed. As for His saying: ﴿bi-maq'adihim (in their seat)﴾, Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, said: it means Madinah, so according to this, al-maq'ad is a noun of place. And Muqatil said: "bi-maq'adihim" means "by their sitting," and according to this it is a verbal noun.

As for His saying: ﴿khilafa Rasul Allah (contrary to the Messenger of Allah)﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

The first, which is the saying of Qutrub, al-Mu'arrij and al-Zajjaj: it means opposition to the Messenger of Allah when he set out and they remained. They said: it is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the meaning is that they sat in order to oppose the Messenger of Allah ﷺ.

The second: al-Akhfash said: khilaf is in the sense of khalf (behind), and Yunus narrated it from 'Isa ibn 'Umar, and its meaning is "after the Messenger of Allah." The reading of one who read "khalfa Rasul Allah" strengthens this aspect. According to this opinion, khilaf is a noun for a specific direction, like khalf, and the reason for this is that a person faces forward, so the direction behind him is contrary to the direction in front of him in that it is a direction he is not facing. Khilaf in the sense of khalf is used; Abu 'Ubaydah recited for al-Ahwas:

"The spring rain came after their khilaf, as though the palm-leaf weavers had spread a mat between them."

As for His saying: ﴿and they disliked to strive with their wealth and their selves in the way of Allah﴾, the meaning is: they rejoiced because of staying behind and disliked going out to the battle.

Know that rejoicing in staying home alongside disliking going out is repeated, but He, exalted is He, mentioned it again for emphasis. Also, perhaps the meaning is that his natural inclination was toward staying, due to his familiarity with that town and his comfort with its people and children, while he disliked going out to battle, because it exposes wealth and self to killing and loss. Also, among what prevented them from going out was the severity of the heat at the time the Messenger of Allah ﷺ set out, and this is what is meant by His saying: ﴿and they said, "Do not go forth in the heat."﴾

Allah, exalted is He, answered this last reason by His saying: ﴿Say, "The Fire of Hell is more intense in heat, if only they understood."﴾ That is: after this abode there is another abode, and after this life there is another life. Also, this hardship is one that ends, while that hardship is one that remains. The author of al-Kashshaf narrated for one of them:

"The joy of ages, after which I encountered
The distress of a day, which is like the idols (anṣāb) of sacrifice."

"So how will you encounter the joy of an hour,
Behind whose passing is the distress of ages?"

Then Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much﴾. Although this came in the form of a command, its meaning is information that this state will indeed occur, and the evidence for it is His saying after it: ﴿as a recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ The meaning of the verse is: though they rejoice and laugh throughout their whole lives, that is little, because the entire world is little; but their grief and weeping in the Hereafter is much, because it is a perpetual punishment that does not cease, and what ceases in comparison to what is permanent is little. For this reason He said: ﴿So let them laugh little and weep much.﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: His saying "jaza'an (as a recompense)" is an object of purpose, and the meaning is: "and let them weep for this purpose." His saying "bima kanu yaksibun (for what they used to earn)" means: in the world, of hypocrisy.

The Mu'tazilah's argument from this verse, that the servant creates his own actions, and that if Allah had brought harm upon them directly, not through their own earning, He would be unjust, is well known; and the refutation of them has been given before this many times, which suffices without repetition.
