[Page 120]

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So if Allah brings you back to a group of them and they ask your permission to go out, say: "You will never go out with me, and you will never fight an enemy with me. You were content to sit at home the first time, so sit with those who stay behind."﴾

Know that when He, exalted be He, had explained the disgraceful conduct of the hypocrites and the evil of their way, He then explained, after informing the Messenger of it, that the right course was not to take them along on his campaigns, because their going out with him would bring about kinds of corruption. So He said: ﴿So if Allah brings you back to a group of them﴾, meaning of the hypocrites, ﴿say: "You will never go out with me"﴾.

His saying, ﴿So if Allah brings you back﴾, means: if Allah returns you to Medina. The meaning of *al-raj'* (return) is the thing coming back to the place where it was. It is said: "I returned it (*raja'tuhu*) a return (*raj'an*), as you say: I returned it (*radadtuhu*) a returning (*radd*)."

His saying, ﴿to a group of them﴾, is specified because not everyone who remained in Medina was a hypocrite; some of them were sincere and had valid excuses. His saying, ﴿and they ask your permission to go out﴾, means: to go to battle with you. ﴿Say: "You will never go out with me"﴾ to a campaign. This carries the force of reproach and condemnation against them, and of exposing their hypocrisy and disgraceful conduct. That is because encouraging the Muslims to jihad is a matter known necessarily from the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him. Then, if these people were prevented from going out to battle after they had taken the initiative of asking permission, that would be an explicit declaration that they had left Islam and were characterised by deceit and treachery; for he, peace be upon him, prevented them from going out only out of caution against their scheming, their plotting and their deception. Thus this meaning, from this aspect, functions as cursing and expulsion.

A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Those left behind will say, when you set out to take the spoils: "Let us follow you"﴾ (Surat al-Fath, 48:15), up to His saying: ﴿Say: "You will never follow us"﴾ (Surat al-Fath, 48:15).

Then He, exalted be He, gave the reason for that prohibition in His saying: ﴿You were content to sit at home the first time﴾. What is meant by this is staying behind from the expedition of Tabuk, meaning that the need for your agreement in the first instance was greater, and after that that need ceased. So when you stayed behind at the time of the greatest need for your presence, then at that point We will not accept you, nor will We pay any heed to you.

There is a point of discussion in the wording, which the author of *al-Kashshaf* mentioned: that the word *marrah* (time) in ﴿the first time﴾ was placed in the position of the plural *marrat* (times), and then the word *al-awwal* (first) was made into a construct with it. It denotes one of the times, so the better form would have been *ula marrah* (the first time).

He answered this by saying that the more common usage of the two languages is to say: "Hind is the greatest (*akbar*) of women," and one does not say: "Hind is the greatest (*kubra*) of women."

Then He, exalted be He, said: ﴿So sit with those who stay behind (*al-khalifin*)﴾. The commentators gave several views on the interpretation of *al-khalif*:

The first: al-Akhfash and Abu Ubayda said: *al-khalifun* is a plural whose singular is *khalif*, meaning one who remains behind a man among his people. The meaning is "with those who remain behind among the men, who stay in the house and do not leave."

The second: that *al-khalifin* is explained as *al-mukhalifin* (those who oppose). Al-Farra' said: it is said, "a slave who is *khalif*" and "a companion who is *khalif*" when he is opposing. Al-Akhfash said: "So-and-so was opposed by his family (*khalafahu*) when he opposed them." Al-Layth said: "This man is a *khalifah*," that is, one who opposes often, and "people are *khalifun*." When you pluralise it you say *al-khalifun*.

The third view: *al-khalif* is the corrupt one. Al-Asma'i said: it is said, "he deteriorated from every good" (*khalafa 'an kulli khayr yakhlufu khulufan*) when he became corrupt, and "the milk went bad" (*khalafa al-laban* and *khalufa*) when it spoiled.

Now, when you know these three aspects, there is no doubt that the word may be taken in any one of them, because those hypocrites were characterised by all of these qualities.

Know that this verse indicates that when a man sees from some of his associates deceit, treachery and scheming, and sees them persisting in it and going to great lengths in establishing its causes, he is obliged to cut off the bond between himself and them, and to guard against keeping their company.

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 84**

[Page 122 of the source is marked here.]

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever, nor stand at his grave. Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they died while they were defiant sinners.﴾

Know that He, the Exalted, commanded His Messenger to strive to humiliate them, degrade them, and abase them. What was mentioned in the first verse, namely their being prevented from going out with him on the campaigns, is a strong cause of their humiliation and degradation. What He mentions in this verse, namely the Messenger being prevented from praying over those among them who die, is another strong cause of their humiliation and abasement.

It is related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him both, that: "When Abdullah ibn Ubayy ibn Salul fell ill, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) visited him. He asked him to pray over him when he died and to stand at his grave. Then he sent to the Messenger, peace and blessings be upon him, asking him for his shirt so that he could be shrouded in it. So he sent him the outer shirt, but he returned it and asked for the one next to his skin, to be shrouded in it. 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: 'Why do you give your shirt to this filthy, unclean one?' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said: 'My shirt will not avail him anything with Allah. Perhaps Allah will bring a thousand people into Islam through it.' The hypocrites never left Abdullah, and when they saw him asking for this shirt and hoping it would benefit him, a thousand of them embraced Islam that day. When he died, his son came to the Prophet and said: 'Pray over him and bury him.' The Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said to his son: 'Pray over him and bury him.' He said: 'If you do not pray over him, O Messenger of Allah, no Muslim will pray over him.' So the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, stood up to pray over him, but 'Umar stood up and placed himself between the Messenger of Allah and the qiblah (the direction of prayer), so that he would not pray over him. Then this verse was revealed, and Jibril, peace be upon him, took hold of his garment and said: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever.﴾"

Know that this indicates a great virtue of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him. This is because revelation descended in accordance with his opinion in many verses:

Among them is the verse on accepting ransom from the captives of Badr, whose explanation has already passed.

Second: the verse prohibiting wine.

Third: the verse on changing the qiblah.

Fourth: the verse commanding women to wear the hijab.

Fifth: this verse. Thus the descent of revelation in conformity with the statement of 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, became a lofty station and an exalted rank for him in the religion. For this reason the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, said concerning him: "If I had not been sent, you would have been sent as a prophet, O 'Umar."

If it is said: How is it permissible to say that the Messenger desired to pray over him after he knew that he was a disbeliever who died in his disbelief? Praying over him is in the category of honouring and magnifying him. Also, if he prayed over him, he would be supplicating for him, and that is forbidden, because He, the Exalted, informed him that He does not forgive the disbelievers at all. Also, giving him the shirt entails honouring him?

The answer: Perhaps the reason is that when he asked the Messenger to send him his shirt that had touched his skin, so that he might be buried in it, it became dominant in the Messenger's assumption, peace and blessings be upon him, that he had turned to faith, because that time is one in which the sinner repents and the disbeliever believes. When he saw him showing Islam and witnessed from him this sign that indicated his entry into Islam, it became dominant in his assumption that he had become a Muslim. He built on this assumption and desired to pray over him. When Jibril, peace be upon him, descended and informed him that he had died in his disbelief and hypocrisy, he refrained from praying over him.

As for giving him the shirt, they have mentioned several reasons for it:

The first: when al-'Abbas, the paternal uncle of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), was taken captive at Badr and they could not find a shirt for him, and he was a tall man, Abdullah clothed him with his shirt.

The second: the polytheists said to him on the day of Hudaybiyyah: "We will not submit to Muhammad, but we will submit to you." He said: "No, for in the Messenger of Allah there is a good example for me." So the Messenger of Allah thanked him for that.

The third: Allah, the Exalted, commanded him not to turn away a petitioner, by His saying: ﴿As for the one who asks, do not repel him harshly.﴾ [al-Duha 93:10]. So when he asked him for the shirt, he gave it to him for this reason.

The fourth: withholding the shirt does not befit people of generosity.

The fifth: his son, Abdullah ibn Abdullah ibn Ubayy, was among the righteous, and the Messenger honoured him because of his son's position.

The sixth: perhaps Allah, the Exalted, revealed to him that when you give your shirt to him, that will lead a thousand hypocrites to enter Islam. So he did that for this purpose. It is narrated that when they witnessed that, a thousand of the hypocrites embraced Islam.

The seventh: mercy and compassion predominated in him, as He said: ﴿And We have not sent you except as a mercy to the worlds.﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:107]. And He said: ﴿It was by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them.﴾ [Al 'Imran 3:159]. So he refrained from praying over him, observing the command of Allah, the Exalted, and he gave him the shirt to display mercy and compassion.

Having known this, we say: His saying, ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died﴾: al-Wahidi said: "Died" (māta) is in the genitive position, because it is an attribute of an indefinite noun, as if it were said: "over any of them who is dead." His saying, ﴿ever﴾, is connected to His saying, ﴿any﴾, and the sense is: "And do not ever pray over any of them." Know that His saying, "and do not ever pray," admits of making the negation perpetual and admits of making the negated thing perpetual, and the intended meaning is the first, because the contextual indications of these verses show that the intended meaning is a total and permanent prohibition on his praying over any of them.

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿And do not stand at his grave.﴾ In this there are two views:

The first: al-Zajjaj said: "Whenever the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) buried the dead, he would stand at his grave and supplicate for him, so here He prohibited him from that."

The second: al-Kalbi said: "Do not take charge of the affairs of his grave." This is from their saying: "So-and-so stood (qama) in charge of so-and-so's affair," when he took care of his affair and undertook it.

Then He, the Exalted, gave as the reason for the prohibition on praying over him and standing at his grave His saying: ﴿Indeed, they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger, and they died while they were defiant sinners.﴾ On this there are questions:

The first question: Defiance (fisq) is a lower state than disbelief (kufr). Since in mentioning the reason for this prohibition He mentioned that he was a disbeliever, what is the benefit of describing him after that as a defiant sinner?

The answer: A disbeliever may be upright in his religion, and he may be a defiant sinner in his religion, vile and detested among his people. Lying, hypocrisy, deception, cunning and plotting are things condemned in all religions. Since the hypocrites were described by these attributes, Allah, the Exalted, described them as defiant sinners after describing them as disbelievers, to draw attention to the fact that the way of hypocrisy is a blameworthy way in the view of all the people of the world.

The second question: Is it not the case that the hypocrite is prayed over when he shows faith while disbelief remains within him?

The answer: Legal obligations are based on the outward, as he, peace and blessings be upon him, said: "We judge by the outward, and Allah, the Exalted, takes charge of the hidden matters."

The third question: His saying, ﴿That is because they disbelieved in Allah and His Messenger﴾, explicitly states that this prohibition is caused by this reason, and that requires that the ruling of Allah, the Exalted, be caused by something, which is impossible, because the ruling of Allah is eternal, while this cause is originated, and causing the eternal by the originated is impossible.

The answer: The discussion of whether the ruling of Allah, the Exalted, may be explained by considerations of benefit or not is a lengthy investigation, and there is no doubt that this apparent meaning indicates it.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 85–87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let not their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

Know that this verse has already been mentioned in this same surah, word for word, and it is mentioned here. There are differences between the two in wording. The first difference is that in the earlier verse He said ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ (fa-la tu'jibka, "so let not... impress you") with the particle فَ (fa), whereas here He said ﴿وَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ (wa-la tu'jibka, "and let not... impress you") with the particle وَ (wa).

The second is that there He said ﴿أَمْوالُهُمْ وَأَوْلادُهُمْ﴾ (their wealth and their children), whereas here the word "لا" (la, "nor") is omitted.

The third is that there He said ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾ (Allah only intends to punish them), with the lam (لِ) of purpose, whereas here He omitted the lam and replaced it with the word "أَنْ" (an, "that").

The fourth is that there He said ﴿فِي الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ (in the life of this world), whereas here He omitted the word "الحياة" (life) and said ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ (in this world). So there are differences between these two verses in these four respects. It is therefore incumbent upon us to mention the benefits of these four differences, and then to mention the benefit of this repetition.

As for the first aspect, we say:

The first type of difference is that He mentioned the phrase ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ with فَ in the first verse, and with وَ in the second. The reason is that in the first verse this statement came after His saying ﴿وَلا يُنْفِقُونَ إِلَّا وَهُمْ كارِهُونَ﴾ (and they do not spend except while they are averse). He described them as being averse to spending, and they were averse to spending only because they were impressed by the abundance of those possessions. For this reason, Allah forbade him from that admiration with the فَ of consequence, saying ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ أَمْوالُهُمْ وَلا أَوْلادُهُمْ﴾. Here, however, this statement has no connection to what precedes it, so He used the particle وَ.

As for the second type, namely that in the first verse He said ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ أَمْوالُهُمْ وَلا أَوْلادُهُمْ﴾, the reason is that this kind of arrangement begins with the lesser and then ascends to the more noble. One says: "The command of the governor does not impress me, nor the command of the vizier." This indicates that these people's admiration for their children was greater than their admiration for their wealth. In this verse, it indicates that there was no difference between the two matters in their eyes.

As for the third type, namely that He said there ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾ and here ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾, the benefit of this is to draw attention to the fact that causation (ta'lil) in the rulings of Allah, may He be exalted, is impossible, and that wherever a particle of causation occurs, its meaning is "أَنْ" (that), as in His saying ﴿وَما أُمِرُوا إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ [al-Bayyina: 5], meaning: "They were only commanded that they should worship Allah."

As for the fourth type, namely that in the first verse He mentioned ﴿فِي الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾, and here He mentioned ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ and dropped the word "الحياة," this is to draw attention to the fact that the worldly life has become so base that it does not deserve to be called "life." Rather, when mentioning it, one must confine oneself to the word "الدنيا" (the lower world), as an indication of its complete lowliness. These are the aspects of the difference between these expressions, and the one who knows the realities of the Qur'an is Allah, may He be exalted.

As for the second aspect, which is explaining the wisdom of the repetition: the thing most powerful in drawing hearts and turning thoughts toward preoccupation with this world is preoccupation with wealth and children. Whatever is of this nature requires warning against it again. However, since the thing most desired and most sought by the believing man is the forgiveness of Allah, may He be exalted, for this reason Allah repeated His saying ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ ما دُونَ ذَلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ [al-Nisa: 48] twice in Surat al-Nisa. In sum, repetition serves for emphasis. Here it is for intensifying the warning, while in the verse of forgiveness it is for intensifying the reassurance. It has also been said that this meaning was repeated because He intended by the first verse a group of hypocrites who had wealth and children at the time of its revelation, and intended by this verse other groups. A single statement, when it needs to be mentioned in connection with many peoples at different times, does not suffice with mentioning it for some of them in place of mentioning it for the others.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, saying: "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth among them ask your leave and say: "Leave us to be with those who sit behind."﴾ ﴿They were content to be with the women who remain behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, explained in the preceding verses that the hypocrites schemed to obtain a concession to stay behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to sit out the expedition. In this verse He added a subtle point, namely that whenever a verse is revealed containing a command to faith and a command to striving alongside the Messenger, those of wealth and power among them ask permission to stay behind from the expedition, and they say to the Messenger of Allah: "Leave us to be with those who sit," that is, with the weak among the people and those residing in the city.

As for His saying ﴿And when a surah is revealed, saying: "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger"﴾, there are several discussions:

The first discussion: "surah" may refer to the whole of it or to a part of it, just as the Qur'an and the Book are applied to all of it and to part of it. It has also been said that the intended surah is Surat Bara'a, because it contains the command to faith and to striving.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿أَنْ آمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ﴾ (an amanu billah). Al-Wahidi said: the position of "أَنْ" is in the accusative, with the preposition deleted, and the implied sense is "bi-an amanu," that is, "by faith."

The third discussion: someone may ask: how does He command the believers to believe, since that entails commanding the obtaining of what is already obtained, which is impossible?

They answered that the meaning of commanding the believers to believe is persistence in it and holding fast to it in the future. I say: there is no need for this answer, since the command is directed at them. He placed the command to faith before the command to striving because the sense is as if it were said to the hypocrites: "Undertaking striving before faith is of no benefit at all. Therefore it is obligatory upon you to believe first, and then to busy yourselves with striving second, so that your busying yourselves with striving may benefit you in your religion." Then He, may He be exalted, related what they say upon the revelation of this surah, saying ﴿اسْتَأْذَنَكَ أُولُو الطَّوْلِ مِنْهُمْ وَقالُوا ذَرْنا نَكُنْ مَعَ الْقاعِدِينَ﴾.

Regarding ﴿أُولُو الطَّوْلِ﴾ (ulu al-tawl) there are two opinions. The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said that it means those of abundance in wealth. The second: al-Asamm said that it means the leaders and the great ones who are looked up to. Regarding the specification of ﴿أُولُو الطَّوْلِ﴾ by mention, there are two opinions. The first: the blame directed at them was obligatory because they were able to travel and to strive. The second: He mentioned those of means because one who has no wealth and no ability to travel does not need to ask for permission.

Then He, may He be exalted, said ﴿رَضُوا بِأَنْ يَكُونُوا مَعَ الْخَوالِفِ﴾ (They were content to be with the khawalif). We have already mentioned the detailed discussion of al-khalif in His saying ﴿فَاقْعُدُوا مَعَ الْخالِفِينَ﴾, and here there are two points:

The first: al-Farra' said that al-khawalif refers to the women who remained behind in the house and did not leave it. The meaning is: they were content to be, in their staying behind from striving, like women.

The second: it is also permissible that al-khawalif be the plural of khalifa, in the sense of one who is inferior. The khalifa is one who is not noble. Al-Farra' said: the plural pattern fa'il does not take the form fawa'il except in two words: faris (rider) and fawaris, and halik and hawalik. The first opinion is preferable, because it more clearly indicates paucity and humiliation. The exegetes said: it was difficult for the hypocrites to be likened to the khawalif.

Then He said ﴿وَطُبِعَ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ فَهُمْ لا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾ (and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand). You already know that in our view, sealing (tab') and stamping (khatm) are expressions for the arising of a strong motive toward disbelief that prevents faith from arising. This is because an act without a motive is impossible, so when a firm and strong motive toward disbelief arises, the heart becomes as if it were sealed upon disbelief. Then, the arising of that motive, if it is from the servant, necessitates an infinite regress (tasalsul), and if it is from Allah, then the intended outcome is achieved.

Al-Hasan said: sealing is an expression for the heart's inclination toward disbelief reaching the point where it is as if it had died to faith. According to the Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that human beings create their own actions), it is an expression for a mark that occurs upon the heart. The full discussion of this is mentioned in Surat al-Baqara in His saying ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ (Allah has sealed their hearts) and His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾, that is, they do not comprehend the secrets of Allah's wisdom in the command to striving.

The second discussion: His saying ﴿أَنْ آمِنُوا بِاللَّهِ﴾ (an amanu billah). Al-Wahidi said: the position of "أَنْ" is in the accusative, with the preposition deleted, and the implied sense is "bi-an amanu," that is, "by faith."

The third discussion: someone may ask: how does He command the believers to believe, since that entails commanding the obtaining of what is already obtained, which is impossible?

They answered that the meaning of commanding the believers to believe is persistence in it and holding fast to it in the future. I say: there is no need for this answer, since the command is directed at them. He placed the command to faith before the command to striving because the sense is as if it were said to the hypocrites: "Undertaking striving before faith is of no benefit at all. Therefore it is obligatory upon you to believe first, and then to busy yourselves with striving second, so that your busying yourselves with striving may benefit you in your religion." Then He, may He be exalted, related what they say upon the revelation of this surah, saying ﴿اسْتَأْذَنَكَ أُولُو الطَّوْلِ مِنْهُمْ وَقالُوا ذَرْنا نَكُنْ مَعَ الْقاعِدِينَ﴾.

Regarding ﴿أُولُو الطَّوْلِ﴾ (ulu al-tawl) there are two opinions. The first: Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan said that it means those of abundance in wealth. The second: al-Asamm said that it means the leaders and the great ones who are looked up to. Regarding the specification of ﴿أُولُو الطَّوْلِ﴾ by mention, there are two opinions. The first: the blame directed at them was obligatory because they were able to travel and to strive. The second: He mentioned those of means because one who has no wealth and no ability to travel does not need to ask for permission.

Then He, may He be exalted, said ﴿رَضُوا بِأَنْ يَكُونُوا مَعَ الْخَوالِفِ﴾ (They were content to be with the khawalif). We have already mentioned the detailed discussion of al-khalif in His saying ﴿فَاقْعُدُوا مَعَ الْخالِفِينَ﴾, and here there are two points:

The first: al-Farra' said that al-khawalif refers to the women who remained behind in the house and did not leave it. The meaning is: they were content to be, in their staying behind from striving, like women.

The second: it is also permissible that al-khawalif be the plural of khalifa, in the sense of one who is inferior. The khalifa is one who is not noble. Al-Farra' said: the plural pattern fa'il does not take the form fawa'il except in two words: faris (rider) and fawaris, and halik and hawalik. The first opinion is preferable, because it more clearly indicates paucity and humiliation. The exegetes said: it was difficult for the hypocrites to be likened to the khawalif.

Then He said ﴿وَطُبِعَ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ فَهُمْ لا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾ (and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand). You already know that in our view, sealing (tab') and stamping (khatm) are expressions for the arising of a strong motive toward disbelief that prevents faith from arising. This is because an act without a motive is impossible, so when a firm and strong motive toward disbelief arises, the heart becomes as if it were sealed upon disbelief. Then, the arising of that motive, if it is from the servant, necessitates an infinite regress (tasalsul), and if it is from Allah, then the intended outcome is achieved.

Al-Hasan said: sealing is an expression for the heart's inclination toward disbelief reaching the point where it is as if it had died to faith. According to the Mu'tazila (a theological school that held that human beings create their own actions), it is an expression for a mark that occurs upon the heart. The full discussion of this is mentioned in Surat al-Baqara in His saying ﴿خَتَمَ اللَّهُ عَلى قُلُوبِهِمْ﴾ (Allah has sealed their hearts) and His saying ﴿فَهُمْ لا يَفْقَهُونَ﴾, that is, they do not comprehend the secrets of Allah's wisdom in the command to striving.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 85–87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So let not their wealth and their children impress you. Allah only intends to punish them through them in this world, and that their souls should depart while they are disbelievers.﴾

Know that this verse has already been mentioned in this same surah, word for word, and it is mentioned here. There are differences between the two in wording. The first difference is that in the earlier verse He said ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ (fa-la tu'jibka, "so let not... impress you") with the particle فَ (fa), whereas here He said ﴿وَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ (wa-la tu'jibka, "and let not... impress you") with the particle وَ (wa).

The second is that there He said ﴿أَمْوالُهُمْ وَأَوْلادُهُمْ﴾ (their wealth and their children), whereas here the word "لا" (la, "nor") is omitted.

The third is that there He said ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾ (Allah only intends to punish them), with the lam (لِ) of purpose, whereas here He omitted the lam and replaced it with the word "أَنْ" (an, "that").

The fourth is that there He said ﴿فِي الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾ (in the life of this world), whereas here He omitted the word "الحياة" (life) and said ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ (in this world). So there are differences between these two verses in these four respects. It is therefore incumbent upon us to mention the benefits of these four differences, and then to mention the benefit of this repetition.

As for the first aspect, we say:

The first type of difference is that He mentioned the phrase ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ﴾ with فَ in the first verse, and with وَ in the second. The reason is that in the first verse this statement came after His saying ﴿وَلا يُنْفِقُونَ إِلَّا وَهُمْ كارِهُونَ﴾ (and they do not spend except while they are averse). He described them as being averse to spending, and they were averse to spending only because they were impressed by the abundance of those possessions. For this reason, Allah forbade him from that admiration with the فَ of consequence, saying ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ أَمْوالُهُمْ وَلا أَوْلادُهُمْ﴾. Here, however, this statement has no connection to what precedes it, so He used the particle وَ.

As for the second type, namely that in the first verse He said ﴿فَلا تُعْجِبْكَ أَمْوالُهُمْ وَلا أَوْلادُهُمْ﴾, the reason is that this kind of arrangement begins with the lesser and then ascends to the more noble. One says: "The command of the governor does not impress me, nor the command of the vizier." This indicates that these people's admiration for their children was greater than their admiration for their wealth. In this verse, it indicates that there was no difference between the two matters in their eyes.

As for the third type, namely that He said there ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ لِيُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾ and here ﴿إِنَّما يُرِيدُ اللَّهُ أَنْ يُعَذِّبَهُمْ﴾, the benefit of this is to draw attention to the fact that causation (ta'lil) in the rulings of Allah, may He be exalted, is impossible, and that wherever a particle of causation occurs, its meaning is "أَنْ" (that), as in His saying ﴿وَما أُمِرُوا إِلَّا لِيَعْبُدُوا اللَّهَ﴾ [al-Bayyina: 5], meaning: "They were only commanded that they should worship Allah."

As for the fourth type, namely that in the first verse He mentioned ﴿فِي الْحَياةِ الدُّنْيا﴾, and here He mentioned ﴿فِي الدُّنْيا﴾ and dropped the word "الحياة," this is to draw attention to the fact that the worldly life has become so base that it does not deserve to be called "life." Rather, when mentioning it, one must confine oneself to the word "الدنيا" (the lower world), as an indication of its complete lowliness. These are the aspects of the difference between these expressions, and the one who knows the realities of the Qur'an is Allah, may He be exalted.

As for the second aspect, which is explaining the wisdom of the repetition: the thing most powerful in drawing hearts and turning thoughts toward preoccupation with this world is preoccupation with wealth and children. Whatever is of this nature requires warning against it again. However, since the thing most desired and most sought by the believing man is the forgiveness of Allah, may He be exalted, for this reason Allah repeated His saying ﴿إِنَّ اللَّهَ لا يَغْفِرُ أَنْ يُشْرَكَ بِهِ وَيَغْفِرُ ما دُونَ ذَلِكَ لِمَنْ يَشاءُ﴾ [al-Nisa: 48] twice in Surat al-Nisa. In sum, repetition serves for emphasis. Here it is for intensifying the warning, while in the verse of forgiveness it is for intensifying the reassurance. It has also been said that this meaning was repeated because He intended by the first verse a group of hypocrites who had wealth and children at the time of its revelation, and intended by this verse other groups. A single statement, when it needs to be mentioned in connection with many peoples at different times, does not suffice with mentioning it for some of them in place of mentioning it for the others.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when a surah is revealed, saying: "Believe in Allah and strive alongside His Messenger," those of wealth among them ask your leave and say: "Leave us to be with those who sit behind."﴾ ﴿They were content to be with the women who remain behind, and a seal was set upon their hearts, so they do not understand.﴾

Know that He, may He be exalted, explained in the preceding verses that the hypocrites schemed to obtain a concession to stay behind from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and to sit out the expedition. In this verse He added a subtle point, namely that whenever a verse is revealed containing a command to faith and a command to striving alongside the Messenger, those of wealth and power among them ask permission to stay behind from the expedition, and they say to the Messenger of Allah: "Leave us to be with those who sit," that is, with the weak among the people and those residing in the city.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 88–89:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But the Messenger and those who believed with him strove with their wealth and their lives. For them are the good things, and it is they who are the successful.﴾ ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great achievement.﴾

Know that when Allah the Exalted explained the condition of the hypocrites in fleeing from jihad, He clarified that the condition of the Messenger and those who believed with him is the opposite of it, since they expended wealth and lives seeking the pleasure of Allah and drawing near to Him. His saying ﴿But﴾ (lakin) carries a benefit, which is that the implication is: if these hypocrites stay behind from the campaign, then there has turned toward it one who is better than them and more sincere in intention and belief, like His saying: ﴿If these disbelieve in it, We have certainly entrusted it to a people who are not disbelievers in it﴾ (al-An'am: 89), and His saying: ﴿And if they are arrogant, then those who are with your Lord﴾ (Fussilat: 38). When He described them with hastening to jihad, He mentioned the benefits and advantages that accrued to them, and these are of several kinds:

The first: His saying: ﴿For them are the good things.﴾ Know that the word "the good things" (al-khayrat) encompasses the benefits of both abodes, because the expression is unrestricted. It was also said: "the good things" refers to the Houris, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿In them are good, beautiful women﴾ (al-Rahman: 70).

The second: His saying: ﴿And it is they who are the successful.﴾ So His saying "for them are the good things" means the reward, and His saying "it is they who are the successful" means deliverance from punishment and torment.

The third: His saying: ﴿Allah has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever.﴾ It is possible that these gardens serve as an explanation of "the good things" and "the success," and it is possible that those good things and success be understood as worldly benefits, such as the campaign's spoils, honor, wealth, power, and victory, while the gardens are understood as the reward of the Hereafter. And ﴿the great achievement﴾ is an expression that this state is an exalted rank and a lofty degree.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who had excuses among the Bedouins came seeking permission, and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back. Those who disbelieve among them will be struck by a painful punishment.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, explained the circumstances of the hypocrites who were in Madinah, He began in this verse to explain the circumstances of the hypocrites from among the Bedouins, with His saying: ﴿And those who had excuses came﴾. He said: Allah has cursed the ones who make excuses (al-mu'adhdhirin), and he went to the view that al-mu'dhir (the one who makes an excuse) is the diligent one who has a genuine excuse, while al-mu'adhdhir with the doubled letter is the one who offers excuses without having an excuse.

The summary: al-mu'dhir is the one who strives fully to present an excuse, and from it comes their saying: "He has given a full warning (a'dhara) to whoever has given warning (andhara)." According to this reading, the meaning of the verse is that Allah, exalted is He, distinguished between the people with genuine excuses and the liars. So al-mu'adhdhirun are those who came with an excuse. It was said: they were the tribes of Asad and Ghatafan. They said: "We have dependents, and we are in hardship, so grant us permission to stay behind." It was also said: they were the household of Amir ibn al-Tufayl, who said: "If we join you in the raid, the Bedouins of Tayy will raid us," so the Messenger of Allah granted them permission. And from Mujahid: a group from Ghatafan who made excuses. Those who read ﴿al-mu'adhdhirun﴾ with the doubled letter, which is the reading of the majority, have two linguistic explanations.

The first explanation: what al-Farra', al-Zajjaj and Ibn al-Anbari mentioned, namely that the original form of this word is al-mu'tadhirun. The vowel of the ta' was moved to the 'ayn, the dhal replaced the ta', and it was assimilated into the dhal that follows it, so the ta' became a doubled dhal. Making an excuse (i'tidhar) may be with falsehood, as in His saying: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 94), and He clarified that this excuse is corrupt by His saying: ﴿Say: Do not make excuses﴾. And it may be with truth, as in the verse of Labid:

"Whoever weeps for a full year has made an excuse (i'tadhara)"
meaning: he has come with a valid excuse.

The second explanation: that ﴿al-mu'adhdhirun﴾ follows the pattern of our saying mufa''iluna from al-ta'dhir, which is falling short. It is said: "a'dhara ta'dhiran" when he fell short and did not exert himself. It is said: "Fulan stood in a manner of ta'dhir" when you asked him to take care of a matter and he fell short in it. If we adopt the light reading, then (al-mu'dhirun) are liars. But if we adopt the doubled reading and interpret it as al-mu'tadhirin, then according to this assessment it is possible that they were truthful and it is possible that they were liars. Some of the exegetes said: al-mu'adhdhirun were truthful, based on the evidence that when Allah mentioned them, He said after them: ﴿and those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾. When He distinguished them from the liars, this indicates that they were not liars. Al-Wahidi related with his chain from Abu 'Amr that when this statement was made to him, he said: "Indeed, some people burdened themselves with an excuse based on falsehood; they are the ones Allah, exalted is He, meant by His saying: ﴿And the ones who make excuses came﴾. And others stayed behind without any excuse or semblance of an excuse, out of audacity toward Allah, exalted is He; they are the ones intended by His saying: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back.﴾" What Abu 'Amr said is possible, except that the first is more apparent.

His saying: ﴿And those who lied to Allah and His Messenger sat back﴾ refers to the hypocrites among the Bedouins who neither came nor made excuses, and it became clear by this that they lied to Allah and His Messenger in their claim of faith. Ubayy read (kadhdhabu) with the doubled letter. ﴿Those who disbelieve among them will be struck by a painful punishment﴾: in this world by killing, and in the Hereafter by the Fire. He said "among them" (minhum) because He, exalted is He, knew that some of them would believe and be spared this punishment, so He used the particle "min," which indicates partiality.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 91–92:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿There is no blame upon the weak, nor upon the sick, nor upon those who do not find anything to spend, when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger. There is no cause for blame against the good-doers. And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might mount them. You said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on." They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears out of sorrow that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained the threat concerning those who give the appearance of having an excuse though they have no excuse, He mentioned those who have genuine excuses, and explained that the obligation imposed by Allah, may He be exalted, to go on expedition and to fight in jihad is dropped from them. They are of several categories.

The first category: those who are physically sound but weak, such as the elderly, and whoever was created weak and frail from birth. These are the ones meant by "the weak" (al-du'afa'). The evidence for this is that He joined the sick to them with a conjunction, and what is conjoined is distinct from what it is conjoined to. Since the weak were not included in the category of those we mentioned, they are not identified with the sick.

As for the sick: this includes the blind, the lame, the chronically disabled, and everyone characterized by an illness that prevents him from being able to fight.

The third category: those who do not find the provisions, the supplies and the mount, and these are the ones who "do not find anything to spend." This is because their presence on the expedition is only beneficial if they are able to spend on themselves, either from their own wealth or from the wealth of another person who helps them with it. If this capacity is not present, they become a burden and a liability to the fighters, and prevent them from occupying themselves with the objective. Then, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned these three categories, He said: there is no blame upon these. The meaning is that it is permissible for them to remain behind from the expedition. The verse does not indicate that it is forbidden for them to go out, because if one of these went out to assist the fighters within his capacity, either by guarding their belongings or by increasing their numbers, provided he does not make himself a burden and a liability upon them, that would be an accepted act of obedience. Then He, may He be exalted, stipulated a specific condition for the permissibility of this delay, which is His saying: ﴿when they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger﴾. Its meaning is that when they remain in the town, they refrain from spreading false rumours and from stirring up strife, and they strive to convey good to the fighters who have travelled, either by attending to the important affairs of their households or by striving to bring glad news from their homes to them. All of these matters are considered a form of assistance to jihad.

[Page 128]

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿There is no cause for blame against the good-doers.﴾ The scholars agreed that what falls under His saying ﴿There is no cause for blame against the good-doers﴾ is that there is no sin upon him because of staying behind from jihad. They differed on whether it indicates generality in all respects. Some of them held that the wording is restricted to this meaning, because this verse was revealed concerning them. Others held that what matters is the generality of the wording and not the specificity of the occasion of revelation. The good-doer (al-muhsin) is one who performs good, and the head and chief of the gates of good is the statement "There is no god but Allah," and whoever says this word and believes in it is among the Muslims. His saying ﴿There is no cause for blame against the good-doers﴾ requires the negation of blame for all Muslims. So this, by its generality, requires that the original state of every Muslim is the innocence of his liability (bara'at al-dhimma), and the absence of any claim by others directed against him in his person or his property. This indicates that the original state regarding his person is the prohibition of killing, unless there is a separate evidence; and the original state regarding his property is the prohibition of taking it, unless there is a separate evidence; and that no obligation should be imposed upon him, unless there is a separate evidence. Thus this verse, by this route, becomes a principle recognized in the Sharia, establishing that the original state is the innocence of liability. If a specific text is revealed indicating the obligation of a specific ruling in a specific case, we decide according to that specific text, giving precedence to the specific over the general. Otherwise, this text is sufficient to establish the original innocence. Some people argue by this against analogical reasoning (al-qiyas). They say: this text indicates that the original state is the innocence of liability and the absence of obligation and imposition. So analogy either indicates the innocence of liability or the occupation of liability. The first is invalid, because since the innocence of liability has been established by the requirement of this text, establishing it by analogy would be pointless. The second is also invalid, because under this assumption that analogy would become a specifier of the generality of this text, and that is not permissible, since it is established that the text is stronger than analogy. They said: By this route the Sharia becomes regulated, known, summarized, far from the disorder and the endless differences. This is because when a sultan sends one of his agents to govern a town and says to him: "O man, my obligations upon you and upon the people of that realm are such and such," and he enumerates for them a hundred kinds of obligations, for example, then says: "After these obligations, no one has any authority over them," this is an explicit statement from him that there is no obligation upon them beyond those hundred categories mentioned. If that sultan were required to state explicitly, by way of detailed negation, everything other than those hundred, that would be impossible, because the door of negation has no end. Rather, it suffices for him in negation to say: "No one has authority over anyone, except in what I have mentioned and detailed." This is what the Literalists (ashab al-zawahir), such as Dawud al-Isfahani and his companions, uphold in establishing this principle.

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the weak, the sick and the poor, He explained that it is permissible for them to remain behind from jihad on condition that they are sincere to Allah and His Messenger, and He explained that they are good-doers and that no one has authority over them. Then He mentioned a fourth category of those excused, saying: ﴿Nor is there blame upon those who came to you that you might mount them. You said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on." They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears out of sorrow that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

If it is said: Are these not included in His saying ﴿nor upon those who do not find anything to spend﴾? What is the benefit of repeating it?

We say: Those who do not find anything to spend are the poor who have with them nothing beyond the means of subsistence. But those mentioned in the final verse are those who possessed the amount needed for expenses, except that they did not find a mount. The commentators have mentioned several reasons for the revelation of this verse:

The first: Mujahid said: they were "three brothers: Ma'qil, Suwayd and al-Nu'man, sons of Muqrin, who asked the Prophet ﷺ to carry them on leather-tanned footwear and stitched sandals. He, peace be upon him, said: 'I cannot find anything to carry you on,' so they turned away weeping."

The second: al-Hasan said: it was revealed concerning "Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and his companions, who came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ asking him to carry them. This coincided with some anger on his part, so he, peace be upon him, said: 'By Allah, I will not carry you, nor do I find anything to carry you on.' So they turned away weeping. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ called them back and gave them camels of the best kind. Abu Musa said: 'Did you not swear, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'As for me, if Allah wills, I will never swear an oath and then see something else better than it, except that I will do what is better and make expiation for my oath.'"

The third narration: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "They asked him to carry them on beasts, and he, peace be upon him, said: 'I cannot find anything to carry you on,' because the distance was great, and a man needs two camels: one to ride and one to carry his water and provisions on." The author of the "al-Kashshaf" said: His saying ﴿they turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears out of sorrow﴾ is like your saying "it overflows with tears," and it is more eloquent than "its tears overflow," because the eye is made as though all of it were overflowing tears.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 91–92:

You said, "I cannot find anything to mount you on." They turned away while their eyes overflowed with tears out of sorrow that they could not find anything to spend.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, had explained the threat concerning those who give the appearance of having an excuse though they have no excuse, He mentioned those who have genuine excuses, and explained that the obligation imposed by Allah, may He be exalted, to go on expedition and to fight in jihad is dropped from them. They are of several categories.

The first category: those who are physically sound but weak, such as the elderly, and whoever was created weak and frail from birth. These are the ones meant by "the weak" (al-du'afa'). The evidence for this is that He joined the sick to them with a conjunction, and what is conjoined is distinct from what it is conjoined to. Since the weak were not included in the category of those we mentioned, they are not identified with the sick.

As for the sick: this includes the blind, the lame, the chronically disabled, and everyone characterized by an illness that prevents him from being able to fight.

The third category: those who do not find the provisions, the supplies and the mount, and these are the ones who "do not find anything to spend." This is because their presence on the expedition is only beneficial if they are able to spend on themselves, either from their own wealth or from the wealth of another person who helps them with it. If this capacity is not present, they become a burden and a liability to the fighters, and prevent them from occupying themselves with the objective. Then, when He, may He be exalted, mentioned these three categories, He said: there is no blame upon these. The meaning is that it is permissible for them to remain behind from the expedition. The verse does not indicate that it is forbidden for them to go out, because if one of these went out to assist the fighters within his capacity, either by guarding their belongings or by increasing their numbers, provided he does not make himself a burden and a liability upon them, that would be an accepted act of obedience. Its meaning is that when they remain in the town, they refrain from spreading false rumours and from stirring up strife, and they strive to convey good to the fighters who have travelled, either by attending to the important affairs of their households or by striving to bring glad news from their homes to them. All of these matters are considered a form of assistance to jihad.

The meaning is: these rich men who ask your permission to remain behind, the way of Allah against them is binding, and the obligation upon them to go out to raiding is incumbent, and they have no excuse whatsoever for staying behind.

If it is asked: What is the position of His saying ﴿they have consented﴾?

We say: It seems to be a resumptive (new) sentence, as if it was said: What is the matter with them that they asked permission while they are rich? So it was said: They have consented to baseness, lowliness, and to being included in the group of those who stay behind.

﴿And Allah has sealed over their hearts﴾ means: the cause of their aversion from jihad is that Allah has sealed over their hearts, and because of that sealing they do not know the benefits of jihad for religion and for the worldly life.

Then He said: ﴿They will make excuses to you when you return to them. Say: "Do not make excuses; we will never believe you."﴾ This is a reason for the prohibition of making excuses, because the aim of one who makes an excuse is that his excuse be accepted. When he knows that the people will deny him in it, it becomes obligatory for him to abandon it. His saying ﴿Allah has already informed us of your news﴾ is a reason for the negation of belief, because when He, the Exalted, informed His Messenger of what was in their inner selves of corruption, deceit and hypocrisy, it became impossible for the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, to believe them in those excuses.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 95–96:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them. So turn away from them. Indeed they are filth, and their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn.﴾ ﴿They swear to you that you may be pleased with them. But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people.﴾

Know that when the Exalted related in the first verse that they make excuses, He mentioned in this verse that they used to reinforce those excuses with false oaths.

As for His words, ﴿They will swear to you by Allah when you return to them, that you may turn away from them⦈, know that this statement indicates that they swore by Allah, but it does not indicate what they swore about. It was said that they swore that they were unable to go out, and that they swore to this so that you would turn away from them, that is, so that you would overlook them and turn away from censuring them.

Then the Exalted said, ﴿So turn away from them⦈. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: He means abandoning speech and greeting. Muqatil said: When the Prophet (ﷺ) arrived in Medina, he said: "Do not sit with them and do not speak to them." The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani, those who study the rhetorical meanings of the Qur'an) said: These people sought the turning away of forgiveness, so they were given the turning away of aversion. Then He mentioned the reason for the obligation to turn away from them, saying: ﴿Indeed they are filth⦈. The meaning is that the corruption of their inner selves is a spiritual filth. Just as it is obligatory to avoid physical filth, avoiding spiritual filth is more obligatory, out of fear of its spreading to a person and out of caution lest a person's nature incline toward those deeds.

Then the Exalted said, ﴿And their refuge is Hell, as recompense for what they used to earn⦈. Its meaning is clear. Since He explained in the verse that they swear by Allah so that the Muslims would turn away from harming them, He also explained that they swear so that the Muslims would be pleased with them. Then the Exalted forbade the Muslims from being pleased with them, saying: ﴿But if you are pleased with them, indeed Allah is not pleased with the defiantly disobedient people⦈. The meaning is: if you are pleased with them while Allah is not pleased with them, then your will would be opposed to the will of Allah, and that is not permissible.

I say: These meanings have been mentioned in the preceding verses, and Allah has repeated them here once more. I think that the first passage is addressed to the hypocrites who were in Medina, and this passage is addressed to the hypocrites among the Bedouin Arabs and the people of the desert. Since the methods of the hypocrites are close to one another, whether they were from the settled population or from the desert dwellers, the discourse with them naturally followed closely similar approaches.

[p. 131]

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The Bedouins are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Among the Bedouins is one who regards what he spends as a loss, and waits for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the circle of evil. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that this verse confirms what we have mentioned: that Allah, exalted is He, only repeated these rulings because their intended audience is the hypocrites among the Bedouins. For this reason He stated that their disbelief and hypocrisy are more intense, and their ignorance of the limits of what Allah has sent down is more complete.

On the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** The scholars of language said: a man is called ʿarabī (Arab) when his lineage is among the ʿArab, and the plural is ʿArab. Just as you say majūsī (Magian) and yahūdī (Jew), and then the yā' of relation (yā' al-nisba) is dropped in the plural, so one says al-majūs and al-yahūd. A man is called aʿrābī (Bedouin) with an alif when he is a nomad, seeking the places where rain falls and pasture grows, whether he is of the Arabs or of their clients (mawālī). The plural of aʿrābī is al-aʿrāb and al-aʿārīb. So if the aʿrābī is addressed as "O ʿArabī," he is pleased, and if the ʿArabī is addressed as "O aʿrābī," he is angered. Whoever settles in the Arab towns are ʿArab, and whoever dwells in the desert are aʿrāb. The following points show the difference:

The first: the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The love of the Arabs is part of faith." But the aʿrāb, Allah has censured them in this verse.

The second: it is not permissible to say of the Emigrants (muhājirūn) and the Helpers (anṣār) that they are aʿrāb; rather they are ʿArab, and they are ahead of the aʿrāb in the ranks of religion. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Let no woman lead a man in prayer, nor a wicked person lead a believer, nor a Bedouin lead an emigrant."

The third: it has been said that the Arabs were named ʿArab because the children of Ishmael grew up in ʿArabah, which is in Tihamah, and so they were attributed to their land. Anyone who inhabits the Arabian Peninsula and speaks their language is one of them, since they descended from the children of Ishmael. It has also been said that they were named ʿArab because their tongues express (muʿribah) what is in their hearts. There is no doubt that the Arabic language is distinguished by kinds of eloquence and forcefulness not found in other languages.

I saw in some books, from some of the wise, that he said: "The wisdom of the Romans is in their brains, because they are capable of wondrous constructions; the wisdom of the Indians is in their imaginations; the wisdom of the Greeks is in their hearts, due to the abundance of their rational investigations; and the wisdom of the Arabs is in their tongues, due to the sweetness of their words and the pleasantness of their expressions."

**The second issue:** Some people said: the definite plural (al-jamʿ al-muḥallā bi-l-alif wa-l-lām) originally refers to a previously known referent (al-maʿhūd al-sābiq). If no previously known referent exists, it is taken to mean comprehensiveness (al-istighrāq, i.e., all members of the class) out of necessity. They said: the plural form suffices for its meaning with three or more, and the alif and lām are for definiteness. If there is a plural that is a previously known referent, it is necessary to refer to it; if not, then it is taken to mean comprehensiveness to avoid vagueness.

They said: once this is established, we say that His saying ﴿al-aʿrāb﴾ refers to a specific group of the hypocrites among the Bedouins who used to be allied with the hypocrites of Medina, so this term is applied to them.

**The third issue:** Allah, exalted is He, has passed two judgments on the Bedouins.

**The first judgment:** They are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy. There are several reasons for this:

The first: the people of the desert resemble wild beasts.

The second: the hot, dry air dominates them, and this produces excess arrogance, pride, vanity, boastfulness and recklessness.

The third: they were not under the governance of any ruler, nor the discipline of any instructor, nor the control of any authority, so they grew up as they wished, and whoever is like this goes out to the most corrupt of directions.

The fourth: whoever morning and evening witnesses the admonition of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), his healing explanations and his complete instructions, how could he be equal to one who did not desire this good and did not hear its report?

The fifth: compare the mountain fruits with the garden fruits, so that you may know the difference between the people of the towns and the people of the desert.

**The second judgment:** His saying ﴿and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger﴾. The word ﴿wa-ajdar﴾ means more fitting and more deserving. The verse contains an ellipsis, and the implied meaning is: "and more deserving that they not know." It has been said that the "limits of what Allah has sent down" means the measures of obligations and rulings. It has also been said that it means the levels of the evidences for justice (ʿadl), monotheism (tawḥīd), prophethood (nubuwwa) and the Return (maʿād). ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing﴾ of what is in the hearts of His creatures, ﴿All-Wise﴾ in what He has made obligatory of His obligations.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Among the Bedouins is one who regards what he spends as a loss﴾. The word maghram is a verbal noun like gharāma (loss, penalty). The meaning is that among the Bedouins is one who believes that what he spends in the way of Allah is a penalty and a loss. He believes this only because he spends merely out of fear of the Muslims and for show, not for the sake of Allah's countenance and seeking His reward. ﴿And waits for misfortunes to befall you﴾, meaning death and killing; that is, he waits for affairs to turn against you through the death of the Messenger, and for the polytheists to prevail over you. Then He returned it to them, saying: ﴿Upon them is the circle of evil.﴾ The word al-dāʾira may be singular, and it may be a dominant descriptive term. It is used only of a calamity that encircles a person such that he has no escape from it. The word ﴿al-sawʾ﴾ has been read with a fatḥa on the sīn and with a ḍamma on it. Al-Farrāʾ said: the fatḥa on the sīn is the preferred reading, because it is the verbal noun of your saying sāʾa yasūʾu sawʾan or musāʾa. Whoever puts a ḍamma on the sīn makes it a noun, as in your saying ʿalayhim dāʾirat al-balāʾ wa-l-ʿadhāb (upon them is the circle of affliction and punishment). A ḍamma on the sīn is not permissible in His saying ﴿What your father was not a man of sawʾ﴾ (Maryam: 28), nor in His saying ﴿and you thought a thought of sawʾ﴾ (al-Fath: 12), for otherwise the meaning would become: "your father was not a man of punishment," and "you thought the thought of punishment," and it is known that this is not permissible.

Al-Akhfash and Abū ʿUbayd said: whoever puts a fatḥa on the sīn, it is like your saying rajul sawʾ (a bad man) and imraʾa sawʾ (a bad woman), and then one adds the alif and lām, saying rajul al-sawʾ (the bad man). Al-Akhfash recited:

*And I was like the wolf of evil (dhiʾb al-sawʾ), when he saw blood on his companion one day, he turned toward the blood.*

Whoever puts a ḍamma on the sīn means by al-sūʾ harm, evil, affliction and what is disliked, as if it were said: "upon them is the circle of defeat and what is disliked," and it encircles them. Abū ʿAlī al-Fārisī said: if the circle were not attributed to sawʾ or sūʾ, the meaning of evil would not be understood from it, because the circle of time (dāʾirat al-dahr) is used only for what is disliked.

Having understood this, we say: the meaning is that affliction and grief turn around them, so they see nothing in Muhammad (peace be upon him) and his religion except what grieves them.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their intentions.

The Qur'an verse: ﴿The Bedouins are more intense in disbelief and hypocrisy, and more likely not to know the limits of what Allah has sent down to His Messenger. And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾ ﴿Among the Bedouins is one who regards what he spends as a loss, and waits for misfortunes to befall you. Upon them is the circle of evil. And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing.﴾

Know that this verse confirms what we have mentioned: that Allah, exalted is He, only repeated these rulings because their intended audience is the hypocrites among the Bedouins. For this reason He stated that their disbelief and hypocrisy are more intense, and their ignorance of the limits of what Allah has sent down is more complete.

Just as you say majūsī (Magian) and yahūdī (Jew), and then the yā' of relation (yā' al-nisba) is dropped in the plural, so one says al-majūs and al-yahūd. A man is called aʿrābī (Bedouin) with an alif when he is a nomad, seeking the places where rain falls and pasture grows, whether he is of the Arabs or of their clients (mawālī). The plural of aʿrābī is al-aʿrāb and al-aʿārīb. So if the aʿrābī is addressed as "O ʿArabī," he is pleased, and if the ʿArabī is addressed as "O aʿrābī," he is angered.
