Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 99:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among the desert Arabs are those who believe in Allah and the Last Day and take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as [means of obtaining] the prayers of the Messenger. Unquestionably, they are a means of nearness for them. Allah will admit them into His mercy. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, explained that among the desert Arabs there are those who regard their spending in the way of Allah as a loss, He also explained that among them there are a people who are believing, righteous, and striving (in jihad), who regard their spending in the way of Allah as a gain.

Know also that He, exalted is He, described this group with two attributes:

The first: that they are believers in Allah and the Last Day. The purpose is to draw attention to the fact that faith must precede all acts of obedience, and in jihad as well.

The second: that they take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as [means of obtaining] the prayers of the Messenger. In this there are two discussions:

The first: Al-Zajjaj said: In "qurubat" three vocalizations are permissible: with a damma on the ra' (qurubāt), with a sukun on it (qurbāt), and with a fatha on it (qurabāt).

The second: The author of "al-Kashshaf" said: "Qurubat" is the second object of yattakhidh (the verb "take"). The meaning is that what he spends is a cause for obtaining nearness to Allah, exalted is He, and the prayers of the Messenger, because the Messenger would supplicate for those who give charity with goodness and blessing, and would seek forgiveness for them. Like his saying (ﷺ): "O Allah, send prayers upon the family of Abu Awfa." And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And pray for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 103]. So when what is spent became a cause for obtaining nearness and prayers, it was said that he takes what he spends as nearness and prayers. And He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Unquestionably, they are a means of nearness for them﴾ [al-Tawbah: 99]. This is a testimony from Allah, exalted is He, to the giver of charity regarding the soundness of what he believed, that his spending is a means of nearness and prayers. Allah, exalted is He, has emphasized this testimony with the particle of alerting, which is His saying ﴿Unquestionably (alā inna)﴾, then He increased the emphasis, saying: ﴿Allah will admit them into His mercy﴾. We have mentioned that the addition of the sin (sa-) here necessitates greater emphasis. Then He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾ of their misdeeds, ﴿Merciful﴾ to them, in that He granted them success in these acts of obedience. Nafi' read (alā inna hā qurubatun lahum) with a damma on the ra', which is the original form, then it was lightened, as in kutbin, rusulin, and tunbin, and the original is the damma, while the sukun is a lightening.

The Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, Verse 100 (Part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness—Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him, and He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the great triumph.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the virtues of the Bedouins who take what they spend as means of nearness to Allah and as prayers of the Messenger, and what He prepared for them of reward, He made clear that above their rank there are higher and greater ranks, namely the ranks of the foremost, the first. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The scholars differed concerning the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, who they are, and they mentioned several views.

The first: Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: they are those who prayed towards both qiblahs and witnessed Badr. And it is reported from al-Sha'bi that they are those who pledged the Pledge of the Tree (bay'at al-ridwan). The view that is correct in my opinion is that they are the foremost in emigration and in support. What indicates this is that He described them as foremost without specifying in what they were foremost, so the expression remains general (mujmal). However, He described them as Emigrants and Helpers, so it is necessary to direct that expression to that by which they became Emigrants and Helpers, namely emigration and support. Therefore it is necessary that what is meant is the foremost, the first, in emigration and support, in order to remove the generality from the expression. Also, precedence in emigration is a great act of obedience, inasmuch as emigration is a deed difficult upon the self and contrary to natural inclination. Whoever undertakes it first becomes an example for others in this obedience, and that strengthens the heart of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and is a cause for the removal of loneliness from his mind. Likewise precedence in support: when the Messenger, peace be upon him, came to Madinah, there is no doubt that those who were first to support and serve gained a great station. For these reasons, it is necessary that what is meant is: "the foremost, the first, in emigration."

Having established this, we say: the one most foremost among people in emigration is Abu Bakr, because he was in the service of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and was his companion in every dwelling and place, so his share of this station was higher than the share of others. As for 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, although he was among the first Emigrants, he only emigrated after the emigration of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and there is no doubt that he remained in Makkah for the affairs of the Messenger. Yet precedence in emigration came only to Abu Bakr, so Abu Bakr's share of this virtue was fuller. Once this is established, Abu Bakr is judged to be one with whom Allah is pleased, and he is pleased with Allah, and that is at the highest degrees of virtue.

And once this is established, it necessarily follows that he is the true imam after the Messenger of Allah, for if his imamate were invalid, he would deserve cursing and abhorrence, and that contradicts attaining such exalted honour. Thus this verse becomes among the strongest proofs of the virtue of Abu Bakr and 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, and of the soundness of their imamate.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible that what is meant is those who embraced Islam first among the Emigrants and Helpers, because these believed when the number of Muslims in Makkah and Madinah was small and weak? Islam was strengthened through them, the number of Muslims increased because of their Islam, the heart of the Messenger was strengthened by their entering Islam, and others followed them. Their situation in this is like that of one who establishes a good practice, for he has its reward and the reward of those who act upon it until the Day of Resurrection. Then we say: Grant that Abu Bakr falls under this verse by virtue of being the first of the Emigrants, but why do you say that he remained in that state? Why is it not permissible to say that he changed from that state, and that this virtue departed from him because of his undertaking that imamate?

The answer to the first: To take "the foremost" as referring to the foremost in time is an arbitrary restriction for which there is no evidence, because the word "foremost" is unrestricted, so taking it to mean precedence in time is no more appropriate than taking it to mean precedence in all matters. We have already shown that taking it to mean precedence in emigration is more appropriate.

As for the claim that it means precedence in Islam: We say that precedence in emigration includes precedence in Islam, whereas precedence in Islam does not include precedence in emigration, so taking the expression to mean precedence in emigration is more appropriate. Moreover, even granting that we take the expression to mean precedence in faith, we still say: His saying "the foremost, the first" is a plural form, so it must be taken to refer to a group, and therefore 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, and others must enter it. Grant that people differed as to whether Abu Bakr's faith was earlier or 'Ali's; yet they agreed that Abu Bakr is among the foremost, the first. The people of hadith agreed that the first man to embrace Islam was Abu Bakr, the first woman Khadijah, the first boy 'Ali, and the first freed slave Zayd. On this basis, Abu Bakr is among the foremost, the first. Also, we have shown that precedence in faith produces great virtue only insofar as it strengthens the heart of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and makes the one who precedes an example for others, and this meaning is most complete in the case of Abu Bakr. When he embraced Islam he was an elderly man well known among the people, and a group of senior Companions followed him. It is reported that when he embraced Islam he went to Talhah, al-Zubayr and 'Uthman ibn 'Affan, presented Islam to them, and then after some days brought them to the Messenger, peace be upon him, and they embraced Islam at the hand of the Messenger, peace be upon him. Thus it became evident that by his entering Islam, strength was added to Islam, and this became an example for others. These meanings did not apply to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, because at that time he was young and was like a boy within the house, so his embracing Islam at that time did not add great strength to Islam, nor did he become an example to others at that time. Therefore it is established that the head and chief in His saying "And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants" is none other than Abu Bakr.

As for his saying, "Why do you say that he remained described by this attribute after his undertaking to seek the imamate?"

We say: His saying, may He be exalted, "Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him" encompasses all states and times, as evidenced by the fact that there is no time or state except that an exception can validly be made from it. It may be said: "Allah is pleased with them, except at the time of seeking the imamate," and the requirement of the exception is to exclude what, were it not for the exception, would have entered under the wording. Or we say: We have shown that He described them as foremost Emigrants, and this requires that what is meant is their being foremost in emigration. Then, when He described them with this description, He established for them what necessitates honour, namely His saying "Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him." Precedence in emigration is a description suitable for honour, and mentioning a judgment immediately after a suitable description indicates that the judgment is caused by that description. This shows that the honour resulting from His saying "Allah is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him" is caused by their being foremost in emigration, and as long as the cause exists, that good pleasure must be present throughout the whole period of their existence. Or we say: He, may He be exalted, said: "And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow," and this requires that He has prepared those gardens and specified them for them, and this requires their remaining in that attribute on account of which they became deserving of those gardens. No one may say that what is meant is that He prepared them for them had they remained in the attribute of faith, for we say: this is an addition of an implied condition, which is contrary to the apparent meaning. Moreover, on this assumption there would be no difference between those mentioned in this praise and the other groups, because He says: "And He has prepared for them gardens beneath which rivers flow," and this would apply equally to Pharaoh, Haman, Abu Jahl and Abu Lahab, had they become believers. It is well known that He mentioned this statement in the context of great praise and complete commendation, and interpreting it according to what they (the objectors) suggested would annul this praise and commendation, so this question falls away. It is thus evident that this verse indicates the virtue of Abu Bakr, and definitively establishes the correctness of the view of his imamate.

* * *

The second issue: The scholars differed as to whether the praise in this verse encompasses all the Companions or only some of them. Some said: it encompasses those who were foremost in emigration and support, and on this view it includes only the earliest Companions, because the particle "min" (of/from) indicates partiality. Others said: rather, it encompasses all the Companions, because the entire body of Companions is described as foremost and first in relation to the rest of the Muslims, and the particle "min" in His saying "of the Emigrants and the Helpers" is not partitive but explanatory (li-l-tabyin), meaning: "and the foremost, the first, who are described as being Emigrants and Helpers," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So shun the abomination of idols﴾ [al-Hajj: 30]. Many people adopted this view. It is related from Humayd ibn Ziyad that he said: "One day I said to Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi: 'Will you not inform me about the companions of the Messenger, peace be upon him, concerning what took place among them?' and I wished to stir up dissension. He said to me: 'Indeed Allah, may He be exalted, has forgiven all of them and made Paradise obligatory for them in His Book, the good among them and the wrongdoers.' I said to him: 'In what place did He make Paradise obligatory for them?' He said: 'Glory be to Allah! Do you not read His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers﴾ to the end of the verse? So Allah made Paradise and good pleasure obligatory for all the Companions of the Prophet, peace be upon him, and stipulated a condition for the Successors (tabi'un), a condition He set for them.' I said: 'And what is that condition?' He said: 'He stipulated for them that they follow them with goodness in deed, that is, that they emulate them in their good deeds and do not emulate them in anything else; or it may be said: the meaning is that they follow them with goodness in speech, that is, that they do not say evil about them, and do not direct criticism at what they undertook.'" Humayd ibn Ziyad said: "It was as if I had never read this verse at all!"

* * *

The third issue: It is reported that 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, used to recite ﴿And the foremost, the first of the Emigrants and the Helpers, and those who followed them in goodness﴾ and he would join "and the Helpers" to "and the foremost," and would omit the waw from "and those who followed them in goodness," making it a description of the Helpers. It is also reported that 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, recited this verse in this manner, and Ubayy said: "By Allah, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ taught it to me in this manner, and you were selling cassia bark at that time in the marketplace of Madinah." 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You are right. You witnessed and we were absent, you were free and we were occupied, and if you wish, you would indeed say: 'We gave refuge and gave support.'" It is also reported that this debate took place between 'Umar and Zayd ibn Thabit, and Zayd cited Ubayy ibn Ka'b as evidence. The difference is that according to 'Umar's reading, the honour resulting from His saying "And the foremost, the first" is restricted to the Emigrants, and the Helpers do not share in it, so greater honour is due to the Emigrants. And Allah knows best. It is also reported that Ubayy argued for the soundness of the well-known reading by the last part of Surah al-Anfal, namely His saying: ﴿And those who believed afterwards and emigrated﴾ after the earlier mention of the Emigrants and Helpers in the first verse, and by the middle of Surah al-Hashr, namely His saying: ﴿And those who came after them﴾, and by the beginning of Surah al-Jumu'ah, namely His saying: ﴿And others among them who have not yet joined them﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 3].

Fifth issue: His saying, ﴿And those who followed them with excellence﴾. 'Ata' reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: he means they mention the Muhajirun and the Ansar with paradise, mercy and supplication for them, and they mention their virtues. In another narration he said: "And those who followed them with excellence" in their religion until the Day of Resurrection. Know that the verse indicates that whoever follows them is only deserving of Allah's good pleasure and reward on the condition that they follow them with excellence. We have explained this excellence as excellence of speech concerning them. A conditional ruling ceases to apply when its condition is absent, so it follows that whoever does not speak well of the Muhajirun and the Ansar is not deserving of Allah the Exalted's good pleasure, and is not among the people of reward for this reason. The people of the religion go to great lengths in honouring the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and do not let their tongues loose in backbiting them or mentioning them with what is not fitting.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 101:

قَوْلُهُ تَعالى: ﴿ومِمَّنْ حَوْلَكم مِنَ الأعْرابِ مُنافِقُونَ ومِن أهْلِ المَدِينَةِ مَرَدُوا عَلى النِّفاقِ لا تَعْلَمُهم نَحْنُ نَعْلَمُهم سَنُعَذِّبُهم مَرَّتَيْنِ ثُمَّ يُرَدُّونَ إلى عَذابٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾

His words, exalted is He: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites, and among the people of Madinah are those who have persisted in hypocrisy. You do not know them; We know them. We will punish them twice; then they will be returned to a great punishment.﴾

اعْلَمْ أنَّهُ تَعالى شَرَحَ أحْوالَ مُنافِقِي المَدِينَةِ، ثُمَّ ذَكَرَ بَعْدَهُ أحْوالَ مُنافِقِي الأعْرابِ، ثُمَّ بَيَّنَ أنَّ في الأعْرابِ مَن هو مُؤْمِنٌ صالِحٌ مُخْلِصٌ، ثُمَّ بَيَّنَ أنَّ رُؤَساءَ المُؤْمِنِينَ مَن هم ؟ وهُمُ السّابِقُونَ المُهاجِرُونَ والأنْصارُ. فَذَكَرَ في هَذِهِ الآيَةِ أنَّ جَماعَةً مِن حَوْلِ المَدِينَةِ مَوْصُوفُونَ بِالنِّفاقِ، وإنْ كُنْتُمْ لا تَعْلَمُونَ كَوْنَهم كَذَلِكَ، فَقالَ: ﴿ومِمَّنْ حَوْلَكم مِنَ الأعْرابِ مُنافِقُونَ﴾ وهم جُهَيْنَةُ وأسْلَمُ وأشْجَعُ وغِفارٌ، وكانُوا نازِلِينَ حَوْلَها.

Know that He, exalted is He, first explained the circumstances of the hypocrites of Madinah, then after that mentioned the circumstances of the hypocrites among the Bedouins. Then He made clear that among the Bedouins there are those who are believers, righteous and sincere. Then He made clear who the leaders of the believers are: they are the foremost, the emigrants (al-Muhajirun) and the helpers (al-Ansar). In this verse He mentioned that a group around Madinah are described with hypocrisy, even though you do not know that they are such, so He said: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾. They are Juhaynah, Aslam, Ashja' and Ghifar, who were dwelling around it.

وأمّا قَوْلُهُ: ﴿ومِن أهْلِ المَدِينَةِ مَرَدُوا عَلى النِّفاقِ﴾ فَفِيهِ بَحْثانِ:

As for His words: ﴿and among the people of Madinah are those who have persisted in hypocrisy﴾, there are two discussions:

البَحْثُ الأوَّلُ: قالَ الزَّجّاجُ: أنَّهُ حَصَلَ فِيهِ تَقْدِيمٌ وتَأْخِيرٌ، والتَّقْدِيرُ: ومِمَّنْ حَوْلَكم مِنَ الأعْرابِ ومِن أهْلِ المَدِينَةِ مُنافِقُونَ مَرَدُوا عَلى النِّفاقِ فَأضْمَرَ (مَن) لِدَلالَةِ (مِن) عَلَيْها كَما في قَوْلِهِ تَعالى: ﴿وما مِنّا إلّا لَهُ مَقامٌ مَعْلُومٌ﴾ (الصّافّاتِ: ١٦٤) يُرِيدُ إلّا مَن لَهُ مَقامٌ مَعْلُومٌ.

The first discussion: al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said that there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir) in it, and the sense is: "And among those around you of the Bedouins and among the people of Madinah are hypocrites, who have persisted in hypocrisy." So he omitted (man, "those who") because the (min, "among") indicates it, as in His words: ﴿And there is none of us but has a known station﴾ (al-Saffat: 164), meaning: "none of us except he who has a known station."

البَحْثُ الثّانِي: يُقالُ: مَرُدَ يَمْرَدُ مَرَدًا فَهو مارِدٌ ومَرِيدٌ إذا عَتا، والمَرِيدُ مِن شَياطِينِ الإنْسِ والجِنِّ، وقَدْ تَمَرَّدَ عَلَيْنا أيْ عَتا، وقالَ ابْنُ الأعْرابِيِّ: المُرادُ التَّطاوُلُ بِالكِبَرِ والمَعاصِي، ومِنهُ: ﴿مَرَدُوا عَلى النِّفاقِ﴾ وأصْلُ المَرُودِ المَلاسَةُ، ومِنهُ صَرْحٌ مُمَرَّدٌ، وغُلامٌ أمْرَدُ، والمَرْداءُ الرَّمْلَةُ الَّتِي لا تُنْبِتُ شَيْئًا، كَأنَّ مَن لَمْ يَقْبَلْ قَوْلَ غَيْرِهِ ولَمْ يَلْتَفِتْ إلَيْهِ، بَقِيَ كَما كانَ عَلى صِفَتِهِ الأصْلِيَّةِ مِن غَيْرِ حُدُوثِ تَغَيُّرٍ فِيهِ البَتَّةَ، وذَلِكَ هو المَلاسَةُ.

The second discussion: It is said: "marada (مَرَدَ) yamradu (يَمْرَدُ) maradan (مَرَدًا), so he is māridun (مارِدٌ) and marid (مَرِيدٌ)," when he becomes rebellious (ata). The marid is one of the rebellious devils of mankind and jinn. "He has rebelled against us" (tamarrada 'alayna) means he became insolent. Ibn al-A'rabi said: what is meant is arrogance through pride and sins, and from this comes ﴿persisted in hypocrisy﴾ (maradu 'ala al-nifaq). The root of marud is smoothness (al-malasah), and from it comes a smooth palace (sarh mumarrad), a beardless youth (ghulam amrad), and al-marda', which is a sandy ground that produces nothing. It is as if one who does not accept the words of others and does not pay attention to them remains in his original state without any change occurring in him at all, and that is smoothness.

صفحة ١٣٨
[Page 138]

إذا عَرَفْتَ أصْلَ اللَّفْظِ فَنَقُولُ: قَوْلُهُ: ﴿مَرَدُوا عَلى النِّفاقِ﴾ أيْ ثَبَتُوا واسْتَمَرُّوا فِيهِ ولَمْ يَتُوبُوا عَنْهُ.
Having understood the root of the word, we say: His words ﴿persisted in hypocrisy﴾ mean they remained firm in it, continued in it, and did not repent from it.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى: ﴿لا تَعْلَمُهم نَحْنُ نَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾ وهو كَقَوْلِهِ: ﴿لا تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ﴾ [الأنفال: ٦٠] والمَعْنى أنَّهم تَمَرَّدُوا في حِرْفَةِ النِّفاقِ فَصارُوا فِيها أُسْتاذِينِ، وبَلَغُوا إلى حَيْثُ لا تَعْلَمُ أنْتَ نِفاقَهم مَعَ قُوَّةِ خاطِرِكَ وصَفاءِ حَدْسِكَ ونَفْسِكَ.

Then He said: ﴿You do not know them; We know them﴾, and it is like His words: ﴿You do not know them; Allah knows them﴾ (al-Anfal: 60). The meaning is that they became rebellious in the craft of hypocrisy, so they became masters in it, and they reached a point where you do not know their hypocrisy, despite the strength of your insight and the clarity of your intuition and your soul.

ثُمَّ قالَ: ﴿سَنُعَذِّبُهم مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾ وذَكَرُوا في تَفْسِيرِ المَرَّتَيْنِ وُجُوهًا كَثِيرَةً:

Then He said: ﴿We will punish them twice﴾, and they mentioned many aspects regarding the explanation of "twice":

الوَجْهُ الأوَّلُ: قالَ ابْنُ عَبّاسٍ - رَضِيَ اللَّهُ عَنْهُما -: يُرِيدُ الأمْراضَ في الدُّنْيا، وعَذابَ الآخِرَةِ، وذَلِكَ أنَّ مَرَضَ المُؤْمِنِ يُفِيدُهُ تَكْفِيرُ السَّيِّئاتِ، ومَرَضُ الكافِرِ يُفِيدُهُ زِيادَةُ الكُفْرِ وكُفْرانُ النِّعَمِ.

The first aspect: Ibn Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: He means illnesses in this world and the punishment of the Hereafter. That is because the illness of a believer brings him the expiation of sins, while the illness of a disbeliever brings him an increase in disbelief and ingratitude for blessings.

الوَجْهُ الثّانِي: رَوى السُّدِّيُّ عَنْ أنَسِ بْنِ مالِكٍ أنَّ «النَّبِيَّ - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - قامَ خَطِيبًا يَوْمَ الجُمُعَةِ فَقالَ: ”اخْرُجْ يا فُلانُ فَإنَّكَ مُنافِقٌ اخْرُجْ يا فُلانُ فَإنَّكَ مُنافِقٌ» “ فَأخْرَجَ مِنَ المَسْجِدِ ناسًا وفَضَحَهم فَهَذا هو العَذابُ الأوَّلُ، والثّانِي عَذابُ القَبْرِ.

The second aspect: al-Suddi narrated from Anas ibn Malik that "the Prophet (ﷺ) stood up delivering a sermon on Friday and said: 'Go out, O so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite. Go out, O so-and-so, for you are a hypocrite.'" So he expelled people from the mosque and exposed them. This is the first punishment, and the second is the punishment of the grave.

والوَجْهُ الثّالِثُ: قالَ مُجاهِدٌ: في الدُّنْيا بِالقَتْلِ والسَّبْيِ وبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ بِعَذابِ القَبْرِ.

The third aspect: Mujahid said: in this world through killing and captivity, and after that through the punishment of the grave.

والوَجْهُ الرّابِعُ: قالَ قَتادَةُ بِالدُّبَيْلَةِ وعَذابِ القَبْرِ، وذَلِكَ أنَّ «النَّبِيَّ - عَلَيْهِ السَّلامُ - أسَرَّ إلى حُذَيْفَةَ اثْنَيْ عَشَرَ رَجُلًا مِنَ المُنافِقِينَ»، وقالَ: سِتَّةٌ يَبْتَلِيهِمُ اللَّهُ بِالدُّبَيْلَةِ سِراجٌ مِن نارٍ يَأْخُذُ أحَدَهم حَتّى يَخْرُجَ مِن صَدْرِهِ، وسِتَّةٌ يَمُوتُونَ مَوْتًا.

The fourth aspect: Qatadah said: through the dubaylah (a festering boil) and the punishment of the grave. That is because "the Prophet (ﷺ) confided to Hudhayfah twelve men among the hypocrites," and said: "Six of them Allah will afflict with the dubaylah, a lamp of fire that seizes one of them until it comes out of his chest, and six will die a natural death."

والوَجْهُ الخامِسُ: قالَ الحَسَنُ: بِأخْذِ الزَّكاةِ مِن أمْوالِهِمْ، وعَذابِ القَبْرِ.

The fifth aspect: al-Hasan said: through the taking of zakat from their wealth, and the punishment of the grave.

والوَجْهُ السّادِسُ: قالَ مُحَمَّدُ بْنُ إسْحاقَ: هو ما يَدْخُلُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِن غَيْظِ الإسْلامِ، ودُخُولُهم فِيهِ مِن غَيْرِ حَسَنَةٍ، ثُمَّ عَذابُهم في القُبُورِ.

The sixth aspect: Muhammad ibn Ishaq said: it is what enters upon them of the rage of Islam, and their entering into it without any good deed, then their punishment in the graves.

والوَجْهُ السّابِعُ: أحَدُ العَذابَيْنِ ضَرْبُ المَلائِكَةِ الوُجُوهَ والأدْبارَ. والآخَرُ عِنْدَ البَعْثِ، يُوَكَّلُ بِهِمْ عُنُقُ النّارِ. والأوْلى أنْ يُقالَ مَراتِبُ الحَياةِ ثَلاثَةٌ: حَياةُ الدُّنْيا، وحَياةُ القَبْرِ، وحَياةُ القِيامَةِ، فَقَوْلُهُ: ﴿سَنُعَذِّبُهم مَرَّتَيْنِ﴾ المُرادُ مِنهُ عَذابُ الدُّنْيا بِجَمِيعِ أقْسامِهِ، وعَذابُ القَبْرِ. وقَوْلُهُ: ﴿ثُمَّ يُرَدُّونَ إلى عَذابٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ المُرادُ مِنهُ العَذابُ في الحَياةِ الثّالِثَةِ، وهي الحَياةُ في القِيامَةِ.

The seventh aspect: one of the two punishments is the angels striking their faces and backs, and the other is at the Resurrection, when the "unuq al-nar" (a fiery guard/keeper of hell) is assigned to them. The better view is to say that the stages of life are three: the life of this world, the life of the grave, and the life of the Resurrection. So His words ﴿We will punish them twice﴾ mean the punishment of this world in all its forms, and the punishment of the grave. And His words ﴿then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾ mean the punishment in the third life, which is life in the Resurrection.

ثُمَّ قالَ تَعالى في آخِرِ الآيَةِ: ﴿ثُمَّ يُرَدُّونَ إلى عَذابٍ عَظِيمٍ﴾ يَعْنِي النّارَ المُخَلَّدَةَ المُؤَبَّدَةَ.

Then He, exalted is He, said at the end of the verse: ﴿then they will be returned to a great punishment﴾, meaning the everlasting, eternal Fire.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 102–103 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and invoke blessings upon them. Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
Page 139

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Regarding His saying, ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, there are two opinions:
The first: they are a group of hypocrites who repented of hypocrisy.
The second: they are a group of Muslims who lagged behind from the expedition to Tabuk, not out of disbelief and hypocrisy, but out of laziness; then they regretted what they had done and then repented. Those who held the first view argued that His saying, ﴿And others﴾, is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying, ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾, and conjunction gives the impression of association. However, He, the Exalted, granted them success until they repented. So when He mentioned the first group by their persistence in hypocrisy and their exaggeration in it, He described this group by repentance and abandoning hypocrisy.

Second issue: It is narrated that they were three: Abu Lubabah Marwan ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Thaʿlabah, and Wadiʿah ibn Hizam. It is also said that they were ten. Seven of them tied themselves up when news reached them of what had been revealed concerning those who lagged behind, and they were certain of destruction, and they tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived, entered the mosque and prayed two rakʿahs, and this was his custom. When he returned from his journey and saw them bound, he asked about them, and it was mentioned to him that they had sworn not to free themselves until the Messenger of Allah himself would free them. He said: "And I swear that I will not free them until I am commanded concerning them." Then this verse was revealed, and he released them and excused them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth, and we only lagged behind you because of it, so give charity from it and purify us." He said: "I was not commanded to take any of your wealth." Then the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ — the verse.

Third issue: Regarding His saying, ﴿acknowledged their sins﴾, the people of language said: iʿtirāf (acknowledgment) is an expression for affirming a matter with knowledge, and its meaning is that they confessed their sin. There is a subtle point in it, as if it were said: they did not offer false excuses for their lagging behind as others did, but they acknowledged against themselves that they had done an evil thing, showed regret, and reproached themselves for that lagging behind.

If it is asked: Does acknowledgment of sin constitute repentance or not?
We say: mere acknowledgment of sin is not repentance. But when it is accompanied by regret for the past, and resolve to abandon it in the future, and this regret and repentance are because it is forbidden by Allah the Exalted, then this combination is repentance. However, the evidence indicates that these people had repented, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, and the commentators said: "Perhaps" from Allah indicates obligation.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad﴾, and in this there are two discussions:
First discussion: Regarding this righteous deed there are several aspects:
First: the righteous deed is their acknowledgment of sin, regret over it, and repentance from it, and the bad deed is lagging behind the raid.
Second: the righteous deed is their going out with the Messenger to the other expeditions, and the bad deed is their lagging behind from the expedition to Tabuk.
Third: this verse was revealed concerning Muslims, and the righteous deed was their hastening to acts of righteousness that proceeded from them.

Second discussion: Someone may say: each of the righteous deed and the bad deed has been described as mixed. So what is it mixed with? The answer is that mixing (khalt) is an expression for general combining. As for your saying "I mixed it," it is fitting only where each of the two blends with the other, and each changes from its original attribute because of that mingling, like your saying "I mixed water with milk." What is fitting for this context is general combination, because when the righteous deed and the bad deed have occurred, each remains as it was according to our school, for with us the doctrine of mutual cancellation (iḥbāṭ) is false, and obedience remains requiring praise and reward, and disobedience remains requiring blame and punishment. So His saying, ﴿They had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad﴾, contains an indication of the negation of the doctrine of mutual cancellation, and that each of them remained as it was without one affecting the other. Among what supports this verse in negating the doctrine of cancellation is that He, the Exalted, described the righteous deed and the bad deed with mixing. Those mixed must necessarily remain while they are mixed, because mixing is an attribute of the things mixed, and the existence of an attribute while the subject is absent is impossible; so this indicates the continuance of both deeds during the mixing.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, and in it there are discussions:
First discussion: Here is a question: the word ʿasā ("perhaps") expresses doubt, and doubt regarding Allah the Exalted is impossible. Its answer is in several aspects:
First aspect: the commentators said: ʿasā from Allah is obligatory, and the evidence for this is His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring the victory﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 52), and He did so. The precise statement on this is that the Qur'an was revealed in accordance with the customary speech of people, and a great sovereign, when a needy person asks him for something, does not grant it except by way of hope, with the word ʿasā or laʿalla, to indicate that no one may oblige me to anything or charge me with anything; rather, everything I do, I do by way of grace and favor. So the benefit of mentioning the word ʿasā is this meaning, while it also conveys certainty of response.
Second aspect: the answer, whose purpose is to show that the accountable person must be between hope and apprehension, because that is further from denial and neglect.
Second discussion: Our companions said: His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, is explicit that repentance is not achieved except by the creation of Allah the Exalted. Reason also indicates this, because the basis of repentance is regret, and regret is not achieved by the servant's choice, for if the will to act or to abandon were an act of the servant, its performance would require another will, and furthermore a person may have a very strong desire for a specific act, then become very regretful over it; while he is desiring it he cannot dispel that desire from his heart, and when he becomes regretful he cannot dispel that regret from his heart. This shows that the servant has no power to bring about regret or to bring about desire. The Mu'tazilah said: what is meant by His saying "Allah accepts repentance" is that He accepts their repentance.
The answer: diverting the word from its apparent meaning is only fitting when it is established by evidence that the wording cannot be taken in its apparent sense. Here, however, the rational evidence is that the wording cannot be taken except in its apparent sense, so how can interpretation be fitting?
Third discussion: His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, requires that this repentance occurs in the future. And His saying, ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, indicates that this acknowledgment occurred in the past, and that indicates that this acknowledgment was not itself the repentance, but was a preliminary to repentance, and that repentance occurs only after it.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾, and in it there are issues:
First issue: People differed concerning the intended meaning. Some said: this refers to those who repented, because they had given their wealth as charity, so Allah the Exalted made its acceptance obligatory, and that became considered in the completeness of their repentance, so that it would serve in their case as an expiation. This is the view of al-Hasan, who used to say: the intended meaning of this verse is not obligatory charity, but rather the charity of expiation for the sin that proceeded from them.

The second view: the zakāt had been obligatory upon them, and when they repented of their lagging behind from the raid, and their Islam became good, and they offered zakāt, Allah commanded His Messenger to take it from them.

The third view: this verse is an independent statement, and its purpose is to make obligatory the taking of zakāt from the wealthy, and most jurists hold this view, for they used this verse as evidence for the obligation of zakāt, and they said that zakāt is purification.

As for those who hold the first view, they argued for the soundness of their position by saying that verses must be coherent and well-ordered; if we took it to mean obligatory zakāt from the outset, this verse would have no connection with what precedes it or what follows it, and would become an alien word, which is not befitting for the speech of Allah the Exalted. As for those who say the intended meaning is taking obligatory zakāt, they said: the connection is also present on this supposition, for when they displayed repentance and regret for lagging behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and admitted that the cause of that lagging was their love of wealth and their intense greed to preserve it from spending, it was as if it were said to them: the soundness of your claim of this repentance and regret will only appear if you pay the obligatory zakāt and are not reluctant about it, for claims are established only by testing, and at the test a man is honored or humiliated. If they paid those zakāt with a contented soul, their sincerity in that repentance and return would be manifest; otherwise they would be liars and deceivers by this means. However, interpreting this verse as a command to pay obligatory zakāt, while the arrangement of these verses remains sound, is preferable. And among what indicates that the intended meaning is obligatory charities is His saying, ﴿by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾, and the meaning is: you purify them from sin by means of taking those charities. This is valid only if we say that had he not taken that charity, the sin would have remained, and that is only valid if the sin would occur in obligatory charities. As for those who hold the first view, they said: when he, upon him be blessings and peace, excused those repentant ones and released them, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth by which we lagged behind you, so give charity from it on our behalf, purify us, and ask forgiveness for us." He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "I have not been commanded to take any of your wealth." So Allah the Exalted revealed these verses, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took one-third of their wealth and left two-thirds, because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾, and did not say "take their wealth," and the word "min" (from) indicates partiality. Know that this report does not contradict the view we have chosen, as if it were said to them: since you were content with giving a charity that is not obligatory, then you should all the more be content with giving the obligatory duties.

* * *

Second issue: This verse indicates many rulings concerning zakāt.

First ruling: His saying, ﴿Take from their wealth﴾, indicates that the amount taken is a part of that wealth, not all of it, since the quantity of that part is not stated here explicitly. Rather, what is mentioned here is His saying, ﴿a charity﴾. It is known that the intended meaning is not indefiniteness such that any portion whatsoever would suffice, even if it were extremely small, like a single grain of wheat or a tiny fraction of gold. Therefore, the intended meaning must be a charity whose attribute, manner, and quantity are known to them, so that His saying, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ is a command to take that known charity, and then the generality is removed. It is known that this charity is none other than the charities which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described and explained in their manner, and the charity which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained is that he commanded

Page 142

[Page 143]

**Issue 2 (of the ruling):** [Wording continues from the previous part:] by taking from twenty-five camels a *bint makhad* (a she-camel in its second year), from thirty-six a *bint labun* (a she-camel in its third year), and so on through the other grades. So His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ is a command to take those specific things and those specific items. The apparent sense of the verse is obligation, so this text indicates that taking them is obligatory, and that implies that the monetary value cannot substitute for them, according to the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

**The second ruling:** His saying ﴿from their wealth a charity﴾ requires that the wealth be theirs. When this is so, the poor person is not a partner of the owner in the *nisab* (the minimum threshold for zakat). It then follows that zakat is attached to the person's liability (*dhimmah*) and has no attachment at all to the *nisab*.

Once this is established, we say: if a person neglects zakat until the *nisab* is destroyed, what has been destroyed is not the locus of the right; rather, the locus of the right remains as it was. Therefore that obligation must remain after the destruction of the *nisab* as it was before. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

**The third ruling:** The apparent generality of this verse requires zakat on the wealth of one who is in debt and on the wealth of one who is a guarantor (*daman*). This is apparent.

**The fourth ruling:** The apparent sense of the verse indicates that zakat is only obligated as a purification from sins. Therefore it is obligated only where it becomes a purification from sins. Its being a purification from sins is only established where sins can occur, and this is conceivable only regarding the one who has reached maturity. Hence it must be that zakat is obligatory only upon the mature, as is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. However, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, responds and says: the verse indicates the taking of charity from their wealth, and taking charity from their wealth entails that it is a purification. So why do you claim that taking zakat from the wealth of a child or a madman is a purification? For it does not follow that the absence of a specific cause entails the absence of the ruling in every respect.

* * *

**Issue 3:** Regarding His saying ﴿to purify them﴾, there are several views:

**The first view:** The implied meaning is: "Take, O Muhammad, from their wealth a charity, for you purify them."

**The second view:** ﴿to purify them﴾ is linked to the charity, and the implied meaning is: "Take from their wealth a charity that purifies them." It is appropriate to describe the charity as purifying because it has been reported that charity is "the filth of people." When charity is taken, that filth is removed, so its removal is considered as purification. And Allah knows best.

According to this view, it must be said that His saying ﴿and cleanse them﴾ is detached from the first part, and the implied meaning is: "Take [O Muhammad] from their wealth a charity which purifies them; that charity [purifies them], and you [O Muhammad] cleanse them by means of it."

**The third view:** The *ta'* in ﴿tutahhiruhum wa-tuzakkihim﴾ is taken as the pronoun of the addressee, and the meaning is: "You, O taker who takes it from them, purify them, and cleanse them by means of that charity."

* * *

**Issue 4:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It has been recited as *tuthhiruhum* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *ha'*), from *athharahu*, meaning *tahharahu* (purified him). And as *tuthhirhum* (with a *jazm*, as a response to the imperative). And ﴿wa-tuzakkihim﴾ has not been recited except with the *ya'* present.

[Page 143 continues]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and cleanse them﴾. Know that since *tazkiyah* (cleansing/growth) is coordinated with *tathhir* (purification), a difference must exist. So it is said: *tazkiyah* is an intensification of *tathhir*. It is also said: *tazkiyah* means growth (*inma'*). The meaning is that He, exalted is He, makes the deficiency that results from giving the amount of zakat a cause of growth. And it is said: charity purifies them from the filth of sin and disobedience, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, cleanses them, elevates their status, and praises them when they give it to the poor.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And pray for them; indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. There are several issues concerning this:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿inna salataka﴾ without a *waw* and with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, in the singular, and the intended meaning is the category. Likewise in Surat Hud, ﴿a-salatuka ta'muruka﴾ [Hud: 87] without a *waw* and in the singular. The rest read *salawatika* in the plural, and likewise in Hud in the plural. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The first recitation is better, because prayer (*salah*) is more frequent; do you not see that He said ﴿Establish prayer﴾? The plural *salawat* is a plural of paucity (*jam' qillah*), as you say "three prayers" and "five prayers." Abu Hatim said: This is an error, because the form *salawat* is not for paucity, since He, exalted is He, said ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27], and He did not intend a small number. And He said ﴿and they will be secure in the upper chambers﴾ (Saba': 37) and ﴿indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ (al-Ahzab: 35).

**The second issue:** Those who withheld zakat in the time of Abu Bakr used this verse as evidence. They said: Allah commanded His Messenger to take charities, then commanded him to pray for them, and mentioned that his prayer is a comfort for them. So the obligation of zakat was conditioned on the attainment of that comfort, and it is known that no one other than the Messenger can stand in his place in attaining that comfort. Therefore it is obligatory to give zakat to no one other than the Messenger, peace be upon him. Know that this argument is weak, because the rest of the verses indicate that zakat is obligated only to meet the need of the poor, as in His saying ﴿Charities are only for the poor﴾ (al-Tawbah: 60), and as in His saying ﴿and in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 19).

* * *

**The third issue:** There is no doubt that *salah* in its original linguistic sense means supplication (*du'a'*). When we say "So-and-so prayed for So-and-so," it conveys supplication according to the original language. However, by custom it has come to convey that he said to him: "O Allah, bless him." For this reason the commentators differed. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: its meaning is "supplicate for them." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sunnah for the imam, when he takes charity, is to supplicate for the giver and say: "May Allah reward you for what you gave, and bless for you what you have kept." Others said: its meaning is that he says: "O Allah, bless So-and-so." They related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that when the family of Abu Awfa brought him charity, he said: "O Allah, bless the family of Abu Awfa." And the judge (al-Qadi), in his *Tafsir*, related from al-Ka'bi in his *Tafsir* that 'Ali said to 'Umar while he was covered [in death]: "Upon you be the prayer and peace." Some people denied this. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: Blessing (*salah*) from one person upon another is not appropriate except regarding the Prophet, peace be upon him.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Our companions prohibit mentioning *salawat* from Allah upon anyone except the Messenger, peace be upon him. The Shi'a mention it regarding 'Ali and his descendants, and they argue against us that the text of the Qur'an indicates that this mention is permissible regarding one who pays zakat. So how can its mention be prohibited regarding 'Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them? I have seen some of them say: Is it not the case that when a man says "Peace be upon you," it is said to him, "And upon you be peace"? This indicates that using this expression is permissible regarding the majority of Muslims. So how can its mention be prohibited regarding the family of the Messenger, peace be upon him? The judge said: It is permissible regarding the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the evidence for this is that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have known the greeting upon you, so how is the blessing upon you?" He said, by way of instruction: "Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham." It is known that there is no prophet among the family of Muhammad, so this includes 'Ali, just as the same may be permitted regarding the family of Abraham. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** I had mentioned some subtleties concerning the statement of some people to others: "Peace be upon you" (*salam 'alaykum*). They are not suitable for this place, but I saw fit to record them here so that they would not be lost. I said: When a man says to another "*salamun 'alaykum*," then His saying "*salamun*" is a predicate (*mubtada'*), and it is indefinite (*nakirah*). They claimed that making an indefinite word the subject is not permissible. They said: this is because a predication only conveys benefit when one predicates an unknown matter of a known subject. However, they said: when the indefinite is qualified (*mawsufah*), it is permissible to make it the subject, as in His, exalted is He, saying ﴿and a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (al-Baqarah: 221).

Having known this, there are two possible explanations here:

**The first:** Indefiniteness indicates perfection. Do you not see His, exalted is He, saying ﴿and you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾ (al-Baqarah: 96)? The meaning is: "You will surely find them the most eager of people for a life that is lasting, perfect, and uninterrupted."

Having established this, His saying "*salam*" is an indefinite word, so the intended meaning is a complete, perfect peace. On this assumption, this indefinite has become qualified, so it is correct to make it a subject, and when that is so, the predicate comes forth, which is His saying "*'alaykum*." The implied meaning is: "A complete, perfect peace upon you."

**The second:** His saying "*'alaykum*" may be taken as a description (*sifah*) of His saying "*salam*," so that the whole of "*salamun 'alaykum*" is the subject, and a predicate is implied for it. The implied meaning is: "A peace upon you that is occurring, existing, and attained." Perhaps the omission of the predicate is more indicative of awe and grandeur.

Having known this, we say: when replying, this order is reversed and one says "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*." The reason for this, as Sibawayh said, is that they put first what is more important, and what they are most concerned with. So when he says "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*," this indicates that this responder's concern for that speaker is strong and complete. Also, His saying "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*" conveys restriction (*hasr*), as though he is saying: "If you have conveyed the peace to me, then I add to it and make the peace specific to you and confined to you, in compliance with His, exalted is He, saying ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, then greet with something better than it, or return it﴾ (al-Nisa': 86)."

One of the subtleties of His saying "*salamun 'alaykum*" is that it is more complete than the saying "*as-salamu 'alayka*." This is because "*salamun 'alayka*" means: a complete, perfect, noble, and exalted peace upon you. As for "*as-salamu 'alayka*," *as-salam* is a singular word with the definite article *al-*, which conveys only the essence of the reality (*asl al-mahiyyah*), and a word indicating the essence of the reality carries no indication of the accidental states of that reality or its perfections. So "*salamun 'alayka*" is more complete than "*as-salamu 'alayka*." What further confirms this meaning is that wherever the word "*salam*" comes from Allah, exalted is He, it comes in the indefinite form, as in His saying ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you﴾ (al-An'am: 54), and His saying ﴿Say: Praise belongs to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ (al-Naml: 59). There is much of this kind in the Qur'an. As for the word "*as-salam*" with the definite article, it has come only from the prophets, peace be upon them, as in the statement of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord, and peace will be upon those who follow guidance﴾ (Ta-Ha: 47). As for Surat Maryam, when Allah mentioned Yahya, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born and the day he dies﴾ (Maryam: 15), and this peace is from Allah, exalted is He. In the story of 'Isa, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born and the day I die﴾ (Maryam: 33), and this is the speech of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Thus it is established by these aspects that His saying "*salamun 'alayka*" is more complete than His saying "*as-salamu*

[Page 145]

...'alayka). For this reason al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) chose, in the recitation of the tashahhud (the testimony recited in prayer), the phrase "salamun 'alayka ayyuha al-nabiyyu" (peace be upon you, O Prophet) in the indefinite form (al-tankir). Among the subtleties of salam is this: there is no doubt that this world is the source of evils, calamities, trials and transgressions. Scholars who investigated the secrets of character disagreed over whether the basic nature of living beings is good or evil. Some said that the basic nature of living beings is evil. This is almost like the consensus (ijma') established among all human beings. Indeed, we go further and say that it is like the consensus among all living beings. The proof is that every person who sees another person approaching him, though he does not know him, finds that his nature drives him to beware of him and to prepare to repel him. Had his nature not witnessed that the basic state of a human being is evil, the natural reason would not have required preparation to repel the evil of that one who approaches him. They also said that this meaning exists in all animals: when one animal is approached by another, the first animal flees from it and avoids it. If it were established in its nature that the basic state of the one arriving is good, it would be necessary for the first to stand still, because the basic nature inclines toward seeking good. If the basic nature of an animal were that its good and evil were balanced and equal, then fleeing and standing still would have to be equal. Since this is not the case, but rather every animal, when another animal of unknown character approaches it, avoids it merely by its original natural disposition, we know that the basic state of the animal is evil.

Once this is established, we say: repelling evil is more important than acquiring good. This is shown by several considerations:

First: repelling evil requires preserving the original state, and preserving the original state is more important than gaining what is additional.

Second: bringing good to every individual is not within capacity, whereas restraining evil from every individual is within capacity, because the first is an act and the second is an abstention. Performing what has no end is not possible, whereas abstaining from what has no end is possible.

Third: if the repelling of evil does not occur, then evil has occurred, and this necessitates the occurrence of pain and grief, which is in the utmost hardship. And if the bringing of good also does not occur, the person remains neither in good nor in evil, but in his original safety, and enduring this state is easy. Thus it is established that repelling evil is more important than bringing good. It is also established that this world is the abode of evils, calamities, trials and afflictions, and that the living being, by its original creation and the requirement of its natural disposition, is a source of evils. When one person reaches another, the most important of all matters is that he inform him that he is with him in safety, security and peace. For this reason the convention was established that conversation begins with mentioning salam, by saying "salamun 'alaykum" (peace be upon you).

Among the subtleties of our saying "salamun 'alaykum" is that its apparent meaning requires conferring peace upon a group. This is so according to reason and according to the Shari'ah. As for the Shari'ah, the Qur'an indicates that a person is never without a group of angels who protect him and watch over his affairs, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ (al-Infitar 82:10-11). Reason also indicates this, because human souls are of different kinds: some are good and rational, some are turbid and wicked, some are appetitive, and some are irascible. For each group of the lower human souls there is a strong higher soul which is like a father to those human souls, and these souls are in relation to that higher soul as children are in relation to a father. It is that higher soul which bestows upon them inspirations, sometimes while awake and sometimes in sleep. Also, the souls separated from their bodies, which resemble these souls in qualities, nature and property, acquire a kind of attachment to this body because of resemblance and affinity, and they become like helpers to this soul in its deeds: if good, then good; if evil, then evil. When you know this secret, a person must necessarily be accompanied by those souls akin to him. Thus his saying "salamun 'alaykum" is an indication of greeting this particular person to all the souls that are attached to him and accompany him because of spiritual companionship.

Among the subtleties of this topic is the following: [Page 146]
When human souls are characterized by true knowledge and noble morals, and they become strong and detached, and then the attachment of some of them to others grows strong, their lights are reflected upon one another, like a shining mirror facing another. For this reason, if a person wishes to recite a litany (wazifah) to his teacher, the proper etiquette is to begin with praising God and extolling the angels and prophets, then to supplicate for his teacher, and then to begin the recitation. Its purpose is to strengthen the connection between his soul and these holy, pure souls, so that, because of the strength of that connection, some of their lights and effects may appear in the soul of this seeker, and some of the overflowing lights from them settle in his intellect, and his soul is strengthened by the support of that overflow in grasping knowledge and sciences. When you know this, then if one says to another "salamun 'alaykum," a strong connection arises between them, and through that connection the souls correspond and the lights are reflected. We shall suffice with this measure on this topic, for we have mentioned that this section is foreign to the present discourse. And God knows best.

The sixth issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. Al-Wahidi said: "Sakan" in the language is that in which one finds tranquility. The meaning is that your prayer for them causes their souls to find tranquility in you. The commentators have various expressions. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: "Your supplication is mercy for them." Qatadah said: "Dignity for them." Al-Kalbi said: "Reassurance for them." Al-Farra' said: "When you seek forgiveness for them, their souls find tranquility in the knowledge that God has accepted their repentance."

I say: the spirit of Muhammad (peace be upon him) was a strong, luminous, pure and dazzling spirit. When Muhammad supplicates for them and mentions them with good, effects from his spiritual strength overflow upon their souls, and for this reason their souls become illuminated, their secrets become pure, and they pass from darkness to light, and from the corporeal to the spiritual. Its establishment is as was stated in the fifth issue.

Then He said: ﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their intentions.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 102–103 (part 1 of 3):

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins; they had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad. Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance. Indeed, Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow, and invoke blessings upon them. Indeed, your invocations are a comfort for them. And Allah is Hearing and Knowing.﴾
Page 139

In the verse there are several issues:

First issue: Regarding His saying, ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, there are two opinions:
The first: they are a group of hypocrites who repented of hypocrisy.
The second: they are a group of Muslims who lagged behind from the expedition to Tabuk, not out of disbelief and hypocrisy, but out of laziness; then they regretted what they had done and then repented. Those who held the first view argued that His saying, ﴿And others﴾, is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon His saying, ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾, and conjunction gives the impression of association. However, He, the Exalted, granted them success until they repented. So when He mentioned the first group by their persistence in hypocrisy and their exaggeration in it, He described this group by repentance and abandoning hypocrisy.

Second issue: It is narrated that they were three: Abu Lubabah Marwan ibn ʿAbd al-Mundhir, Aws ibn Thaʿlabah, and Wadiʿah ibn Hizam. It is also said that they were ten. Seven of them tied themselves up when news reached them of what had been revealed concerning those who lagged behind, and they were certain of destruction, and they tied themselves to the pillars of the mosque. Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) arrived, entered the mosque and prayed two rakʿahs, and this was his custom. When he returned from his journey and saw them bound, he asked about them, and it was mentioned to him that they had sworn not to free themselves until the Messenger of Allah himself would free them. He said: "And I swear that I will not free them until I am commanded concerning them." Then this verse was revealed, and he released them and excused them. They said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth, and we only lagged behind you because of it, so give charity from it and purify us." He said: "I was not commanded to take any of your wealth." Then the words of Allah were revealed: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ — the verse.

Third issue: Regarding His saying, ﴿acknowledged their sins﴾, the people of language said: iʿtirāf (acknowledgment) is an expression for affirming a matter with knowledge, and its meaning is that they confessed their sin. There is a subtle point in it, as if it were said: they did not offer false excuses for their lagging behind as others did, but they acknowledged against themselves that they had done an evil thing, showed regret, and reproached themselves for that lagging behind.

If it is asked: Does acknowledgment of sin constitute repentance or not?
We say: mere acknowledgment of sin is not repentance. But when it is accompanied by regret for the past, and resolve to abandon it in the future, and this regret and repentance are because it is forbidden by Allah the Exalted, then this combination is repentance. However, the evidence indicates that these people had repented, by the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, and the commentators said: "Perhaps" from Allah indicates obligation.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad﴾, and in this there are two discussions:
First discussion: Regarding this righteous deed there are several aspects:
First: the righteous deed is their acknowledgment of sin, regret over it, and repentance from it, and the bad deed is lagging behind the raid.
Second: the righteous deed is their going out with the Messenger to the other expeditions, and the bad deed is their lagging behind from the expedition to Tabuk.
Third: this verse was revealed concerning Muslims, and the righteous deed was their hastening to acts of righteousness that proceeded from them.

Second discussion: Someone may say: each of the righteous deed and the bad deed has been described as mixed. So what is it mixed with? The answer is that mixing (khalt) is an expression for general combining. As for your saying "I mixed it," it is fitting only where each of the two blends with the other, and each changes from its original attribute because of that mingling, like your saying "I mixed water with milk." What is fitting for this context is general combination, because when the righteous deed and the bad deed have occurred, each remains as it was according to our school, for with us the doctrine of mutual cancellation (iḥbāṭ) is false, and obedience remains requiring praise and reward, and disobedience remains requiring blame and punishment. So His saying, ﴿They had mixed a righteous deed with another that was bad﴾, contains an indication of the negation of the doctrine of mutual cancellation, and that each of them remained as it was without one affecting the other. Among what supports this verse in negating the doctrine of cancellation is that He, the Exalted, described the righteous deed and the bad deed with mixing. Those mixed must necessarily remain while they are mixed, because mixing is an attribute of the things mixed, and the existence of an attribute while the subject is absent is impossible; so this indicates the continuance of both deeds during the mixing.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, and in it there are discussions:
First discussion: Here is a question: the word ʿasā ("perhaps") expresses doubt, and doubt regarding Allah the Exalted is impossible. Its answer is in several aspects:
First aspect: the commentators said: ʿasā from Allah is obligatory, and the evidence for this is His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will bring the victory﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 52), and He did so. The precise statement on this is that the Qur'an was revealed in accordance with the customary speech of people, and a great sovereign, when a needy person asks him for something, does not grant it except by way of hope, with the word ʿasā or laʿalla, to indicate that no one may oblige me to anything or charge me with anything; rather, everything I do, I do by way of grace and favor. So the benefit of mentioning the word ʿasā is this meaning, while it also conveys certainty of response.
Second aspect: the answer, whose purpose is to show that the accountable person must be between hope and apprehension, because that is further from denial and neglect.
Second discussion: Our companions said: His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, is explicit that repentance is not achieved except by the creation of Allah the Exalted. Reason also indicates this, because the basis of repentance is regret, and regret is not achieved by the servant's choice, for if the will to act or to abandon were an act of the servant, its performance would require another will, and furthermore a person may have a very strong desire for a specific act, then become very regretful over it; while he is desiring it he cannot dispel that desire from his heart, and when he becomes regretful he cannot dispel that regret from his heart. This shows that the servant has no power to bring about regret or to bring about desire. The Mu'tazilah said: what is meant by His saying "Allah accepts repentance" is that He accepts their repentance.
The answer: diverting the word from its apparent meaning is only fitting when it is established by evidence that the wording cannot be taken in its apparent sense. Here, however, the rational evidence is that the wording cannot be taken except in its apparent sense, so how can interpretation be fitting?
Third discussion: His saying, ﴿Perhaps Allah will accept their repentance﴾, requires that this repentance occurs in the future. And His saying, ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, indicates that this acknowledgment occurred in the past, and that indicates that this acknowledgment was not itself the repentance, but was a preliminary to repentance, and that repentance occurs only after it.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾, and in it there are issues:
First issue: People differed concerning the intended meaning. Some said: this refers to those who repented, because they had given their wealth as charity, so Allah the Exalted made its acceptance obligatory, and that became considered in the completeness of their repentance, so that it would serve in their case as an expiation. This is the view of al-Hasan, who used to say: the intended meaning of this verse is not obligatory charity, but rather the charity of expiation for the sin that proceeded from them.

The second view: the zakāt had been obligatory upon them, and when they repented of their lagging behind from the raid, and their Islam became good, and they offered zakāt, Allah commanded His Messenger to take it from them.

The third view: this verse is an independent statement, and its purpose is to make obligatory the taking of zakāt from the wealthy, and most jurists hold this view, for they used this verse as evidence for the obligation of zakāt, and they said that zakāt is purification.

As for those who hold the first view, they argued for the soundness of their position by saying that verses must be coherent and well-ordered; if we took it to mean obligatory zakāt from the outset, this verse would have no connection with what precedes it or what follows it, and would become an alien word, which is not befitting for the speech of Allah the Exalted. As for those who say the intended meaning is taking obligatory zakāt, they said: the connection is also present on this supposition, for when they displayed repentance and regret for lagging behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and admitted that the cause of that lagging was their love of wealth and their intense greed to preserve it from spending, it was as if it were said to them: the soundness of your claim of this repentance and regret will only appear if you pay the obligatory zakāt and are not reluctant about it, for claims are established only by testing, and at the test a man is honored or humiliated. If they paid those zakāt with a contented soul, their sincerity in that repentance and return would be manifest; otherwise they would be liars and deceivers by this means. However, interpreting this verse as a command to pay obligatory zakāt, while the arrangement of these verses remains sound, is preferable. And among what indicates that the intended meaning is obligatory charities is His saying, ﴿by which you purify them and cause them to grow﴾, and the meaning is: you purify them from sin by means of taking those charities. This is valid only if we say that had he not taken that charity, the sin would have remained, and that is only valid if the sin would occur in obligatory charities. As for those who hold the first view, they said: when he, upon him be blessings and peace, excused those repentant ones and released them, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, this is our wealth by which we lagged behind you, so give charity from it on our behalf, purify us, and ask forgiveness for us." He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "I have not been commanded to take any of your wealth." So Allah the Exalted revealed these verses, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ took one-third of their wealth and left two-thirds, because He, the Exalted, said: ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾, and did not say "take their wealth," and the word "min" (from) indicates partiality. Know that this report does not contradict the view we have chosen, as if it were said to them: since you were content with giving a charity that is not obligatory, then you should all the more be content with giving the obligatory duties.

* * *

Second issue: This verse indicates many rulings concerning zakāt.

First ruling: His saying, ﴿Take from their wealth﴾, indicates that the amount taken is a part of that wealth, not all of it, since the quantity of that part is not stated here explicitly. Rather, what is mentioned here is His saying, ﴿a charity﴾. It is known that the intended meaning is not indefiniteness such that any portion whatsoever would suffice, even if it were extremely small, like a single grain of wheat or a tiny fraction of gold. Therefore, the intended meaning must be a charity whose attribute, manner, and quantity are known to them, so that His saying, ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ is a command to take that known charity, and then the generality is removed. It is known that this charity is none other than the charities which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ described and explained in their manner, and the charity which the Messenger of Allah ﷺ explained is that he commanded
