[Page 143]

**Issue 2 (of the ruling):** [Wording continues from the previous part:] by taking from twenty-five camels a *bint makhad* (a she-camel in its second year), from thirty-six a *bint labun* (a she-camel in its third year), and so on through the other grades. So His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ is a command to take those specific things and those specific items. The apparent sense of the verse is obligation, so this text indicates that taking them is obligatory, and that implies that the monetary value cannot substitute for them, according to the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

**The second ruling:** His saying ﴿from their wealth a charity﴾ requires that the wealth be theirs. When this is so, the poor person is not a partner of the owner in the *nisab* (the minimum threshold for zakat). It then follows that zakat is attached to the person's liability (*dhimmah*) and has no attachment at all to the *nisab*.

Once this is established, we say: if a person neglects zakat until the *nisab* is destroyed, what has been destroyed is not the locus of the right; rather, the locus of the right remains as it was. Therefore that obligation must remain after the destruction of the *nisab* as it was before. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him.

**The third ruling:** The apparent generality of this verse requires zakat on the wealth of one who is in debt and on the wealth of one who is a guarantor (*daman*). This is apparent.

**The fourth ruling:** The apparent sense of the verse indicates that zakat is only obligated as a purification from sins. Therefore it is obligated only where it becomes a purification from sins. Its being a purification from sins is only established where sins can occur, and this is conceivable only regarding the one who has reached maturity. Hence it must be that zakat is obligatory only upon the mature, as is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. However, al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, responds and says: the verse indicates the taking of charity from their wealth, and taking charity from their wealth entails that it is a purification. So why do you claim that taking zakat from the wealth of a child or a madman is a purification? For it does not follow that the absence of a specific cause entails the absence of the ruling in every respect.

* * *

**Issue 3:** Regarding His saying ﴿to purify them﴾, there are several views:

**The first view:** The implied meaning is: "Take, O Muhammad, from their wealth a charity, for you purify them."

**The second view:** ﴿to purify them﴾ is linked to the charity, and the implied meaning is: "Take from their wealth a charity that purifies them." It is appropriate to describe the charity as purifying because it has been reported that charity is "the filth of people." When charity is taken, that filth is removed, so its removal is considered as purification. And Allah knows best.

According to this view, it must be said that His saying ﴿and cleanse them﴾ is detached from the first part, and the implied meaning is: "Take [O Muhammad] from their wealth a charity which purifies them; that charity [purifies them], and you [O Muhammad] cleanse them by means of it."

**The third view:** The *ta'* in ﴿tutahhiruhum wa-tuzakkihim﴾ is taken as the pronoun of the addressee, and the meaning is: "You, O taker who takes it from them, purify them, and cleanse them by means of that charity."

* * *

**Issue 4:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* said: It has been recited as *tuthhiruhum* (with a *damma* on the *ta'* and a *kasra* on the *ha'*), from *athharahu*, meaning *tahharahu* (purified him). And as *tuthhirhum* (with a *jazm*, as a response to the imperative). And ﴿wa-tuzakkihim﴾ has not been recited except with the *ya'* present.

[Page 143 continues]

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿and cleanse them﴾. Know that since *tazkiyah* (cleansing/growth) is coordinated with *tathhir* (purification), a difference must exist. So it is said: *tazkiyah* is an intensification of *tathhir*. It is also said: *tazkiyah* means growth (*inma'*). The meaning is that He, exalted is He, makes the deficiency that results from giving the amount of zakat a cause of growth. And it is said: charity purifies them from the filth of sin and disobedience, and the Messenger, peace be upon him, cleanses them, elevates their status, and praises them when they give it to the poor.

* * *

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And pray for them; indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. There are several issues concerning this:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read ﴿inna salataka﴾ without a *waw* and with a *fatha* on the *ta'*, in the singular, and the intended meaning is the category. Likewise in Surat Hud, ﴿a-salatuka ta'muruka﴾ [Hud: 87] without a *waw* and in the singular. The rest read *salawatika* in the plural, and likewise in Hud in the plural. Abu 'Ubaydah said: The first recitation is better, because prayer (*salah*) is more frequent; do you not see that He said ﴿Establish prayer﴾? The plural *salawat* is a plural of paucity (*jam' qillah*), as you say "three prayers" and "five prayers." Abu Hatim said: This is an error, because the form *salawat* is not for paucity, since He, exalted is He, said ﴿the words of Allah would not be exhausted﴾ [Luqman: 27], and He did not intend a small number. And He said ﴿and they will be secure in the upper chambers﴾ (Saba': 37) and ﴿indeed the Muslim men and the Muslim women﴾ (al-Ahzab: 35).

**The second issue:** Those who withheld zakat in the time of Abu Bakr used this verse as evidence. They said: Allah commanded His Messenger to take charities, then commanded him to pray for them, and mentioned that his prayer is a comfort for them. So the obligation of zakat was conditioned on the attainment of that comfort, and it is known that no one other than the Messenger can stand in his place in attaining that comfort. Therefore it is obligatory to give zakat to no one other than the Messenger, peace be upon him. Know that this argument is weak, because the rest of the verses indicate that zakat is obligated only to meet the need of the poor, as in His saying ﴿Charities are only for the poor﴾ (al-Tawbah: 60), and as in His saying ﴿and in their wealth there is a right for the beggar and the deprived﴾ (al-Dhariyat: 19).

* * *

**The third issue:** There is no doubt that *salah* in its original linguistic sense means supplication (*du'a'*). When we say "So-and-so prayed for So-and-so," it conveys supplication according to the original language. However, by custom it has come to convey that he said to him: "O Allah, bless him." For this reason the commentators differed. It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: its meaning is "supplicate for them." Al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, said: The sunnah for the imam, when he takes charity, is to supplicate for the giver and say: "May Allah reward you for what you gave, and bless for you what you have kept." Others said: its meaning is that he says: "O Allah, bless So-and-so." They related from the Prophet, peace be upon him, that when the family of Abu Awfa brought him charity, he said: "O Allah, bless the family of Abu Awfa." And the judge (al-Qadi), in his *Tafsir*, related from al-Ka'bi in his *Tafsir* that 'Ali said to 'Umar while he was covered [in death]: "Upon you be the prayer and peace." Some people denied this. And it is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, that he said: Blessing (*salah*) from one person upon another is not appropriate except regarding the Prophet, peace be upon him.

* * *

**The fourth issue:** Our companions prohibit mentioning *salawat* from Allah upon anyone except the Messenger, peace be upon him. The Shi'a mention it regarding 'Ali and his descendants, and they argue against us that the text of the Qur'an indicates that this mention is permissible regarding one who pays zakat. So how can its mention be prohibited regarding 'Ali, al-Hasan, and al-Husayn, may Allah be pleased with them? I have seen some of them say: Is it not the case that when a man says "Peace be upon you," it is said to him, "And upon you be peace"? This indicates that using this expression is permissible regarding the majority of Muslims. So how can its mention be prohibited regarding the family of the Messenger, peace be upon him? The judge said: It is permissible regarding the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the evidence for this is that they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have known the greeting upon you, so how is the blessing upon you?" He said, by way of instruction: "Say: O Allah, bless Muhammad and the family of Muhammad, as You blessed Abraham and the family of Abraham." It is known that there is no prophet among the family of Muhammad, so this includes 'Ali, just as the same may be permitted regarding the family of Abraham. And Allah knows best.

* * *

**The fifth issue:** I had mentioned some subtleties concerning the statement of some people to others: "Peace be upon you" (*salam 'alaykum*). They are not suitable for this place, but I saw fit to record them here so that they would not be lost. I said: When a man says to another "*salamun 'alaykum*," then His saying "*salamun*" is a predicate (*mubtada'*), and it is indefinite (*nakirah*). They claimed that making an indefinite word the subject is not permissible. They said: this is because a predication only conveys benefit when one predicates an unknown matter of a known subject. However, they said: when the indefinite is qualified (*mawsufah*), it is permissible to make it the subject, as in His, exalted is He, saying ﴿and a believing slave is better than a polytheist﴾ (al-Baqarah: 221).

Having known this, there are two possible explanations here:

**The first:** Indefiniteness indicates perfection. Do you not see His, exalted is He, saying ﴿and you will surely find them the most eager of people for life﴾ (al-Baqarah: 96)? The meaning is: "You will surely find them the most eager of people for a life that is lasting, perfect, and uninterrupted."

Having established this, His saying "*salam*" is an indefinite word, so the intended meaning is a complete, perfect peace. On this assumption, this indefinite has become qualified, so it is correct to make it a subject, and when that is so, the predicate comes forth, which is His saying "*'alaykum*." The implied meaning is: "A complete, perfect peace upon you."

**The second:** His saying "*'alaykum*" may be taken as a description (*sifah*) of His saying "*salam*," so that the whole of "*salamun 'alaykum*" is the subject, and a predicate is implied for it. The implied meaning is: "A peace upon you that is occurring, existing, and attained." Perhaps the omission of the predicate is more indicative of awe and grandeur.

Having known this, we say: when replying, this order is reversed and one says "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*." The reason for this, as Sibawayh said, is that they put first what is more important, and what they are most concerned with. So when he says "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*," this indicates that this responder's concern for that speaker is strong and complete. Also, His saying "*wa 'alaykumu as-salam*" conveys restriction (*hasr*), as though he is saying: "If you have conveyed the peace to me, then I add to it and make the peace specific to you and confined to you, in compliance with His, exalted is He, saying ﴿When you are greeted with a greeting, then greet with something better than it, or return it﴾ (al-Nisa': 86)."

One of the subtleties of His saying "*salamun 'alaykum*" is that it is more complete than the saying "*as-salamu 'alayka*." This is because "*salamun 'alayka*" means: a complete, perfect, noble, and exalted peace upon you. As for "*as-salamu 'alayka*," *as-salam* is a singular word with the definite article *al-*, which conveys only the essence of the reality (*asl al-mahiyyah*), and a word indicating the essence of the reality carries no indication of the accidental states of that reality or its perfections. So "*salamun 'alayka*" is more complete than "*as-salamu 'alayka*." What further confirms this meaning is that wherever the word "*salam*" comes from Allah, exalted is He, it comes in the indefinite form, as in His saying ﴿And when those who believe in Our signs come to you, say: Peace be upon you﴾ (al-An'am: 54), and His saying ﴿Say: Praise belongs to Allah, and peace upon His servants whom He has chosen﴾ (al-Naml: 59). There is much of this kind in the Qur'an. As for the word "*as-salam*" with the definite article, it has come only from the prophets, peace be upon them, as in the statement of Musa, peace be upon him: ﴿We have certainly come to you with a sign from your Lord, and peace will be upon those who follow guidance﴾ (Ta-Ha: 47). As for Surat Maryam, when Allah mentioned Yahya, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿And peace is upon him the day he was born and the day he dies﴾ (Maryam: 15), and this peace is from Allah, exalted is He. In the story of 'Isa, peace be upon him, He said: ﴿And peace is upon me the day I was born and the day I die﴾ (Maryam: 33), and this is the speech of 'Isa, peace be upon him. Thus it is established by these aspects that His saying "*salamun 'alayka*" is more complete than His saying "*as-salamu*

[Page 145]

...'alayka). For this reason al-Shafi'i (may God have mercy on him) chose, in the recitation of the tashahhud (the testimony recited in prayer), the phrase "salamun 'alayka ayyuha al-nabiyyu" (peace be upon you, O Prophet) in the indefinite form (al-tankir). Among the subtleties of salam is this: there is no doubt that this world is the source of evils, calamities, trials and transgressions. Scholars who investigated the secrets of character disagreed over whether the basic nature of living beings is good or evil. Some said that the basic nature of living beings is evil. This is almost like the consensus (ijma') established among all human beings. Indeed, we go further and say that it is like the consensus among all living beings. The proof is that every person who sees another person approaching him, though he does not know him, finds that his nature drives him to beware of him and to prepare to repel him. Had his nature not witnessed that the basic state of a human being is evil, the natural reason would not have required preparation to repel the evil of that one who approaches him. They also said that this meaning exists in all animals: when one animal is approached by another, the first animal flees from it and avoids it. If it were established in its nature that the basic state of the one arriving is good, it would be necessary for the first to stand still, because the basic nature inclines toward seeking good. If the basic nature of an animal were that its good and evil were balanced and equal, then fleeing and standing still would have to be equal. Since this is not the case, but rather every animal, when another animal of unknown character approaches it, avoids it merely by its original natural disposition, we know that the basic state of the animal is evil.

Once this is established, we say: repelling evil is more important than acquiring good. This is shown by several considerations:

First: repelling evil requires preserving the original state, and preserving the original state is more important than gaining what is additional.

Second: bringing good to every individual is not within capacity, whereas restraining evil from every individual is within capacity, because the first is an act and the second is an abstention. Performing what has no end is not possible, whereas abstaining from what has no end is possible.

Third: if the repelling of evil does not occur, then evil has occurred, and this necessitates the occurrence of pain and grief, which is in the utmost hardship. And if the bringing of good also does not occur, the person remains neither in good nor in evil, but in his original safety, and enduring this state is easy. Thus it is established that repelling evil is more important than bringing good. It is also established that this world is the abode of evils, calamities, trials and afflictions, and that the living being, by its original creation and the requirement of its natural disposition, is a source of evils. When one person reaches another, the most important of all matters is that he inform him that he is with him in safety, security and peace. For this reason the convention was established that conversation begins with mentioning salam, by saying "salamun 'alaykum" (peace be upon you).

Among the subtleties of our saying "salamun 'alaykum" is that its apparent meaning requires conferring peace upon a group. This is so according to reason and according to the Shari'ah. As for the Shari'ah, the Qur'an indicates that a person is never without a group of angels who protect him and watch over his affairs, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians, noble writers﴾ (al-Infitar 82:10-11). Reason also indicates this, because human souls are of different kinds: some are good and rational, some are turbid and wicked, some are appetitive, and some are irascible. For each group of the lower human souls there is a strong higher soul which is like a father to those human souls, and these souls are in relation to that higher soul as children are in relation to a father. It is that higher soul which bestows upon them inspirations, sometimes while awake and sometimes in sleep. Also, the souls separated from their bodies, which resemble these souls in qualities, nature and property, acquire a kind of attachment to this body because of resemblance and affinity, and they become like helpers to this soul in its deeds: if good, then good; if evil, then evil. When you know this secret, a person must necessarily be accompanied by those souls akin to him. Thus his saying "salamun 'alaykum" is an indication of greeting this particular person to all the souls that are attached to him and accompany him because of spiritual companionship.

Among the subtleties of this topic is the following: [Page 146]
When human souls are characterized by true knowledge and noble morals, and they become strong and detached, and then the attachment of some of them to others grows strong, their lights are reflected upon one another, like a shining mirror facing another. For this reason, if a person wishes to recite a litany (wazifah) to his teacher, the proper etiquette is to begin with praising God and extolling the angels and prophets, then to supplicate for his teacher, and then to begin the recitation. Its purpose is to strengthen the connection between his soul and these holy, pure souls, so that, because of the strength of that connection, some of their lights and effects may appear in the soul of this seeker, and some of the overflowing lights from them settle in his intellect, and his soul is strengthened by the support of that overflow in grasping knowledge and sciences. When you know this, then if one says to another "salamun 'alaykum," a strong connection arises between them, and through that connection the souls correspond and the lights are reflected. We shall suffice with this measure on this topic, for we have mentioned that this section is foreign to the present discourse. And God knows best.

The sixth issue: His saying: ﴿Indeed, your prayer is a comfort for them﴾. Al-Wahidi said: "Sakan" in the language is that in which one finds tranquility. The meaning is that your prayer for them causes their souls to find tranquility in you. The commentators have various expressions. Ibn 'Abbas (may God be pleased with them both) said: "Your supplication is mercy for them." Qatadah said: "Dignity for them." Al-Kalbi said: "Reassurance for them." Al-Farra' said: "When you seek forgiveness for them, their souls find tranquility in the knowledge that God has accepted their repentance."

I say: the spirit of Muhammad (peace be upon him) was a strong, luminous, pure and dazzling spirit. When Muhammad supplicates for them and mentions them with good, effects from his spiritual strength overflow upon their souls, and for this reason their souls become illuminated, their secrets become pure, and they pass from darkness to light, and from the corporeal to the spiritual. Its establishment is as was stated in the fifth issue.

Then He said: ﴿And God is All-Hearing﴾ of their words, ﴿All-Knowing﴾ of their intentions.

[Page 147]

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 9, verse 104:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they not know that it is God who accepts repentance from His servants and takes the charities, and that God is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful?﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, related of the people already mentioned that they had repented of their sins and given charity, and in that passage He mentioned only His saying: ﴿It may be that God will turn to them [in forgiveness]﴾, and that was not explicit about the acceptance of repentance, He mentioned in this verse that He accepts repentance and takes charities. The purpose is to encourage those who had not repented to repent, and to encourage all the disobedient to obedience. There are several issues in the verse:

The first issue: Abu Muslim said: His saying ﴿Do they not know﴾, although it is in the form of a question, its purpose is affirmation in the soul. It is a custom of the Arabs, in order to make the addressee aware and remove doubt from him, to say: "Do you not know that whoever taught you is owed your service? Do you not know that whoever has done good to you is owed your gratitude?" So God, may He be exalted, gave these repentant people the good news of the acceptance of their repentance and their charities.

Then He added emphasis to it with His saying: ﴿He is the Ever-Relenting, the Most Merciful﴾.

[Page 147 continues]

The second issue: The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari) said: It was read as (*a-lam yaʿlamū*, "do they not know") with the *yāʾ* and with the *tāʾ*, and in it there are two aspects:

The first: that the intended meaning of this verse is those who repented, meaning: (Do they not know), before repentance was accepted from them and their charities were accepted, that God accepts sincere repentance and accepts charities given out of purity of intention.

The second: that the intended meaning of this verse is those who had not repented, as an encouragement to them to repent. It is related that when the Messenger of God (ﷺ) judged the soundness of their repentance, he said: "Those who did not repent, these who repented were with us yesterday, they were not spoken to and not sat with, so what is wrong with them?" Then this verse was revealed.

The third issue: His saying ﴿He accepts repentance﴾ contains several benefits:

The first benefit: He, may He be exalted, named Himself here by the name Allah. Then He said after it: ﴿He accepts repentance﴾, and in this there is an alert that His being God necessitates the acceptance of repentance. That is because God is the One to whom increase and decrease cannot reach; His state cannot be increased by the obedience of the obedient, nor diminished by the disobedience of the sinners. It is also impossible that He has a desire for obedience and an aversion to disobedience, such that it could be said that His aversion and anger move Him to retribution. Rather, the purpose of the prohibition of disobedience and the encouragement to obedience is that everything that calls the heart to the world of the Hereafter and the abodes of the blessed, and forbids it from occupying itself with futile material things, is worship, the true deed, and the righteous path; and everything that is the opposite of it is disobedience and futile deeds. So the sinner harms only himself, and the obedient benefits only himself. As He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿If you do good, you do good for yourselves, and if you do evil, it is for them﴾ (al-Isra, 17:7). If God is merciful, wise, and generous, and His anger toward the sinner is not because he has harmed Him by his disobedience, then when the servant moves from disobedience to obedience, His generosity is as if it necessitated upon Him the acceptance of his repentance. So it is established that since divinity is an expression of absolute independence, and absolute independence is impossible to be attained by other than Him, the acceptance of repentance from others is as if impossible, except for another separate cause, or for an opposing or contrary factor.

The second benefit: In this specification, the acceptance of repentance does not belong to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), but to God, who accepts repentance at one time and rejects it at another. So direct your intention to God with it, and turn it toward Him. It was also said to these repentant people: act, for your deed is not hidden from God, whether it is good or evil.

* * *

The fourth issue: The Mu'tazilah said: The acceptance of repentance is obligatory upon God, may He be exalted, by reason. Our companions (the Ash'aris) said: The acceptance of repentance is obligatory by the judgment of His promise, His bounty, and His kindness, but not by reason. The arguments of our companions for the non-obligation of the acceptance of repentance are several:

The first: The meaning of obligation is not established except if it is such that, if the doer does not do it, he deserves blame. So if the acceptance of repentance were obligatory upon God, may He be exalted, it would be such that if He did not accept it, He would become deserving of blame, and this is impossible; because whoever is like that is perfected by the act of acceptance, and what is perfected by another is deficient in its essence, and that is impossible with regard to God, may He be exalted.

The second: Blame prevents an act only when the one blamed is such that he is hurt by hearing that blame and recoils by his nature, and a deficiency in his state appears to him because of it. As for one who is exalted above desire, aversion, increase, and decrease, it is not conceivable that obligation is realized with regard to him in this sense.

The third: He, may He be exalted, praised Himself by accepting repentance in this verse, and if it were obligatory, He would not have praised Himself with it; because the performance of an obligation does not bring praise, commendation, or glorification.

The fifth issue: The (*ʿan*, "from") in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿from His servants﴾ has two aspects:

The first: There is no difference between His saying ﴿from His servants﴾ and His saying (*min ʿibādihi*, "from His servants"). It is said: "I took this from you and I took this from you."

The second: The judge (al-Qadi) said: Perhaps (*ʿan*) is more eloquent, because it indicates acceptance together with facilitating the path to the repentance that was accepted. I say: he did not explain how the word (*ʿan*) indicates this meaning. What I say is that the word (*ʿan*) and the word (*min*) are close in meaning, but the word (*ʿan*) conveys distance. So when it is said: "So-and-so sat to the right of the emir (*ʿan yamīn al-amīr*)," it conveys that he sat on that side but with a kind of distance. So His saying ﴿from His servants﴾ conveys that the repentant one must believe of himself that he has become distanced from God's acceptance of him because of that sin, and there occurs in him the brokenness of a servant whom his master has driven away and removed from His presence. So the word (*ʿan*) is like an alert that this meaning must be present in the repentant one.

* * *

The sixth issue: His saying ﴿and takes the charities﴾. There is a question in it: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that the one who takes is God. His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ indicates that the one who takes is the Messenger, upon him be peace. His saying, upon him be peace, to Mu'adh: ("Take it from their wealthy") indicates that the one who takes those charities is Mu'adh. When the charity is given to the poor, the senses witness that the one who takes it is the poor man. So how can these expressions be reconciled?

The answer has two aspects:

The first: When He, may He be exalted, made clear in His saying ﴿Take from their wealth a charity﴾ that the one who takes is the Messenger, then mentioned in this verse that the one who takes is God, the intended meaning is that the Messenger's taking stands in place of God's taking. The purpose is to alert to the magnification of the status of the Messenger, inasmuch as his taking of the charity is as if God were taking it. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed those who pledge allegiance to you are only pledging allegiance to God﴾ (al-Fath, 48:10), and His saying: ﴿Indeed those who harm God﴾ (al-Ahzab, 33:57), and what is meant by it is harming the Prophet, upon him be peace.

The second answer: It is attributed to the Messenger, upon him be peace, in the sense that he orders its taking and conveys God's ruling in this matter to the people, and it is attributed to the poor man in the sense that he is the one who directly takes it. A parallel to this is that He, may He be exalted, attributed death (*tawaffī*) to Himself by His saying: ﴿And it is He who takes you back [in death]﴾ (al-An'am, 6:60), and attributed it to the Angel of Death, which is His saying: ﴿Say: The Angel of Death will take you﴾ (al-Sajdah, 32:11), and attributed it to the angels who are the followers of the Angel of Death, which is His saying: ﴿until, when death comes to one of you, Our messengers take him﴾ (al-An'am, 6:61). So it is attributed to God by creation, to the Angel of Death for his headship in that kind of action, and to the followers of the Angel of Death, meaning that they are the ones who directly carry out the actions at which God creates death. So it is likewise here.

Having known this, we say: His saying ﴿and takes the charities﴾ is a great honor for this act of obedience, and the reports about it are numerous. From the Prophet, upon him be peace, it is related that he said: "Indeed God accepts charity, and accepts from it only what is good, and He accepts it with His right hand and nurtures it for its giver, just as one of you nurtures his foal or his young camel, until a morsel is greater in God's sight than Uhud." And he, upon him be peace, said: "By Him in whose hand is the soul of Muhammad, no Muslim servant gives a charity which reaches the one to whom it is given except that it falls into the hand of God." When al-Hasan related these two reports, he said: God's right hand, His palm, and His grip are not described [as a physical thing]: "There is nothing like unto Him" (al-Shura, 42:11). Know that the words "right hand" and "palm" are among the expressions of sanctification.

[Page 149]

The Almighty said: ﴿And say, "Work, for Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers. And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed, and He will inform you of what you used to do."﴾

Concerning this there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Know that this statement combines encouragement (tarhib... *al-targhib*, encouragement) and warning (*al-tarhib*). This is because if the one worshipped does not know the deeds of His servants, the servant does not benefit from his act. For this reason Ibrahim, peace be upon him, said to his father: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees and cannot avail you at all?﴾ (Maryam: 42). I said in some gatherings: the purpose of this argument that Ibrahim, peace be upon him, made was not to disparage the divinity of the idol, because everyone knows by necessity that it is a stone and wood, and that it is subject to the manipulation of those who manipulate it. Whoever wishes burns it, and whoever wishes breaks it. And how can a rational person imagine that such a thing is a god? Rather, the purpose is that most of the idol-worshippers in the time of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, were followers of the philosophers (*falasifa*), who held that the God of the universe is a necessitating cause by its essence (*mujab bi'l-dhat*), and is not an originator by will and choice. So he said: a necessitating cause by its essence, if it does not know the good things, and is not able to benefit or harm, and does not hear the supplication of the needy nor see the humility of the poor, then what benefit is there in worshipping it? Thus the purpose of Ibrahim's proof, peace be upon him, was to refute the claim of one who says that the God of the universe is a necessitating cause by its essence. However, if He is an agent who chooses, and is knowing of particulars, then great benefits accrue to the servants. This is because when the servant obeys, the One worshipped knows his obedience and is able to convey reward to him in this world and the Hereafter; and if he disobeys, the One worshipped knows that and is able to convey punishment to him in this world and the Hereafter. So His saying: ﴿Work, for Allah will see your deeds﴾ is a great encouragement for the obedient and a great warning for the sinners. It is as if He, exalted is He, said: strive in the future, for your deeds have a judgment in this world and a judgment in the Hereafter. As for their judgment in this world, it is that Allah sees them, the Messenger sees them, and the Muslims see them. If it is an act of obedience, great praise and great reward result from it in this world and the Hereafter; and if it is an act of disobedience, great blame results from it in this world and severe punishment in the Hereafter. Thus it is established that this single expression comprises everything that a person needs in his religion, his worldly life, his livelihood, and his return.

* * *

**The second issue:** The verse indicates several principles of usul (foundations of jurisprudence and theology).

**The first ruling:** It indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is a seer of visible things. This is because the verb *ra'a* (to see) when transitive to one object means "to perceive by sight" (*al-ibsar*), and when transitive to two objects means "to know," as when you say: *ra'aytu Zaydan faqihan* ("I saw Zayd as a jurist"). Here, *al-ru'ya* is transitive to one object, so it means sight (*al-ibsar*), and this indicates that He is a perceiver of things, just as Ibrahim's statement, peace be upon him: ﴿Why do you worship that which neither hears nor sees﴾ (Maryam: 42), indicates that Allah, exalted is He, is a perceiver and a seer of things. Among what strengthens the point that this *ru'ya* cannot be understood here as knowledge is that He, exalted is He, described Himself with knowledge after this verse, saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. If this seeing were knowledge, it would entail unbeneficial repetition, and that is false.

**The second ruling:** The position of our companions (*ashabuna*, i.e., the Ash'arites) is that everything that exists can be seen. They argued for it with this verse and said: We have shown that the seeing mentioned in this verse is transitive to one object, and the linguistic rules bear witness that *al-ru'ya* transitive to one object means sight. So this seeing means sight. Then He, exalted is He, related this seeing to their deeds, and deeds are divided into deeds of the heart, such as desires, aversions, and glances, and deeds of the limbs, such as movements and stillnesses. Therefore it is obligatory that He, exalted is He, sees all of them, and this indicates that all these things are visible to Allah, exalted is He.

As for al-Jubba'i, he used to argue with this verse that He, exalted is He, sees movements, stillnesses, gatherings, and separations. When it was said to him: if this inference is valid, then it would necessitate that He, exalted is He, sees deeds of the heart, he answered that He, exalted is He, joined to it His saying: ﴿and His Messenger and the believers﴾, and they only see deeds of the limbs. So since this seeing is restricted to deeds of the limbs with respect to the conjoined, it must be restricted by this restriction with respect to the one conjoined to. This is far-fetched, because conjunction (*'atf*) only conveys the basic sharing (*al-tashrik*). As for full equality in all matters, it is not obligatory. Therefore, the entry of restriction into the conjoined does not necessitate the entry of restriction into the one conjoined to.

The answer to the basic inference may also be given: the seeing of Allah, exalted is He, is present now. The meaning indicated by the wording of the verse is His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾, which is a matter not yet present now, because the particle *sin* (the future marker) is specific to the future. Thus it is established that what is meant is the recompense for the deeds. So His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾ means: so He will convey to you the recompense of your deeds. And someone who objects may answer this by saying that conveying the recompense to them is mentioned by His saying: ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾. So if we take this seeing to mean the conveying of recompense, it would entail repetition, and that is not permissible.

* * *

**The third issue:** Regarding His saying: ﴿Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers﴾, there is an objection: that their deeds are not seen by everyone, so what is the meaning of this statement?

The answer: its meaning is the arrival of the news of that deed to everyone. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If a man performs a deed on a rock that has no door and no window, his deed will come out to the people, whatever it may be."

If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning the Messenger and the believers after mentioning Allah, regarding their seeing the deeds of these repentant ones?

We say: there are two aspects to this.

**The first aspect:** What most motivates a person to righteous action is the praise and honor he receives, and the esteem that accrues to him at that time. So when he knows that if he does that deed the Messenger and the believers will honor him, his joy at that increases and his desire for it grows. What alerts to this subtle point is that He mentioned the seeing of Allah first, then mentioned right after it the seeing of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers. It is as if it were said: if you are among those who are truly rightly guided in servitude to the Truth, then perform righteous deeds for the sake of Allah, exalted is He; and if you are among the weak who are preoccupied with the praise of creation, then perform righteous deeds so that you may gain the praise of creation, which is that of the Messenger and the believers.

**The second aspect of the answer:** what Abu Muslim mentioned: that the believers are witnesses of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾ (al-Baqarah: 143), and the Messenger is a witness over his nation, as He said: ﴿How, then, when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?﴾ (al-Nisa': 41). Thus it is established that the Messenger and the believers are the witnesses of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and testimony is not valid except after seeing. So Allah mentioned that the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers see their deeds, and the purpose is to alert that they will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection, in the presence of the first and the last, that they are people of truthfulness, uprightness, chastity, and right guidance.

* * *

Then the Almighty said: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

[Page 151]

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "the unseen (*al-ghayb*) is what they keep secret, and the witnessed (*al-shahada*) is what they make apparent." I say: it is not far-fetched that the unseen is what arises in their hearts of motives and deterrents, and the witnessed is the deeds that appear on their limbs. I also say: the position of the philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*) is that the existents that are hidden from the senses are causes, or like causes, of the sensible existents. In their view, knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect. So it is obligatory that knowledge of the unseen precedes knowledge of the witnessed. For this reason, wherever this phrase occurs in the Qur'an, the unseen is mentioned before the witnessed.

**The second issue:** If we take His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾ to mean seeing, then it becomes evident that its meaning differs from the meaning of His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. If we take that seeing to mean knowledge or the conveying of reward, then we make His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ function as an explanation of His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾. Its meaning is: by manifesting praise, commendation, and honor in this world, or by manifesting their opposites. And His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ means: what will become manifest on the Day of Resurrection of the state of reward and punishment.

Then He said: ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, and the meaning is: He will make you know the states of your deeds, then He will recompense you for them, because recompense from Allah, exalted is He, does not occur in the Hereafter except after making known; so that everyone may know that what he has reached is justice and not injustice. If he is among the people of reward, his joy and happiness will be greater; and if he is among the people of punishment, his grief and loss will be greater.

The philosophers of Islam said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾ is an allusion to the spiritual reward. This is because when the servant bears various kinds of hardships in the matters that his master has commanded him, and the servant knows that his master sees his bearing of those hardships, his joy becomes great and his delight in them grows strong, and that becomes for him sweeter than precious robes and great wealth.

As for His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, what is meant by it is making known the punishment of disgrace and scandal. An example of this: a servant whom the sultan has favored with many kinds of kindness, but who then commits many kinds of disobedience; when that servant is brought before that sultan and his various ugly deeds and disgraces are enumerated to him, his grief grows strong, his sorrow becomes great, and his disgrace is complete. This is a kind of spiritual punishment. A rational person may sometimes accept the most severe kinds of physical punishment rather than this. The purpose of this verse is to make known this kind of spiritual punishment. We ask Allah for protection from it and from all other punishment.

* *

The Almighty said: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command: either He will punish them or He will accept their repentance, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *mur-jawna* without a hamza, while the rest read it with a hamza, and both are dialects (*lughatan*). One says *arja'tu al-amr* and *arjaytuhu* (I postponed the matter), with the hamza and without it, when you delay it. The Murji'ah (those who "postpone," *al-Murji'ah*) were named with this name because they do not affirm definitively the forgiveness of the penitent, but defer it to the will of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Awza'i said: it is because they postpone deeds from faith.

**The second issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, divided those who stayed behind from the struggle (*jihad*) into three categories.

**The first category:** the hypocrites who persisted in hypocrisy.

[Page 152]

**The second category:** the repentant ones, who are the ones intended by His saying: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, and Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He accepted their repentance.

The third category: those who were left in suspense, and they are the ones mentioned in this verse. The difference between the second category and this third one is that those [in the second] hastened to repentance, whereas these did not hasten to it. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "This verse was revealed concerning Kaʿb ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabiʿ, and Hilal ibn Umayyah. Kaʿb said: 'I am the most robust of the people of Madinah with a mount; whenever I wish, I can catch up with the Messenger.' So he delayed for some days, and after that he despaired of catching up with him, and he regretted his conduct, and so did his two companions. When the Messenger of Allah arrived, Kaʿb was told: 'Apologise to him for your conduct.' He said: 'No, by Allah, not until my repentance is revealed.' As for his two companions, they apologised to him, peace be upon him, and he said: 'What kept you behind from me?' They said: 'We have no excuse except our sin.' Then there was revealed the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾. So the Messenger, after the revelation of this verse, put them in isolation and forbade the people from sitting with them, and commanded them to keep away from their wives and to send them back to their families. Hilal's wife came asking to be allowed to bring him food, for he was an elderly man, and he permitted her in that matter alone. A messenger came from Syria to Kaʿb, enticing him to join them, and Kaʿb said: 'My sin has reached such a point that the polytheists have come to desire me.' He said: 'The earth became constricted for me despite its vastness.' Hilal ibn Umayyah wept until his sight was feared for. When fifty days had passed, their repentance was revealed with the saying: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ (al-Tawbah: 117), and with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And to the three who were left behind, until the earth became constricted for them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 118), the verse." Al-Hasan said: By His saying ﴿And others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾ He means a people among the hypocrites whom the Messenger of Allah deferred from his presence. Al-Asamm said: He means the hypocrites, and this is like His saying: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾. Allah deferred them and did not inform about them what He knew of them, and warned them through this verse that if they did not repent, He would send down a Qur'an concerning them.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: One may say: the words "either... or" (imma... imma) indicate doubt, and Allah the Exalted is far above that.
The answer: What is intended is that their state should be one of fear and hope. So some people began to say: "They are ruined if Allah does not send down an excuse for them," while others said: "Perhaps Allah will forgive them."

The second issue: There is no doubt that the people were regretful for their delay from the expedition and their staying behind from the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then He, the Exalted, did not judge them to be repentant, but said: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and this indicates that regret alone is not sufficient for the soundness of repentance.
If it is said: What are those conditions?
We say: Perhaps they feared the Messenger's command to harm them, or they feared shame and disgrace. On this assumption, their repentance was neither sound nor accepted. So the non-acceptance of repentance continued until the people's attitudes toward their censure and praise became easy, and at that point they regretted the sin for the very fact that it was a sin, and at that point their repentance was sound.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that Allah the Exalted does not pardon anyone who is not repentant, because He said concerning these sinners: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and this indicates that there is no ruling except one of these two matters, either punishment or repentance. As for pardoning a sin without repentance, that is a third category. Since Allah the Exalted omitted mention of it, this shows that it is invalid and not to be considered.
Page 153
The answer: We do not affirm with certainty that pardon is granted to all sinners; rather, we affirm with certainty that pardon is granted in general, while as for each individual specifically, that is uncertain. Do you not see that He the Exalted said: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. So He affirmed the forgiveness of everything other than shirk, but not for every person; rather, for whomever He wills. Thus the absence of pardon regarding these people does not entail the absence of pardon absolutely. Also, the absence of mention does not indicate non-existence. Do you not see that He the Exalted said: ﴿Faces that day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ (Abasa: 39), and they are the believers; ﴿And faces that day will have upon them dust, darkness covering them﴾, ﴿those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ (Abasa: 40). So here those mentioned are either believers or disbelievers. Then the absence of mention of a third category did not, according to al-Jubba'i, indicate its negation, and so it is here.
As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾, that is: ﴿Knowing﴾ of what is in the hearts of these believers, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He decides concerning them and judges over them.

[Page 149]

**The third issue:** Regarding His saying: ﴿Allah will see your deeds, and so will His Messenger and the believers﴾, there is an objection: that their deeds are not seen by everyone, so what is the meaning of this statement?

The answer: its meaning is the arrival of the news of that deed to everyone. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "If a man performs a deed on a rock that has no door and no window, his deed will come out to the people, whatever it may be."

If it is said: what is the benefit of mentioning the Messenger and the believers after mentioning Allah, regarding their seeing the deeds of these repentant ones?

We say: there are two aspects to this.

**The first aspect:** What most motivates a person to righteous action is the praise and honor he receives, and the esteem that accrues to him at that time. So when he knows that if he does that deed the Messenger and the believers will honor him, his joy at that increases and his desire for it grows. What alerts to this subtle point is that He mentioned the seeing of Allah first, then mentioned right after it the seeing of the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers. It is as if it were said: if you are among those who are truly rightly guided in servitude to the Truth, then perform righteous deeds for the sake of Allah, exalted is He; and if you are among the weak who are preoccupied with the praise of creation, then perform righteous deeds so that you may gain the praise of creation, which is that of the Messenger and the believers.

**The second aspect of the answer:** what Abu Muslim mentioned: that the believers are witnesses of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And thus We have made you a justly balanced nation﴾ (al-Baqarah: 143), and the Messenger is a witness over his nation, as He said: ﴿How, then, when We bring from every nation a witness and bring you, [O Muhammad], as a witness against these?﴾ (al-Nisa': 41). Thus it is established that the Messenger and the believers are the witnesses of Allah on the Day of Resurrection, and testimony is not valid except after seeing. So Allah mentioned that the Messenger, peace be upon him, and the believers see their deeds, and the purpose is to alert that they will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection, in the presence of the first and the last, that they are people of truthfulness, uprightness, chastity, and right guidance.

* * *

Then the Almighty said: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. Concerning this there are several issues:

[Page 151]

**The first issue:** Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: "the unseen (*al-ghayb*) is what they keep secret, and the witnessed (*al-shahada*) is what they make apparent." I say: it is not far-fetched that the unseen is what arises in their hearts of motives and deterrents, and the witnessed is the deeds that appear on their limbs. I also say: the position of the philosophers of Islam (*hukama' al-Islam*) is that the existents that are hidden from the senses are causes, or like causes, of the sensible existents. In their view, knowledge of the cause is a cause of knowledge of the effect. So it is obligatory that knowledge of the unseen precedes knowledge of the witnessed. For this reason, wherever this phrase occurs in the Qur'an, the unseen is mentioned before the witnessed.

**The second issue:** If we take His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾ to mean seeing, then it becomes evident that its meaning differs from the meaning of His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾. If we take that seeing to mean knowledge or the conveying of reward, then we make His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ function as an explanation of His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾. Its meaning is: by manifesting praise, commendation, and honor in this world, or by manifesting their opposites. And His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ means: what will become manifest on the Day of Resurrection of the state of reward and punishment.

Then He said: ﴿and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾, and the meaning is: He will make you know the states of your deeds, then He will recompense you for them, because recompense from Allah, exalted is He, does not occur in the Hereafter except after making known; so that everyone may know that what he has reached is justice and not injustice. If he is among the people of reward, his joy and happiness will be greater; and if he is among the people of punishment, his grief and loss will be greater.

The philosophers of Islam said: what is meant by His saying: ﴿so Allah will see your deeds﴾ is an allusion to the spiritual reward. This is because when the servant bears various kinds of hardships in the matters that his master has commanded him, and the servant knows that his master sees his bearing of those hardships, his joy becomes great and his delight in them grows strong, and that becomes for him sweeter than precious robes and great wealth.

As for His saying: ﴿And you will be returned to the Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾, what is meant by it is making known the punishment of disgrace and scandal. An example of this: a servant whom the sultan has favored with many kinds of kindness, but who then commits many kinds of disobedience; when that servant is brought before that sultan and his various ugly deeds and disgraces are enumerated to him, his grief grows strong, his sorrow becomes great, and his disgrace is complete. This is a kind of spiritual punishment. A rational person may sometimes accept the most severe kinds of physical punishment rather than this. The purpose of this verse is to make known this kind of spiritual punishment. We ask Allah for protection from it and from all other punishment.

* *

The Almighty said: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command: either He will punish them or He will accept their repentance, and Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise.﴾

Concerning the verse there are several issues:

**The first issue:** Hamzah, Nafi', al-Kisa'i, and Hafs from 'Asim read *mur-jawna* without a hamza, while the rest read it with a hamza, and both are dialects (*lughatan*). One says *arja'tu al-amr* and *arjaytuhu* (I postponed the matter), with the hamza and without it, when you delay it. The Murji'ah (those who "postpone," *al-Murji'ah*) were named with this name because they do not affirm definitively the forgiveness of the penitent, but defer it to the will of Allah, exalted is He. Al-Awza'i said: it is because they postpone deeds from faith.

**The second issue:** Know that He, exalted is He, divided those who stayed behind from the struggle (*jihad*) into three categories.

**The first category:** the hypocrites who persisted in hypocrisy.

[Page 152]

**The second category:** the repentant ones, who are the ones intended by His saying: ﴿And others have acknowledged their sins﴾, and Allah, exalted is He, made clear that He accepted their repentance.

The third category: those who were left in suspense, and they are the ones mentioned in this verse. The difference between the second category and this third one is that those [in the second] hastened to repentance, whereas these did not hasten to it. Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) said: "This verse was revealed concerning Kaʿb ibn Malik, Murarah ibn al-Rabiʿ, and Hilal ibn Umayyah. Kaʿb said: 'I am the most robust of the people of Madinah with a mount; whenever I wish, I can catch up with the Messenger.' So he delayed for some days, and after that he despaired of catching up with him, and he regretted his conduct, and so did his two companions. When the Messenger of Allah arrived, Kaʿb was told: 'Apologise to him for your conduct.' He said: 'No, by Allah, not until my repentance is revealed.' As for his two companions, they apologised to him, peace be upon him, and he said: 'What kept you behind from me?' They said: 'We have no excuse except our sin.' Then there was revealed the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾. So the Messenger, after the revelation of this verse, put them in isolation and forbade the people from sitting with them, and commanded them to keep away from their wives and to send them back to their families. Hilal's wife came asking to be allowed to bring him food, for he was an elderly man, and he permitted her in that matter alone. A messenger came from Syria to Kaʿb, enticing him to join them, and Kaʿb said: 'My sin has reached such a point that the polytheists have come to desire me.' He said: 'The earth became constricted for me despite its vastness.' Hilal ibn Umayyah wept until his sight was feared for. When fifty days had passed, their repentance was revealed with the saying: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾ (al-Tawbah: 117), and with the saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And to the three who were left behind, until the earth became constricted for them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 118), the verse." Al-Hasan said: By His saying ﴿And others are deferred until the command of Allah﴾ He means a people among the hypocrites whom the Messenger of Allah deferred from his presence. Al-Asamm said: He means the hypocrites, and this is like His saying: ﴿And among those around you of the Bedouins are hypocrites﴾. Allah deferred them and did not inform about them what He knew of them, and warned them through this verse that if they did not repent, He would send down a Qur'an concerning them.
* * *
Then Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and in it there are issues:

The first issue: One may say: the words "either... or" (imma... imma) indicate doubt, and Allah the Exalted is far above that.
The answer: What is intended is that their state should be one of fear and hope. So some people began to say: "They are ruined if Allah does not send down an excuse for them," while others said: "Perhaps Allah will forgive them."

The second issue: There is no doubt that the people were regretful for their delay from the expedition and their staying behind from the Messenger, peace be upon him. Then He, the Exalted, did not judge them to be repentant, but said: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and this indicates that regret alone is not sufficient for the soundness of repentance.
If it is said: What are those conditions?
We say: Perhaps they feared the Messenger's command to harm them, or they feared shame and disgrace. On this assumption, their repentance was neither sound nor accepted. So the non-acceptance of repentance continued until the people's attitudes toward their censure and praise became easy, and at that point they regretted the sin for the very fact that it was a sin, and at that point their repentance was sound.

The third issue: Al-Jubba'i used this verse to argue that Allah the Exalted does not pardon anyone who is not repentant, because He said concerning these sinners: ﴿Either He will punish them or He will turn to them in forgiveness﴾, and this indicates that there is no ruling except one of these two matters, either punishment or repentance. As for pardoning a sin without repentance, that is a third category. Since Allah the Exalted omitted mention of it, this shows that it is invalid and not to be considered.
Page 153
The answer: We do not affirm with certainty that pardon is granted to all sinners; rather, we affirm with certainty that pardon is granted in general, while as for each individual specifically, that is uncertain. Do you not see that He the Exalted said: ﴿And He forgives what is less than that for whomever He wills﴾ [al-Nisa': 48]. So He affirmed the forgiveness of everything other than shirk, but not for every person; rather, for whomever He wills. Thus the absence of pardon regarding these people does not entail the absence of pardon absolutely. Also, the absence of mention does not indicate non-existence. Do you not see that He the Exalted said: ﴿Faces that day will be bright, laughing, rejoicing﴾ (Abasa: 39), and they are the believers; ﴿And faces that day will have upon them dust, darkness covering them﴾, ﴿those are the disbelievers, the wicked﴾ (Abasa: 40). So here those mentioned are either believers or disbelievers. Then the absence of mention of a third category did not, according to al-Jubba'i, indicate its negation, and so it is here.
As for His saying the Exalted: ﴿And Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾, that is: ﴿Knowing﴾ of what is in the hearts of these believers, ﴿Wise﴾ in what He decides concerning them and judges over them.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and to cause division among the believers and as a station of observation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger before. And they will surely swear, "We intended only the best." And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, mentioned the categories of the hypocrites and their various methods, He said: ﴿And those who took a mosque for harm and disbelief and to cause division among the believers﴾. And concerning this there are several issues:

The first issue: Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited (alladhina attakhadhu, "those who took") without a waw, and likewise it is so in the codices of the people of Medina, while the rest recited it with a waw, and likewise it is so in the codices of Mecca and Iraq. The first reading is that it is a substitution (badal) for His saying: ﴿and others await the command﴾. The second is that the implied sense is: "And among them are those who took a mosque for harm."

The second issue: al-Wahidi said: Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Qatadah and the majority of the people of exegesis – may Allah be pleased with them – said: those who took a mosque for harm were twelve men from the hypocrites who built a mosque to harm by it the Mosque of Quba. I say that He, may He be exalted, described it with four attributes:

The first attribute: harm (dirar). Harm (ḍirār) is the attempt to inflict injury, just as opposition (shiqaq) is the attempt to cause hardship. Al-Zajjaj said: His saying ﴿harm﴾ is in the accusative because it is an object of purpose (maf'ul lahu), and the meaning is: they took it for harm and for the other matters mentioned after it. When the preposition (lam) was dropped, the verb required it, so it was put in the accusative. He said: It is also permissible that it be a verbal noun (masdar) understood in meaning, and the implied sense is: they took a mosque by which they harmed, a harm.

The second attribute: His saying: ﴿and disbelief﴾. Ibn 'Abbas – may Allah be pleased with them both – said: He means by it harm to the believers and disbelief in the Prophet – peace be upon him – and in what he brought. Others said: they took it so that they might disbelieve in it by reviling the Prophet – peace be upon him – and Islam.

The third attribute: His saying: ﴿and to cause division among the believers﴾, that is, they divide, through it, the community of the believers. That is because the hypocrites said: "We will build a mosque and pray in it, and we will not pray behind Muhammad. If he comes to us in it, we will pray with him. And we will separate it from him and from those who pray in his mosque," and that leads to discord in the word and the nullification of unity.

The fourth attribute: His saying: ﴿and as a station of observation for those who had warred against Allah and His Messenger﴾. They said: the intended one is Abu 'Amir the monk, the father of Handhalah whom the angels washed, and whom the Messenger of Allah ﷺ named the Fasiq. He had become Christian in the pre-Islamic period, took up monasticism and sought knowledge. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went out, he opposed him, because his leadership had vanished, and he said: "I do not find a people who fight you except that I will fight you along with them." He continued fighting him until the day of Hunayn. When Hawazin was defeated, he went out to Syria and sent to the hypocrites: "Prepare what you can of strength and weaponry, and build for me a mosque, for I am going to Caesar and will come back from him with an army, and I will expel Muhammad and his companions." So they built this mosque and awaited the coming of Abu 'Amir so that he might lead them in prayer in that mosque. Al-Zajjaj said: al-irṣad means waiting. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-irṣad means waiting combined with enmity. Most of them said: al-irṣad means preparation. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed your Lord is in observation﴾ (al-Fajr: 14).

His saying: ﴿before﴾ means before the building of the mosque of harm. Then, when He, may He be exalted, described this mosque with these four attributes, He said: ﴿And they will surely swear, "We intended only the best."﴾ That is: they will surely swear that by its building they intended only the good deed, which is kindness to the Muslims by way of accommodating the weak, the sick and those unable to reach the mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. That is because they said to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: "We have built a mosque for the one with an illness and need, and for the rainy night and the wintry night."

Then He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And Allah testifies that indeed they are liars.﴾ The meaning is that Allah, may He be exalted, informed the Messenger that they swore falsely.

Know that His saying: ﴿And those who⁠﴾ has a place in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence, and its predicate is omitted, meaning: "And among those we mentioned are those who..."

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 108:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not ever stand in it. A mosque founded upon righteousness from the first day is more worthy that you stand in it. In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves﴾ ﴿Is one who founded his building upon fear of Allah and [seeking] His approval better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling cliff, so it collapsed with him into the fire of Hell? And Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ ﴿Their building which they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts unless their hearts are cut to pieces. And Allah is Knowing and Wise﴾

The exegetes said: When the hypocrites built that mosque for those corrupt purposes, during the absence of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the expedition to Tabuk, they said: "O Messenger of Allah, we have built a mosque for the sick, for the nights of rain and the cold. We love that you pray in it for us and invoke blessing upon us there." He, peace be upon him, said: "I am on the point of a journey, and when we return, if Allah wills, we will pray in it." So when he returned from the expedition to Tabuk, they asked him to come to the mosque, and this verse was revealed. He summoned some of the people and said: "Go to this mosque whose people are wrongdoers, and demolish it and destroy it." They did so, and he commanded that its site be made a dunghill where carrion and refuse would be thrown. Al-Hasan said: The Messenger of Allah ﷺ intended to go to that mosque, and Jibril, peace be upon him, called out: "Do not ever stand in it."

Having understood this, we say: His saying, ﴿Do not stand in it﴾ is a prohibition to him, peace be upon him, against standing in it. Ibn Jurayj said: They finished building that mosque on Friday, and prayed in it that day, and on Saturday and Sunday, and it collapsed on Monday. Then Allah, exalted is He, explained the reason for this prohibition: that since one of the two mosques was founded upon righteousness from the first day, and praying in the other mosque would prevent praying in the mosque of righteousness, it is necessarily known that it would prohibit praying in the second mosque.

If it is said: That one of the two mosques is more excellent does not necessitate prohibiting prayer in the second mosque.

We reply: The causal reasoning is based on the combination of both matters, namely that the mosque of harm was a cause of the four corruptions mentioned, while the mosque of righteousness included many goods. Among the Rafidah there are those who say: Allah, exalted is He, made clear that the mosque which was built from the outset upon righteousness has more right to be stood in than one that is not so. And it is established that Ali never disbelieved in Allah for the blink of an eye, so he must be more worthy of the leadership than one who disbelieved in Allah at the beginning of his affair. Our answer is that the causal reasoning is based on the combination of the mentioned matters, so this objection is removed.

They differed regarding what the mosque of righteousness is. It was said: It is the Mosque of Quba, and he, peace be upon him, used to come to it every year and pray in it. Most of them said it is the Mosque of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab said: The mosque founded upon righteousness is the Mosque of the Messenger, peace be upon him. He mentioned that two men disagreed about it: one of them said, "It is the Mosque of the Messenger," and the other said, "It is Quba." So they asked him, peace be upon him, and he said, "It is this mosque of mine."

Al-Qadi said: Their both being included under this mention is not prevented, because His saying ﴿a mosque founded upon righteousness﴾ is like the saying of one who says: "A righteous man is more worthy that you sit with him." So that is not restricted to one only.

If it is said: Why did He say "more worthy that you stand in it," when standing in the other is not permissible?

We reply: The meaning is that if that were permissible, this one would be more worthy, for the reason mentioned.

[Page 156]

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾ On this verse there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** He, the Exalted, preferred the Mosque of Piety (masjid al-taqwa) for two reasons. The first is that it was founded on piety, which has already been explained.

The second is that in it are men who love to purify themselves. Regarding the meaning of this purification there are two opinions.

The first is that it means purification from sins and disobedience. This opinion is the necessary one, for several reasons.

The first reason is that purification from sins and disobedience is what effectively brings nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and merits His reward and praise.

The second reason is that He, the Exalted, described the people of the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-dirar) as harming the Muslims, disbelieving in Allah, and dividing the Muslims. It is therefore necessary that these people be the opposite of those qualities. And that is nothing but their being free of disbelief and sins.

The third reason is that the purity of the outward body has an effect and a value with Allah only if the purity of the inner self from disbelief and sins is also attained. But if the inner self is purified from disbelief and sins, while outward cleanliness is not attained, the purity of the inner self still has an effect. So the purity of the inner self takes precedence.

The fourth: Sahib al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari, author of al-Kashshaf) narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ walked, accompanied by the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), until he stood at the door of the Mosque of Quba, and there were the Ansar sitting. He said: "Are you believers?" The people were silent, then he repeated it. Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are indeed believers, and I am with them." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you accept the decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be patient in trials?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you give thanks in ease?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Kaaba." Then he said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah has praised you. What is it that you do in wudu'?" They said: "We follow the water with the stone." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾, the verse.

The second opinion is that what is meant is purification with water after using a stone. This is the opinion of most of the exegetes among the people of narrations (ahl al-akhbar).

The third opinion is that the word is to be understood as covering both meanings. There is an objection to this: the word purification (tahharah) is literal (haqiqah, its primary meaning) for purification from material impurities (najasat 'ayniyyah), and figurative (majaz, its extended meaning) for freedom from sins and wrongdoings, and it is not permissible to use one word in both its literal and figurative senses at the same time.

The answer: the word najas (impurity) is a name for what is repugnant, and that common quality is a shared concept between the two categories. On this basis the objection disappears.

Then He, the Exalted, returned to the first cause, which is that the mosque was founded on piety, and He said: ﴿Is one who founded his building on piety from Allah and approval better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell?﴾ On this verse there are several discussions.

**The First Discussion:** Al-bunyan (the building) is a verbal noun like al-ghufran (forgiveness), and what is meant here is the thing built. Using a verbal noun for the thing acted upon is a well-known figure of speech. One says: "This is the beating of the commander" and "the weaving of Zayd," meaning what is beaten and what is woven. Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible that bunyan be the plural of bunyanah, if you take it as a noun, since they said bunyanah in the singular.

**The Second Discussion:** Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited (أُسِّسَ بُنْيانُهُ, "was founded, its building") in the passive form, and the agent of that is the builder and the founder. As for His saying ﴿on piety from Allah and approval﴾, that means: out of fear of Allah's punishment and desire for His reward. This is because obedience is not obedience except with this fear and this hope. The sum of the matter is that when the builder constructed that building for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and out of fear of His punishment and desire for His reward, that building was better and more perfect than the building that its builder constructed out of the motive of disbelief in Allah and harm to the servants of Allah. As for His saying ﴿or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾, there are several discussions on it:

**The First Discussion:** Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited (جُرْفٍ, "bank") with a sukun on the rā'. The rest recited it with a ḍammah on the rā'. These are two dialects: jurufun and jurfun, like shughul and shughl, and 'unuq and 'unq.

**The Second Discussion:** Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-shafa is the brink (al-shafir), and the shafa of a thing is its edge. From this one says: "He overlooked such-and-such" when he came near to it. And al-juruf is that which, when the flood flows and the valley bends, remains at the edge of the flood as wet mud overhanging collapse moment by moment. That thing is the juruf. As for His saying ﴿crumbling (hari)﴾, al-Layth said: al-hawr is the verbal noun of hara al-jurufu yahuru, when it splits from behind and is still in its place, and it is a crumbling, collapsing bank. When it falls, it has collapsed and crashed down.

Having understood these terms, we say: the meaning is: Is one who founded the building of his religion on a strong and firm foundation, namely the truth, which is the piety of Allah and His approval, better? Or one who founded it on the weakest and least lasting foundation, which is falsehood, and hypocrisy? Hypocrisy is like the edge of a crumbling bank from the valleys of Hell. Because it is "the edge of a crumbling bank," it overhangs collapse, and because it is at the edge of Hell, when it collapses it falls into the depths of Hell. We see no example in the world more fitting to the affair of the hypocrites than this example. The sum of the matter is that one of the two buildings was intended by its builder for the piety of Allah and His approval, and the second building was intended by its builder for disobedience and disbelief. So the first building is noble and must be preserved, and the second is base and must be demolished.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The building that they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾. The meaning is that the construction of that building became a cause for doubt arising in their hearts, so the building itself was described as doubt because it was a cause of doubt. Regarding its being a cause of doubt there are several aspects:

The first: the hypocrites greatly rejoiced in the building of the Mosque of Harm. When the Messenger ﷺ ordered its demolition, this weighed heavily on them, their hatred for him increased, and their doubt about his prophethood increased.

The second: when the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) ordered the demolition of that mosque, they thought that he had ordered its demolition only out of envy. Their security from him was removed, and their fear of him grew greater at all times, and they became doubtful about whether he would leave them as they were or would order their killing and the plundering of their wealth.
