The third: they believed that they had been doing good in building that mosque. When the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) ordered its demolition, they remained doubtful and uncertain about why he had ordered its demolition.

The fourth: they remained doubtful and uncertain about whether Allah, the Exalted, would forgive that disobedience, I mean their effort in building that mosque. The correct aspect is the first.

Then He said: ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾. On this there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Hamzah recited (أَنْ تَقَطَّعَ, "to be cut") with a fatḥah on the tā' and the ṭā' doubled, meaning tataqatta'u (they are cut), so one of the two tā's was dropped. The rest recited with a ḍammah on the tā' and a shaddah on the ṭā', in the passive form. From Ibn Kathir: (تَقْطَعُ) with a fatḥah on the ṭā' and a sukun on the qāf, (qulubahum, "their hearts") in the accusative, meaning: you yourself do that cutting to their hearts. His saying ﴿their hearts are cut﴾ means: their hearts are made into pieces and divided into parts, either by the sword or by grief and weeping. Then that doubt would disappear. The intended meaning is that this doubt remains in their hearts forever, and they will die upon this hypocrisy. It was also said: its meaning is: unless they repent with a repentance by which their hearts are cut off through regret and sorrow over their neglect. It was also said: until their hearts split apart from grief and remorse. Al-Hasan recited (إلى أنْ, "until"). In the recitation of 'Abdullah it is (وَلَوْ قُطِّعَتْ قُلُوبُهم, "even if their hearts were cut to pieces"). From Talhah it is (وَلَوْ قَطَّعْتَ قُلُوبَهم, "even if you cut their hearts to pieces"), addressing the Messenger ﷺ or every addressee.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. The meaning is: All-Knowing of their conditions, All-Wise in the rulings by which He judges them.

[Page 156]

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves, and Allah loves those who purify themselves.﴾ On this verse there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** He, the Exalted, preferred the Mosque of Piety (masjid al-taqwa) for two reasons. The first is that it was founded on piety, which has already been explained.

The second is that in it are men who love to purify themselves. Regarding the meaning of this purification there are two opinions.

The first is that it means purification from sins and disobedience. This opinion is the necessary one, for several reasons.

The first reason is that purification from sins and disobedience is what effectively brings nearness to Allah, the Exalted, and merits His reward and praise.

The second reason is that He, the Exalted, described the people of the Mosque of Harm (masjid al-dirar) as harming the Muslims, disbelieving in Allah, and dividing the Muslims. It is therefore necessary that these people be the opposite of those qualities. And that is nothing but their being free of disbelief and sins.

The third reason is that the purity of the outward body has an effect and a value with Allah only if the purity of the inner self from disbelief and sins is also attained. But if the inner self is purified from disbelief and sins, while outward cleanliness is not attained, the purity of the inner self still has an effect. So the purity of the inner self takes precedence.

The fourth: Sahib al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari, author of al-Kashshaf) narrated that when this verse was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ walked, accompanied by the Emigrants (al-Muhajirun), until he stood at the door of the Mosque of Quba, and there were the Ansar sitting. He said: "Are you believers?" The people were silent, then he repeated it. Umar said: "O Messenger of Allah, they are indeed believers, and I am with them." He (peace be upon him) said: "Do you accept the decree?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you be patient in trials?" They said: "Yes." He said: "Will you give thanks in ease?" They said: "Yes." He (peace be upon him) said: "Believers, by the Lord of the Kaaba." Then he said: "O assembly of the Ansar, Allah has praised you. What is it that you do in wudu'?" They said: "We follow the water with the stone." Then the Prophet (peace be upon him) recited: ﴿In it are men who love to purify themselves﴾, the verse.

The second opinion is that what is meant is purification with water after using a stone. This is the opinion of most of the exegetes among the people of narrations (ahl al-akhbar).

The third opinion is that the word is to be understood as covering both meanings. There is an objection to this: the word purification (tahharah) is literal (haqiqah, its primary meaning) for purification from material impurities (najasat 'ayniyyah), and figurative (majaz, its extended meaning) for freedom from sins and wrongdoings, and it is not permissible to use one word in both its literal and figurative senses at the same time.

The answer: the word najas (impurity) is a name for what is repugnant, and that common quality is a shared concept between the two categories. On this basis the objection disappears.

Then He, the Exalted, returned to the first cause, which is that the mosque was founded on piety, and He said: ﴿Is one who founded his building on piety from Allah and approval better, or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell?﴾ On this verse there are several discussions.

**The First Discussion:** Al-bunyan (the building) is a verbal noun like al-ghufran (forgiveness), and what is meant here is the thing built. Using a verbal noun for the thing acted upon is a well-known figure of speech. One says: "This is the beating of the commander" and "the weaving of Zayd," meaning what is beaten and what is woven. Al-Wahidi said: it is permissible that bunyan be the plural of bunyanah, if you take it as a noun, since they said bunyanah in the singular.

**The Second Discussion:** Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited (أُسِّسَ بُنْيانُهُ, "was founded, its building") in the passive form, and the agent of that is the builder and the founder. As for His saying ﴿on piety from Allah and approval﴾, that means: out of fear of Allah's punishment and desire for His reward. This is because obedience is not obedience except with this fear and this hope. The sum of the matter is that when the builder constructed that building for the sake of Allah, the Exalted, and out of fear of His punishment and desire for His reward, that building was better and more perfect than the building that its builder constructed out of the motive of disbelief in Allah and harm to the servants of Allah. As for His saying ﴿or one who founded his building on the edge of a crumbling bank that collapsed with him into the fire of Hell﴾, there are several discussions on it:

**The First Discussion:** Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, recited (جُرْفٍ, "bank") with a sukun on the rā'. The rest recited it with a ḍammah on the rā'. These are two dialects: jurufun and jurfun, like shughul and shughl, and 'unuq and 'unq.

**The Second Discussion:** Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-shafa is the brink (al-shafir), and the shafa of a thing is its edge. From this one says: "He overlooked such-and-such" when he came near to it. And al-juruf is that which, when the flood flows and the valley bends, remains at the edge of the flood as wet mud overhanging collapse moment by moment. That thing is the juruf. As for His saying ﴿crumbling (hari)﴾, al-Layth said: al-hawr is the verbal noun of hara al-jurufu yahuru, when it splits from behind and is still in its place, and it is a crumbling, collapsing bank. When it falls, it has collapsed and crashed down.

Having understood these terms, we say: the meaning is: Is one who founded the building of his religion on a strong and firm foundation, namely the truth, which is the piety of Allah and His approval, better? Or one who founded it on the weakest and least lasting foundation, which is falsehood, and hypocrisy? Hypocrisy is like the edge of a crumbling bank from the valleys of Hell. Because it is "the edge of a crumbling bank," it overhangs collapse, and because it is at the edge of Hell, when it collapses it falls into the depths of Hell. We see no example in the world more fitting to the affair of the hypocrites than this example. The sum of the matter is that one of the two buildings was intended by its builder for the piety of Allah and His approval, and the second building was intended by its builder for disobedience and disbelief. So the first building is noble and must be preserved, and the second is base and must be demolished.

* * *

Then He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The building that they built will not cease to be a source of doubt in their hearts﴾. The meaning is that the construction of that building became a cause for doubt arising in their hearts, so the building itself was described as doubt because it was a cause of doubt. Regarding its being a cause of doubt there are several aspects:

The first: the hypocrites greatly rejoiced in the building of the Mosque of Harm. When the Messenger ﷺ ordered its demolition, this weighed heavily on them, their hatred for him increased, and their doubt about his prophethood increased.

The second: when the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) ordered the demolition of that mosque, they thought that he had ordered its demolition only out of envy. Their security from him was removed, and their fear of him grew greater at all times, and they became doubtful about whether he would leave them as they were or would order their killing and the plundering of their wealth.

The third: they believed that they had been doing good in building that mosque. When the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) ordered its demolition, they remained doubtful and uncertain about why he had ordered its demolition.

The fourth: they remained doubtful and uncertain about whether Allah, the Exalted, would forgive that disobedience, I mean their effort in building that mosque. The correct aspect is the first.

Then He said: ﴿Unless their hearts are cut to pieces﴾. On this there are several discussions:

**The First Discussion:** Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Hamzah recited (أَنْ تَقَطَّعَ, "to be cut") with a fatḥah on the tā' and the ṭā' doubled, meaning tataqatta'u (they are cut), so one of the two tā's was dropped. The rest recited with a ḍammah on the tā' and a shaddah on the ṭā', in the passive form. From Ibn Kathir: (تَقْطَعُ) with a fatḥah on the ṭā' and a sukun on the qāf, (qulubahum, "their hearts") in the accusative, meaning: you yourself do that cutting to their hearts. His saying ﴿their hearts are cut﴾ means: their hearts are made into pieces and divided into parts, either by the sword or by grief and weeping. Then that doubt would disappear. The intended meaning is that this doubt remains in their hearts forever, and they will die upon this hypocrisy. It was also said: its meaning is: unless they repent with a repentance by which their hearts are cut off through regret and sorrow over their neglect. It was also said: until their hearts split apart from grief and remorse. Al-Hasan recited (إلى أنْ, "until"). In the recitation of 'Abdullah it is (وَلَوْ قُطِّعَتْ قُلُوبُهم, "even if their hearts were cut to pieces"). From Talhah it is (وَلَوْ قَطَّعْتَ قُلُوبَهم, "even if you cut their hearts to pieces"), addressing the Messenger ﷺ or every addressee.

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is All-Knowing, All-Wise﴾. The meaning is: All-Knowing of their conditions, All-Wise in the rulings by which He judges them.

[p. 158]

Allah, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for paradise. They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed. That is a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an. And who is truer to his covenant than Allah? So rejoice in the bargain you have made, for that is the supreme triumph.﴾

Know that when Allah, the Exalted, began to explain the disgraceful conduct and vices of the hypocrites, because of their staying behind from the expedition to Tabuk, and when He had completed that explanation and clarification, mentioned their categories, and assigned to each category what was fitting for it, He returned to explaining the excellence of jihad and its reality. So He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives...﴾ There are several issues in this verse.

The first issue: al-Qurtubi said: "When the Ansar pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ on the night of al-'Aqabah in Makkah, and they were seventy persons, 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah said: 'Stipulate for your Lord and for yourself whatever you wish.' He said: 'I stipulate for my Lord that you worship Him and do not associate anything with Him, and for myself that you protect me as you protect yourselves and your properties.' They said: 'If we do that, what will we get?' He said: 'Paradise.' They said: 'The bargain is profitable; we will not cancel it, nor will we ask for its cancellation.'" Then this verse was revealed. Mujahid, al-Hasan, and Muqatil said: "He [Allah] took them as customers and made their price high."

The second issue: The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani, those who study the semantic meanings of the Qur'an) said: It is not permissible that Allah truly purchases anything, since a buyer only buys what he does not own. For this reason al-Hasan said: "He purchased lives which He Himself created, and properties which He Himself provided." Rather, Allah mentioned it for the sake of gently inviting people to obedience. The reality of this is that when the believer fights in the cause of Allah until he is killed, so that his soul departs, and spends his wealth in the cause of Allah, he receives from Allah in the Hereafter paradise as a reward for what he did. So this is treated as an exchange and a purchase. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for paradise﴾, that is, "for paradise." Likewise was the reading of 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and al-A'mash. Al-Hasan said: "Listen! By Allah, it is a profitable transaction and a weighty return, which Allah has concluded with every believer. By Allah, there is no believer on earth but that he has entered into this pledge." Al-Sadiq, peace be upon him, said: "Your bodies have no price except paradise, so do not sell them except for it." His saying "and their properties" means the wealth they spend in the cause of Allah, and on themselves, their families, and their dependents. There are subtle points in this verse:

The first subtle point: A buyer must have a seller, and here the seller is Allah and the buyer is Allah. This is valid only in the case of a guardian managing the affairs of a child who cannot himself look after his interests in buying and selling, and the validity of this sale is conditional upon securing a great benefit. So this example serves as a reminder that the servant resembles a child who is not guided to protect his own interests, and that He, the Exalted, is the one who looks after his interests on condition of complete benefit. The purpose of this is to indicate ease, leniency, pardon for sins, and attainment of the ranks of good and the degrees of felicity.

The second subtle point: He, the Exalted, attributed the lives and properties to them. Therefore, the fact that the lives and properties are attributed to them requires two distinct matters for them, and the matter is so in itself. For the human being is an expression for the original, enduring essence, while this body functions as an instrument, a tool, and a composite. Likewise, wealth was created as a means to securing the interests of this composite. So the Truth, glory be to Him, purchased from the human being this composite and this wealth in exchange for paradise. This is the realization of the matter, because as long as a person remains attached in heart to the interests of the world of the changing, transforming body, namely the body and wealth, he is barred from reaching the lofty felicities and noble ranks. But when his attachment to them is severed, and that severance reaches the point of exposing the body to killing and wealth to spending in pursuit of the good pleasure of Allah, he has reached the point of preferring guidance over desire, the Master over the world, and the Hereafter over the present life. At this point he is among the happy righteous and the excellent virtuous. Thus the seller is the essence of the holy spirit, the buyer is Allah, one of the two exchanged items is the decaying body and the perishing wealth, and the second exchanged item is enduring paradise and everlasting felicities. So the profit is achieved and sorrow and grief disappear. For this reason He said: ﴿So rejoice in the bargain you have made﴾.

Then He said: ﴿They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed.﴾ The author of al-Kashshaf said: His saying "they fight" carries the sense of a command, like His saying: ﴿and strive in the cause of Allah with your wealth and your lives﴾ [al-Saff: 11]. It was also said that He made "they fight" like an explanation of that pledge, and like a necessary consequence of it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with the object placed before the subject, meaning they are killed while being fighters; the rest read it with the subject placed before the object. As for placing the subject before the object, the meaning is evident: they kill the disbelievers and do not turn away from them until they themselves become killed. As for placing the object before the subject, the meaning is: a large group of Muslims, even if they become killed, that will not deter the rest from fighting; rather, after that they remain fighting alongside the enemies, fighting them to the extent possible. This is like His saying: ﴿So they did not weaken for what befell them in the cause of Allah﴾ [Al 'Imran: 146], that is, those who remained among them did not weaken. Scholars differed over whether striving against enemies through argument, commanding right and forbidding wrong, is included under this verse or not. Some said it is specific to jihad through fighting, because He explained that pledge by fighting in His saying: ﴿They fight in the cause of Allah, so they kill and are killed.﴾ Others said that all types of jihad are included in it, as evidenced by the report we narrated from 'Abdullah ibn Rawahah. Moreover, jihad through argument and calling to the proofs of monotheism has more complete effects than fighting. For this reason the Prophet ﷺ said to 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him: "That Allah guides a man through you is better for you than what the sun rises upon." Also, jihad through fighting does not have its good effect except after jihad through argument has been put forward. As for jihad through argument, it is independent of jihad through fighting. The soul's essence is a noble substance, which Allah, the Exalted, singled out with greater honor in this world, and there is no corruption in its essence; corruption lies only in the attribute established in it, namely disbelief and ignorance. Whenever it is possible to remove the corrupt attribute while preserving the essence and substance, that is preferable. Do you not see that since the hide of a dead animal can be benefited from in some respects, the Law urged its preservation, saying: "Why did you not take its hide and tan it, so that you could benefit from it?" Thus jihad through argument is like tanning, which preserves the essence while removing the corrupt attribute, whereas jihad through fighting is like annihilating the essence. So the first station is preferable and more excellent.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿a promise binding upon Him in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "The word 'promise' (wa'dan) is in the accusative on the basis of meaning, because the meaning of His saying ﴿in exchange for paradise﴾ is that He promised them paradise, so 'promise' is a verbal noun of emphasis." Scholars differed over what this is that occurred in the Books:

The first view: this promise He made to those who strive in the cause of Allah is a firm promise, which Allah established in the Torah and the Gospel just as He established it in the Qur'an.

The second view: the meaning is that Allah, the Exalted, made clear in the Torah and the Gospel that He purchased from the community of Muhammad, peace be upon him, their lives and properties in exchange for paradise, just as He made it clear in the Qur'an.

The third view: the command to fighting and jihad exists in all the revealed laws.

Then Allah, the Exalted, said: ﴿And who is truer to his covenant than Allah?﴾ The meaning is that breaking a covenant is a lie; moreover it is deception and treachery, and all of these are vices. They are vile in a human being even though he needs them, so the One who is free of all needs is more deserving of being exempt from them. His saying ﴿And who is truer to his covenant﴾ is an interrogative used in the sense of denial, meaning: no one is more faithful to what He has promised than Allah.

Then He said: ﴿So rejoice in the bargain you have made, for that is the supreme triumph.﴾ Know that this verse contains kinds of emphasis:

[p. 160]
The first of them is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties﴾, so the buyer is Allah, who is exalted above lying and betrayal, and this is among the strongest indications of the firmness of this covenant.

The second: He expressed the conferral of this reward through buying and selling, and that is firm emphasis.

The third: His saying "a promise" (wa'dan), and the promise of Allah is true.

The fourth: His saying "binding upon Him" ('alayhi), and the word 'alaa ("upon") indicates obligation.

The fifth: His saying "true" (haqqan), which is emphasis for affirmation.

The sixth: His saying ﴿in the Torah, the Gospel, and the Qur'an﴾, which functions like calling all the divine books and all the prophets and messengers to witness this pledge.

The seventh: His saying ﴿And who is truer to his covenant than Allah?﴾, which is an extreme form of emphasis.

The eighth: His saying ﴿So rejoice in the bargain you have made﴾, which is also an exaggeration in emphasis.

The ninth: His saying ﴿for that is the triumph﴾.

The tenth: His saying "supreme" (al-'azim). Thus it is established that this verse includes these ten aspects of emphasis, affirmation, and confirmation. We conclude the verse with a closing remark: Abu al-Qasim al-Balkhi cited this verse as evidence that there must be compensations ('iwad) for the pains of children and animals. He said: The verse indicates that it is not permissible to inflict the pain of killing and the seizure of wealth upon adults except in exchange for a price, which is paradise. Therefore He said: ﴿Indeed, Allah has purchased from the believers their lives and their properties in exchange for paradise﴾. So it must be the case that the same applies to children and animals. And if they were capable of wishing, they would wish that their pains be multiplied so that they might obtain those lofty and noble compensations. We say: We do not deny that children and animals obtain goods in return for these pains; the disagreement is only that such compensation, according to us, is not obligatory, while according to you it is obligatory, and the verse is silent about the establishing of obligation.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 112 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travelers, the bowers, the prostrators, those who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil, and those who guard the limits of Allah. And give good tidings to the believers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned in the first verse that He ﴿purchased from the believers their lives and their properties, for which theirs is the Garden﴾, He then explained in this verse that those believers are the ones described by these nine attributes. There are two issues concerning this.

The first issue: concerning the nominative case (raf') of His saying ﴿the repentant, the worshippers, the praisers, the travelers﴾, there are several aspects:

The first: it is in the nominative on the basis of praise (al-madh), and the implied meaning is: they are the repentant, meaning the believers mentioned in His saying ﴿purchased from the believers their lives﴾ are the repentant.

The second: al-Zajjaj said: It is not far-fetched that His saying "the repentant" is a subject (mubtada'), and its predicate is omitted, i.e., "the repentant, the worshippers, [and] those from among the people of the Garden as well, even if they did not fight, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And to each Allah has promised the best﴾ [al-Nisa': 95]." This is a good aspect, because on this reading the promise of the Garden is attained by all believers, whereas if we make His saying "the repentant" follow the beginning of the speech, the promise of the Garden is attained only by those who fight.

The third: "the repentant" is a subject, or it is in the nominative as a substitute (badal) for the pronoun in His saying "they fight".

The fourth: His saying "the repentant" is a subject, and His saying "the worshippers" up to the end of the verse is a predicate following a predicate, i.e., the ones who are truly repentant from disbelief are those who combine these qualities. Ubayy and Abdullah read "the repentant" (al-ta'ibin) with a yā' up to His saying "the guarders" (al-hafizin), and in this there are two aspects:
One of them: that this is in the accusative on the basis of praise.
The second: that it is in the genitive, as an attribute of "the believers."

* * *

Page 161

The second issue: concerning the explanation of these nine attributes.

As for the first attribute, His saying "the repentant": Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "the repentant from polytheism." al-Hasan said: "the repentant from polytheism and hypocrisy." The usuliyyun said: "the repentant from every sin," and this is preferable, because repentance may be repentance from disbelief and may be repentance from sin. His saying "the repentant" is a general form marked by the definite article (al-alif wa-l-lam), so it encompasses all; restricting it to repentance from disbelief is pure arbitrariness.

Know that we have elaborated on the reality of repentance in our explanation of His saying in Surat al-Baqarah: ﴿Then Adam received from his Lord words, and He accepted his repentance﴾ [al-Baqarah: 37].

Know that repentance is only realized upon the occurrence of four matters:
The first: the heart burning at the moment over the committing of that sin.
The second: regret for what has passed.
The third: resolve to abandon it in the future.
The fourth: that the motive for these three matters is seeking the pleasure of Allah, exalted is He, and His worship. If his purpose in them is to repel people's blame and to obtain their praise, or any other aims, then he is not among the repentant.

As for the second attribute, His saying, exalted is He, "the worshippers": Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, said: those who regard the worship of Allah as obligatory upon them. The theologians (al-mutakallimun) said: they are those who perform worship, which is an expression for performing an act that indicates glorifying Allah, exalted is He, in the most complete forms of glorification. For Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with both of them, one may say that knowledge of Allah and acknowledgment of the obligation of obeying Him is a deed of the heart, and the realization of the name in the affirmative sense is satisfied by the realization of one instance of that reality. al-Hasan said: "the worshippers" are those who worshipped Allah in ease and in hardship. Qatadah said: they are a people who exerted their bodies by night and by day.

The third attribute: His saying "the praisers" (al-hamidun), who are those who genuinely perform the thanks of Allah, exalted is He, for His favors, in religion and in worldly life, and who make the manifestation of that a habit for themselves. We have mentioned that glorifying (tasbih), declaring His oneness (tahlil), and praising (tahmid) is the attribute of those who worshipped Allah before the creation of the world, namely the angels, since He, exalted is He, reported about them that they said before the creation of Adam: ﴿and we glorify You with Your praise﴾. It is also the attribute of those who worship Allah after the ruin of the world, since He, exalted is He, reported about the people of the Garden that they praise Allah, exalted is He, and it is ﴿their final call is: "Praise be to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾ [Yunus: 10]. They are the ones intended by His saying "the praisers."

The fourth attribute: His saying "the travelers" (al-sa'ihun), and concerning it there are opinions:

The first opinion: the majority of exegetes said they are the fasting ones (al-sa'imun). Ibn 'Abbas said: everything mentioned in the Qur'an concerning siyahah (travel/wandering) is fasting. The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The wandering (siyahah) of my community is fasting." From al-Hasan: that this refers to obligatory fasting. It was also said: they are those who maintain fasting continually. Regarding the meaning for which describing the sa'ih as the sa'im is apt, there are two aspects:
The first: al-Azhari said: the fasting person is called sa'ih because one who wanders on the earth in devotion without provision, holding back from eating, and the fasting person refrains from eating; for this resemblance the fasting person is called a traveler.
The second: the essence of siyahah is continuing to go on the earth like flowing water (sayh al-ma'), and the fasting person continues in performing obedience and abandoning desires, namely eating, drinking and intercourse. And in my view there is another aspect: when a person refrains from eating, drinking and intercourse, and closes upon himself the doors of desires, the doors of wisdom are opened to him and the lights of the world of majesty are revealed to him. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever sincerely devotes himself to Allah for forty mornings, the springs of wisdom will gush from his heart onto his tongue." Thus he becomes among the travelers in the world of Allah's majesty, moving from station to station and from rank to rank, and so he attains a wandering in the world of spirituality.

The second opinion: that what is meant by the travelers are seekers of knowledge who move from city to city in seeking knowledge. This is the view of Ikrimah. From Wahb ibn Munabbih: travel was practiced among the Children of Israel, and when a man wandered for forty years he would see what the travelers before him used to see. A son of a prostitute among them wandered for forty years and saw nothing, so he said: "My Lord, what is my sin, that my mother did wrong?" At that point Allah showed him what He had shown the travelers. I say: wandering has a great effect in perfecting the soul, because one encounters various kinds of harm and hardship, so one must be patient with them; his provision may run out, so he needs to rely upon Allah; he may meet distinguished people of differing views, and benefit from each one a particular benefit; he may meet the great among people and belittle himself before them; he may attain many desired things and benefit from them; and he may observe the differing conditions of the people of the world, due to what Allah, exalted is He, created in every region of special conditions for them, so his knowledge grows stronger. In sum, wandering has strong effects on religion.

The third opinion: Abu Muslim said: "the travelers" (al-sa'ihun) are those who journey on the earth, derived from sayh, the flowing of water, and what is meant by it is one who goes out as a fighter and emigrant. Its explanation is that He, exalted is He, urged the believers in the first verse to jihad, then mentioned this verse to describe the attributes of the fighters, so they should be described with the totality of these attributes.

The fifth and sixth attributes: His saying "the bowers, the prostrators" (al-raki'un al-sajidun), and what is meant by it is the performance of the prayers. al-Qadi said: He made the mention of bowing and prostration a metonymy for prayer, because the other forms of the one praying are conventional, namely standing and sitting. What departs from custom in this is bowing and prostration, and by it the distinction between the one praying and others becomes evident. It may be said: standing is the first degree of humility before Allah, exalted is He, bowing is its middle, and prostration is its extreme. He specified bowing and prostration for mention because they indicate the utmost humility and servitude, alerting that the purpose of prayer is the utmost submission and glorification.

The seventh and eighth attributes: His saying "those who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil." Know that the book on the rulings of enjoining good and forbidding evil is a great work mentioned in the science of usul al-fiqh, so it is not possible to set it out here. In it there is an indication of the obligation of jihad, because the head of what is good is faith in Allah, and the head of what is evil is disbelief in Allah. Jihad necessitates encouraging faith and deterring from disbelief. Jihad falls within the category of enjoining good and forbidding evil. As for the entry of the waw in His saying "and those who forbid what is evil," there are aspects:
The first aspect: equalization (al-taswiyah) sometimes comes with waw and sometimes without waw. He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Forgiver of sin, Acceptor of repentance, severe in punishment, the Owner of bounty﴾ [Ghafir: 3], where some came with waw and some without waw.
The second aspect: the purpose of these verses is to encourage jihad, so Allah, glorified is He, mentioned the nine attributes, then said: ﴿those who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil﴾. The meaning is: those described by the six attributes, and those who enjoin what is good and forbid what is evil. We have mentioned that the head and chief of enjoining good and forbidding evil is jihad, so the purpose of introducing the waw before it is to alert to what we have mentioned.

Page 162

The third aspect: concerning the introduction of the waw before these, it is because every attribute preceding them is a worship a person performs for himself, with no connection of any of them to others. As for forbidding evil, it is a worship connected to others, and this forbidding necessitates the stirring of anger and the appearance of enmity; perhaps the one forbidden will attack the one forbidding, and perhaps he will try to kill him. So forbidding evil is the most difficult category of worships and acts of obedience, and so the waw was introduced before it to alert to the added hardship and trial involved in it.

The ninth attribute: His saying "and those who guard the limits of Allah." The purpose is that Allah's obligations are many, and they are confined to two types:
One of them: what relates to acts of worship.
The second: what relates to dealings (mu'amalat).
As for acts of worship, they are those which Allah commanded not for a worldly benefit that is observed, but for benefits observed in religion: such as prayer, zakat, fasting, hajj, jihad, manumission, vows, and all other acts of righteousness. As for dealings, they are either for attracting benefits or for repelling harms.

The first type, which concerns the attracting of benefits: those benefits are either intended primarily or secondarily. As for benefits intended primarily, they are the benefits attained through the five senses:
The first of them: what is tasted. This includes the book of foods and drinks in jurisprudence. Since food may be vegetable or animal, and an animal cannot be eaten except after slaughter, and Allah stipulated specific conditions for slaughter, for this reason the books of hunting and slaughter and the book of sacrificial animals entered into jurisprudence.
The second: what is touched. This includes the rules of intercourse, among them what makes it permissible, which is the book of marriage, and also the book of nursing; and among them is what is an inquiry into the necessary consequences of marriage, such as the dower, maintenance and dwelling, and connected to it are the matters of division and disobedience; and among them is what is an inquiry into the causes that dissolve marriage, which includes the books of divorce, khul', ila', zihar, and li'an. Among the rulings relating to what is touched is the inquiry into what is permissible to wear and what is not, and what is permissible to use and what is not, such as using gold and silver vessels; and the discussion of the jurists in this chapter is lengthy.
The third: what is seen. This is the chapter on what is permissible to look at and what is not.
The fourth: what is heard. This is the chapter on whether it is permissible to hear it or not.

[p. 163 continued]

Fifth: the things smelled (al-mashmumat), with which the jurists (fuqaha') have no concern. As for the benefits that are sought secondarily, they are property (al-amwal). The discussion of them has three aspects.

The first: the causes that confer ownership (al-milk). These are either sale (al-bay') or other than sale. Sale is either the sale of substances (a'yan) or the sale of usufruct (manafi'). The sale of substances is either the exchange of a substance for a substance, or the exchange of a debt for a substance, which is the salam (advance sale), or the exchange of a substance for a debt, as when one buys something described as a liability (fi al-dhimmah), or the exchange of a debt for a debt. It has been said that this is not permissible, on the basis of what is narrated: "He (ﷺ) forbade the sale of kali' for kali'" (peace be upon him). However, an example of it occurs in the Sharia, namely the settlement of two debts. As for the sale of usufruct, it includes the book of ijarah (hire), the book of ju'alah (contract of reward), and the book of mudarabah (profit-sharing contract). As for the remaining causes that make ownership obligatory, they are inheritance (al-irth), gift (al-hibah), bequest (al-wasiyyah), reviving dead land (ihya' al-mawat), finding lost property (al-iltiqat), taking fay' (booty without battle) and spoils of war (al-ghana'im), and taking zakat and other dues. There is no way to define the causes of ownership except through induction (al-istiqra').

The second type, among the subjects of the jurists, is the causes that make it permissible for someone other than the owner to dispose of a thing, which is the chapter of agency (wakalah), deposit (wadi'ah), and other such matters.

The third type is the causes that prevent the owner from disposing of his own property, namely pledge (rahn), insolvency (tafliss), hire (ijarah), and others. This is the definition of the categories of God's obligations in the domain of attracting benefits. As for God's obligations in the domain of repelling harms

[p. 164]

we say: the categories of harm are five, because harm either occurs to souls, or to property, or to religion, or to lineage, or to intellect. As for the harms that occur to souls, they are either inflicted upon the whole soul, and the ruling concerning it is either qisas (retaliation), or diyah (blood money), or kaffarah (expiation); or they are inflicted upon some part of the body, such as cutting off a hand or other limbs, and what is obligatory in that case is either qisas, or diyah, or arsh (compensation for injury). As for the harms that occur to property, such harm either takes place openly and publicly, which is the book of ghasb (usurpation), or secretly, which is the book of sariqah (theft). As for the harms that occur to religion, they are either disbelief (kufr) or innovation (bid'ah). As for disbelief, it includes the rulings concerning apostates (al-murtaddin). The jurists have no established book on the rulings concerning innovators. As for the harms that occur to lineage, connected with this are the prohibition of adultery (zina) and sodomy (liwat) and the explanation of the prescribed punishment for both. Also included is the chapter on the punishment for slander (hadd al-qadhf) and the chapter on mutual imprecation (li'an). Here is another discussion: no one can secure his rights to benefits and repel harms by himself, because he may be weak, so his opponent will not pay attention to him. For this reason God the Exalted appointed the Imam to enforce the rulings, and it is necessary that this Imam have deputies, who are the commanders (umara') and the judges (qudah). Since the statement of one party against another cannot be accepted except with proof (hujjah), the Sharia established a specific proof for the manifestation of truth, which is testimony (shahadah). It is also necessary that the claim (da'wa) and the establishment of evidence (bayyinah) have specific conditions, so there must be a chapter that comprises them. This is the definition of the foundations of God the Exalted's obligations, His rulings, and His limits (hudud). Since these are numerous, and God the Exalted has explained them throughout the Qur'an, sometimes in detail and sometimes by commanding the Messenger (peace be upon him) to explain them to the responsible persons (mukallafin), it is inevitable that He summarized their mention in this verse. So He said: ﴿And those who guard the limits of Allah﴾, and this encompasses the whole of these obligations.

Know that the jurists thought that what they mentioned in explaining the obligations was the whole; but the matter is not so. The deeds of responsible persons are of two kinds: deeds of the limbs and deeds of the hearts. The books of fiqh contain an explanation of the categories of obligations related to deeds of the limbs. As for the obligations related to deeds of the hearts, they have not discussed them at all, nor have they composed books, chapters, or sections on them, nor have they investigated their subtleties. Without doubt, the investigation of them is more important, and elaborating the disclosure of their realities is more appropriate, because deeds of the limbs are intended only for the sake of achieving deeds of the hearts. The numerous verses in the Book of God the Exalted speak to this. However, His saying, glorified be He: ﴿And those who guard the limits of Allah﴾ comprehends all these categories in a comprehensive and encompassing manner.

Know that when God the Exalted mentioned these nine attributes, He said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾. The purpose of this is that in the preceding verse He said: ﴿So rejoice in your transaction which you have made﴾ (At-Tawbah: 111), then He mentioned these nine attributes, and then after them said: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾ who possess these attributes.

If it is said: what is the reason that God the Exalted mentioned those eight attributes in detail, then after them mentioned in this ninth attribute the remaining categories of obligations in summary?

We say: because repentance, worship, occupation with glorifying God, wandering in search of knowledge (siyahah li-talab al-'ilm), bowing and prostration, enjoining good and forbidding evil, are matters from which a responsible person is not free for most of his time. Therefore God the Exalted mentioned them in detail. As for the rest, the responsible person may be free of them for most of his time, such as the rulings of buying and selling, and the knowledge of the rulings on crimes against persons (al-jinayat). Furthermore, those eight matters are deeds of the hearts, even though they are deeds of the limbs; but what is intended from them is the manifestation of the states of the hearts. You have known that attending to the states of the hearts is more important than attending to the states of the outward. For this reason He mentioned this category in detail,

[p. 165]

and mentioned this category in summary.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 113–114 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists, even if they should be near relatives, after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ ﴿And the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him. But when it became clear to him that he was an enemy to Allah, he disassociated himself from him. Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾

Know that when He, may He be exalted, made clear from the beginning of this surah up to this point the obligation of openly disavowing the disbelievers and the hypocrites in every respect, He explained in this verse that disavowal is obligatory even regarding their dead, even if they were in the closest relation to a person, such as a father or mother, just as disavowal was made obligatory regarding their living. The purpose of this is to show the obligation of cutting off contact with them to the utmost extent and prohibiting maintaining any kind of connection with them. In this regard there are several issues:

The first issue: They have mentioned several reports concerning the occasion of revelation of this verse.

The first: Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, said: "When Allah, exalted is He, opened Makkah, the Prophet (ﷺ) asked, 'Which of his two parents is most recent in his remembrance?' It was said, 'Your mother.' So he went to her grave and stood in front of it, then sat beside her head and wept. Then ʿUmar asked him and said: 'You forbade us from visiting graves and from weeping, and yet you visited and wept.' He said: 'I was permitted to do so. When I realized her condition from the punishment of Allah, and that I could not avail her anything against Allah, I wept out of mercy for her.'"

The second: It is related from Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab, from his father, who said: "When death approached Abu Talib, the Messenger (ﷺ) said to him: 'O uncle, say: There is no god but Allah, so that I may plead for you with it before Allah.' Abu Jahl and ʿAbdullah ibn Abi Umayyah said: 'Do you turn away from the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib?' He said: 'I am upon the religion of ʿAbd al-Muttalib.' Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said: 'I will surely ask forgiveness for you as long as I am not forbidden from you.' Then this verse was revealed."

His saying: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you love﴾. Al-Wahidi said: al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl considered this unlikely, because this surah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, while the death of Abu Talib occurred in Makkah at the beginning of Islam. I say: this consideration seems unlikely to me. What harm is there in saying that the Prophet (ﷺ) continued to seek forgiveness for Abu Talib from that time until the revelation of this verse? For the severity toward the disbelievers only appeared in this surah, so perhaps the believers were permitted to seek forgiveness for their disbelieving parents, and the Prophet (ﷺ) too would do so; then, when this surah was revealed, Allah forbade them from it. Thus this is not entirely unlikely.

The third: It is narrated from ʿAli that he heard a man seeking forgiveness for his two polytheist parents. He said: "I said to him: Do you seek forgiveness for your parents while they are polytheists? He said: Did not Abraham seek forgiveness for his parents while they were polytheists? I mentioned that to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and then this verse was revealed."

The fourth: It is narrated that a man came to the Messenger (ﷺ) and said: "My father in the Jahiliyyah used to maintain the ties of kinship, host guests, and give from his wealth. Where is my father?" He said: "Did he die as a polytheist?" He said: "Yes." He said: "He is in a shallow part of the Fire." The man turned away weeping, so the Prophet (ﷺ) called him back and said: "My father and your father and the father of Abraham are in the Fire. Your father never once said: I seek refuge in Allah from the Fire."

* * *

Page 166

The second issue: His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ may mean that it is not fitting for them to do so, in which case it is descriptive, or it may mean they are not permitted to do so, in the sense of a prohibition.

As for the first: its meaning is that prophethood and faith prevent seeking forgiveness for the polytheists.

As for the second: its meaning is "do not seek forgiveness"; the two meanings are close. The reason for this prohibition is what Allah mentioned in His saying: ﴿after it has become clear to them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire﴾. He also said: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not forgive that partners be associated with Him, but He forgives what is less than that for whom He wills﴾ [an-Nisa': 48]. The meaning is that when He, exalted, informed us that He will cause them to enter the Fire, asking forgiveness for them is like asking that Allah break His promise and His threat, and that is impermissible. Also, since Allah's decree that He will punish them has already preceded, if they asked for His forgiveness they would be rejected, and that would entail a diminishing of the rank of the Prophet (ﷺ) and a lowering of his station. Also, He said: ﴿Call upon Me, I will respond to you﴾ [Ghafir: 60], and He said of them that they are companions of the Blazing Fire; so this seeking of forgiveness would entail contradicting one of these two texts, and that is impermissible. Abu Hashim permitted that a servant ask his Lord for something after Allah has informed that He will not do it, and he argued for this with the saying of the people of the Fire: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 107], although they knew that He would not do that. This is extremely far-fetched in several respects:

First: This is based on his doctrine that the people of the Hereafter do not become ignorant or lie, and that is disputed; rather the text of the Qur'an refutes it, namely His saying: ﴿Then their trial will be only that they say: By Allah, our Lord, we were not polytheists﴾ [al-An'am: 23] ﴿See how they lied against themselves﴾ [al-An'am: 24].

Second: Regarding them, it is fitting to turn them away from that request and silence them, but regarding the Messenger (ﷺ) this is not permissible, because it would entail a diminishing of his rank.

Third: A request of this kind, which is known to have no benefit, is either futile or sinful; both are permissible for the people of the Fire and impermissible for the great prophets, upon them be peace.

The third issue: Since He, exalted, made clear that the reason preventing this seeking of forgiveness is the clarity that they are among the companions of the Fire, and this reason does not differ whether they are close relatives or distant ones, for this reason He said: ﴿even if they should be near relatives﴾. That the occasion of revelation is what we have related strengthens what we have said.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are several views:

The first: that its purpose is that no one should suppose that Allah prohibited Muhammad from something He had permitted Abraham to do.

The second: it is said that we mentioned, regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, the emphasis on requiring separation from the disbelievers, living and dead. Then He, exalted, explained that this ruling is not specific to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ); rather, the emphasis on establishing the obligation of separation was also prescribed in the religion of Abraham, upon him be peace, so the emphasis on establishing the obligation of boycotting and disassociating from the disbelievers is stronger.

The third: He, exalted, described Abraham, upon him be peace, in this verse as forbearing, i.e., slow to anger, and as ʾawwah, i.e., greatly grieved and distressed when harm befalls people. The point is that whoever is described with these qualities, the inclination of his heart toward seeking forgiveness for his father would be strong; so it is as if it were said: Abraham, despite his great rank and being described as ʾawwah and forbearing, Allah prevented him from seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father; so for someone else to be prevented from this matter is more fitting.

The second issue: The Qur'an indicates that Abraham, upon him be peace, sought forgiveness for his father. He, exalted, said, relating about him: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 86]. He also said about him: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾ [Ibrahim: 41]. He, exalted, also said, relating about him in Surah Maryam: ﴿Peace be upon you; I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ [Maryam: 47], and He said: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. It is established that seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is impermissible, so this indicates that this sin proceeded from Abraham, upon him be peace.

Know that He, exalted, answered this difficulty with His saying: ﴿And the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾. There are two views regarding this:

The first: that the one who made the promise was Abraham's father, upon Abraham be peace, and the meaning is that his father promised him that he would believe, so Abraham would seek forgiveness in order that this outcome might be achieved; then when it became clear to him that he would not believe and that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him and abandoned that seeking of forgiveness.

The second: that the one who made the promise was Abraham, upon him be peace, for he promised his father that he would seek forgiveness for him, hoping for his conversion. ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him.﴾ The evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is the reading of al-Hasan ("wa'adaha abahu," with the preposition bāʾ). Some people mentioned two other views regarding the answer.

The first of these two other views: what is meant by Abraham's seeking forgiveness for his father is his calling him to faith and Islam; he would say to him: "Believe, so that you may be freed from punishment and attain forgiveness," and he would humbly beseech Allah to grant him the faith that necessitates forgiveness. This is the seeking of forgiveness. Then when Allah informed him that he would die persisting in disbelief, he abandoned that call.

The second view in the answer: some people understood His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ as referring to the funeral prayer. By this route, there is no impediment to seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever, since the benefit of such seeking is the lightening of punishment. They said: the evidence that what we have mentioned is what is meant is that He prohibited praying over the hypocrites, as in His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ [at-Tawbah: 84]. In this verse He generalized this ruling and prohibited praying over the polytheists, whether he was a hypocrite or openly held to that polytheism. This is a strange view.

* * *

The third issue: They differed concerning the cause by which it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of Allah. Some said: by his persistence and death. Some said: by his persistence alone. Others said: it is not far-fetched that Allah made him aware of that through revelation, and at that point he disassociated himself from him. So He, exalted, was saying: When it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him; so you too should be like that, because I have commanded you to follow Abraham in His saying: ﴿Follow the religion of Abraham﴾ [an-Nahl: 123].

Know that when He, exalted, mentioned Abraham's condition in this incident, He said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ Know that the derivation of ʾawwah is from a man's saying "awwah" at the height of his grief. The reason for this is that in grief the inner spirit of the heart becomes constricted and its burning intensifies, so a person exhales that burning breath from the heart to lighten some of what he feels; this is the origin of the derivation of this word. The exegetes have various expressions about it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The ʾawwah is the humble one who beseeches." And from ʿUmar: that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the ʾawwah, and he said: "The one who supplicates much." It is also narrated that Zaynab spoke in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) in a way that changed his color, and ʿUmar disapproved, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave her, for she is an ʾawwah." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the ʾawwah?" He said: "The one who calls upon Him, humble and beseeching." It was also said: the meaning of Abraham being ʾawwah is that whenever he remembered

the Arabic: "لِنَفْسِهِ تَقْصِيرًا" means "for himself, a shortcoming" — translate.

Translation:

for a shortcoming on his own part, or something of the severities of the Hereafter was mentioned to him, he would groan out of fear of that and out of magnifying it. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "al-Awwah" is the one who believes with fear (al-khashyah). As for describing him as ḥalīm (forbearing), it is well known. Know that Allah, exalted, described him with these two attributes in this context, because He described him with intense tenderness, compassion, fear and anxiety; and whoever is like this, his tenderness toward his father and children is great. So Allah, exalted, made clear that despite this habit he disowned his father and his heart became harsh toward him when his persistence in disbelief became manifest to him. So you are more entitled to this meaning. Likewise He also described him as ḥalīm, because one of the causes of forbearance is tenderness of heart and intensity of kindness; for when a person's state is like this, his forbearance becomes strong at the time of anger.

Third: A request of this kind, which is known to have no benefit, is either futile or sinful; both are permissible for the people of the Fire and impermissible for the great prophets, upon them be peace.

The third issue: Since He, exalted, made clear that the reason preventing this seeking of forgiveness is the clarity that they are among the companions of the Fire, and this reason does not differ whether they are close relatives or distant ones, for this reason He said: ﴿even if they should be near relatives﴾. That the occasion of revelation is what we have related strengthens what we have said.

* * *

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: Regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, there are several views:

The first: that its purpose is that no one should suppose that Allah prohibited Muhammad from something He had permitted Abraham to do.

The second: it is said that we mentioned, regarding the connection of this verse to what precedes it, the emphasis on requiring separation from the disbelievers, living and dead. Then He, exalted, explained that this ruling is not specific to the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ); rather, the emphasis on establishing the obligation of separation was also prescribed in the religion of Abraham, upon him be peace, so the emphasis on establishing the obligation of boycotting and disassociating from the disbelievers is stronger.

The third: He, exalted, described Abraham, upon him be peace, in this verse as forbearing, i.e., slow to anger, and as ʾawwah, i.e., greatly grieved and distressed when harm befalls people. The point is that whoever is described with these qualities, the inclination of his heart toward seeking forgiveness for his father would be strong; so it is as if it were said: Abraham, despite his great rank and being described as ʾawwah and forbearing, Allah prevented him from seeking forgiveness for his disbelieving father; so for someone else to be prevented from this matter is more fitting.

The second issue: The Qur'an indicates that Abraham, upon him be peace, sought forgiveness for his father. He, exalted, said, relating about him: ﴿And forgive my father, for he was among the astray﴾ [ash-Shu'ara': 86]. He also said about him: ﴿Our Lord, forgive me and my parents﴾ [Ibrahim: 41]. He, exalted, also said, relating about him in Surah Maryam: ﴿Peace be upon you; I will ask my Lord to forgive you﴾ [Maryam: 47], and He said: ﴿I will surely ask forgiveness for you﴾ [al-Mumtahanah: 4]. It is established that seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever is impermissible, so this indicates that this sin proceeded from Abraham, upon him be peace.

Know that He, exalted, answered this difficulty with His saying: ﴿And the plea for forgiveness by Abraham for his father was only because of a promise he had made to him﴾. There are two views regarding this:

The first: that the one who made the promise was Abraham's father, upon Abraham be peace, and the meaning is that his father promised him that he would believe, so Abraham would seek forgiveness in order that this outcome might be achieved; then when it became clear to him that he would not believe and that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him and abandoned that seeking of forgiveness.

The second: that the one who made the promise was Abraham, upon him be peace, for he promised his father that he would seek forgiveness for him, hoping for his conversion. ﴿So when it became clear to him that he was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him.﴾ The evidence for the soundness of this interpretation is the reading of al-Hasan ("wa'adaha abahu," with the preposition bāʾ). Some people mentioned two other views regarding the answer.

The first of these two other views: what is meant by Abraham's seeking forgiveness for his father is his calling him to faith and Islam; he would say to him: "Believe, so that you may be freed from punishment and attain forgiveness," and he would humbly beseech Allah to grant him the faith that necessitates forgiveness. This is the seeking of forgiveness. Then when Allah informed him that he would die persisting in disbelief, he abandoned that call.

The second view in the answer: some people understood His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ as referring to the funeral prayer. By this route, there is no impediment to seeking forgiveness for a disbeliever, since the benefit of such seeking is the lightening of punishment. They said: the evidence that what we have mentioned is what is meant is that He prohibited praying over the hypocrites, as in His saying: ﴿And do not pray over any of them who has died, ever﴾ [at-Tawbah: 84]. In this verse He generalized this ruling and prohibited praying over the polytheists, whether he was a hypocrite or openly held to that polytheism. This is a strange view.

* * *

The third issue: They differed concerning the cause by which it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of Allah. Some said: by his persistence and death. Some said: by his persistence alone. Others said: it is not far-fetched that Allah made him aware of that through revelation, and at that point he disassociated himself from him. So He, exalted, was saying: When it became clear to Abraham that his father was an enemy of Allah, he disassociated himself from him; so you too should be like that, because I have commanded you to follow Abraham in His saying: ﴿Follow the religion of Abraham﴾ [an-Nahl: 123].

Know that when He, exalted, mentioned Abraham's condition in this incident, He said: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was compassionate and forbearing.﴾ Know that the derivation of ʾawwah is from a man's saying "awwah" at the height of his grief. The reason for this is that in grief the inner spirit of the heart becomes constricted and its burning intensifies, so a person exhales that burning breath from the heart to lighten some of what he feels; this is the origin of the derivation of this word. The exegetes have various expressions about it. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "The ʾawwah is the humble one who beseeches." And from ʿUmar: that he asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the ʾawwah, and he said: "The one who supplicates much." It is also narrated that Zaynab spoke in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ) in a way that changed his color, and ʿUmar disapproved, so the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Leave her, for she is an ʾawwah." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, what is the ʾawwah?" He said: "The one who calls upon Him, humble and beseeching." It was also said: the meaning of Abraham being ʾawwah is that whenever he remembered

the Arabic: "لِنَفْسِهِ تَقْصِيرًا" means "for himself, a shortcoming" — translate.

Translation:

for a shortcoming on his own part, or something of the severities of the Hereafter was mentioned to him, he would groan out of fear of that and out of magnifying it. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father: "al-Awwah" is the one who believes with fear (al-khashyah). As for describing him as ḥalīm (forbearing), it is well known. Know that Allah, exalted, described him with these two attributes in this context, because He described him with intense tenderness, compassion, fear and anxiety; and whoever is like this, his tenderness toward his father and children is great. So Allah, exalted, made clear that despite this habit he disowned his father and his heart became harsh toward him when his persistence in disbelief became manifest to him. So you are more entitled to this meaning. Likewise He also described him as ḥalīm, because one of the causes of forbearance is tenderness of heart and intensity of kindness; for when a person's state is like this, his forbearance becomes strong at the time of anger.

Tafsir of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, verses 115–116:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah would never misguide a people after He had guided them until He makes clear to them what they should fear. Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things.﴾ ﴿Indeed, to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death. And you have not, other than Allah, any ally or helper.﴾

In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when He, exalted is He, forbade the believers from seeking forgiveness for the polytheists, and the Muslims had sought forgiveness for the polytheists before the revelation of this verse (for before the revelation of this verse they used to seek forgiveness for their fathers, mothers and all their relatives who had died in disbelief), then when this verse was revealed they feared, because of what had proceeded from them before that of seeking forgiveness for the polytheists. Also, groups of the Muslims who had sought forgiveness for the polytheists had died before the revelation of this verse, so fear fell upon the hearts of the Muslims as to what their condition would be. Allah, exalted is He, removed that fear from them by this verse, and made clear that He, exalted is He, does not take them to account for any action except after He has made clear to them that it is obligatory upon them to fear Him and guard against it. This is a good connection in the arrangement of the verses. It was also said that the intended meaning is: from the beginning of the surah up to this point is an explanation of the prohibition of associating with the disbelievers and the hypocrites, the obligation of disassociating from them, and the avoidance of allying with them. So it is as if it were said: How is it fitting for the merciful, generous God to impose this severe strictness regarding these disbelievers and hypocrites? It was answered that He, exalted is He, does not take peoples to punishment after He has called them to right guidance until He makes clear to them what it is obligatory for them to fear. As for after He has done that, and removed the excuse and eliminated the cause, then He may take them to account with the most severe kinds of accountability and punishment. And in His saying, exalted is He, (to misguide, liyudilla) there are several aspects:

The first: the meaning is that He led him astray from the path of Paradise, that is, He turned him away from it and prevented him from turning toward it.

The second: the Mu'tazilah said: the intended meaning of this misguidance is passing judgment upon them as being in error. They argued with the verse of al-Kumayt:

"And a group has declared me an unbeliever for love of you"

Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: this interpretation is invalid, because when the Arabs intend that meaning they say: dalla-la yudill (he declared him astray). Their argument with the verse of al-Kumayt is false, because it does not follow from our saying "akfara" in the sense of judging as unbeliever that our saying "adalla" is correct; and not every form that is valid with af'ala is valid in every case. Do you not see that one may say kasarahu (he broke it), but one may not say aksarahu (he broke it, causative), rather in this one must return to what is heard from the Arabs.

The third aspect regarding the interpretation of the verse: and Allah would not cause error to fall into their hearts after guidance, until there comes from them the matter for which punishment is deserved.

The second issue: The Mu'tazilah said: the sum of the verse is that He, exalted is He, does not take anyone to account except after He has made clear to him that that act is ugly and forbidden. They established this by His being knowing of all things, which is His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, and by His being capable of all possibilities, which is His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death﴾. So the implication is: whoever is knowing and capable in this way is not in need, and a knowing, capable, self-sufficient one does not do what is ugly or punish before clarification. Removing the excuse is ugly, so it is obligatory that Allah, exalted is He, not do it. Thus the arrangement of the verse is sound only if we interpret it in this way, and this implies that it is ugly for Allah, exalted is He, to begin with punishment, and you do not hold this.

The answer: what you have mentioned indicates that He, exalted is He, does not punish except after clarification, removal of the excuse, and removal of the cause; and there is no indication in it that He, exalted is He, does not have that right. So what you have mentioned in this matter falls away.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He gives life and causes death﴾. In mentioning this meaning here there are several benefits:

The first: when He, exalted is He, commanded disassociation from the disbelievers, He made clear that to Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth; so if He is your helper, they cannot harm you.

The second: the Muslims said: since You have commanded us to cut ties with the disbelievers, we cannot then mix with our fathers, children and brothers, for many of them are likely disbelievers. The meaning is: if you become deprived of their assistance and support, then the God who is the owner of the heavens and the earth, who gives life and causes death, is your helper, so their severing from you does not harm you.

The third: when He, exalted is He, commanded these arduous obligations, it is as if He said: it is obligatory upon you to submit to My judgment and My commandment, because I am your God and because you are My servants.
