Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 117:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved. Then He turned to them in forgiveness. Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them.﴾

Page 170
Know that when He, exalted is He, had fully explained the circumstances of the Battle of Tabuk, and clarified the situation of those who stayed behind from it, and extended discourse on that in the order we summarized in this tafsir, He returned in this verse to explaining what remained of its rulings. Among the remaining rulings is that a kind of lapse proceeded from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, similar to that first one, and a kind of lapse also proceeded from the believers. So He mentioned that He showed favour to them and turned to them in forgiveness for those lapses. He said: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾. In the verse there are several issues:

The first issue: The reports indicate that this journey was extremely arduous upon the Messenger, peace be upon him, and upon the believers, as its explanation will come. This calls for praise, so how does His saying ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants﴾ fit with it?

The answer has several aspects:

The first: Something of the category of leaving what is better (tark al-afdal) proceeded from the Prophet, peace be upon him, and this is what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿May Allah pardon you. Why did you give them permission?﴾ (al-Tawbah: 43). Also, when the hardship of this campaign intensified upon the believers, as its explanation will come, there may have occurred in the hearts of some of them a kind of aversion to that journey, and it may have occurred to some of them that we are not able to flee. I do not say they resolved upon it; rather I say they were whisperings that occurred in their hearts. So God, exalted is He, made clear at the end of this surah that by His grace He pardoned them. He said: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him﴾.

The second aspect in the answer: A person throughout his life is not free from lapses and slips, either of the category of minor sins or of the category of leaving what is better. Then, when the Prophet, peace be upon him, and all the believers bore the hardships and toils of this journey, and endured those trials and tribulations, God, exalted is He, informed that bearing those hardships became an expiation for all the lapses that proceeded from them throughout their lives, and stood in place of repentance accompanied by sincerity for all of them. For this reason God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾, and so on.

The third aspect in the answer: When the time became harsh upon them in that journey, and whisperings were occurring in their hearts, whenever a whispering occurred in the heart of one of them he repented to God from it and humbly implored God to remove it from his heart. Because of their frequent turning to repentance on account of the thoughts of those whisperings passing through their minds, God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet﴾, and so on.

The fourth aspect: It is not far-fetched that kinds of disobedience proceeded from those groups, but God, exalted is He, turned to them in forgiveness and pardoned them because they bore the hardships of that journey. Then, God, exalted is He, joined the mention of the Messenger, peace be upon him, to their mention, as an indication of the greatness of their ranks in religion, and that they had reached the degree for the sake of which He joined the Messenger, peace be upon him, with them in the acceptance of repentance.

* * *
The second issue: Regarding the meaning of "the hour of hardship" there are two opinions:

The first opinion: It is specific to the Battle of Tabuk, and what is meant by it is the time when the matter became extremely difficult for them in that journey. ʿUsrah (hardship) means the impracticability and difficulty of a matter. Jabir said: there occurred the hardship of mounts, the hardship of water, and the hardship of provisions. As for the hardship of mounts, al-Hasan said: ten of the Muslims would go out on one camel, taking turns riding it among themselves. As for the hardship of provisions, a group would sometimes suck a single date, taking turns with it, until nothing remained of the date but the pit; and they had with them some barley that was infested with weevils, so whenever one of them put a morsel into his mouth he would pinch his nose because of the stench of the morsel. As for the hardship of water, ʿUmar said: We set out in intense summer heat, and we were afflicted with severe thirst, to the point that a man would slaughter his camel, squeeze its stomach contents, and drink them.

Know that this campaign is called the Campaign of Hardship (Ghazwat al-ʿUsrah), and whoever went out in it is the Army of Hardship (Jaysh al-ʿUsrah). ʿUthman and others among the Companions equipped them, may Allah be pleased with them all.

The second opinion: Abu Muslim said: It is permissible that what is meant by the hour of hardship is all the difficult states and times upon the Messenger and upon the believers, so it includes the Battle of the Trench and others. God has mentioned some of them in His Book, such as His saying: ﴿And when the eyes swerved and the hearts reached the throats﴾ (al-Ahzab: 10), and His saying: ﴿And Allah had certainly fulfilled His promise to you when you were killing them by His permission, until when you lost courage﴾ (Al ʿImran: 152), and the purpose of this is to describe the Emigrants and the Helpers as having followed the Messenger, peace be upon him, in the severe times and the difficult states, and that conveys the utmost praise and exaltation.

* * *
Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾, and in it there are discussions:

The first discussion: The subject of (kāda, "nearly") may be (qulūb, "hearts"), with the sense: the hearts of a group of them nearly swerved. It may also be that in it is the pronoun of the matter and affair, and the verb and subject are an explanation of the matter, and the meaning is: they nearly did not remain steadfast in following the Messenger, peace be upon him, in that campaign because of the severity of the hardship.

The second discussion: Ḥamzah and Ḥafs, from ʿAsim, read (yazīgh) with the yā' because the verb is placed first; the rest read it with the tā' because (qulūb, "hearts") is feminine. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah it is: ﴿min baʿdi mā zāghat qulūbu farīqin minhum﴾.

The third discussion: (kāda) according to some indicates only approximation, and according to others indicates approximation together with non-occurrence. Thus the repentance mentioned is repentance from that approximation. They differed about what occurred in their hearts. It was said: some of them intended, at that great hardship, to part from the Messenger, but he endured and sought reward; therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾, when they endured, remained steadfast, and regretted that matter, however slight. Others said: rather, that was a stirring of the self (ḥadīth al-nafs), which is the precursor of resolve; when hardship befell them, that occurred in their hearts, yet they corrected this slight matter out of fear that it might be disobedience; therefore God, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾.

If it is said: He mentioned repentance at the beginning of the verse and at its end, so what is the benefit of the repetition?

We say: There are several aspects to this:

The first aspect: He, exalted is He, began with mention of repentance before mention of the sin, to console their hearts; then He mentioned the sin, and then followed it once more with mention of repentance, and the purpose of this is to magnify their station.

The second aspect: When it is said, "The ruler pardoned so-and-so; then he pardoned him," this indicates that that pardon is an emphasized pardon that reached the utmost degree in perfection and strength. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed Allah forgives the sin of a Muslim man twenty times." This is the meaning of Ibn ʿAbbas's saying regarding His words ﴿Then He turned to them in forgiveness﴾: he means He increased in His pleasure with them.

The third aspect: He said: ﴿Indeed Allah has turned in forgiveness to the Prophet and the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship﴾, and this arrangement indicates that the meaning is that He turned to them in forgiveness from the whisperings that occurred in their hearts in the hour of hardship. Then He added to it, saying: ﴿after the hearts of a group of them had nearly swerved﴾. This addition conveys that strong whisperings had occurred; therefore, inevitably, He followed it with mention of repentance once more, so that no doubt would remain in the mind of any of them about being held accountable for those whisperings.

Then He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, He is Kind and Merciful to them﴾. These are two attributes of God, exalted is He, and their meanings are close. It seems that ra'fah (kindness) is an expression for striving to remove harm, and raḥmah (mercy) is an expression for striving to bring benefit. It was also said: one of them refers to past mercy, and the other to future mercy.

[p. 173]

**His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [He turned in mercy also] toward the three who were left behind, until, when the earth was constricted for them despite its vastness, and their souls were constricted for them, and they knew that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him, then He turned to them in mercy that they might repent. Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾**

There are several issues in the verse.

**The first issue:** This is conjoined (ma'tuf) to the previous verse, and the implied meaning is: "Allah has certainly turned in mercy to the Prophet, the Emigrants and the Helpers who followed him in the hour of hardship, and to the three who were left behind." The benefit of this conjunction is that we have explained that whoever has his repentance mentioned alongside the repentance of the Prophet (ﷺ) is thereby shown to be honoured and esteemed. This conjunction requires that the acceptance of the repentance of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) and the repentance of the Emigrants and the Helpers be under one ruling, and this requires elevating their status and affirming that they deserve this.

**The second issue:** These three are the ones mentioned in His saying: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command﴾ [al-Tawbah: 106]. The commentators differed about the reason for which they were described as "left behind," and they mentioned several views:

First: It is not meant that these people were commanded to stay behind, nor that the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) approved of that. Rather, it is like your saying to your companion, "Where did you leave so-and-so?" and he says, "At such-and-such a place," not meaning that he ordered him to stay behind; perhaps he even forbade him from it, but he simply means that he stayed behind from him.

Second: It is not impossible that these three had intended to go out to the raid, and the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) gave them leave for the time needed to prepare the equipment and tools. When they remained for a period, laziness and sluggishness became apparent, and so it is correct to say: "The Messenger left them behind."

Third: The verse relates the story of groups of people, and they are the ones meant by His saying: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command.﴾ So the meaning of these people being "left behind" is that they were delayed in the acceptance of repentance, compared with the first group. Ka'b ibn Malik, who was one of these three, said: "The saying of Allah, exalted is He, concerning us: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind﴾ does not refer to our staying behind. It is only the delay of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in deciding our matter, to allude thereby to His saying: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command.﴾"

[p. 173 continued]

**The third issue:** The author of *al-Kashshaf* (al-Zamakhshari's commentary) said: It has been read as (khalafū), meaning they became successors (khulafa') to those who went out to the raid, and they were corrupted, from *al-khalifah* and *khulūf al-fam* (the bad smell of the mouth). Ja'far al-Sadiq read (khālafū), and al-A'mash read (wa-ʿalā al-thalāthati al-mukhallafīn).

**The fourth issue:** These three were Ka'b ibn Malik, the poet; Hilal ibn Umayya, concerning whom the verse of *li'an* was revealed; and Murara ibn al-Rabi'. There are two views concerning this story:

The first view: They went out following the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Al-Hasan said: One of them had land worth one hundred thousand dirhams, and he said: "O my land! It was only your command that kept me from the Messenger of Allah. Go, for you are in the way of Allah." Then he said, "I shall certainly endure the deserts until I reach the Prophet (ﷺ)," and he did so. The second had a family, and he said: "O my family! It was only your command that kept me from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). I shall certainly endure the deserts until I reach him," and he did so. The third had neither wealth nor family, and he said: "I have no cause except my attachment to life. By Allah, I shall certainly endure the deserts until I reach the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)." So they joined the Messenger (ﷺ), and Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿And others are deferred until Allah's command.﴾

The second view, which is the view of most scholars, is that they did not go out after the Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him). Ka'b said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved my conversation. When I delayed in going out with him, he (peace and blessings be upon him) said: 'What has held Ka'b back?' When he came to Madinah, the hypocrites offered excuses, and he accepted their excuses. I came to him and said: 'My camel and my provisions were present, but I was detained by my own sin. So ask forgiveness for me.' The Messenger refused that. Then he (peace and blessings be upon him) forbade people from sitting with these three and commanded that they be shunned, to the extent that he commanded this to their wives as well. So the earth became constricted for them despite its vastness. The wife of Hilal ibn Umayya came and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, Hilal has wept so much that I fear for his sight.' When fifty days had passed, Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿Certainly Allah has turned in mercy to the Prophet and the Emigrants﴾ and He revealed His saying: ﴿And upon the three who were left behind.﴾ At that, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out to his chamber, while he was with Umm Salama, and said: 'Allah is greatest! Allah has revealed the excuse of our companions.' When he prayed the dawn prayer, he mentioned that to his companions and gave them the good news that Allah had turned in mercy to them. So they set out to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited to them what had been revealed concerning them." Ka'b said: "My repentance to Allah the Exalted is that I give my wealth away as charity." He said: "No." I said: "Then half of it." He said: "No." I said: "Then a third of it." He said: "Yes."

Know that He, exalted is He, described these three with three attributes:

**The first attribute:** His saying: ﴿Until, when the earth was constricted for them despite its vastness.﴾ The exegetes said: its meaning is that the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) turned away from them, forbade the believers from speaking with them, and commanded their wives to keep away from them. They remained in this state for fifty days, and it was said: more. The meaning of (and the earth was constricted for them despite its vastness) has already been explained in this surah.

**The second attribute:** His saying: ﴿And their souls were constricted for them.﴾ What is meant is the constriction of their hearts due to grief and distress, and being shunned by friends and loved ones, and people looking upon them with the eye of contempt.

**The third attribute:** His saying: ﴿And they knew that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him.﴾ Its meaning is close to his (peace and blessings be upon him) supplication: "I seek refuge in Your pleasure from Your wrath, and I seek refuge in Your pardon from Your anger, and I seek refuge in You from You." Some people said the meaning of His saying (and they knew) is "they were certain," as in His saying: ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord﴾ [al-Baqarah: 46]. The evidence for this is that He mentioned this description of them in the context of praise and commendation, and this would not be so unless they knew that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him. Others said: their matter was left pending revelation, and they were not certain that Allah would send down revelation clearing them of hypocrisy, but they considered it possible that the period of their hardship would be prolonged. So the objection returns to their considering that period might be short. When Allah described them with these three attributes...

* * *

He said: ﴿Then He turned to them in mercy﴾, and concerning it there are issues:

**The first issue:** Know that a supposition (idmar) is necessary here. The meaning is: "Until, when the earth was constricted for them despite its vastness, and their souls were constricted for them, and they knew that there is no refuge from Allah except in Him, He turned to them [in mercy], then He turned to them in mercy." So what is the benefit of this repetition?

We say: This repetition is good for emphasis, just as when a king wishes to stress his pardon for one of his servants, he says: "I have pardoned you, I have pardoned you."

If it is asked: What is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in mercy that they might repent﴾?

We say: There are several views concerning it:

The first: Our companions said: its purpose is to show that the act of the servant is created by Allah, the Exalted. So His saying: ﴿Then He turned to them in mercy﴾ indicates that repentance is the act of Allah, and His saying (that they might repent) indicates that it is the act of the servant. This is the clear statement of our position. Its parallel is (so let them laugh) alongside His saying: ﴿And it is He who makes people laugh and weep﴾ [al-Najm: 43], and His saying: ﴿As your Lord brought you out﴾ [al-Anfal: 5] alongside His saying: ﴿When those who disbelieved drove him out﴾ [al-Tawbah: 40], and His saying: ﴿It is He who enables you to travel﴾ [Yunus: 22] alongside His saying: ﴿Say: Travel﴾ [al-Naml: 69].

The second: What is meant is that Allah turned to them in the past, so that this would be an incentive for them to repent in the future.

The third: The original meaning of repentance is return. So what is meant is: "Then He turned to them in mercy, so that they might return to their former state and habit of mixing with the believers, and the separation would end, so that their souls would then be at peace."

The fourth: (He turned to them in mercy that they might repent) means: that they might persist in repentance, and not return to what nullifies it.

The fifth: (Then He turned to them in mercy) so that they might benefit from repentance, and its reward would be complete for them. These two benefits are only attained after Allah's turning to them in mercy.

**The second issue:** Our companions used this verse to argue that it is not obligatory upon Allah, by reason, to accept repentance. They said: The conditions of repentance for these people were fulfilled from the very beginning. Then the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him) did not accept them, did not turn to them, and left them for fifty days or more. Had accepting repentance been obligatory by reason, this would not have been permissible.

Al-Jubba'i answered this by saying: It is said that this repentance was accepted from the very beginning, but it is said: He intended to tighten the obligation upon them, so that no one would dare to stay behind from the Messenger in what he commanded of jihad or other things. Also, his (peace and blessings be upon him) prohibition of speaking with them was not a punishment, but was in the manner of tightening the obligation. The Qadi said: The Messenger (peace and blessings be upon him) singled out these three for this tightening because they submitted to the truth and acknowledged their sin. What is done to them, in their state, is more effective in deterrence than what is done to those hypocrites who display an excuse.

The response: We hold to the apparent meaning of His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then He turned to them in mercy.﴾ The word (then, thumma) indicates delay, so the implication of this wording is the postponement of the acceptance of repentance. If you interpret that as a postponement of the public manifestation of this acceptance, that would be a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence.

[p. 175]

If they say: What necessitates this departure is His saying: ﴿And it is He who accepts repentance from His servants﴾ [al-Shura: 25].

We say: The form (yaqbalu, he accepts) is for the future, and by consensus it does not at all indicate immediacy. Furthermore, He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is the Accepting of repentance, the Merciful.﴾

Know that the mention of the Merciful immediately after the mention of the Accepter of repentance indicates that the acceptance of repentance is for the sake of pure mercy and generosity, not because it is obligatory. This strengthens our position that it is not obligatory upon Allah, by reason, to accept repentance.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 119:

﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and be with the truthful.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, decreed the acceptance of the repentance of these three, He mentioned something that serves as a deterrent against doing what had passed, namely lagging behind the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in jihad. So He said: ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ regarding opposing the command of the Messenger, ﴿and be with the truthful﴾, meaning, with the Messenger and his companions in the military campaigns, and do not be among those who lag behind from them, or who sit with the hypocrites in their homes. There are several issues concerning the verse:

The first issue: Allah, exalted is He, commanded the believers to be with the truthful. Whenever being with the truthful is obligatory, the truthful must necessarily exist at every time. This prevents all of them from agreeing upon falsehood, and when it is impossible for all of them to agree upon falsehood, it is necessary that when they agree upon something, they are correct. This indicates that the consensus (ijma') of the community is a proof (hujjah).

If it is said: Why is it not permissible to say that what is meant by ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ is: follow the way of the truthful, just as when a man says to his child, "Be with the righteous," this conveys nothing but that? We grant that, but we say: this command existed only during the time of the Messenger. So this was a command to be with the Messenger, and it does not indicate the existence of a truthful person in all other times. Granting that as well, why is it not permissible that the truthful one is the infallible (ma'sum) whose existence the time of obligation cannot be devoid of, as the Shi'ah maintain?

The answer to the first: His saying ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ is a command to agree with the truthful and a prohibition against separating from them, and this is conditional upon the existence of the truthful, and whatever an obligation cannot be completed without is itself obligatory. So this verse indicates the existence of the truthful. As for his saying that it is to be understood as "to be upon the way of the truthful," we say: this is a departure from the apparent meaning without evidence. As for his saying that this command is specific to the time of the Messenger, peace be upon him:

We say: This is invalid for several reasons:

The first: It is established by the apparent mass-transmission (tawatur) from the religion of Muhammad, peace be upon him, that the obligations mentioned in the Qur'an are directed at the responsible persons until the Resurrection, so the command in this obligation is likewise.

The second: The wording encompasses all times, as shown by the validity of making an exception (istithna') [from it].

The third: Since the specific time is not mentioned in the wording of the verse, applying the verse to some times is no more appropriate than applying it to the rest. Either it is applied to none of the times, which leads to nullification, and this is false, or to all of them, which is what is sought.

The fourth: His saying ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾ is a command to them to have taqwa, and this command only applies to one who could possibly not be pious, and that would only be the case if he were capable of error. So the verse indicates that whoever is capable of error must follow one who is obligatorily free from error, and they are those whom Allah, exalted is He, has decreed to be truthful. This indicates that it is obligatory for one capable of error to be with one who is protected from error (ma'sum 'an al-khata'), so that the one protected from error prevents the one capable of error from erring. This meaning persists in all times, so it must be realized in all times.

If it is said: Why is it not permissible that what is meant is the believer's being with the infallible who exists in every time?

We say: We acknowledge that there must be an infallible person in every time. However, we say that this infallible one is the totality of the community, while you say that this infallible one is one individual among them. We say: this second view is false, because Allah, exalted is He, obligated each one of the believers to be with the truthful. This is possible for him only if he knows who that truthful one is, not if he is ignorant of who he is. So if he were commanded to be with him, that would be a burden of what cannot be borne, and that is impermissible. But we do not know any specific human being described by the attribute of infallibility, and knowledge that we do not know this person is attained by necessity. Thus it is established that His saying ﴿and be with the truthful﴾ is not a command to be with a specific individual. Since this is invalid, what remains is that what is meant is being with the totality of the community, and this indicates that the statement of the totality of the community is true and correct. There is no meaning to our saying "consensus is a proof" except this.

* * *

The second issue: The verse indicates the excellence of truthfulness and the perfection of its rank. Among the aspects that support that the matter is so are several points:

The first: It is narrated that a man came to the Prophet, peace be upon him, and said: "I am a man who wants to believe in you, but I love wine, fornication, theft, and lying, and people say that you prohibit these things, and I have no ability to abandon them all. So if you are content with my abandoning just one of them, I will believe in you." The Prophet, peace be upon him, said, "Abandon lying." He accepted that, then embraced Islam. When he left the presence of the Prophet, peace be upon him, they offered him wine, and he said: "If I drink and the Messenger asks me about drinking it and I lie, then I have broken the covenant; and if I tell the truth, he will impose the prescribed punishment (hadd) upon me." So he abandoned it. Then they offered him fornication, and that thought came to him, so he abandoned it. Likewise with theft. Then he returned to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "How excellent is what you did! When you prevented me from lying, the doors of sins were closed to me." And he repented of all of them.

The second: It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Upon you is truthfulness, for it leads to righteousness (birr), and righteousness leads to Paradise. A servant continues to be truthful until he is recorded with Allah as a truthful one (siddiq). Beware of lying, for lying leads to wickedness (fujur), and wickedness leads to the Fire. A man continues to lie until he is recorded with Allah as a great liar. Do you not see that it is said: 'You spoke truly and were righteous,' and 'You lied and were wicked'?"

The third: It has been said regarding His saying, exalted is He, quoting Iblis: ﴿By Your might, I will surely mislead them all, ﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ (Sad: 82-83). Iblis mentioned this exception only because, had he not mentioned it, he would have been a liar in claiming to mislead all of them. So it is as if he disdained lying, and therefore mentioned this exception. If lying is something Iblis disdains, then the Muslim is more deserving of disdaining it.

The fourth: Among the virtues of truthfulness is that faith (iman) is from it and not from the rest of the acts of obedience, and among the defects of lying is that disbelief (kufr) is from it and not from the rest of the sins. People have differed regarding what is the cause (muqtada) of its ugliness. Our companions (the Ash'arites) said: the cause of its ugliness is that it disrupts the interests of the world and the interests of the self. The Mu'tazilah said: the cause of its ugliness is that it is falsehood (kadhib). Our evidence is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, if a wicked person brings you a report, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful﴾ (al-Hujurat: 6), meaning: do not accept the statement of the wicked, for perhaps it is a lie, and from accepting that lie an act would result over which you would become regretful. This indicates that He, exalted is He, only obligated the rejection of what may possibly be a lie because of the possibility that it leads to what contradicts the interests. So the cause of the ugliness of lying must be that it leads to harms. The qadi (al-Qadi 'Abd al-Jabbar) argued for his view that whoever is driven to seek a benefit or to avert a harm, and is able to reach that by lying or by truthfulness, it is known by the immediate intuition of reason that it is not permissible for him to turn away from truthfulness to lying. And if he were able to reach that through two truthful means, it would be permissible for him to switch from one to the other. So if lying were good for a benefit or for removing a harm, its status would be the same as truthfulness. Since it is not so, it is known that it is only ugly. Also, if it were permissible for it to be good, it would be permissible for Allah, exalted is He, to command it when it is an interest, and that leads to the consequence that His reports could not be trusted. This is what he mentioned in the tafsir. It is said in reply to the first: when a person has, from the beginning of his life, established the ugliness of lying because of its disrupting the interests of the world, that becomes before his eyes and the image of his imagination. Then, when that rare image happens to be judged, the firmly established habit judges it to be ugly. So if you assume that a person is free of this habit, and you assume that truthfulness and lying are equal in leading to the desired end, then on this assumption we do not grant that preference is achieved. And it is said in reply to the second argument: you establish the impossibility of lying upon Allah, exalted is He, by its being ugly because it is lying. So if you established this meaning by the impossibility of its issuing from Allah, it would entail circular reasoning (dawr), and that is invalid.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 120–121:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those of the desert Arabs around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to prefer themselves over his own self. That is because they are not afflicted with thirst, nor fatigue, nor hunger in the way of Allah, nor do they tread upon a path that enrages the disbelievers, nor do they gain any gain from an enemy except that a righteous deed is written for them thereby. Indeed Allah does not waste the reward of the good-doers.﴾ ﴿And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large, nor do they cross a valley, except that it is written for them, so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do.﴾

Know that when Allah, exalted is He, commanded by His saying: ﴿Be with the truthful ones﴾, the obligation of being in accordance with the Messenger, upon him be peace, in all the expeditions and battles, He confirmed that, and so in this verse He forbade remaining behind from him. He said: ﴿It was not for the people of Medina and those of the desert Arabs around them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah﴾. The desert Arabs who were around Medina were Muzayna, Juhayna, Ashja', Aslam and Ghifar; this is what Ibn Abbas said. It was said: rather, this includes all the desert Arabs who were around Medina, for the wording is general, and specification is arbitrary. On both views, it is not permissible for them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah, nor to seek for themselves safety and ease while the Messenger of Allah is in heat and hardship. His saying: ﴿nor to prefer themselves over his own self﴾: it is said, "I turned myself away from this matter," meaning I stopped from it and left it; and "I turn away with so-and-so from this," meaning I withhold it from him and do not leave it. The meaning: it is not for them to be averse to themselves to what the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace, desires for himself.

Page 178

Know that the apparent meaning of these words is the obligation of jihad upon all of these people. However, we say: the sick, the weak and the incapable are excluded by the evidence of reason, and also by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Allah does not burden a soul beyond its capacity﴾ (al-Baqarah: 286), and also by His saying: ﴿There is no blame upon the blind﴾ (al-Nur: 61), and so on. As for jihad not being obligatory upon every individual person, consensus (ijma') has indicated it, so it is specified from this generality; and what remains beyond these two cases remains included under this generality.

Know that when He forbade remaining behind, He explained that in that journey there does not befall them any kind of hardship except that it entails a great reward with Allah, exalted is He. Then He mentioned five matters:

The first: His saying: ﴿That is because they are not afflicted with thirst﴾, which is intense thirst; it is said "Zami'a fulan" when his thirst became intense.

The second: His saying: ﴿nor fatigue﴾, meaning exhaustion and weariness.

The third: ﴿nor hunger in the way of Allah﴾, meaning severe hunger by which the belly becomes visibly empty; from this it is said: "so-and-so is slender-bellied."

The fourth: His saying: ﴿nor do they tread upon a path that enrages the disbelievers﴾, that is, a person does not place his foot, nor his horse place its hoof, nor his camel place its sole, in a way that becomes a cause of the disbelievers' rage. Ibn al-A'rabi said: it is said "ghaza-hu, ghayyaza-hu and aghaza-hu" with one meaning, that is, he angered him.

The fifth: His saying: ﴿nor do they gain any gain from an enemy﴾, that is, captivity, killing, or defeat, whether little or much, ﴿except that a righteous deed is written for them thereby﴾, that is, except that this becomes a means of nearness for them with Allah. We say: this verse indicates that whoever intends obedience to Allah, his standing, his sitting, his walking, his moving and his resting are all good deeds recorded with Allah. Likewise the matter is in the opposite direction regarding disobedience. How great is the blessing of obedience, and how great is the ill-omen of disobedience!

They differed. Qatadah said: this ruling is among the special features of the Messenger of Allah, when he went out to battle in person; so it is not permissible for anyone to remain behind from him except with an excuse.

Ibn Zayd said: this was when the Muslims were few; when they increased, Allah abrogated it (naskh) by His saying: ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ (al-Tawbah: 122). Atiyyah said: it is not for them to remain behind from the Messenger of Allah when he calls them and commands them; and this is the correct view, because answering and obeying the Messenger of Allah becomes binding when he commands; likewise for other rulers and leaders when they are summoned and appointed; for if we permitted the one who is summoned to hold back, it would not be specific to some and not others, and that would lead to the suspension of jihad.

Then He said: ﴿And they do not spend any expenditure, small or large﴾, meaning a date or more, and the lash-cord or more; ﴿nor do they cross a valley﴾. The valley (wadi) is every open space between mountains and hills that serves as a channel for floodwater; its plural is awdiyah. Except that Allah writes for them that expenditure and that journey.

Then He said: ﴿so that Allah may reward them with the best of what they used to do﴾, and in this there are two views:

The first: that "the best" is a description of their action, and within it are the obligatory, the recommended and the permissible; Allah rewards them for the best of it, which is the obligatory and the recommended, not the permissible.

The second: that "the best" is a description of the reward, meaning He rewards them with a reward that is better than their deeds, greater and more excellent, and that is the thawab (reward).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, verse 122**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It was not for the believers to go forth all together. Why should not a party from every group of them go forth, so that they may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people when they return to them, so that they may beware?﴾

[Page 179]

There are several issues concerning the verse.

**The first issue:** Know that it may be said that this verse belongs to the remaining rulings concerning jihad, and it may also be said that it is an independent statement with no connection to jihad.

As for the first possibility, it is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with them both) that: "When the Prophet (ﷺ) went out on a military expedition, none would stay behind except a hypocrite or someone with an excuse. When Allah, glorified is He, exposed the faults of the hypocrites at the Battle of Tabuk, the believers said: 'By Allah, we will not stay behind from any expedition with the Messenger (ﷺ), nor from any detachment.' When the Messenger (ﷺ) came to Medina and sent the detachments against the disbelievers, the Muslims all went forth to fight and left him alone in Medina, so this verse was revealed." The meaning is: it is not permissible for the believers to go forth in their entirety to raid and fight; rather, they must divide into two groups. One group remains in the service of the Messenger, and another group goes forth to fight. This is because at that time Islam was in need of raiding, jihad, and the subduing of disbelief. Moreover, obligations were arising and laws were being revealed, and the Muslims needed people who would remain in the presence of the Messenger (ﷺ), learn those laws, preserve those obligations, and convey them to those who were absent. It is therefore established that at that time it was obligatory for the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to divide into two parts: one part goes forth to raid and fight, and the second part remains in the presence of the Messenger. The party that goes forth to raid acts as a substitute for those who remain behind in the raid, and the party that remains acts as a substitute for those who go forth in gaining understanding. By this means the affair of the religion is completed through these two parties.

Having understood this, we say that according to this view there are two possibilities:

One of them is that the remaining party are those who gain understanding in the religion, because they constantly attended the service of the Messenger (may the blessings and peace of Allah be upon him) and witnessed the revelation and the sending down. Whenever an obligation was revealed or a law arose, they came to know it and memorized it. Then, when the party that went forth on the raid returned to them, the remaining party would warn them of the obligations and laws they had learned. According to this interpretation, the verse necessarily requires an implied element, and the meaning is: "Why should not a party from every group of them go forth, and a party remain, so that those who remain may gain understanding in the religion and warn their people, meaning those who went forth to raid, when they return to them, so that they may beware of the disobedience of Allah, glorified is He, upon that learning."

The second possibility is that gaining understanding is an attribute of the party that goes forth. This is the view of al-Hasan (al-Basri). The meaning of the verse is: "Why should not a party from every group of them go forth, so that this party that goes forth may become scholars of the religion." That understanding intended here is that they witness the victory of the Muslims over the polytheists, and that a small number of them overcome a whole world of polytheists. Then they know that this is because Allah, glorified is He, has singled them out for help and support, and that He wills to elevate the religion of Muhammad (ﷺ) and strengthen his law. So when they return from that expedition to their people among the disbelievers, they warn them with what they witnessed of the signs of help, conquest, and triumph, so that perhaps they will beware, abandoning disbelief, doubt, and hypocrisy. This view is also possible. Al-Qadi criticized this view, saying: "This perception is not considered understanding in the religion." It may be answered that when they witness that a small group, who have no weapons or provisions, overcome a great multitude of disbelievers whose provisions and weapons are abundant and whose power is strong, then they become aware of what is the true purpose: that this matter is from Allah, glorified is He, and not from humans. For if it were from humans, the few would not have overcome the many, and this religion would not have continued to grow and rise every day. Awareness of understanding these subtleties and finer points is undoubtedly a form of gaining understanding.

[Page 180]

As for the third possibility, namely that this verse is not among the remnants of the rulings of jihad, but is an independent and self-standing ruling, its explanation is as follows: When Allah, glorified is He, explained in this surah the matter of emigration (hijrah), and then the matter of jihad, both of which are acts of worship involving travel, He also explained the act of worship of gaining understanding from the side of the Messenger (ﷺ), which also involves travel. He said: "It was not for the believers to go forth all together to the presence of the Messenger in order to gain understanding in the religion." Rather, that is neither obligatory nor permissible. And its status is not like the status of jihad with him, which every person without an excuse must go forth to perform.

Then He said: ﴿Why should not a party from every group of them go forth﴾, meaning from the groups residing in the lands, a party should go to the presence of the Messenger in order to gain understanding in the religion, to learn what is lawful and unlawful, and return to their homelands, and warn and admonish their people so that they may turn back from their disbelief. According to this interpretation, the meaning is that it is obligatory to go forth to the presence of the Messenger for the sake of gaining understanding and learning.

If it is asked: Does the verse indicate an obligation to go forth in search of understanding in every age?

We answer: Whenever a person is unable to gain understanding except by travelling, travel becomes obligatory for him. In the time of the Messenger (may the peace of Allah be upon him) the situation was like this, because the law was not yet settled; rather, a new obligation and a fresh ruling would arise every day. As for our time, the law has become settled, so if a person can obtain knowledge in his homeland, travel is not obligatory for him. However, since the wording of the verse indicates travel, we have indeed seen that blessed and beneficial knowledge is not acquired except through travel.

* * *

**The second issue:** Concerning the explanation of the words mentioned in this verse. ﴿Lawlā﴾ (why not), when it is followed by a verb, has the meaning of urging (taḥḍīḍ), like the word hallā (why not). It is permissible for lawlā to mean hallā because hallā consists of two words: hal, which is interrogative and an offer (ʿarḍ), since when you say to a man, "Do you eat?" or "Do you enter?" it is as if you are offering that to him; and lā, which is negation. So hallā is composed of two matters: the offer and the negation. When you say, "Why did you not do such and such?", it is as if you said, "Did you do it?", and then you added with it "lā" meaning, "I did not do it." This contains an alert to the obligation of the act, and an alert that this obligatory act has been neglected. The same applies to lawlā, because when you say, "Why did you not enter upon me?" or "Why did you not eat with me?", its meaning is also an offer and an expression of your pleasure should he do it. The same applies to lawmā, and from it is His saying: ﴿Why do you not bring us the angels?﴾ (al-Hijr 15:7). Thus it is established that lawlā, hallā, and lawmā are closely related expressions, and the purpose of all of them is encouragement and urging. So His saying: ﴿Why should not a party from every group of them go forth﴾ means: "Why did they not do that?"

* * *

**The third issue:** This verse is a strong proof for those who hold that the report of a single narrator (khabar al-wahid) is a valid proof (ḥujjah). We have elaborated on this at length in the book *al-Mahsul min al-Usul* (The Harvest from the Principles). What we say here is that every three constitute a group (firqah). Allah, exalted is He, has required that from every group a party should go forth, and whoever goes forth from three will be two or one. It follows that the party must be either two or one. Then He, exalted is He, required acting upon their reports, because His saying: ﴿and warn their people﴾ refers to their reporting. And His saying: ﴿so that they may beware﴾ is an obligation upon their people to act upon their reports. This requires that the report of one or two persons be a proof in the law.

Al-Qadi said: This verse does not indicate the obligation of acting upon the report of a single narrator, because the party may be a group whose report yields a proof, and because the saying: ﴿and warn their people﴾ is valid even if acceptance is not obligatory, just as a single witness is obliged to testify even though acceptance is not obligatory for him. Also, warning includes intimidation, and this alone does not necessitate the obligation of acting upon it.

[Page 181]

The answer: As for his saying, "the party may be a group," we answer: We have shown that every three constitute a group. Since Allah, exalted is He, has required that from every group a party should go forth, it follows that the party must be either two or one. This nullifies the claim that the party is a group whose report produces certainty.

If they say: He, exalted is He, required acting upon the words of those parties, and perhaps they became numerous to the extent that certainty is attained through their words.

We say: He, exalted is He, required each party to return to their people, and this requires that each party return to a specific people. Then He, exalted is He, required knowledge (ʿilm) through the words of that party, and this establishes what is sought.

As for his saying: ﴿and warn their people﴾ is valid even if acceptance is not obligatory, we say: We do not rely, in establishing the obligation of acting upon the report of a single narrator, on His saying "and warn," but on His saying: ﴿so that they may beware﴾, which is an encouragement from Him, exalted is He, toward beware, on the basis that such warning requires the obligation of acting in accordance with that warning. By this answer the response to his third objection is also complete, namely his saying: "Warning includes intimidation, and this alone does not necessitate the obligation of acting upon it."

* * *

**The fourth issue:** The verse indicates that the purpose of gaining understanding and learning must be calling people to the truth and guiding them to the upright religion and the straight path. This is because the verse shows that He, exalted is He, commanded them to gain understanding in the religion so that, when they return to their people, they may warn them with the true religion, and those people may beware of ignorance and disobedience and be eager to accept the religion. Therefore, whoever gains understanding and learns for this purpose is upon the upright method and the straight path. Whoever turns away from it and seeks worldly gain through religion is among "the greatest losers in deeds, whose effort is lost in the life of this world while they think they are doing well in their work" (al-Kahf 18:103–104).

**Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on Surah 9, Verse 123:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, fight those of the disbelievers who are near you, and let them find harshness in you, and know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾

Know that it is reported from al-Hasan (al-Basri) that he said: "This verse was revealed before the command to fight the polytheists collectively. Then it was abrogated (mansukh) by His saying: ﴿And fight against the polytheists collectively﴾ (al-Tawbah: 36)." As for the muhaqqiqun (the careful scholars and verifiers), they rejected this abrogation (naskh) and said: "When He, may He be exalted, commanded fighting the polytheists collectively, He guided them in that matter to the most correct and beneficial method, which is to begin with the nearest and then proceed to the farther, and then the farthest. Do you not see that the command to da'wah (the call to Islam) followed this order? He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And warn your closest kinsmen﴾ (al-Shu'ara': 214). And the command for military campaigns (ghazawat) followed this same order, because he, peace be upon him, fought his own people, then moved from them to campaigning against the rest of the Arabs, then moved from them to campaigning against al-Sham (Greater Syria). And the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, when they finished with the matter of al-Sham, entered Iraq. We have said that beginning the campaign with the nearby places is preferable for several reasons:

The first: confronting all of them at once is impossible. Since all of them were equal in the obligation to fight, because of their disbelief and their waging war, and since combining them all was impossible, it became necessary to prioritize. Nearness is an evident factor of preference, as in da'wah and in all other important matters. Do you not see that in enjoining what is good and forbidding what is evil, beginning with those present is preferable to going off to distant lands for this matter? Therefore it is obligatory to begin with the nearest.

The second: beginning with the nearest is preferable because the expenses in it are less, and the need for mounts, equipment and tools is less.

The third: if the fighting group passes over the nearest and goes on to the farther, they expose the families and offspring (dhurriyyah) to temptation (fitnah).

The fourth: those who border the abode of Islam are either strong or weak. If they are strong, their aggression against the abode of Islam is more severe and more frequent than the aggression of distant disbelievers, and a stronger, greater evil deserves to be repelled first. If they are weak, the Muslims' conquest over them is easier, and the honor of Islam resulting from their defeat is nearer and easier to achieve. So beginning with them is preferable.

The fifth: a person's knowledge of the condition of those close to him is easier than his knowledge of the condition of those far from him. When this is so, the Muslims' ability to fight the nearer ones is easier, because they know their conditions, the quantities of their weapons, and the numbers of their armies.

The sixth: the abode of Islam is vast. When the people of each land occupy themselves with fighting the disbelievers who are near them, the burden is lighter and the goal is more easily achieved.

The seventh: when two obligations are combined and one of them is easier to accomplish, it must be given precedence. Nearness is a cause of ease, so it is obligatory to begin with the nearest.

The eighth: we have shown that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ began his da'wah with the nearest and then the nearer, and in campaigns with the nearest and then the nearer, and in all important matters in the same way. When the Bedouin sat at the table and kept reaching his hand to the far sides of that table, the Prophet, peace be upon him, said to him: "Eat from what is near you." These considerations indicate that beginning with the nearest and then the nearer is obligatory.

If it is said: Perhaps passing over the nearest to the farther is more beneficial, because the farther one would feel that he was passed over only because he is not considered worthy of any regard.

We say: That is one possibility, whereas what we have mentioned are many possibilities. The interests of this world are built on preferring what is more beneficial over what is less beneficial. What we have said applies only when combining the fighting of the nearer and the farther is impossible. As for when combining all of them is possible, there is no dispute that the better course is to combine them. Thus it is established that this verse is not abrogated at all.

As for His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and let them find harshness in you﴾, al-Zajjaj said: "In it there are three readings (lughat): opening the ghayn (ghilzah), its dammah, and its kasrah." The author of al-Kashshaf said: "Al-ghilzah with a kasrah means great severity. Al-ghilzah is like al-dagh'tah (a pressing), and al-ghilzah is like al-sukhtah (a displeasure)." This verse indicates a command to be harsh toward them. Its parallels are His saying: ﴿And be harsh with them﴾ (al-Tawbah: 73), and His saying: ﴿And do not weaken﴾ (Al 'Imran: 139), and His saying describing the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them: ﴿humble toward the believers, mighty against the disbelievers﴾ (al-Ma'idah: 54) — and His saying: ﴿harsh against the disbelievers﴾ (al-Fath: 29). The mufassirun have various expressions in explaining ghilzah: it was said to be courage, it was said to be severity, and it was said to be anger.

Know that ghilzah is the opposite of riqqah (tenderness), and it is severity in carrying out retribution. Its benefit is that it is more effective in restraining and preventing one from wrongdoing. Then, the matter in this domain is not uniform; sometimes it requires gentleness and kindness, and at other times it requires force. For this reason He said: ﴿and let them find harshness in you﴾, drawing attention to the fact that it is not permissible to rely on harshness alone, for it repels and causes the people to disperse. So His saying: ﴿and let them find harshness in you﴾ indicates the minimization of harshness, as if it was said: "It is necessary that you be such that if they searched your characters and natures, they would find harshness in you." This statement applies only to one whose predominant state is mercy and compassion, and even with that, he is not free from some degree of harshness.

[p. 183]

Know that this harshness is considered only in matters connected with calling to the religion. That is either by establishing the proof and clear evidence, or by fighting and jihad. As for this harshness applying to matters connected with buying and selling, sitting together, and eating together, it does not.

Then He said: ﴿And know that Allah is with the righteous.﴾ The meaning is that his advancing into jihad and fighting should be because of taqwa of Allah, not because of seeking wealth or status. If he sees the enemy before Islam, he should refrain from fighting him; if he sees him inclined to accept the jizyah, he leaves him; and if the enemy is numerous, he takes the spoils in accordance with the ruling of Allah, may He be exalted.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verses 124–125:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And whenever a surah is revealed, among them are some who say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?" As for those who believed, it has increased them in faith, and they rejoice.﴾ ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease, it has added defilement to their defilement, and they died while disbelievers.﴾

Know that when He, exalted is He, mentioned the disgraceful conduct of the hypocrites and their vile deeds, He said: "And whenever a surah is revealed, among the hypocrites are some who say, 'Which of you has had his faith increased by this?'" They differed. Some said: some hypocrites say it to other hypocrites, and their aim is to strengthen their own people in hypocrisy. Others said: rather, they say it to groups of Muslims, and their purpose is to turn them away from faith. Others said: rather, they mention it in mockery. All of these are possible, and it is not possible to apply it to all of them, because the narration of a state does not indicate generality.

Then He, exalted is He, answered, saying that two things occurred for the believers because of the revelation of this surah, and two things also occurred for the disbelievers. As for what occurred for the believers:

The first: it increases them in faith, since upon its revelation they must acknowledge it and confess that it is the truth from Allah. The discussion of the increase and decrease of faith has been mentioned by us in detail at the beginning of Surah al-Anfal.

The second: what they obtain of rejoicing (al-istibshar, "seeking glad tidings"). Some interpreted it as the reward of the Hereafter, some interpreted it as what they obtain in this world of victory and triumph, and some interpreted it as the joy and delight arising from those additional obligations, insofar as it is a means to greater reward. Then He combined for the hypocrites two things opposite to the two mentioned for the believers, saying: ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾, meaning the hypocrites, ﴿it has added defilement to their defilement﴾. The meaning of "defilement" (rijs) is either false beliefs or blameworthy character traits. If it is the first, the meaning is that they used to deny the surahs revealed before that, and now they have become deniers of this new surah, so disbelief has been added to disbelief. If it is the second, the meaning is that they were in envy, enmity, and devising ways of deception and scheming, and now those blameworthy traits have increased because of the revelation of this new surah.

The second matter: they die upon their disbelief. This state is thus like the opposite of the rejoicing that occurred among the believers. This state is worse and more repugnant than the first state, because the first state is an expression of an increase in filth, while this state is an expression of persistence in disbelief and dying upon it.

Our companions argued from His saying, ﴿it has added defilement to their defilement﴾, that He, exalted is He, may turn people away from faith and divert them from it. They said: He, exalted is He, knew that hearing this surah would produce envy and spite in their hearts, and that this envy would produce additional disbelief in their hearts. They replied and said: the revelation of that surah does not necessitate that additional disbelief, as evidenced by the fact that others heard that surah and increased in faith; thus it is established that this defilement they themselves brought about from their own selves.

We say: we do not claim that hearing this surah is an independent cause that tips the balance toward disbelief over faith. Rather, we say that hearing this surah, for a particular soul described by a specific character and a specific habit, necessitates disbelief. The proof of this is that a envious person, if he wants to remove the trait of envy from himself, can refrain from the acts that indicate envy, but he cannot remove from himself the inner state called envy. The same applies to all character traits. The basic capacity is one thing, the act is another, and the trait is another; the basic capacity is present in everyone, but people differ in their traits. The summary is that a pure, clean soul, free from love of this world, characterized by the dominance of love of Allah, exalted is He, and of the Hereafter, when it hears the surah, its hearing necessitates an increase in its desire for the Hereafter and its aversion from this world. But a soul greedy for this world, devoted to its pleasures, desiring its good things, heedless of the love of Allah, exalted is He, and of the Hereafter, when it hears this surah, which includes jihad and the exposure of the self to killing and of wealth to plunder, its disbelief is increased upon its disbelief. Thus it is established that the sending down of this surah with respect to this disbeliever necessitates that he increases in defilement upon defilement, so its revelation was a cause of strengthening disbelief in the heart of the disbeliever. This indicates what we mentioned, that He, exalted is He, may turn a person away and prevent him from faith and right guidance, and cast him into error and disbelief.

Several discussions remain concerning the verse:

The first: the "ma" in His saying, ﴿And whenever a surah is revealed﴾ is an emphatic extra particle (silah muakkadah).

The second: al-istibshar means seeking glad tidings, because whenever one remembers that blessing, the glad tidings arise in him; by means of renewing that remembrance he seeks the renewal of the glad tidings.

The third: His saying, ﴿As for those in whose hearts is a disease﴾ indicates that the soul has a disease, whose disease is disbelief and blameworthy traits, and whose health is knowledge and virtuous traits. And Allah knows best.

[Page 184]
