Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 126:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do they not see that they are tested every year once or twice? Then they do not repent, nor do they take heed.﴾

Know that when God, exalted is He, explained that those in whose hearts is a sickness will die while they are disbelievers, and that this indicates the punishment of the Hereafter, He explained that they are not freed, once or twice every year, from the punishment of this world. And in this are several issues:

The first issue: Hamzah recited ﴿أوَلا تَرَوْنَ﴾ (awa-la tarawna, "do you not see?") with the ta' (ta), addressing the believers, while the rest recited it with the ya' (ya), as a report about the hypocrites. According to the recitation in the second person, the meaning is that the believers are alerted to the hypocrites' turning away from reflection and contemplation. According to the recitation in the third person, the meaning is a rebuke of the hypocrites for turning away from taking lesson from what befalls them of matters that call for taking lesson.

The second issue: Al-Wahidi, may God have mercy on him, said: His saying ﴿أوَلا يَرَوْنَ﴾ (awa-la yarawna, "do they not see?"): this alif is the interrogative particle (alif al-istifham) entering upon the waw of conjunction, so it is connected to the mention of the hypocrites, and it is an address in the manner of alerting. Sibawayh said, quoting al-Khalil, regarding His saying:
Page 185
﴿Do you not see that God sends down water from the sky?﴾ [al-Zumar: 21] The meaning is: God sent down water from the sky, so it became such and such.

The third issue: They mentioned several aspects regarding this trial (fitnah):

First: Ibn Abbas, may God be pleased with him and his father, said: they are tested with sickness once or twice every year, and then they do not repent of that hypocrisy, nor do they take admonition from that sickness, as the believer takes admonition from it when he falls ill, for then he remembers his sins and his standing before God, and that increases him in faith and fear of God, and this becomes a cause for his deserving more mercy and good pleasure from God.

Second: Mujahid said: (they are tested) by drought and hunger.

Third: Qatadah said: they are tested by the expedition and jihad, for God, exalted is He, commanded expedition and jihad, so if they stay behind, they fall into people's tongues with cursing, disgrace, and ill repute, and if they go out to the expedition while being disbelievers, they have exposed themselves to killing and their wealth to plunder for no benefit.

Fourth: Muqatil said: the Messenger of God will expose them by making their hypocrisy and disbelief apparent. It was said: they used to gather to mention the Messenger with slander, and Gabriel, peace be upon him, would descend to him and inform him of what they had said about him, so he would mention that incident to them, rebuke them for it, and admonish them, yet they would not take admonition nor desist.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 127:

God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And whenever a surah is sent down, some of them look at others, [asking], "Does anyone see you?" Then they turn away. God has turned their hearts away because they are a people who do not understand.﴾

Know that this is another kind of the disgraceful conduct of the hypocrites. Whenever a surah was revealed that contained mention of the hypocrites and an explanation of their disgrace, they were distressed by hearing it. Some of them would look at others with a particular glance that indicated disparagement of that surah, mockery of it, and belittling of its standing. It is also possible that this was not limited to the surah that exposed the hypocrites, but that they treated the Qur'an lightly: whenever they heard a surah, they mocked it and disparaged it, and began to wink and laugh in a spirit of derision and ridicule. Then some of them said to others: "Does anyone see you?" That is, "If anyone saw you [doing this]." There are several interpretations of this:

The first: that glance indicated what was inwardly of intense denial and complete aversion. They feared that one of the Muslims would see that glance and those conditions, which indicated hypocrisy and disbelief. At that point they said: ﴿Does anyone see you?﴾, that is, "If anyone saw you with this glance and this appearance, he would harm you greatly."

The second: when they heard that surah, they were distressed by hearing it and wished to leave the mosque. So some of them said to others: ﴿Does anyone see you?﴾, meaning: "If someone sees you, do not leave; if no one sees you, leave the mosque, so that you may escape this harm."

The third: ﴿Does anyone see you?﴾ means: "You could say, 'We love it,' so we must leave the mosque." God said: ﴿Then they turn away.﴾ It is possible that the intended meaning is their very flight from the place of revelation and from listening to the Qur'an. It is also permissible that it means: "Then they turned away from listening to the Qur'an to finding fault with it," even if they remained in their places.

If it is said: What is the difference between this verse and the preceding verse, which is His saying: ﴿And whenever a surah is sent down, some of them say, "Which of you has had his faith increased by this?"﴾?

We reply: In that verse, He related that they uttered their statement: ﴿"Which of you has had his faith increased by this?"﴾. In this verse, He related that they were content with glancing at one another in mockery, and sought to flee.

Then God, the Exalted, said: ﴿God has turned their hearts away because they are a people who do not understand.﴾ Our companions (the Ash'aris) cited this as evidence that God turned them away from faith and barred them from it, and this is correct in its meaning. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "[He turned them away] from every guidance, good and right direction." Al-Hasan said: "God turned their hearts away and sealed them because of their disbelief." Al-Zajjaj said: "God misguided them." The Mu'tazila (the rationalist school that held that human acts are created by humans and that God is just in a way that precludes such guidance) said: "If God is the one who turned them away from faith, then how does He say: ﴿How are they turned away?﴾ [9:30], and how does He punish them for turning away from faith?" The Qadi (ʿAbd al-Jabbar) said: "The apparent meaning of the verse indicates that this turning away is a punishment for them because of their turning away. But turning away from faith cannot be a punishment, for if it were, then just as He may command His prophets to establish the hadd punishments, He could also command them to turn people away from faith. Permitting that would lead to the conclusion that what the Messenger brought cannot be trusted." Then he said: "This turning away may bear two meanings:

One: that God turned their hearts by what He inflicted upon them of grief and treachery.

Two: that He turned them away from the lutf (divine favour or assistance, which in Mu'tazili theology is what God specifically grants to those who believe and are guided)."

The response: The meanings that the Qadi mentioned are, as is apparent, very strained. As for the correct meaning, to which every sound intellect attests, it is that an act depends on the occurrence of a motive (da'i). Otherwise, it would follow that one of two equal possibilities is preferred over the other without a preponderant cause, and that is impossible. The occurrence of that motive does not come from the servant, for otherwise an infinite regress would follow; rather, it comes from God, the Exalted. So the servant only proceeds to disbelief when the motive of disbelief arises in his heart, and that arising is from God, the Exalted. When that motive arises, that heart turns from the side of faith to the side of disbelief. This is what is meant by the turning of the heart. This is a proposition established by a decisive proof, and it accords with this text, so it reaches the highest degree of clarity.

Among what remains of the discussions of this verse is what is reported from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, who said: "Do not say, 'We turned away from the prayer,' for some people turned away and God turned their hearts. Rather say, 'We have completed the prayer.'" The purpose of this was to express optimism by avoiding this expression, which is found in matters that are not fitting, and to encourage the use of that expression which is found in good matters. For God, the Exalted, said: ﴿And when the prayer is concluded, disperse in the land and seek of God's bounty﴾ (Surah al-Jumu'ah, 62:10).

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 128:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿There has certainly come to you a Messenger from among yourselves; grievous to him is your suffering; he is anxious over you; with the believers he is kind and merciful.﴾

Concerning it there are several issues:

The first issue: Know that when Exalted God commanded His Messenger, peace be upon him, to convey to creation in this surah duties that are heavy, severe and difficult, which cannot be borne except by one whom God Exalted has specially favoured with the means of success and honour, He concluded the surah with what makes these duties easier to bear, namely that this Messenger is from among you, so all the honour and nobility he gains in this world returns to you. Moreover, he is in a state where your harm grieves him and his desire to bring you the good of this world and the Hereafter is great. He is therefore like a compassionate physician and a merciful father toward you. A compassionate physician may undertake painful treatments that are hard to bear, and a merciful father may impose severe disciplines; yet, once it is known that the physician is skilful and the father compassionate, those painful treatments become bearable and those disciplines are taken as kindness. So here too: once you know that he is a Messenger of truth from God, accept from him these heavy duties so that you may win every good. Then He said to the Messenger, peace be upon him: If they do not accept them but turn away and refuse, then leave them, do not turn to them, rely upon God, and return in all your affairs to God. ﴿Say: God is sufficient for me; there is no god but Him; in Him I have put my trust, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾ This conclusion of this surah came in the utmost of beauty and the height of perfection.
* * *
The second issue: Know that Exalted God described the Messenger in this verse with five kinds of attributes:

The first attribute: His saying, ﴿from among yourselves﴾. Concerning its interpretation there are several views:

The first: It means he is a human being like you, as in His saying: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people that We revealed to a man from among them?﴾ (Yunus: 2) and His saying: ﴿I am only a human being like you﴾ (Fussilat: 6). The purpose is that if he were of the kind of the angels, the matter would be difficult for people because of him, as has been established in the commentary on Surah al-An'am.

The second: ﴿from among yourselves﴾ means from the Arabs. Ibn 'Abbas said: There is no tribe among the Arabs but that the Prophet, peace be upon him, descended from it through the grandmothers: Mudar, Rabi'a and Yaman. The Mudarites and Rabi'ites are the 'Adnanites, and the Yamanites are the Qahtanites. A parallel to this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God certainly conferred a favour upon the believers when He sent among them a Messenger from among themselves﴾ (Al 'Imran: 164). The purpose of it is to encourage the Arabs to support him and to serve him, as if it were said to them: All the power and elevation he gains in this world is a cause of your honour and pride, because he is from you and from your lineage.

The third: ﴿from among yourselves﴾ is an address to the people of the Haram, because the Arabs used to call the people of the Haram "the people of God and His special ones," and they used to serve them and attend to their affairs. It is as if it were said to the Arabs: Before his coming you were zealous and diligent in serving his forefathers and ancestors, so why are you lax in serving him, when he has no lesser claim to nobility and elevation than his forefathers?

The fourth view: The purpose of mentioning this attribute is to draw attention to his purity, as if it were said: He is from your kin; you know him for truthfulness, trustworthiness, chastity and protection, and you know that he is eager to repel calamities from you and to bring blessings to you, and that sending one of such a state and description is among the greatest of God's blessings upon you. It is also recited as ﴿min anfasikum﴾, that is, from your noblest and best; and it is said that this is the recitation of the Messenger of God, Fatima and 'A'isha, may God be pleased with them both.

The second attribute: His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿grievous to him is your suffering﴾. Know that 'aziz means the one who prevails and is severe, and 'izza means dominance and severity. When hardship reaches a person, he knows that he was unable to repel it, for if he had been able to repel it he would not have fallen short in that repelling; since he did not repel it, he knows that he was powerless to repel it and that it overcame him. For this reason, when something weighs heavily upon a person he says: "This is grievous to me" (ʿazza ʿalayya hadha). As for 'anat, it is said: "'anita al-rajul ya'nat 'anatan" when a man falls into a hardship and severity from which he cannot escape. From this is His saying: ﴿That is for him who fears falling into difficulty among you﴾ (An-Nisa: 25) and His saying: ﴿Had God willed, He would have made you suffer﴾ (Al-Baqara: 220). Al-Farra' said: "ma" in His saying ﴿ma 'anittum﴾ is in the nominative position, and the meaning is: "Your suffering is grievous to him," that is, your harm is burdensome to him. The most important of harms to repel is the harm of God's punishment, and he was sent only to repel this harm.

The third attribute: His saying, ﴿he is anxious over you﴾. Anxiety cannot be attached to their essences; rather the meaning is that he is anxious to bring you the good things of this world and the Hereafter.
Know that under this interpretation, His saying ﴿grievous to him is your suffering﴾ means: his strong distress at any calamity of this world and the Hereafter reaching you. With this interpretation, repetition does not occur. Al-Farra' said: "haris" means "shahih" (miserly), and the meaning is that he is miserly toward you that you should enter the Fire; but this is far-fetched, because it entails being empty of benefit.

The fourth and fifth attributes: His saying, ﴿with the believers he is kind and merciful﴾. Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, said: God named him with two of His names. There remain two questions here:

The first question: How can this be so, when in this surah He imposed upon them kinds of heavy duties which none can bear except one whom God has granted success?

We say: We have given for this meaning the example of the skilful physician and the compassionate father. The meaning is that He did this to them only so that they might be saved from everlasting punishment and win everlasting reward.

The second question: When He said ﴿grievous to him is your suffering, he is anxious over you﴾, this arrangement would require that it be said: "kind and merciful to the believers"; why did He abandon this arrangement and say ﴿with the believers he is kind and merciful﴾?

The answer: His saying ﴿with the believers he is kind and merciful﴾ conveys restriction, in the sense that he has no kindness or mercy except toward the believers. As for the disbelievers, he has no kindness or mercy toward them. This serves as a complement to the measure of severity that occurred in this surah, as if He were saying: Although I have been strict in this surah, that strictness is directed at the disbelievers and hypocrites, while My mercy and kindness are specific to the believers alone. For this subtlety He departed from that arrangement.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 9, verse 129:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So if they turn away, say: "Allah is sufficient for me; there is no god but Him. On Him I have relied, and He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne."﴾

As for His saying ﴿So if they turn away﴾, it means the polytheists and the hypocrites. Then it has been said: (turn away) means: they turned away from you. It has also been said: they turned away from obedience to Allah, exalted is He, and from affirming the Messenger, upon him be blessings and peace. And it has been said: they turned away from accepting the burdensome obligations mentioned in this surah. And it has been said: they turned away from supporting you in jihad. Know that the purpose of this verse is to show that if the disbelievers turned away and did not accept these obligations, no grief or sorrow would enter the heart of the Messenger, because Allah is sufficient for him and suffices him in his victory over the enemies, and in bringing him to the stations of blessings and favours. ﴿There is no god but He﴾. And since there is no god but He, it must be that no one originates any of the possible things and no one creates any of the created things except Him; and since He is the One who sent me with this message and commanded me to this proclamation, victory and help from Him are to be awaited.

Then He said: ﴿On Him I have relied﴾, and this implies restriction, meaning: I rely on no one but Him. ﴿And He is the Lord of the Mighty Throne.﴾ The reason for specifying this by mention is that whenever the effects are greater and more noble, the majesty of the one who produces them becomes more evident to the intellect and the mind; and since the greatest of bodies is the Throne, the purpose of mentioning it is to magnify the majesty of Allah, glorified is He.

(Page 189)

If they say: the Throne is not perceptible, so its existence is not known except after the establishment of the Shari'ah; how then is it possible to mention it in the context of explaining the greatness of Allah, exalted is He?

We say: the existence of the Throne is a well-known matter, and the disbelievers heard of it from the Jews and the Christians. It is also not far-fetched that they had heard of it from their forefathers. And some people read His saying (al-'Azim) with a nominative ending (ḍamma), so that it is an attribute of the Lord, glorified is He. Abu Bakr said: this reading is more fitting, because making al-'Azim an attribute of Allah, exalted is He, is preferable to making it an attribute of the Throne. Moreover, if we make it an attribute of the Throne, the meaning of its being great is the size of its body, the vastness of its dimensions and the breadth of its sides, as is mentioned in the reports; but if we make it an attribute of Allah, glorified is He, the meaning of greatness is the necessity of existence, His being exalted above corporeality, parts and divisions, perfection of knowledge and power, and His being far beyond being imagined in fancies or reached by understandings.

Al-Hasan said: these two verses are the last of what Allah sent down of the Qur'an, and nothing was revealed after them. Ubayy ibn Ka'b said: the most recent of the Qur'an in terms of its connection to Allah, Mighty and Majestic, are these two verses, and this is also the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr. Some say: the last of what was revealed of the Qur'an is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And fear a Day when you will be returned to Allah﴾ (al-Baqarah: 281).

It is related from Hudhayfah that he said: you call this surah "al-Tawbah," but it is the surah of punishment; it has not left anyone without touching him, and by Allah, you do not recite a quarter of it.

Know that this report must be rejected, because if we permitted it, it would be evidence that addition and deficiency reach the Qur'an, and that would take it out of being a proof. There is no doubt that the claim of this is false, and Allah, exalted is He, knows best what He intends.

This is the end of the commentary on this surah, and to Allah belongs all praise and thanks.

The author, may Allah have mercy on him, finished its commentary on Friday, the fourteenth of Ramadan, in the year six hundred and eleven. All praise is for Allah alone, and blessings upon our master Muhammad, his family and all his companions.

The fifteenth part is complete; followed, God willing, by the sixteenth part, whose beginning is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Fight them; Allah will punish them by your hands﴾ from the beginning of Surah Yunus. May Allah help in completing it.
